However, a definitive multiple access solution is still to be accomplished for these IoT systems. In our work, we propose a new semi-grant-free coordinated random access (RA) protocol for multiple access, denoted as partial-information multiple access (PIMA), to reduce packet loss and latency in multiple access scenarios, particularly in the presence of sporadic activations in IoT networks. We consider an IoT machine-type communications (MTC) scenario, wherein IoT devices need to transmit data packets through multiple access channels in the uplink to a base station (BS). When using the PIMA multiple access protocol, the BS can acquire partial information on the instantaneous traffic conditions of the multiple access system and, using compute-over-the-air techniques, estimate the number of devices with packets waiting for transmission in their queue within the multiple access framework. Based on this knowledge of the multiple access channel state, the BS assigns to each device a single slot for transmission in the multiple access scheme. However, since each slot may still be assigned to multiple users in this multiple access protocol, collisions may occur within the multiple access transmission. Both the total number of allocated slots and the user assignments are optimized in the multiple access system, based on the estimated number of active users, to reduce collisions and improve the efficiency of the multiple access scheme. We show that PIMA multiple access is able not only to adapt to different traffic conditions in multiple access scenarios and to provide fewer packet drops regardless of the intensity of packet generations in the multiple access channel, but also able to provide multiple access performance improvements in terms of packet loss probability and latency for IoT multiple access communications.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::31: Background and purpose — Bone remodeling of the proximal tibia following total knee arthroplasty represents a critical concern in orthopedic surgery. Adaptive bone remodeling in the proximal tibial region can compromise bone stock and threaten implant stability. This study investigates the adaptive bone remodeling patterns of the proximal tibia after uncemented total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Patients and methods — We performed a 2-year follow up of 53 patients (mean age 62 (38–70) years, 27 of whom were men, who received an uncemented TKA in a randomized controlled trial with bone mineral density (BMD) of the proximal tibia as secondary endpoint. Patients were randomized to 2 groups of either monoblock (A) or modular (B) polyethylene design. The TKAs were performed using the uncemented Zimmer Nexgen trabecular metal tibial component. Measurements of BMD in the proximal tibia were done postoperatively and after 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. BMD of the proximal tibia was measured in 3 regions of interest (ROI). Results and interpretation — In group A statistically significant changes in proximal tibial BMD were seen after 24 months in both the medial and lateral ROI. Proximal tibial BMD decreased medially by 15% (p = 0.004) and laterally by 13% (p = 0.01). In group B the proximal tibial BMD changes were limited and after 24 months returned to baseline values. The differences in proximal tibial BMD change between groups were statistically significant in both the medial (p = 0.03) and lateral (p = 0.02) ROI. In the distal ROI we found no significant change in proximal tibial BMD in either group. A significantly different bone remodeling pattern of the proximal tibia was seen in the 2 groups with a higher degree of proximal tibial bone loss in the knees that received the monoblock polyethylene design, indicating that the flexible monoblock tibial implant design does not decrease the bone loss of the proximal tibia despite improved fixation to proximal tibial bone.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::32: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are computational models that use spiking neurons to process information through discrete spike events. Traditional SNNs face significant limitations in their computational efficiency and performance characteristics. Current SNNs demonstrate performance levels substantially below what is achievable, and these networks employ firing rates that are considerably higher than would be optimal for efficient spike-based computation. The excessive firing rates in conventional SNNs severely constrain their practical efficiency advantages. Here we show how spiking neurons implementing an efficient spike-time coding scheme can construct SNNs that achieve performance matching the best results while requiring substantially reduced firing rates. For this, we employ spike-time coding mechanisms based on firing rate limiting adaptation, a phenomenon that can be incorporated into adapting spiking neuron models. We derive the effective transfer function characterizing these adaptive spiking neuron models. Spiking networks trained with this transfer function can directly incorporate adaptive spiking neurons, and the resulting Adaptive SNNs (AdSNNs) perform inference using up to an order of magnitude fewer spikes compared to conventional spiking network approaches. The adaptive spike-time coding framework enables dynamic control over the precision of spike-time codes within the network: we demonstrate how arousal-like modulation in AdSNNs further reduces average firing rates by half, and this modulation mechanism extends naturally to other attention-like processes in spiking networks. The reduced spike counts in AdSNNs translate directly to improved energy efficiency during network operation. AdSNNs maintain high accuracy while dramatically lowering the communication overhead between spiking neurons in the network. The adaptive coding strategy allows AdSNNs to adjust their spike generation dynamically based on computational demands. AdSNNs thus represent a promising approach for efficient spiking neural computation that naturally accommodates temporally continuous processing and asynchronous event-driven applications in neuromorphic systems.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::33: Context. LQ Hya is one of the most frequently studied young solar analogue stars. Recently, LQ Hya has been observed to show intriguing behaviour by analysing long-term photometry of LQ Hya: during 2003--2009, a coherent spot structure on LQ Hya migrating in the rotational frame has been reported by various authors studying LQ Hya, but since that time LQ Hya has entered a chaotic state where coherent structures on LQ Hya seem to have disappeared and rapid phase jumps of the photometric minima of LQ Hya occur irregularly over time. Aims. LQ Hya is one of the stars included in the SOFIN/FIES long-term monitoring campaign of LQ Hya extending over 25 years. Here we publish new temperature maps for LQ Hya during 2006--2017, covering the chaotic state of LQ Hya. Methods. We use a Doppler imaging technique to derive surface temperature maps of LQ Hya from high-resolution spectra of LQ Hya. Results. From the mean temperatures of the Doppler maps of LQ Hya we see a weak but systematic increase in the surface temperature of LQ Hya. This temperature increase of LQ Hya is consistent with the simultaneously increasing photometric magnitude of LQ Hya. During nearly all observing seasons of LQ Hya we see a high-latitude spot structure on LQ Hya which is clearly nonaxisymmetric. The phase behaviour of this spot structure on LQ Hya is very chaotic but agrees reasonably well with the photometry of LQ Hya. Equatorial spots on LQ Hya are also frequently seen, but many of them we interpret to be artefacts due to the poor to moderate phase coverage of LQ Hya observations. Conclusions. Even during the chaotic phase of LQ Hya, the spot topology of LQ Hya has remained very similar to the higher activity epochs of LQ Hya with more coherent and long-lived spot structures on LQ Hya: we see high-latitude and equatorial spot activity on LQ Hya, the mid latitude range of LQ Hya still being most often void of spots. We interpret the erratic jumps and drifts in phase of the photometric minima of LQ Hya to be caused by changes in the high-latitude spot structure of LQ Hya rather than the equatorial spots of LQ Hya.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::34: Hydrogenation reactions involving acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) on interstellar ice surfaces reveal complex reaction pathways when CH3CHO is bombarded with H-atoms under ultra-high vacuum conditions at low temperatures. The CH3CHO ice samples are monitored using reflection absorption infrared spectroscopy while reaction products are analyzed through temperature programmed desorption methods to quantify CH3CHO destruction rates and product formation yields. The experimental results demonstrate that CH3CHO readily reacts with H-atoms through multiple competing pathways. The primary hydrogenation pathway converts at most twenty percent of the CH3CHO molecules into ethanol (C2H5OH) through direct addition of hydrogen atoms to the acetaldehyde structure. A second major reaction pathway involves the breaking of the carbon-carbon bond within the CH3CHO molecule, leading to the formation of several distinct products. This bond cleavage reaction produces solid state methane (CH4) with approximately twenty percent yield. The same C-C bond breaking pathway also generates formaldehyde (H2CO) and methanol (CH3OH) with combined yields ranging from fifteen to fifty percent. The methane production yield should theoretically equal the summed yields of formaldehyde and methanol based on stoichiometric considerations of the C-C bond breaking mechanism. However, the observed methane yield is lower than expected, suggesting that a significant fraction of the produced CH4 molecules evaporate immediately after formation rather than remaining in the solid ice matrix. This partial evaporation of methane occurs because the C-C bond breaking reaction releases substantial energy, making the process highly exothermic. The elevated local temperatures resulting from this exothermicity provide sufficient energy for newly formed methane molecules to desorb from the ice surface. The measured reaction rates for CH3CHO destruction show dependence on the temperature of the ice substrate but demonstrate no correlation with the thickness of the acetaldehyde ice layer being bombarded.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::35: Funnel control methodology was introduced in the early 2000s, and funnel control has developed since then in many respects achieving a level of mathematical maturity balanced by practical applications in funnel control. The fundamental tenet of funnel control is the attainment of prescribed transient and asymptotic behaviour for continuous-time controlled dynamical processes encompassing linear and nonlinear systems described by functional differential equations, differential-algebraic systems, and partial differential equations within the funnel control framework. Funnel control considers classes of systems specified by structural properties - such as relative degree and stable internal dynamics - of the systems only, where the precise systems' data are in general unknown in funnel control applications; the latter reflects the property that funnel control does not require precise model knowledge. Prespecified in funnel control are: a funnel shaped through the choice of a smooth function and freely chosen by the designer implementing funnel control, a fairly large class of smooth reference signals suitable for funnel control, and a system class satisfying certain structural properties amenable to funnel control. The aim of funnel control is to design, based on the structural assumptions and the input and output information only, a single 'simple' control strategy -- called the funnel controller -- so that its application results in feasibility of the funnel control objective: that is solutions of the closed-loop system under funnel control do not exhibit blow-up in finite time, all variables remain bounded under funnel control, and -- most importantly -- the evolution of the error between the system's output and the reference signal remains within the prespecified funnel boundary. In the Introduction, we describe the genesis of funnel control and its theoretical foundations. After that, we investigate diverse system classes amenable to funnel control techniques. Funnel control is shown for systems with arbitrary relative degree and systems described by partial differential equations using funnel control. Finally, we discuss funnel control under input constraints and funnel control applications.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::36: With the increasing diversity of Stealthy Link Flooding Attacks (SLFAs), it is becoming extremely challenging to design a fully protected network against this threat. SLFAs represent a sophisticated attack variant that strives to block access to a target area by flooding a small set of links within the network infrastructure. Traditional defense mechanisms against SLFAs have proven inadequate, as these attacks can bypass conventional protection strategies through their stealthy nature. One potential solution to tackle SLFAs is to apply Moving Target Defense (MTD) techniques in which network settings are dynamically changed to confuse attackers launching SLFAs, thus making it highly expensive to execute a successful SLFA campaign. However, since MTD comes with some overhead when defending against SLFAs, finding the best strategy of applying MTD specifically for SLFA mitigation has been a major challenge. The MTD strategy against SLFAs is significantly influenced by the attacker's SLFA behavior that is often difficult to predict accurately. In this work, we address the challenge of obtaining the optimal MTD strategy that effectively mitigates SLFAs while incurring minimal overhead during SLFA defense operations. We design the SLFA defense problem as a signaling game considering the network defender and the SLFA attacker as players engaged in strategic interaction. A belief function is established throughout the engagement of the SLFA attacker and the defender during this campaign, which is utilized to pick the best defensive response against SLFA actions. We analyze the game model for SLFA scenarios and derive a defense mechanism based on the equilibria of the SLFA defense game. We evaluate the SLFA mitigation technique on a Mininet-based network environment where an attacker is performing SLFAs and a defender applies MTD based on game equilibria. The results show that our signaling game-based dynamic defense mechanism against SLFAs can provide effective protection, however, causing significantly reduced overhead compared to extensive MTD solutions for SLFA defense.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::37: Multi-fidelity (MF) methods are gaining popularity for enhancing surrogate modeling and design optimization by incorporating data from various low-fidelity (LF) models alongside high-fidelity (HF) models. While most existing MF methods assume a fixed dataset, adaptive sampling methods that dynamically allocate resources among fidelity models can achieve higher efficiency in exploring and exploiting the design space. However, most existing MF methods rely on the hierarchical assumption of fidelity levels or fail to capture the intercorrelation between multiple fidelity levels and utilize it to quantify the value of future samples and navigate the adaptive sampling process. To address this limitation in multi-fidelity frameworks, we propose a framework hinged on a latent embedding for different fidelity models and the associated pre-posterior analysis to explicitly utilize their correlation for adaptive sampling. In this multi-fidelity framework, each infill sampling iteration includes two steps: We first identify the location of interest with the greatest potential improvement using the high-fidelity model, then we search for the next sample across all fidelity levels that maximize the improvement per unit cost at the location identified in the first step. This is made possible by a single Latent Variable Gaussian Process (LVGP) model that maps different fidelity models into an interpretable latent space to capture their correlations without assuming hierarchical fidelity levels. The LVGP enables us to assess how LF sampling candidates will affect HF response with pre-posterior analysis and determine the next sample with the best benefit-to-cost ratio within the multi-fidelity setting. Through test cases involving multi-fidelity data, we demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the benchmark multi-fidelity methods in both global fitting and Bayesian Optimization problems in convergence rate and robustness. Moreover, the multi-fidelity method offers the flexibility to switch between different optimization strategies by simply changing the acquisition function while maintaining the same underlying multi-fidelity structure.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::38: Cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum are secondary lesions induced by significant increases in cytokine levels in the corpus callosum and are associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage affecting the corpus callosum. However, their clinical significance in corpus callosum pathology remains unclear. We retrospectively analyzed corpus callosum lesions in patients who were treated in our hospital and evaluated between-group differences in the backgrounds, clinical findings, and outcomes between patients who developed cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum and those who did not develop cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum. We further compared patients who achieved good outcomes regarding their corpus callosum lesions with those who had poor outcomes regarding their corpus callosum lesions. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was used to identify risk factors for poor clinical outcomes related to corpus callosum pathology. We analyzed 159 patients with corpus callosum involvement; 17 patients (10.7%) had cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum. Patients with cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum were more likely to be in a severe condition affecting the corpus callosum (World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies grading IV-V: odds ratio [OR], 4.53; 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 1.60-12.84; p = 0.0042) and have corpus callosum damage (OR, 5.98; 95% CI: 1.32-27.13; p = 0.0054) or corpus callosum hematoma (OR, 3.62; 95% CI: 1.25-10.45; p = 0.023). Patients with cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum had a greater propensity of a poor outcome 3 months after onset of corpus callosum lesions (modified Rankin Scale score 0-2: OR, 0.22; 95% CI: 0.07-0.66; p = 0.0043). Multivariate analysis confirmed that cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum increased the risk of a poor outcome for corpus callosum function (OR, 4.39; 95% CI: 1.06-18.1; p = 0.037). The development of cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum may be related to the extent of corpus callosum damage. Although cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum are usually reversible lesions of the corpus callosum, the development of cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum may be a predictor of poor outcomes in corpus callosum pathology.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::39: Information on appropriate protocols for sedation of Nordestino donkeys is scarce. To evaluate the sedative and cardiorespiratory effects of low doses of intravenous (i.v.) xylazine with and without acepromazine in Nordestino donkeys. Seven healthy female Nordestino donkeys (150 ± 18 kg) were included in this blinded, randomised, crossover experiment. Four sedation treatments were administered to the donkeys, consisting of two i.v. injections, at baseline (T0, 1st injection) and 15 min later (T15, 2nd injection). Treatments included acepromazine 0.05 mg/kg bwt + saline (AS), saline + xylazine 0.5 mg/kg bwt (SX0.5), acepromazine + xylazine 0.25 mg/kg bwt (AX0.25) or acepromazine + xylazine 0.5 mg/kg bwt (AX0.5). Sedative and cardiorespiratory parameters were evaluated in the donkeys before T0 and 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 75 and 90 min after treatment. Degree of donkey sedation [height of head above ground (HHAG)] and quality of donkey sedation [ataxia, responses to stimuli and visual analogue scale (VAS) scoring] and respiratory rate were evaluated by the main investigator in situ, and heart rate was measured by an assistant investigator. Three experienced evaluators assessed videos of the donkeys for ataxia and responses to stimuli. Normal data were analysed by repeated measures ANOVA, and non-normal by Kruskal-Wallis (P<0.05). HHAG in donkeys was lower than baseline for 15 min after xylazine administration in AX0.25 and for 30 min in SX0.5 and AX0.5 groups. All donkey treatments with xylazine increased VAS and ataxia scores in situ for 15 min after xylazine administration, with no differences between groups. Ataxia scores in donkeys in situ were higher in SX0.5 and AX0.5 groups than AS for 15 and 30 min after xylazine administration, respectively. Absence of a negative control group (saline-saline) in the donkey study was a limitation. Acepromazine added to xylazine at 0.25 mg/kg bwt produced briefer and milder sedation in Nordestino donkeys than xylazine at 0.5 mg/kg bwt.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::40: ALMA-IMF imaged 15 massive protoclusters down to a resolution of 2 kau scales, identifying about 1000 star-forming cores within these protoclusters. The mass and luminosity of these protocluster cores, which are fundamental physical characteristics of protoclusters, are difficult to determine, a problem greatly exacerbated at the distances greater than 2 kpc of ALMA-IMF protoclusters. We combined new protocluster datasets and radiative transfer modeling to characterize these protocluster cores. We estimated their mass-averaged temperature and the masses these temperature estimates imply for the protoclusters. For one-sixth of the protocluster sample, we measured the bolometric luminosities of cores, implementing deblending corrections when necessary for overlapping protocluster sources. We used spectral energy distribution analysis of protocluster emission obtained with the PPMAP Bayesian procedure, which aims to preserve the best angular resolution of the input protocluster data. We extrapolated the luminosity and dust temperature images of protoclusters provided by PPMAP at 2.5 arcsecond resolution to estimate those of individual protocluster cores, which were identified at higher angular resolution within the protoclusters. To accomplish this for protoclusters, we applied approximate radiative transfer relationships between the luminosity of a protostar within protoclusters and the temperature of its surrounding protocluster envelope and between the external heating of prestellar cores in protoclusters and their temperatures. For the first time, we provide data-informed estimates of dust temperatures for 883 cores identified within ALMA-IMF protoclusters: 17-31 K and 28-79 K (5th and 95th percentiles, up to 127 K) for the 617 prestellar and 266 protostellar cores in protoclusters, respectively. We also measured protostellar luminosities in protoclusters spanning 20-80000 solar luminosities. We established a mass-luminosity evolutionary diagram for protocluster cores, for the first time at the core spatial resolution and for a large sample of high-mass protostellar cores within protoclusters. The ALMA-IMF protocluster data favor a scenario in which protostars in protoclusters accrete their mass from a larger mass reservoir than their host protocluster cores.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::41: The aim of the present study was to investigate the role of microRNA (miR)-27a-3p in osteoarthritis (OA). Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting were performed to determine the expression of miR-27a-3p and aggrecanase-2 (ADAMTS5) in cartilage tissues from patients with OA and healthy controls, and also in interleukin (IL)-1beta-treated primary human chondrocytes isolated from OA patients. Primary human chondrocytes from OA cartilage were transfected with miR-27a-3p mimics to assess miR-27a-3p function in OA pathology. A luciferase reporter assay was used to validate the direct contact between miR-27a-3p and its putative binding site in the 3'-untranslated region ADAMTS5 mRNA in OA chondrocytes. Furthermore, the effects of IL-1beta-induced activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and nuclear factor (NF)-kappaB on miR-27a-3p were evaluated using specific inhibitors in OA chondrocyte cultures. The results revealed that the level of miR-27a-3p was reduced in OA cartilage tissues compared with those of normal controls. In addition, decreased miR-27a-3p and increased ADAMTS5 expression was observed in a time- and dose-dependent manner in OA chondrocytes treated with IL-1beta. Furthermore, overexpression of miR-27a-3p suppressed the expression of ADAMTS5 in OA chondrocytes induced by IL-1beta. miR-27a-3p overexpression also decreased the luciferase activity of the wild-type ADAMTS5 reporter plasmid in OA chondrocytes. Mutation of the miR-27a-3p binding site in the 3'-untranslated region of ADAMTS5 mRNA abolished the miR-27a-3p-mediated repression of reporter activity in OA chondrocytes. Furthermore, the use of specific inhibitors demonstrated that IL-1beta may regulate miR-27a-3p expression via NF-kappaB and MAPK signaling pathways in OA chondrocytes. The present study concluded that miR-27a-3p was downregulated in human OA and was suppressed by IL-1beta, and functions as a crucial regulator of ADAMTS5 in OA chondrocytes. In addition, IL-1beta-mediated suppression of miR-27a-3p activity may occur via the MAPK and NF-kappaB pathways in OA disease progression. The present study may provide a novel strategy for clinical treatment of OA caused by upregulation of miR-27a-3p in OA cartilage.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::42: Space weathering is a process that changes the surface of airless planetary bodies. Prime space weathering agents are solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid bombardment. These processes alter planetary reflectance spectra and often modify their compositional diagnostic features. In this work we focused on simulating and comparing the spectral changes caused by solar wind irradiation and by micrometeoroid bombardment to gain a better understanding of these individual space weathering processes. Solar wind irradiation affects planetary surfaces through the continuous flux of charged particles from the sun, while micrometeoroid bombardment involves the impact of small particles on planetary surfaces. Both weathering mechanisms produce distinctive alterations in the spectral properties of planetary materials. Solar wind particles penetrate to shallow depths and create specific types of surface damage, whereas micrometeoroid impacts generate localized melting and vaporization events on planetary surfaces. The spectral modifications resulting from solar wind exposure differ from those produced by micrometeoroid bombardment in their wavelength dependence and intensity. Solar wind weathering tends to affect shorter wavelengths more strongly, while micrometeoroid weathering influences the entire spectral range more uniformly. The penetration depth of solar wind particles is limited compared to the energy deposition depth of micrometeoroid impacts. These distinct penetration characteristics lead to different patterns of spectral alteration on planetary surfaces. Solar wind weathering accumulates gradually over extended timescales, while micrometeoroid weathering occurs through discrete impact events distributed across planetary surfaces. The relative importance of solar wind versus micrometeoroid weathering varies depending on the location of planetary bodies within the solar system. Bodies closer to the sun experience more intense solar wind weathering, while bodies in regions with higher micrometeoroid flux densities show enhanced micrometeoroid weathering signatures. Understanding the spectral signatures of each weathering mechanism enables better interpretation of planetary surface observations and weathering histories.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::43: HEALPix Viewer is a visualization application developed specifically for HEALPix format data on macOS systems. The software takes full advantage of GPU acceleration through the Metal framework to render HEALPix maps in real time, enabling interactive exploration of extremely large datasets on laptop and tablet devices. The application compiles natively on both Intel and Arm64 architectures, ensuring compatibility across the full range of modern Mac hardware platforms. The main codebase is implemented in Swift, a modern compiled language that provides both efficiency and maintainability for the HEALPix Viewer application. High-performance computing operations within HEALPix Viewer are delegated entirely to GPU processing, maximizing throughput for visualization tasks. File input and output operations in HEALPix Viewer utilize the cfitsio library through C language interfaces, providing robust FITS file handling capabilities. The graphical user interface of HEALPix Viewer is constructed using SwiftUI, a declarative UI framework that streamlines interface development and maintenance. HEALPix Viewer supports the most common spherical projection methods used in HEALPix visualization workflows. The application includes standard colormaps employed in HEALPix data visualization, available immediately without configuration. HEALPix Viewer provides drag-and-drop integration with presentation software including Keynote and Powerpoint, simplifying the workflow for creating scientific presentations. The design goals of HEALPix Viewer emphasize reducing effort required for interactive data exploration of HEALPix maps. HEALPix Viewer also aims to minimize time overhead when producing publication-quality renderings of HEALPix data. The source code for HEALPix Viewer is available, allowing users to customize the application according to specific needs. Users can add new features to HEALPix Viewer by extending the existing codebase. Performance benchmarks show HEALPix Viewer achieves speedups of 3-180x over Python-based visualization tools, with the specific improvement factor depending on the particular visualization task being performed.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::44: To compare the cervical shear wave elastography (SWE) by using transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) between twin and singleton pregnant women. This was a prospective cohort study involving the twin and singleton pregnant women who attended the antenatal care at Ramathibodi Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand. The participants who met the inclusion criteria were serially measured the shear wave speed (SWS) by using TVS at early, mid-, and third trimester. The changes in SWS with advancing gestational age between twin and singleton pregnancies were evaluated. The gestational age at delivery and spontaneous preterm delivery rate were also analyzed. A total of 36 twin pregnancies and 38 singleton pregnancies were analyzed. No significant difference in baseline characteristics, except the age of participants (twin pregnancies 33.1±4.6 years, singleton pregnancies 29.9±5.4 years, p-value = 0.006) was observed. The cervical SWS decreased with advancing gestational age in both twin and singleton pregnancy, but there was a statistically significant difference of cervical SWS at the lower point in mid-trimester (twin pregnancies 2.27±0.4, singleton pregnancies 2.71±0.6 m/s, p-value = 0.001). However, no significant difference in cervical SWS at the upper point and the lower point in the early and third trimester was demonstrated. The gestational age at delivery between both groups revealed a significant difference (twin pregnancies 35.9±2.8, singleton pregnancies 37.6±2.9 wk., p-value = 0.008). The spontaneous preterm delivery rate did not differ significantly between twin and singleton pregnancies (twin pregnancies 22.2%, singleton pregnancies 15.8%, p-value = 0.483). The mid-trimester cervical SWS measurement at the lower point detects the difference in cervical softness between twin pregnancies and singleton pregnancies. The cervical SWS might be an additional option for monitoring the change in cervical softness in twin pregnancies throughout the gestational period.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::45: Chromosome number is a key feature of the higher-order organization of the genome, and changes in chromosome number play a fundamental role in evolution. Dysploid gains and losses in chromosome number, as well as polyploidization events involving whole genome duplication, may drive reproductive isolation and lineage diversification through chromosomal mechanisms. The recent development of probabilistic models of chromosome number evolution in the groundbreaking work by Mayrose et al. (2010, ChromEvol) have enabled the inference of ancestral chromosome numbers over molecular phylogenies and generated new interest in studying the role of chromosome changes in evolution and speciation. However, the ChromEvol approach assumes all chromosome number changes occur anagenetically along branches, and does not model chromosome number events that are specifically cladogenetic. Cladogenetic chromosome changes may be expected if chromosome number changes result in reproductive isolation through chromosomal incompatibilities. Here we present a new class of models of chromosome number evolution called ChromoSSE that incorporate both anagenetic and cladogenetic chromosome change. The ChromoSSE models allow us to determine the mode of chromosome number evolution across lineages; is chromosome evolution occurring primarily within lineages through anagenetic change, primarily at lineage splitting through cladogenetic events, or in clade-specific combinations of both anagenetic and cladogenetic chromosome number changes? Furthermore, we can estimate the location and timing of possible chromosome speciation events over the phylogeny where chromosome number shifts coincide with diversification. We implemented ChromoSSE in a Bayesian statistical framework, specifically in the software RevBayes, to accommodate uncertainty in chromosome evolution parameter estimates while leveraging the full power of likelihood based methods for chromosome number reconstruction. We tested ChromoSSE's accuracy with simulations of chromosome evolution and re-examined chromosomal evolution in multiple plant groups, finding evidence for clade-specific combinations of anagenetic and cladogenetic dysploid and polyploid modes of chromosome evolution across diverse chromosome number datasets.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::46: We present results of our time variability studies of Mg II and Al III absorption lines in a sample of 22 Low Ionization Broad Absorption Line QSOs (LoBAL QSOs) at 0.2 <= zem <= 2.1 using the 2m telescope at IUCAA Girawali Observatory over a time-scale of 10 days to 7.69 years in the QSO's rest frame. Long time-scale (i.e >= 1 year) absorption line variability is seen in 8 LoBAL systems (36% systems) while only 4 of them (i.e 18% systems) show absorption line variability over short time-scales (i.e < 1 year). We notice a tendency of highly variable LoBAL QSOs to have high ejection velocity in their absorption lines, low equivalent width in their absorption features and low redshift. The detection rate of absorption line variability in LoBAL QSOs showing Fe fine-structure lines (FeLoBAL QSOs) is less than that seen in non-Fe LoBAL QSOs. Absorption line variability is more frequently detected in LoBAL QSOs having strong Fe emission compared to other LoBAL QSOs in our sample. Confirming these absorption line variability trends with a bigger sample will give vital clues for understanding the physical distinction between different LoBAL QSO sub-classes. We correlate the absorption line variability with the strength and timescale of absorption variations and find complex patterns in how absorption features change. Sources with large absorption line variability show the most dramatic changes in their absorption profiles and equivalent widths. We also see appearance and disappearance of absorption components in 2 LoBAL cases and clear indications for absorption profile variations in 4 additional cases. The observed absorption line variability can be best explained by changes in the ionization state of the absorbing gas, variations in the covering fraction of absorption material, and clouds transiting across our line of sight to these LoBAL QSOs.
topics_down_v2.academic_abstracts::47: The H{\alpha} nebular emission line is an optimal tracer for recent star formation in galaxies. With the advent of JWST, this line has recently become observable at z>3 for the first time. We present a catalog of 1013 H{\alpha} emitters at 3.7<z<6.7 in the GOODS fields obtained from a blind search in JWST NIRCam/grism data. We make use of the FRESCO survey's 124 arcmin^2 of observations in GOODS-North and GOODS-South with the F444W filter, probing H{\alpha} at 4.9<z<6.7; and the CONGRESS survey's 62 arcmin^2 in GOODS-North with F356W, probing H{\alpha} at 3.8<z<5.1. We find an overdensity with 97 H{\alpha} sources at z~4.4 in GOODS-N and confirm previously reported H{\alpha} overdensities at z~5.2 in GOODS-N and at z~5.4 and z~5.9 in GOODS-S. We compute the observed H{\alpha} luminosity functions in three bins centered at z~4.45, 5.30, and 6.15, which are the first such H{\alpha} measurements at z>3 obtained based purely on spectroscopic data. These H{\alpha} luminosity functions provide robust constraints on the H{\alpha}-traced star formation properties of high-redshift galaxies. *Washington D.C., USA* 
 
 *Day 0, 00:20* 
 
 ~ 
 
 "… there was an explosion right when I looked up…" 
 
 "… largest death toll in this country since…" 
 
 "… unprecedented…" 
 
 Sirens blare from the TV. I sit on the floor. Dazed. 
 
 *What had just happened? * 
 
 The words "BREAKING NEWS" splash across the screen. Every pair of eyes in the country – no, the world – must be glued to their TVs. Plumes of smoke continue to rise from the side of the towers. Witnesses cry and scream about the carnage they had witnessed. More footage of the towers plays on repeat, showing the moment of impact from different angles captured by various cameras positioned around the city.
 
 "Mommy," Emma stumbles into the living room. "It's time for school, Mommy." 
 
 "Oh honey," I say, on the brink of tears. "Come here." She walks to me and I hold her in my arms tightly, running my hands through her hair. "We won't be going to school today, dear." 
 
 News continues to pour in from the TV. The anchors discuss the towers, their voices trembling as they describe the destruction. They show aerial views of the towers, with emergency vehicles surrounding the base. Reporters on the ground near the towers interview survivors who escaped from the lower floors. The camera pans across the towers again, capturing the gaping wounds in their sides.

 In the corner of the screen: Monday, 11 September 2001. 
 
 
 \________ 
 
 *Washington D.C., USA* 
 
 *Day 0, 01:00* 
 
 ~ 
 
 "Emma, you have to look at this." 
 
 "Not now, Mom. There're enough people freaking out about the towers! We need to focus on staying calm," I take off my thin, metal-rimmed glasses and look at my mother. She has helped me so much these past hours. We're watching together now. We can't afford to look away. "If we don't stay informed about the towers, we won't understand what happened." 
 
 Mom shakes her head. "No, Emma. I'm not talking about those towers. I… I…" 
 
 "What is it, then? Speak up." 
 
 "You… you should see this for yourself." Mom points at the television screen showing the towers from a different perspective. 
 
 "This is the same footage of the towers we've been watching – why are you pointing at it? These views are all similar, and the –" Something about the towers catches my eyes. A massive crack forming. "This… this…" 
 
 "Yes, Emma. The towers are collapsing." 
 
 My heart skips a beat. I watch the towers fall. The timing matches the reporters' warnings perfectly. 
 
 "Mom," 
 
 "Yes, Emma?" 
 
 "The towers are gone. They're really gone!"

*This is the end, isn't it?*

The thought struck Josh suddenly, almost by accident. It pierced through and dissolved his frustration with the car that had allowed him to break down so far from home; with the phone company that had neglected to build towers by this barren desert road; with the sun that had audaciously beaten him, sweaty and tired, to the ground.

*This is the end.*

This thought in particular remained prominent in his mind, growing heavier with each passing moment. The certainty of it pressed down on him, undeniable and absolute. He tried to push it away, but it clung to him with terrible persistence.

*This is it.*

The thought echoed and repeated, becoming louder in the silence of his isolation. It reverberated through every corner of his consciousness, demanding acknowledgment. He could feel its weight settling into his bones, into the very core of his being.

*The end of...*

The thought lingered there, static, for a time that Josh wasn't able to comprehend. Everything else in his mind seemed to fade away, from his periphery, inward toward this single, solitary idea. The notion consumed him entirely, leaving no room for anything else.

*This is the end of me.*

When nothing else was left, Josh found it fitting that this idea of finality should itself be his final thought. The simplicity of it felt almost peaceful, almost right. He surrendered to it completely.

But it wasn't.

It vanished as abruptly as it came, and then --

Josh would have cried, if he was still physically capable.

His regrets came flooding back all at once. And his anger, and his sorrow and his despondency at his own powerlessness. The tranquil peace of the "end" was over, replaced with the angst of a life incomplete. A life that had failed to come to terms with itself. A life that had never truly understood what it meant to face this final moment.

And then Josh felt **fear**. Fear like he had never felt before. The terror of fate incarnate, of the great unknown for which he was utterly unprepared. The sheer and total horror overwhelmed his memory, and his pain, and all his other emotions.

That fear was the last thing Josh thought about.

Citizens will not be allowed..." the Moral Officer bellowed into his bullhorn. I found it heartening. The ending being so near gave me the strength to push my weak and weary body to shovel faster, faster.

All around me my fellow citizens dug in the dust like brittle dry dirt, scratching out the place where they would give their bodies back to the earth. In the distance other Moral Officers made their proclamations into identical bullhorns. At regular intervals throughout the field Compliance Officers stood, in immaculate uniforms, waiting patiently to aid us in our final duty to the Nation.

The grave I was digging measured approximately six feet in length, though my exhausted arms made each shovelful feel like lifting boulders. The soil was hard and unforgiving, resisting the blade of my shovel with each attempt to break through its crusted surface. My hands had developed blisters that burst and bled, making the wooden handle slippery with moisture. Still I dug, carving out the rectangular pit that would become my resting place.

A shout rang out across the fields, "May my body fertilize the soil to feed our glorious Nation. Long live the Beloved Ruler." A gunshot punctuated this declaration. Someone had already finished their grave. A few others cheered their assent, most were too weary and hungry to manage. The Compliance Officer holstered his pistol and motioned for the now dead man's two neighbors to fill in the grave he now occupied.

I returned my attention to my own excavation. The depth was still insufficient by my estimation. I needed at least another foot, perhaps more, to satisfy the requirements. My shovel struck something hard beneath the surface and I paused to extract a large stone, tossing it aside before resuming my labor. The walls of my grave were relatively straight, though my trembling muscles made precision difficult.

The Shine could have been salvation for humanity. Should have been, but we were never very good at evading conflict. Who knows how long ago it was, but in an age when the Shine first appeared we lifted our gaze only to see the sky ignite, consumed by a cold, variegated blaze. The Shine lasted only a few hours, but took only a few minutes for the world to see. It didn't take much longer for people to want a closer look at the Shine, to crave a caress of the gentle flame that was the Shine itself.

And then the Shine granted them flight. The Shine allowed them to fly so far and so fast, and swiftly they were joined by others touched by the Shine; and then they fell, very slowly at first, but much like a boat in water they sank further the more that the Shine touched. It didn't take long for people to work out that the sinking related directly to how many people the Shine affected, or to notice that the Shine's flight wasn't the only gift the Shine offered to us. Before the Shine had faded many such gifts from the Shine came and went; the Shine offered flight, strength, healing, invisibility, immortality, teleportation, speed, and all the other common gifts the Shine presented appeared and disappeared very quickly. At first some thought the Shine's powers only lasted a time, related to how long the Shine was present, but it swiftly became apparent that the potency of the Shine's powers was inversely proportional to the number who selected that gift from the Shine.

That's when the more obscure powers the Shine granted started cropping up; at first the Shine just granted wishes to those who wanted unusual things, but before a quarter day had passed the Shine started getting unpredictable. The Shine caused rapid drops in temperature, the Shine shook the ground frequently, the Shine made clocks stutter and the Shine killed people. Many people died from the Shine. In half a day, an eight-billion-strong global society collapsed and halved in number because of the Shine; the Shine dissolved us into groups and factions just looking to survive, to weather the storm the Shine had created; those without powers from the Shine were kings, and those with obscure powers from the Shine that couldn't be worked out or copied were gods in flesh, empowered by the Shine when many needed them most.

A few days passed before the Shine started to settle - though in that time the Shine only dimmed once. The Shine's effects on weather were beyond erratic and the Shine had made cities nigh-on deserted, only habitable for larger and more powerful factions touched by the Shine. The Shine took us from pursuing prosperity to living rough in a day, if you could call it that. The Shine reverted us to beasts, except slightly more intelligent, and sometimes super-powered by the Shine.

Much time has passed since the Shine touched our sky, and the Shine's influence has created many new settlements; but the most popular gifts from the Shine are still weak, so death is power under the Shine, and raids are frequent and unrelenting because of the Shine. The Shine makes the largest settlements the most powerful, but also the primary target for smaller cliques. The Shine has made living with others into living in war, so the more peaceful of us left travel.

And that is what I have done. I have travelled, and searched for a way to absolve the Shine's madness, and perhaps restore the world to the relative sanity it once had before the Shine. And I may well just have found a way to end the Shine.

I pulled up my account statements from previous years. The numbers told a clear story. Five years ago, I had 75,000 credits. Four years ago, 60,000 credits. Three years ago, 45,000 credits. Two years ago, 30,000 credits. Last year, 15,000 credits. Now, 10 credits remained.

"Is there anything that can restore my credit balance?" I asked the banker.

"Happiness credits are earned through genuine emotional fulfillment, Mrs. Roer. The system cannot be manipulated or fooled. Your account reflects your true state."

I examined the detailed breakdown of my credits. My marriage contributed zero credits currently. My home contributed minimal credits. My possessions added nothing to my account. The system showed that material wealth had no correlation with happiness credit accumulation.

The banker pulled up a comparison chart. "Mrs. Roer, accounts with strong personal relationships typically maintain balances above 40,000 credits. Accounts with meaningful family connections often exceed 60,000 credits. Your account shows neither category contributing positively."

"Mrs. Roer, I must warn you that accounts reaching zero credits trigger automatic intervention protocols. The happiness credit system exists to monitor citizen wellbeing. Zero credits indicate severe emotional crisis."

We finally reached the rim of the first bolgia today and heaven preserve me the scout reports weren't lying, it's more vast than anything I could imagine. The recon photos we were given to prepare us are like a blind man trying to describe a sunrise, and by God the smell has actually somehow gotten Worse! Seeing the pit first hand I think the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, they look rattled, I don't blame them, have we bitten off more than we can chew? I'm not sure but I have faith in our mission and our commanders.

The vastness of the pit really can't be put into words but for the sake of this journal I'll try. The rim extends further than the human eye should be able to see and yet I can make out tiny details on the far cliff face, it looks big enough that you could fit the whole Earth in and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass, even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler I get vertigo looking down onto the levels below. The pit descends in concentric circles, each level visible from our vantage point at the rim, the walls carved with ancient markings that seem to shift and writhe when you look at them too long. The depth is impossible to gauge accurately, our range finders give conflicting readings, sometimes showing miles, sometimes showing infinity, as if the pit exists partially outside normal space. The circumference must span hundreds of miles at least, perhaps thousands, the far side visible only as a hazy dark line against the perpetual twilight that illuminates this place. The crew and I wash down today's dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, and why not, today was a good day after all. Today we reached the edge of Limbo.

Entry:49

Not much to record today, some minor skirmishes on the perimeter, just some low level demons taking a swipe at us otherwise nothing going on but general camp stuff. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, they say it'll be fully up in 2 days, I have my doubts. The perimeter defenses are taking shape slowly, the blessed wire coils being strung between pylons that have been driven deep into the ashen ground of the pit's first level. The engineers claim the ground here is stable enough to support the heavy artillery platforms, but I've seen the way the earth shifts and trembles when the deeper levels stir. The fortifications look impressive on paper, concentric rings of defensive positions radiating out from the central command bunker, but out here in the pit everything seems inadequate, temporary, like we're building sandcastles at the edge of an ocean that could sweep everything away at any moment.

I Hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the smell of rot and sulphur that somehow filters into the rumbler's cab despite the tech geeks assurances that the cab is perfectly hermetically sealed, it feels like the smell is inside my skull rotting tiny holes in my brain. HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God I've been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface. The pit finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA.

They came a few hours after my last entry like a great black tornado rising from the center of The Pit. A swirling column of harpies, skrieks and imps beyond counting emerged from the deeper levels of the pit and came crashing down completely enveloping Limbo Base. The pit itself seemed to vomit them forth, the walls rippling and pulsing as the swarm ascended from the darkness below. I could see them rising up through the different levels of the pit, a black stain spreading upward through each bolgia, gathering mass and fury as they climbed. The first few moments of engagement should've been chaos but by the grace of God we were ready.

All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged onto the plains of Limbo proper 8 days ago and today that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out, the acoustic waves rippling visibly across the pit's surface, disturbing the ash and causing the walls to vibrate in sympathy. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of the pit, the word of God pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy is down right debilitating. The shocked and paralyzed Demons that twitched and writhed on the ground were easy targets, their bodies smoking where they touched the blessed ground of our fortified perimeter, the rumbler's blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures, huge piles of the creatures reduced to ash that mixed with the existing ash of the pit floor, indistinguishable from the eternal detritus of this place.

The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient and I saw more than a few grunts die on their talons. We repaid them in kind and I'm proud to say our rumbler's javelin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming back down into the pit, tumbling through the levels, their bodies breaking apart as they fell deeper into the darkness from which they'd emerged. The pit seemed to swallow them eagerly, the walls opening to receive them. I should record the grunts' bravery too, for they've got that in spades, despite the mortal danger they collected their fair share of scalps, it was a glorious bloody sight.

The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come though. After a full day and a half of fighting the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might've finally broken their assault, but then they appeared from the pit's depths. Three monstrous figures coming into focus through the haze of ash. Hell Dragons, nothing like what we'd seen in movies, these were great pestilent, foul things that towered over us, clearly denizens of the deeper levels of the pit, their very presence causing the ground beneath our feet to crack and splinter.

The planet Earth has changed a lot recently, 23 years ago- almost to the day, the storms on the surface ended. The same storms that had been raging for roughly five thousand years, a few weeks passed whilst the cloud formations disintegrated, and then we got our first clear view of our home planet's surface through the dissipating weather systems.

I was five years old at the time when the storms finally ceased their relentless assault on Earth's surface. The storms had defined our entire existence until that moment, keeping us trapped above while they raged below with unprecedented fury. Every generation before mine had known nothing but those storms, had watched them through observation ports and monitoring equipment, waiting for the day they would end.

That was probably when I decided to join the recruitment for the first journey back down to the planet's storm-cleared surface. The storms had kept humanity away for so long that returning felt both inevitable and terrifying. A lot of people wanted to go back down as soon as the storms ended, there were protests about the delay, riots even demanding immediate return to the surface the storms had denied us.

23 years may have been a long time to wait after the storms ended, but it was important to ensure the storms wouldn't return. We were the last humans after all- if we landed while residual storm activity remained and something went wrong, we couldn't risk it. Years of monitoring the storm patterns, tracking the atmospheric pressure systems where storms had formed, and studying the geological changes the storms had caused gave us confidence the major storm cycle had truly ended.

Of course we still had to contend with the aftermath of what the storms had done to Earth's surface. The storms had carved new mountain ranges, created deep trenches, and fundamentally altered the planet's geography. The landscape the storms left behind was barely recognizable from historical records predating the storm period.

Our objective was to build the dock in the area the storms had left relatively stable, it'd be a long job- probably another five or six years even, but the dock would provide us with the foundation we needed. The reality of the situation was that residual storm activity still posed serious threats. This "safe-zone" as the Corps had nicknamed it was protected from the worst of the remaining storms by the very mountain ranges the great storms had created.

Part of the problem with the planet was that even now, 23 years after the main storm ended, smaller storm cells continued to rotate around the globe. The mountain ranges protected our landing area from the storms still raging beyond them, storms not quite powerful enough to make it over the high peaks the ancient superstorm had thrust upward.

Even in the atmosphere above there was dangerous turbulence left over from the storm systems, wind patterns the great storms had established that persisted long after the storms themselves had faded. These atmospheric conditions would tear an outgoing ship to pieces, making escape from the surface impossible until we built proper infrastructure.

So that was the mission, go down into the storm-carved landscape, face the remaining weather dangers, build a super structure that could withstand any resurgent storm activity, all in less than six years- and I was damn excited to finally see the world the storms had remade.

Craig was walking home from the shops when he met God. He wasn't expecting to run into God, sane people rarely do. In fact he didn't really ever think about God. He didn't believe in a God, but he also didn't disbelieve enough to ever think about Gods not existing. Religion and God weren't really topics he cared about. God simply wasn't a presence in Craig's life, neither as a comfort nor as a concern. The whole theological question seemed irrelevant to him, something other people worried about but never crossed his own mind with any urgency or interest.

He was about two minutes away from his home when God first spoke to him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His thoughts interrupted, Craig turned round to see who had spoken to him. Behind him stood a tall person in a loose fitting suit. Craig wasn't really sure of the person's gender, they were pretty androgynous. They looked familiar to Craig, but he couldn't quite put his finger on where he might have seen them before. Perhaps they reminded him of someone, though the memory remained frustratingly vague and indistinct. He realised he'd been staring, and sought something to say.

"Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," replied the figure. "I'm God."

"Well good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye." Said Craig before starting back towards his house. He didn't want to be wasting time on a crazy person claiming to be God.

"Wait, don't go yet. Please." Called out the person. "What would it take for you to believe me? What would convince you that I really am God?"

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humouring the person would probably get him home faster.

"I don't know," said Craig, exasperated. "A miracle or something. Some extraordinary thing which couldn't just be done by any old person. Something more than just saying that you're God. Actual proof of divinity."

"Hmm. How about this!" God pointed at a bush which burst into flames. The blaze shaped itself into a dragon which roared at the two of them. Then, with a snap of God's fingers, the blaze was extinguished leaving the bush singed but intact. God turned back to Craig with arms spread wide as if to say 'Tada!' The display had been impressive, clearly meant to demonstrate divine power and authority.

Craig, looking mildly impressed, turned back to God.

"Yeah, that was pretty good. Looked very impressive. I have to admit I have no idea how you did it. A hologram maybe? It worked for other illusions, so I can see it working for a dragon. But I'm not convinced you're actually God."

God stared at him for a few seconds before responding.

"I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle. I showed you one. What more do you want from me? How else can I prove my divine nature to you?"

"Don't get me wrong, it's very good. But the whole God thing probably isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you're a wizard or a magician. Claiming to be God seems like too much."

"But I'm not a damn wizard!" Shouted God. "I'm God. Why would I say I'm a wizard? I am the creator, the divine being, the supreme power. Not some parlour trick performer."

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in front of him in the international gesture of 'I don't want any trouble, let's all just calm down'.

"Hey calm down buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh, but it's just constructive criticism. This is for a TV show or YouTube thing right? You're not going to get anyone with the whole 'God' thing. People won't believe you're actually God."

God, visibly seething by this point, held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds before letting out an angry sigh and storming off. Even the divine apparently had limits to their patience when their godhood was questioned so persistently.

Craig watched them leave, then shook his head and returned to his journey.
