*This is the conclusion, isn't it?*

That realization struck Josh suddenly, almost accidentally. It pierced through and dissolved his frustration with the vehicle that had allowed him to malfunction so far from home; with the telephone company that had neglected to construct towers by this barren desert highway; with the sun that had audaciously beaten him, sweaty and exhausted, to the ground.

*This is the finale.*

That notion in particular remained prominent in his consciousness, even as he realized that he had already seen Heather for the final time. And... and Joey, who was still so proud about that geometry examination. And Dale, and the enterprise Dale would inherit, the venture that would serve as an unexpected legacy.

*This is it.*

Dale, who had told him that this journey was a fool's errand, and made a joke about what he would say at Josh's funeral; this recollection, too, failed to shake the contemplation from Josh's head.

*The conclusion of...*

That reflection lingered there, static, for a duration that Josh wasn't able to comprehend. Everything else in his mind seemed to fade away, from his periphery, inward toward this single, solitary concept.

*This is the termination of me.*

When nothing else was left, Josh found it fitting that this awareness of finality should itself be his ultimate consideration.

But it wasn't.

It vanished as abruptly as it came, and then --

Josh would have cried, if he was still physically capable.

His regrets came flooding back all at once. And his anger, and his sorrow and his despondency at his own powerlessness. The tranquil peace of the "conclusion" was over, replaced with the angst of a life incomplete. An existence that had failed to come to terms with itself.

And then Josh felt **fear**. Dread like he had never experienced before. The terror of fate incarnate, of the great unknown for which he was utterly unprepared. The sheer and total horror overwhelmed his memory, and his pain, and all his other emotions.

That fright was the last thing Josh pondered.

All around me my fellow residents excavated in the dust like brittle parched soil, scratching out the place where they would surrender their flesh back to the ground. In the distance other Moral Officers made their proclamations into identical loudspeakers. At regular intervals throughout the field Compliance Officers stood, in immaculate uniforms, waiting patiently to aid us in our final obligation to the Nation.

Then the whispers turned to fully voiced complaints when items began disappearing from the allotments, never to reappear again. Soon protein had almost become a memory and fully grown, healthy looking vegetables were rare.

When the State News Agency, in a special broadcast, finally announced the famine, nobody was surprised. We were instructed that we must, as always, stand united, robust and proud in the face of this Straining Test. Everyone must do their part to bear this hardship and our Immaculate Society would clear this hurdle and emerge triumphant. Even the Beloved Ruler was limiting his consumption, we were told. It was apparent, yes undoubtably evident, that this was some ploy by the dissidents and the outsiders, attempting to destroy our resolve, to make us turn back from the principles of the revolution. That a number of inhabitants would be randomly selected from the population to give glorious sacrifice of faith and righteousness for the Nation, to help ease the burden of sustenance. "Residents shall not be permitted to perish until they have completed excavating their own burial pit." The Moral Officer chanted into his megaphone.

"Inhabitants shall not be authorized..."

Daniel's wife stood at his side, absolutely coming apart at the edges, not that anyone else but him would be able to tell. Okay maybe that was a bit of an exaggeration, but she was a touch anxious. Nervous? Whatever she was feeling, something wasn't quite right, and she was doing that little nose twitch that never happens when she's calm.

"Imani," he called out and her head tipped down to where he was seated in acknowledgement. "It's going to be fine." She gave him a weak smile that didn't quite reach her eyes before reaching out to squeeze his hand. Of course he said it to comfort her, but he honestly felt like everything was going to be okay. They already crossed the worst bits. He survived the car accident, then he survived the surgery to make sure the universe didn't decide to change its mind later, then afterwards the amputations, the implants. With a roll of his eyes he squeezed her fingers back. "Honestly, this has been the easy part, we have plenty of time."

"The easy part? Since when do we ever get easy!" she reached out to swat his ears, her eyes crinkling with mirth. "That's up there with 'What could possibly go wrong?' Don't jinx it," she scolded. He leaned in to tell her all that worrying could do nothing good when the door slammed open, the solid thump echoing through the large room.

"Oops," the tall man in the doorway looked sheepish. "I tripped into the door there. How are you two today?" he inquired friendly, striding into the space and the sunlight from the windows poured over his lanky form. "Ready to give it another go?" Daniel flexed his legs, neat and secured into his new running blades.

"Since the second I put these on, Mason!" he replied earnestly and the easygoing man gave him a thumbs up before reaching out his hands.

"That's what we like to hear! Alright, let's get you up and moving then." With one last look at his wife, who was standing back with an apprehensive expression but held up crossed fingers, he reached for the other man's palms. These were the fourth pair of running blades he had tried. The other ones had issues, despite their so-called custom fits. Too long. Too short. These hurt. Those felt like they were going to fall off. But as Daniel wobbled to his feet he knew these were it. It took a moment to steady himself. They had a different sort of balance and give to them than his normal prosthetic, and his fitness wasn't quite where he wanted it to be. His heart raced as he shifted his weight from one foot to the other, hearing the blades flex in response. Left. Right. Left. Right. Left right, left right, left right, bounce. They felt nothing like his old limbs. But all the same... they felt right. Slowly Mason let go and then backed away to the other side of the room, his gaze never leaving Daniel's position. When he hit the wall he called out to them.

"Great! Now start at a walk and work up to as fast as you feel comfortable doing," a sly tone crept into his voice. "And remember, the room is padded and we're all friends here. Face plants are nothing to worry about." Daniel scoffed at the insinuation. As if he'd let these things get the better of him. Confident, he took a shaky step forward and his arms wheeled around a bit before he braced his core to maintain balance. Then he took another. And another, and soon he had a slow bobbing jog going, carefully moving between his wife and physical therapist. He did this until finally, Mason signaled for him to stop. He sprinted down the space to the happy couple with a look of great excitement.

"It looks like we got it this time!" He stepped back and gave him one final look over. "We just need to run a few more tests, make sure that everything is adjusted correctly, but I think we found your golden pair here. So, how do you feel?"

His mind began to wander as he turned inward, trying to find the words that could even begin to describe what he was experiencing. All he could think about were the things he thought he had lost forever when he hazily woke up from surgery that faithful day, looking down to see the sheet cave in where his lower limbs had once been. The sound of the crowd screaming his name as he tore down the field. The heady sensation of sprinting down a track, the world narrowing almost into blackness as he pushed himself to the limit. The lightness of a casual game of tag with his wife, catching thin air as she slipped by him with laughter dancing in her eyes. Bouncing on his new blades once more he felt weightless. Invincible. With a strength he hadn't experienced in a long time he hugged Imani and spoke over her head, his face aching with a smile.

"Alive."

-- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -

So let it be known I did absolutely no research on the subject for such a quiet piece and just went off of memory and educated guessing. So if anything is terribly wrong, that's why! This disclaimer stands as written because accuracy wasn't prioritized during composition. The author acknowledges potential inaccuracies stemming from lack of proper investigation into prosthetics, rehabilitation processes, or medical procedures depicted within this narrative.

Her warning delivered, the lady turned and started to leave the ornate sitting room. As she reached the door, Lord Aerlman called to her.

He caressed the photograph with his thumb, before setting it back down. All of the energy drained from him and he sagged, turning towards the visitor with a beaten look.

"Fine. Do it. Make the call." He dismissed her with a wave and then sank into one of the large leather chairs, pouring himself a generous whiskey, which he immediately downed. As he poured another, Laura excused herself and closed the entrance quietly. She had a phone conversation to initiate.

"Antonia. I know you're here." Glowing runes twisted across his skin, and his left eye was covered by an eyepatch. His right eye was the color of polished metal, and it quickly scanned the space. Everything after that was a blur, and Antonia couldn't recall any details, except the corpses, and the gore.

She remembered a voice in her head, then her companions all screaming, fire pouring from their eyes as they charged the sword-bearing intruder while shouting in some language Antonia had never heard. As her friends threw themselves at the assailant, she turned and leapt through the bay window, falling the three stories and landing with a sickening crunch. She remembered her legs feeling surprisingly good for such a fall, and then running. The voice in her mind was louder, and she couldn't understand it, but it was hurting her.

As she ran through the streets, the voice was chanting, and every person she passed turned to stare at her, their eyes spewing flames before they turned and charged the direction she had come. She didn't understand what was happening, who the stranger was, or why he pursued her. She didn't comprehend anything! Next thing she knew, she was concealed in the warehouse, where the assailant found her again, his curved blade and pistol both covered in blood. "Why, greetings, Ma'am," I declared easily, rising upward and offering her a seat with my usual grace. "Bertram Proudfoot at your service. Whom do I have the pleasure of addressing?"

"I'd rather not reveal that, if it's all the same to you," she replied, settling down.

"Alright," I responded comfortably. "What can the Hobbiton Detective and Gossip Agency accomplish for you?"

"Well," stated the lady, rubbing her hands together nervously. "It's like this." She paused.

"Like what, Ma'am?" I inquired kindly, lighting my pipe and leaning back in my seat.

"My husband is deceased," she announced.

"Oh my dear, I am sorry!" I exclaimed, though I must admit there was part of me that felt less than sorry. What can I mention? I am only a Hobbit, and this lady possessed the most beautiful feet I had ever laid eyes on. "Tell me everything that occurred."

"We were out boating on the Brandywine three nights ago," she recounted. "And all of a sudden, a rock flew out of nowhere and struck my poor spouse in the head. He keeled over in the water. I screamed for help, but he drowned."

Now of course I had already known it must have been something like this from the moment she walked through the door. I have an uncanny sense for things like that. An instinct, you might call it, honed over years of investigative work in the Shire.

I looked as grave as I could, given the circumstances. "I see," I remarked, blowing another perfect smoke ring up towards the ceiling. "And you would like me to locate and prosecute the perpetrator of this event."

"Yes," confirmed the lady.

"I will do my best, I can promise you that," I assured, and I witnessed her visibly sigh with relief. "May I offer you a cup of tea? Something stronger, perhaps?"

"No thank you," she declined, and without another word she showed herself out.

I promptly made my way to the Brandywine River dock. My first line of inquiry would be to interrogate the man who rented out boats. An odd fellow, and an unusual profession—not many sane hobbits choose to be out in the middle of the water by their own free will. And indeed, this hobbit's boat-renting business was not doing well financially.

After a long consultation of his records he informed me that he had rented out two vessels on the evening in question, and only one of those was by a couple. The pair had been a one Drogo Baggins and a one Primula Brandybuck. Primula, that was the dame's name. But why had she not wanted to reveal it to me initially?

Had this boat fellow heard any commotion on the water, any cries for assistance? No he had not. Did he remember who returned the vessel to him? It hadn't been returned, he explained. In fact, that particular craft had been left floating in the middle of the river. Strange indeed.

Next I walked up and down both banks of the waterway. Not much to garner here, except that whoever had thrown the stone must have been quite a shot. Remarkable accuracy, really.

Having thoroughly investigated the river, my next step was to discover more about Priscilla and Drogo. After visiting several pubs in the areas of Buckland and Hobbiton, I had gathered this: Primula and Drogo were long married, though perhaps not happily wedded. They had one son, now twelve years old, named Frodo Baggins. Strangely, it seemed that Primula had not been witnessed by anyone except me since Drogo's demise. In fact, most of the gentlehobbits that I spoke with seemed to be of the belief that both Drogo *and* Primula had perished three nights ago during the boating accident.

Facts were not adding up properly. Before I could do anything else, I had to speak with my mysterious client again so as to straighten things out completely. Though I had no method of contacting her directly, I knew she would return to my offices in short order. A hunch, if you will.

The following day, she did just that.

"Good afternoon, Primula," I greeted upon her entrance.

Her face betrayed surprise, but she did not deny the name outright.

"I have a few things I need to clarify with you about the case," I explained, and proceeded to outline what I had discovered during my investigation. "So I'm afraid I must ask again," I finished carefully. "What transpired that night?"

And without a word, the dame got up and departed. Just like that. Abruptly.

I did not hear from her again, and two days later, her body was found floating down the Brandywine. I was saddened but not surprised by this development.

My suspicion had been this: having been unhappily married for some time, Primula had pushed her husband into the water herself and boated back to the shore with the intent of disappearing forever from the Shire. Everyone would think that they both were deceased, and so would not suspect any foul play whatsoever. However, upon eavesdropping on the lawyer's meetings that quickly followed, she realized that custody of her son would go to an extended cousin, none other than the famous crackpot Bilbo Baggins himself.

Understandably, Primula did not want her offspring to fall under the influence of said crackpot eccentric, and so she came to me in the hopes that I would believe her story and deflect suspicion away from herself, all in a desperate attempt to maintain custody of her child. But I, having seen through her ruse completely, prevented this outcome. Seeing no alternative she then drowned herself in grief and despair. Shame—I had just begun to think there may have been a very beneficial alternative for the both of us romantically.

I sat back and began polishing my pipe thoughtfully. It was another case solved by the estimable Bertram Proudfoot, but perhaps another opportunity lost forever. I had solved countless mysteries, but opportunities of the other sort came only now and again infrequently. Like I mentioned, it was a shame truly.

I blew another smoke ring toward the ceiling as my thoughts turned to crazed old Mr. Baggins. I felt sympathy for the young Mr. Frodo, who was now cursed enough to fall into the elderly hobbit's custody unfortunately. Who knows what old Baggins would pass on to the impressionable young fellow going forward. As I'm sure you're all aware, Mr. Bilbo Baggins suddenly disappeared many years ago and then returned just as suddenly a year later with hoards of gold and many tall tales to tell. Having been a very respectable hobbit before he departed, whatever he experienced on his journey seemed to have addled his mind completely. He came back a changed hobbit entirely, and not for the better unfortunately.

He was so transformed, in fact, that it is my personal suspicion that the hobbit currently inhabiting Bag End is not the real Bilbo Baggins at all, but rather an impersonator or impostor. There is plenty of evidence to suggest this theory: particularly the fact that "Mr. Baggins" appears much younger than a hobbit of his years has any right to look naturally.

I shall have to explore that line of inquiry further some day soon.

They soared so far and so fast, and swiftly they were joined by others; and then they fell, very slowly at first, but much like a boat in water they sank further the more that accompanied them. It didn't take long for individuals to work out that the sinking related directly to how many humans flew, or to notice that flying wasn't the only *option* available to us. Before the Shine had faded many such choices came and went; flight, strength, healing, invisibility, immortality, teleportation, speed, and all the other common abilities appeared and disappeared very quickly. At first some thought the powers only lasted a time, related to how long the Shine was present, but it swiftly became apparent that the potency of capabilities was inversely proportional to the number who selected that *option*.

That's when the more obscure powers started cropping up; at first it was just salarymen who decided they wanted to shit gold, or kids who decided they wanted to control animals, but before a quarter day had passed things started getting weird. Rapid drops in temperature, the ground shook frequently, clocks would stutter and folks died. Many individuals perished. In half a day, an eight-billion-strong global society of the most intelligent and durable species on Earth collapsed and halved in number; we dissolved into groups and factions just looking to survive, to weather the storm; those *without* abilities were kings, and those with obscure capabilities that couldn't be worked out or copied were gods in flesh, right there to worship when many needed them most.

A few days passed before things started to settle - though in that time the sun only traversed once. Weather was beyond erratic and cities were nigh-on deserted, only habitable for larger and more powerful factions. We went from pursuing prosperity to living rough in a day, if you could call it that. We reverted to beasts, except slightly more intelligent, and sometimes super-powered.

Much time has elapsed since the Shine touched our sky, and humanity has created many new settlements; but the most popular options are still weak, so death is power, and raids are frequent and unrelenting. The largest communities are the most powerful, but also the primary target for smaller cliques. Living with others is dwelling in war, so the more peaceful of us left travel.

And that is what I have done. I have travelled, and searched for a way to absolve this madness, and perhaps restore the planet to the relative sanity it once had. And I may well just have found it.

The man before Councilwoman Asaarha met the gaze of her and her fellow Arbiters with cold blue eyes. Despite the 140 cycles of temporal isolation he had endured before his trial, Sacha Markes stood tall and unbroken. He radiated power and command, even now, stripped of his rank, fleet, and army. The final human was a testament to the species.

The silence before he spoke seemed louder to the Councilwoman than the crashing waves of her ocean home. The time it took for this defendant to respond seemed longer than the span of the galaxy.

"Guilty," he said with a simple finality.

The Arbiters nodded their heads solemnly. None of them had expected this one to beg for mercy.

Asaarha keyed the sentence into the terminal before her. The other six judges did the same. The blue lights of Markes's uniform and restraints changed to red. The screen on the psionic inhibitor around his head changed to read GUILTY in Galactic Standard.

Though the courtroom was empty save for the Tribunal and Markes, Asaarha could hear the roars of vengeance that were surely reverberating throughout the galaxies. Each proceeding involving the humans had been broadcast in its entirety. Each had ended in a condemnation verdict.

"Sacha Markes, formal Admiral of the Seventh Human Expeditionary Fleet, High Captain of the Royal Guard, Commander-in-Chief of the Human Expeditionary Force, and Primarch of the Solar Empire, you are sentenced to Psionic Stripping and Execution by black hole. The prisoner threw his head back defiantly and turned his gaze on the camera nearest him. Addressing the billions of life forms throughout the cosmos, he began the concluding soliloquy of the human race.

"We brought you up out of the mud we discovered you in. We gave you art, culture, and science. Our golden fleets created a civilization that will never be matched; not for 100,000 turns of the galaxy. We are responsible for all that you are.

You have sacrificed googles of lives and thousands of civilizations to bleed your gods dry and bind them in chains. Your worlds are shattered. Your cities gone; wiped from history in an instant. War Journal of P1C Henry Whiticker, First Divine Armored.

Entry:48

We finally reached the rim of the initial bolgia today and heaven preserve me the scout reports weren't lying, it's more vast than anything I could imagine. The recon photos we were given to prepare us are like a blind man trying to describe a sunrise, and by God the stench has actually somehow gotten Worse! Seeing the pit firsthand I think the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, they look rattled, I don't blame them, have we bitten off more than we can chew? I'm not sure but I have faith in our mission and our commanders.

The vastness of the chasm really can't be put into words but for the sake of this journal I'll try. The edge extends further than the human eye should be able to see and yet I can make out tiny details on the far cliff face, it looks big enough that you could fit the whole Earth in and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass, even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler I get vertigo looking down onto the levels below, if it wasn't for the special anti-psychotics the docs give us I'm sure what I witness on the lower tiers might have some lasting horrific effect on me. My crewmates and I wash down today's dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, and why not, this particular day was good after all. We reached the boundary of Limbo.

Entry:49

Not much to record presently, some minor skirmishes on the perimeter, just some low level demons taking a swipe at us otherwise nothing going on but general camp stuff. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, they say it'll be fully up in two days, I have my doubts. After their fiasco at the river they've got a lot of face to save, two Rumblers, four squads of troops and a Screacher lost because of their damn barges. Bastards.

I Hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the odor of rot and sulphur that somehow filters into the vehicle's cabin despite the tech geeks assurances that the compartment is perfectly hermetically sealed, it feels like the reek is inside my skull rotting tiny holes in my brain.

Entry:51

HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God I've been waiting for this moment since the initial days of the war for the surface. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA.

They came a few hours after my last entry like a great black tornado. A swirling column of harpies, skrieks and imps beyond counting rising up from the center of The Pit and came crashing down completely enveloping Limbo Base. The first few moments of engagement should've been chaos but by the grace of God we were ready.

All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged from the maze of caves and onto the plains of Limbo proper eight days ago and presently that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell, the divine scripture pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy is down right debilitating. The shocked and paralysed Demons that twitched and writhed on the ground were easy targets, the rumblers blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures as if the misted holy liquid were strong acid, huge piles of the beasts were reduced to ash in seconds.

The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient and I saw more than a few grunts die on their talons, their sanctified body armor little better than cardboard. We repaid them in kind and I'm proud to say our vehicle's javelin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion impaled on our gleaming silver spears. I should note so it doesn't seem like I'm diminishing the infantry's efforts, their bravery and ferocity in combat too, for they've got that in spades, despite the mortal danger they collected their fair share of scalps, pinning the massive monsters with their silver pikes and finishing them off with their chain sickles. It was a glorious bloody sight, like something out of a nature documentary.

The greatest trial of the engagement was yet to come though. After a full day and a half of fighting the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might've finally broken their assault, but then they appeared. Three monstrous figures coming into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion. Hell Dragons, nothing like what we'd seen in movies or our stories from childhood, these were great pestilent, foul things that towered over us. Snub nosed heads the size of a grand cathedral covered in spines, long armored bodies like an insect's, their faces and joints slick with thick black tar that bubbled and hissed as it fell from them and stained the plains of Limbo.

Screachers focused their assault and prevented the titans from overrunning the base, the vehicle's water tanks and javelin cannons ran dry just trying to keep them at bay, our brave infantry held back the black swarm, fighting tirelessly which allowed us time to retreat, resupply and reenter the fray. And so it went for hours on end and for all our efforts the Hell Dragons seemed to be none the worse.

Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps. Of all people! Through our struggles we had given them enough time to secure and assemble Limbo Base's major defenses, Sanctified Artillery and the Holy Rail Gun. The Rail Gun punctured the Dragon's thick armor spewing geysers of tar onto the battlefield while the artillery smashed into the beast's vulnerable exposed points lodging shells etched with scripture deep in their bodies wracking them with pain and agony. The attack still went on for many hours and we lost a great deal of our force but after nearly two months since we first descended into this place we finally have established a forward base to launch our offensive on Hell. One Bolgia down eight to go. This is the first day here that the smell doesn't bother me at all anymore.

Our world has transformed dramatically lately, 23 years ago—almost to this day, the tempests across the surface ceased. Those same hurricanes had been ravaging for roughly five thousand years; several weeks elapsed whilst the atmospheric formations disintegrated, and then we received our initial clear view of our homeworld.

I was five years old then and entertained mostly by the hues, the beautiful azure and emerald were like nothing aboard the Ark. We had water—sure, but not reservoirs large enough to give that sapphire colour. We had vegetation too, but the conditions were far from optimal and made the flora a dirty olive rather than lush. I wanted to see it closer—touch it—feel it.

That was probably when I decided to join the recruitment for the first journey. The initial voyage was—as the name implies—the pioneering expedition back down to the planet. A lot of people wanted to return down as soon as the tempests ceased, there were protests—riots even. People demanded the Ark head straight back down—Idiots.

23 years may have been a long time to wait, but it was important... We were the last humans after all—if we landed and something went wrong? We couldn't risk it. Years of geological scans, and low atmosphere scouting gave us the perfect landing spot. Minimal damage to local environment, enough space to develop a community, plenty of food—reservoirs—and importantly a lot of natural protection taking the form of Cataclysm-formed mountain ranges, and deep trenches filled with the darkest sapphire liquid.

Of course something as massive as the Ark couldn't simply just descend though... No—that was where the pioneering voyage came into the picture. We were the initial guys to go planetside—and live permanently in over seven generations. Our objective was to construct the dock, it'd be a lengthy job—probably another five or six years even, but the harbour would provide us with a much needed start—as well as mapping out local geography much more clearly, learning about flora, fauna. The reality of the situation is that we were going in blind—this "safe-zone" as the Corps had nicknamed it could very easily become a deathtrap. The problem with the safezone was that because of its location once we went in, our shuttle wouldn't be able to make it out.

Part of the dilemma with the world was the hurricanes—even now 23 years after the main cyclone ended smaller cells continued to rotate... The mountainous barriers protected the area from the tempests still ravaging—not quite powerful enough to make it over the high peaks though.

Even in the atmosphere above there was a vicious gale that constantly blew... It would tear an outgoing vessel to pieces, only a craft as massive as the Ark would be able to survive it—and the Ark needed a harbour in order to perform a takeoff.

So that was the mission, descend down, face possible death, construct a superstructure, all in less than six years—and I was damn excited. The challenge ahead seemed insurmountable yet thrilling, representing humanity's desperate gamble for survival and rebirth on our ancestral homeworld after millennia of exile.

"Hey, observe those chickadees over in the birdbath." Kylo whooped and puffed out his chest, nearly toppling off his perch.

"Don't be a troglodyte, bro," Atticus groused, pecking at his seeds, "You're a wren. That isn't even the same family."

"I don't care. I'm gonna go talk to them." Kylo took off, swerving through the air like a leaf trapped in a gust. Atticus sighed and departed after him. He'd have to keep close tabs on his companion or else they'd get kicked out again.

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash. Droplets flew in every direction, drenching the occupants of the basin. They squawked with indignation as Kylo emerged from beneath the surface, shaking the wetness from his head. He trotted up to a group of soaked finches and gave his wings a shake. "Hey, birds. Nice tits."

"We're not tits." A purple finch stepped forward from the cluster, and she launched into a tirade on how overused that pickup line was. Atticus alighted on the rim of the bath and began to walk around, apologizing to everyone for Kylo's behavior and pleading with them not to summon the bouncer over.

"Okay, sorry," Kylo interrupted, "let me make it up to you: how about you and I head over there—" He motioned to the bird feeder. "—and I share my seeds with you?" If birds had lips, Kylo would be smirking right now.

The finches began to flap their wings angrily, splashing Kylo with liquid. "You're such a boor. Get out of here!" Many of the onlookers chirped in agreement, and some of the bigger birds began to puff their chests threateningly. Atticus shoved Kylo to the side and raised his wings. "On behalf of my friend here, I apologize. He's clearly had too much nectar; we'll just be going now..."

"Oh, you think we're going to fall for that?" The purple finch spat a nut shell at his feet. "He's just trying to play wingbird for you, isn't he? Let him take the fall for you, and swoop in to appear better by comparison." The other avians chorused in agreement, their voices rising in collective disapproval of the pair's transparent strategy.

"I think these two need to be taught a lesson." A blue jay fluttered over to Atticus, towering a full inch above him. He spread his wings menacingly, blocking Atticus from taking off. "Why don't you peck on someone your own size?" The onlookers broke into cheers, shouting for a fight.

"Well, you're kind of larger than me." Atticus took a step back into the bath. He felt feathers ruffle against him as the crowd pressed around him, urged him back towards the jay. "That wouldn't be my own size now, would it?"

Kylo staggered in front of him and began to hop around. "Don't worry, Atticus; we got this."

"Hey, this is a one-on-one fight." The jay looked around. "If you get backup, then—"

"Who on earth placed all this here?" A door opened, and the birds began to scatter, screaming, "Human!" Atticus grabbed Kylo and urged him into the air, and the duo lost themselves amongst the cloud of fleeing birds. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw the person scratching his head in front of the birdbath.

"Make sure to thank that individual for bailing you out of yet another mess," Atticus said.

Kylo scoffed. "We could've totally taken that guy." As the pair flew over the Toyota in the driveway, he let loose a dropping that landed right in the center of the windshield.

He used to strike me constantly.

I'd never even consumed alcohol, and he inflicted cracked ribs, damaged kidneys and loosened teeth upon me. To ensure I never became what he was.

Once while sober he mentioned drinking because of how he grew up. He spoke like wanting my empathy, my forgiveness. As if unable to see that my arm was fractured from him protecting me from liquor the week prior. As though blind to himself standing over me crying blood and mucus and tears, mocking. Unable to recall what was so terrible about his childhood, couldn't remember why he needed it for sleeping at night, to stop waking screaming, to stop wetting himself during nightmares.

He made me sick, my father. My breath catches sometimes, and one wrist never healed properly, leaving me half crippled in that hand. I have eleven false teeth. At twenty three, all this damage.

I didn't attend his funeral, though I celebrated it. I didn't consume alcohol though, could never do that. I cry myself to sleep most evenings, can't help screaming if someone approaches suddenly. Lately I've noticed considerable blood appearing when I cough. I won't let him defeat me though, won't give him this small victory.

When my son was born it was the happiest day of my existence. For the first time in my life, someone wanted and needed me. His mother departed soon afterward, saying she didn't want entrapment in a lifestyle she didn't choose (after carrying a child for nine months, she abandons it in three weeks. Never during those nine months did she reject that lifestyle).

Honestly, after she left everything became too overwhelming for me. I left my son with my mother for the evening, and went and had a drink. It was perfect. It was the best I've felt in my entire existence. For several hours, I wasn't scared or self-loathing or on edge. Just calm and okay, I could handle everything a little better. I think I'll probably have a few more now, just to maintain the buzz going. Sobriety now frightens me even more, now that I know there's such an easy alternative, which is so much superior.

When I collected my son in the morning mom looked at me strangely, but I dismissed her. I was in a bit of a rush, I'd heard positive things about whisky, and was eager to try it.

But don't worry, I won't let my son grow up like I did, I'll ensure he knows alcohol is evil. I won't expose him to that pain, to that fear. I'll make certain he hates me for as long as possible as much as possible. He'll associate liquor with me, and I'm bad, so he'll break the cycle. I'm not strong enough, but he will be. I know he'll be powerful enough. I'll make him calloused enough outside, and cold and hard enough inside. He'll be able to overcome it. Like I cannot. I'll teach him through suffering what words never could. Through discipline and harshness he'll learn to resist temptation. My failures will become his lessons, my weakness his strength.
lexical_diversity_up_s.writingprompts::38:
Craig was strolling homeward from the market when he encountered the Almighty. He wasn't anticipating running into the Divine, rational individuals rarely do. Actually, he didn't really ever contemplate the Supreme Being. He didn't accept a Deity's existence, but he also didn't reject enough to ever ponder divinity's nonexistence. Theology and the Creator weren't really subjects he considered important.

A subject he valued deeply was that of those delicious treats. If you don't know, these confections are a rather scrumptious chocolatey biscuit type thing composed of several layers of wafer encased in sweet coating, and Craig was obsessed with them. He may not have been spiritual, but his feelings on these snacks came close. The reason behind his trip to the market was to purchase more of these goodies, and his brain was full of anticipation as he headed back to his dwelling.

He was about two minutes away from his residence, and treat satisfaction when the Lord first addressed him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His snack contemplation interrupted, Craig turned round to see who had called to him. Behind him stood a tall figure in a loose fitting outfit. Craig wasn't really sure of the figure's gender, they were pretty androgynous, looking not dissimilar to Diamond Dogs era David Bowie. They looked familiar to Craig, but he couldn't quite put his finger on where he might have seen them before. He realised he'd been staring, and sought something to say.

"Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," replied the Bowie lookalike. "I'm the Almighty."

"Well good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye." Said Craig before starting back towards his house. He had those chocolate wafers in his bag, and didn't want to be wasting time on a lunatic.

"Wait, don't go yet. Please." Called out the individual. "What would it take for you to accept me?"

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humouring the stranger would probably get him to his treats faster.

"I don't know," said Craig, exasperated. "A miracle or something. Some extraordinary feat which couldn't just be accomplished by any old individual. Something more than just claiming that you're divine."

"Hmm. How about....*this*!" The Supreme Being pointed at a shrub which burst into flames. The blaze shaped itself into a dragon which roared at the two of them. Then, with a snap of fingers, the inferno was extinguished leaving the plant singed but intact. The Creator turned back to Craig with arms spread wide as if to say 'Tada!'

Craig, looking mildly impressed, turned back to face the mysterious person.

"Yeah, that was pretty good. Looked very spectacular. I have to admit I have no idea how you accomplished it. A hologram maybe? It worked for Tupac, so I can see it working for a mythical beast."

The Deity stared at him for a few seconds before responding.

"I did it by being what I am. You requested a supernatural display. I showed you one. What more do you want from me?"

"Don't get me wrong, it's very impressive. But the whole divinity claim probably isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to accept you're a sorcerer."

"But I'm not a damn magician!" Shouted the Lord. "I'm the Eternal One. Why would I claim I'm a spellcaster?"

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in front of him in the international gesture of 'I don't want any trouble, let's all just calm down'.

"Hey relax buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh, but it's just constructive feedback. This is for a television program or internet video right? You're not going to convince anyone with the whole 'Supreme Being' angle."

The Almighty, visibly seething by this point, held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds before letting out an angry sigh and storming off.

Craig watched them depart, then shook his head and returned to his journey. He considered examining the scorched vegetation to see if he could get any clues as to how the illusion had been performed, but decided against it. Whoever had been filming the incident was probably still observing, waiting for Craig to do exactly that. So he pushed it out of his mind, and set off homeward. After all, there were those beloved chocolate-covered wafer biscuits waiting for him.

"Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy?" 

"Get it yourself, Ser Whyte. I'm not your bloody squire no more." 

"Right. Well then, my liege. Would you do me the honor of fetching my wine so I can die drunk and happy?" 

"As you wish, sir-knight." 

"I hate you, Patsy." 

The bedridden husk of a former warrior bellowed a harshly cough. His rusty suit of white armor clinked and clanked as he jerked up violently. Greasy, gray hair shot up in an instant. Sputtering still, he downed the little glass container of burgundy liquid in his hand. The belch was loud as the lightning's thunder, striking down on a rainy evening. 

Besides him, there sat a young man. A little silver crown, chipped and beaten from torn away gemstones, rested upon his short locks of brown. Deep green eyes, far too youthful to experience what it means to rule, gaze down upon the Knight Whyte. His warrior. 

"Tell me." The armored man's limb, weak and weary, placed his container on the bedside. "How is Isabella faring? I haven't been able to receive a letter from you for months." 

"We've shut down the postal service, remember? The courier system handles delivery for packages, but messages go through that fancy tele-ma-gram contraption." 

"Hah. What an era your realm has come to. Bows that spew steel and fire. Scribes who control entire townships. Pretty soon, even my kind will be out of work." 

The monarch chuckled, though it sounded forced and awkward through his lips. He had no need for warriors anymore. Neither did any neighboring realm. They were now just artifacts. Artifacts that talked and drank and fought. No, conflict in this time was determined by how much gold you could carry, how many people you could take, and how many flags you can plant on some hill. 

"What's with that look, sovereign? Has that queen kicked you out of your palace again? You're more than welcome to take some sleep in my fortress here. Just remember to clean the corpses out from their beds." 

"That's a terrible joke, Whyte." 

"So, we're dropping the titles? I don't think we need another repeat of Georgie bringing about another revolution. The guillotines, they were only a little uncomfortable." 

"A little?" 

"A little." 

The precipitation outside appeared to stop, the lightning-storm ceased in its steps. The ruler got up to the windowsill to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time. 

"Hmm. You see that, Whyte?" 

The figure in rusting armor had gotten up out of his mattress, placing his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the youthful sovereign's shoulder. A gust of wind came bellowing through, slapping its cold blanket of winter breeze against the faces of the two men. The ruler's smile flashed warmly at the warrior, who responded in kind. With wet eyes, the younger fellow turned to the armored figure. 

"How ironic. I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this." 

"And you will say good-bye on a snowy evening too." 

"I'm glad to have called you my protector." 

"And you my liege." 

The armored warrior turned back to his deathbed. His legs suddenly shook with a fury, sending him down to the hard wood floor. His sovereign moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised gauntlet, still coppery-red and faded. With a great effort, the dying man made it to his resting place, taking his gauntlets off and throwing them right out the windowsill. 

"I guess it's about time I've gotten rid of those. Too old for me." 

"I've seen older. Take a look at the person who wore them." 

"You always were a cheeky little patsy." Skin falls over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink. "I grow tired. Would you tell me a tale?" 

"What am I, your mother?" 

"Just tell me that tale." 

"That tale. Yes, after all, we only know that one tale." 

"Don't play cute with me, Patsy." 

"Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after?" 

The sovereign sighed, taking a knee on the side of the mattress. The dying warrior smiled, eyelids finally drooping over his vision. Hands clasped over his chest as the beating of the organ grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the freezing air. Through hot tears, the kneeling monarch began speaking. 

"Once upon a time, in a village far, far away..."

The atmosphere feels cool here. Fog rises off the gardens and the climate remains heavy with the perfume of flowers. A shout comes from the tower. Stranger approaching from the south.

There is nothing to the south. Just sand and dust and perhaps, if the barbarians are to be believed, the bones of monsters.

He is a tattered man. Along the march he lost his sandals. The bottom of his feet are bloodied. Rags hang off the bones of his shoulders and hips. He only alive through the grace of the gods.

Before he can be shown to the commander he must be cleaned. Fed and dressed as well. Rewarded - not yet. It is not known if he deserted.

The water almost kills him. He screams like a babe, thrashing in the pool and sobbing for his mother, his father, his commanding officer... He begs for death.

It is not given to him. Soon he is silent. The slaves scrub him until he is clean. His wounds are not grievous. As he is being dressed a sentry mutters that he is not yet a grown soldier. The armor must be stolen.

When food is brought to him, he does not eat. Bread agrees with him though. He is not allowed to gorge himself.

The commanding officer asks about the others. A hundred thousand strong, it had been whispered, a host of the strongest and most loyal. The warriors who feared nothing.

They are all dead. The youth looked stunted. Fear had stolen his nerve and his will, but not his honor.

They had walked thousands of leagues. When they entered a valley the sun and stars were lost to them. There were monstrous things - half humans with sloping torsos and sharp teeth, cats twice the size of a horse made of fire and smoke, beasts with snakes for noses and tusks like a boar that roared like a thousand trumpets.

Deeper they must have walked. The jungle must have been Pluto's garden. Everything brought death.

They did not have a hundred thousand warriors, only five thousand. By the time they found it - the thing of nightmares, the titan's aborted fetus - they numbered in the hundreds.

It came at night, drawn by the fires.

It was here the youth stopped. He trembled. His teeth ground so hard they might have broken in his mouth. But he had honor, and spoke of what he had seen.

It must have been drawn by the flames. Maybe it remembered the hell it had come from, or in the blaze it saw strength.

The appearance was sudden. It fell near the campfire, stirring it up and sending sparks into the atmosphere. It had small claws and was armored like a fish. It was not large. The youth gestured to his waist. He was missing half his hand. About the size of war dog. It had wings like a bat.

It drank the fire. The gods gave it power and it rose up and slaughtered a hundred the first night.

The host fled through the hell garden. Some were felled by the plants, the creatures. One soldier awoke screaming in the darkness. Insects had eaten away at his flesh. They swarmed through his mouth and nose and the sockets of his eyes.

After that no one slept.

Was that how the youth lost his hand? No. That was on the fifth day.

The soldiers had begun to go mad. Every tree was the same. Every rock and puddle and patch of dirt.

They came to a cliff. They must climb it, someone said. So they did.

The youth was quick. Some soldiers were quicker and stood along the top of the world and helped the others up. When the youth pulled himself over he saw the piles of bodies and called below. This is death above, wearing the face of their brothers. One of the soldiers tried to kill him. Instead he lost half of his hand to a rock. It was crushed and mangled. The youth hauled himself up and scrambled away.

He left the soldiers and headed north. The host was scattered. The youth walked north. He could see the sky again. His hand felt tight and hot. His fingers turned white, then red. On the fifth day he gnawed them off.

The seventh he lost one sandal. He threw the other away, and in a fit of madness stripped off his clothes. The forest became thinner. He was burnt by the sun. There was no water, no nourishment. Once he saw a golden eagle and followed it. But there was no eagle. On the ninth day he found a person hung from a tree.

The youth stripped the body of clothes and dressed himself in the dead.

As he walked north his hand leaked blood and his feet cramped and trembled. One night he built a campfire. It started a great fear in him. He was brave enough to put his hand inside and stop the rot from spreading. Afterwards he crawled away and cried until the sun rose again.

As he walked he left the grasslands. He wanted to see water. He wanted to die.

On the tenth day he saw the beast again. Or it may have been a different one. It had the body of canine, upright. It had long claws and chattered like a bird. It was the size of a person's leg, from the ground to his knee. There was a flock of them. They called to each other. The youth followed them.

The creatures took down a beast - the one with a snake for a nose. It had leather for skin and wailed as it died. After the canine-creatures left the youth ate what he could.

The youth stopped there. What else? There was nothing else. He had come to the sand and walked. His voice was quiet. Tired. His body told the toll his voice could not.

Could he die now? No. Not yet. More would want to hear of this.

The subway halted abruptly. Laurentius awoke with a gasp. He struggled to comprehend his surroundings: It was frigid, that was certain. He examined his armour: His hands were covered with gloves that appeared to be made of cow hide. His boots were black, fur-lined and warm. Underneath a thick ebony coat was a soft white shirt, with clasps holding it together in the front. A red strip of fabric reached around his neck and descended to just past his stomach. "*What is this, *" he thought. "*Is that how I perished? Do we wear tokens of our demise? *" His eyes met those of a rotund darker-skinned woman, who was reading a curious layered-parchment device on her lap. He looked around her throat: a cross. He gazed at her sympathetically. "*I suppose so. *" 

Tubes of light illuminated the metal chamber he occupied. A smooth ding announced itself, and the doors closed shut. To Laurentius' surprise, the metallic enclosure began to move again. He stood, and made his way to a man he assumed was in charge. The fellow, covered in what seemed to be traditional dress for the era, with the exception of a large silver wig, and glasses that read "2015" across the front. 

"*Salve*," Laurentius began. 

The gentleman returned a confused look, then resumed gazing out the window. He smelled of wine. 

"*Aut ubi sum? Quis hic locus? *" 

The metallic enclosure shook once again, slightly, disrupting Laurentius' balance. A voice rang out over the loudspeaker, but Laurentius couldn't make out what it had announced. The vehicle made another stop, but Laurentius wasn't prepared. He fell onto the floor below as a wave of people exited. He got up and followed the crowd, which weaved through tunnels. He struggled to absorb everything around him: Musicians lined the enclosed street. Few vendors, from what he understood. He continued until he reached a flight of stairs. He ascended, and was astounded by what he witnessed. 

Bright lights flashed around him, in all directions. What had been the steady hum of voices, interrupted occasionally by an outburst, had now turned into an onslaught of sound and action. To his left and right, the streets were lined with pedestrians all moving towards a central location, where a large spire reached into the heavens. Atop this tower was a sphere. He peered into the sky. 

No stars? 

No stars. He pondered. Suddenly, a realization came to him, and with it, a wave of happiness and relief. There were no celestial bodies, for he was above them all: Might these be the plains of Asphodel? They were more beautiful than he'd ever imagined. 

Suddenly, a fellow in a similar outfit – an ebony coat, dark pants, pale shirt – ran up to him. Black metal covered his eyes, and frost came out of his mouth when he spoke. 

"Dick!" he exclaimed, grabbing Laurentius by the arm. So overwhelmed, Laurentius had no expectation of arguing. He followed this stranger. 

"Dick, where have you been? We've been searching all over – the audience's waiting, and they ain't happy. Kathy's been doing what she can, but..." 

Laurentius paused. Clearly, he must learn the language of the afterlife. He noticed some of the throng had begun to direct their attention towards him. He returned the same greeting he received. 

"Dick," he uttered, nodding his head at the passers-by as he was carried off by the stranger he had encountered. 

"Dick," he repeated once more, this time at a young girl. Her ears were covered immediately by her mother, who left a scathing glare in her wake. 

A few minutes of navigating the bustling streets passed, and Laurentius passed by other similarly-dressed gentlemen who padded him down. After greeting both formally, he was ushered up steep metallic stairs, and onto a platform which overlooked the massive throng below. The stage held a lady, red-haired, who was holding a microphone. "Dick!" she exclaimed, "Where have you been? We're on in 2." 

"Dick," Laurentius smiled. 

"Well, you know what I like." 

Someone handed Laurentius a plastic cord with a bud on the end. He observed the lady, who had it placed in her ear, and did the same. Perhaps this was part of the welcoming ceremony. 

He heard the redhead speak with the operator behind a larger metallic contraption, one with a folded glass mirror in the centre. 

"Live in 30." 

"Alright. You ready?" she inquired, staring directly at Laurentius. He nodded. She handed him another metallic stick with fur at the end, much like the one she was grasping. She stared into the apparatus. Her lips formed a grin, and Laurentius couldn't help but beam himself. 

A small crimson light went on in the corner of the metal-glass apparatus. There was a brief pause. The redhead nudged Laurentius expectantly. 

Laurentius beamed and inhaled deeply. "Dick," he proclaimed, and regarded expectantly once again the redhead to his right.

*** 
The Author 
*** 

I can't shake this sensation. You know, that feeling creeping along your spine waiting to take up residence in the base of your skull like some kind of parasite. It's an indeterminable awareness you're being watched. I cannot dismiss it. I am sure I understand what this is, but I'm not ready to admit my comprehension. The... *writer* let's call him. He is observing, waiting, constructing. Even as I think these thoughts, he is scratching them down in his chicken-scratch scrawl, touching the pen against his teeth in contemplation. I can sense it; I can see it in my mind's eye. He's trying to figure out how to kill me. 

I suppose this is my own fault. See I kept asking, I needed to comprehend. I had to find out if there was some directing hand to existence. If mankind had a purpose, a reason, I needed to appreciate what goal we worked toward. There's a moment, one of particular realization, which caught me and held fast. Like my apprehension regarding an observer; only, this emotion was deeper, more primal. I *knew*, I mean really *understood*; all of it is a narrative. Existence is a story. Which inevitably led me to the conclusion -- there needs to be an architect, an *author*. 

The car narrowly missed me. I had an inkling of pressure against my chest verging on the edge of panic. I didn't cross when the green man displayed on the crossing signal, instead I took a step back. My *spidey-sense* tingled. The taxi-cab driver never saw me, I hadn't seen him either. His drunken sprawling vehicle slammed into the same traffic signal post I had been, until recently, standing by. Can I tell you how fucked up that is, I have this realization, followed by a sudden wave of fear. If I hadn't heeded my gutless compulsion, I might have been splattered between the cabbie's automobile and the hard place which was the traffic pole. I turned my gaze upward, burning eyes and clenching jaw notwithstanding, and decried whoever worked at compiling this tale. 

"What the actual fuck was that?" I said. 

Okay, so I realize my choice of words probably did not fall into the definition of circumspect, but hell we're talking about some kind of god-figure deciding on my time to perish. 

*Are you sure?* My logical brain asked. 

I pondered my position, both in the physical and meta-physical sense. 

*Yeah, I'm fucking certain,* I replied to myself internally. *How else do you explain the sudden epiphany and subsequently my almost immediate demise. There's a* writer *and he doesn't want to be discovered.* 

I'm not sure how I knew the *scribe* didn't want to be revealed, or the fact he was male, but I figured it was something in my general make-up granting me the knowledge. Oh don't get all high and mighty and preach at me now, I'm not talking religion or spirituality, I want to live damnit. I stood, still staring up at the heavens, trying to impart my utter disgust and frustration when the pole creaked, unnaturally so. I adjusted my head so my vision was level with the metal. 

The steel appeared warped, and I realized that the vehicle had burst into flames. 

*When had that happened?* I thought. *Nevermind, run stupid.* 

My internal dialog is not always the most kind; I'm a blunt sort. So, I ran. What I was running from, if Mr. Omniscient *creator* was already in my head, he could follow me anywhere. Hell, I could have an inopportune flashback, and he could hit me with a mack truck. If this *narrator* decided I was going to perish, why didn't he do it already? 

*Fuck me,* I thought. *It's about the drama; the plot.* 

"Sick fuck," I said. I knew he'd hear me, or he'd inscribe that in his juvenile scrawl, knowing I intended it for him. 

*What if I stop?* 

I looked up again, and said, "What are you going to do with a character who won't cooperate, huh?" 

Naturally, he didn't respond. It wasn't like I expected a voice from the heavens, but I figured he might strike me down with lightning or something, I mean he potentially it's within his ability, right? He might decide my awareness of the scheme labeled me as a liability. 

*What the hell is the scheme anyway?* 

I don't know, I guess the design is for me to expire. Perhaps, he's not into the mundane. Maybe, just maybe, he wants my ending to be something significant, something of a show. I bet that's it. I got the sensation again; a gut punch to my stomach making my insides roil like they were leaking to the outside, and the rumbling in my belly suggested I take a step back. I did. Something pierced the flesh in my back. It was a fluid, smooth motion that parted the tissue. I felt the warm blood mixing with my sweat as it soaked the back of my flannel shirt. 

A quiet voice whispered in my ear. "Hello protagonist," she said. "I'm your antagonist, the *writer* says hello." 

That was all she uttered. She didn't have a scent, like you would expect. She was a ghost from the shadows. I don't know who she was, or why her specifically, but she'd made it clear... I was right. Take that fucker. I didn't have the strength to say it aloud, but I know he heard me. The confirmation settled over me like a shroud, heavy and undeniable. My suspicions had been validated, my paranoia justified, my instincts proven accurate. Everything I had feared was true.

If I don't return. Dan. Love always.

lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::1: Nutritional supplements may improve development of infants born small (preterm or small for gestational age [SGA]) but may increase the risk of later metabolic disease. We conducted a review and analysis to assess the effects of macronutrient supplements for infants born small on later development and metabolism. We searched OvidMedline, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Cochrane Database of Reviews from inception to April 1, 2019, and controlled-trials.com, clinicaltrials.gov, and anzctr.org.au. Trials were included if the intention was to increase macronutrient intake to improve development of infants born small and assessed outcomes. Outcomes were cognitive impairment and metabolic risk, evaluated in toddlers (<3 years), childhood (3 to 8 years), and adolescence (9 to 18 years). Two reviewers extracted data. Quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and data were pooled using random-effect models. Twenty-one trials and one trial of variable quality involving 3,680 infants were included. In toddlers born small, supplementation did not alter cognitive impairment (relative risk [RR] 1.00; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.49; P = 0.99), and there were no differences in cognitive outcomes (mean difference [MD] 0.57; 95% CI -0.71 to 1.84; P = 0.38) or motor outcomes (MD 1.16; 95% CI -0.32 to 2.65; P = 0.12) between supplemented groups and unsupplemented groups. However, fewer supplemented toddlers had motor impairment (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; P = 0.01). In analyses, supplementation improved cognitive outcomes in boys (MD 5.60; 95% CI 1.07 to 10.14; P = 0.02), but not girls born small (MD -2.04; 95% CI -7.04 to 2.95; P = 0.42), and did not alter cognitive outcomes or motor outcomes in the subgroup of infants born SGA. In childhood, there was no difference in cognitive impairment (RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.26 to 2.57; P = 0.72) or cognitive outcomes (MD 1.02; 95% CI -1.91 to 3.95; P = 0.50) between supplemented groups and unsupplemented groups. There were also no differences in blood pressure, triglyceride, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) concentrations (all P > 0.05). However, supplemented groups had lower fasting glucose (mmol/L: MD -0.20; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.06; P = 0.005) and higher high-density lipoprotein (HDL) concentrations (mmol/L: MD 0.11; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19; P = 0.02). In analyses, there was no evidence of differences in blood pressure between supplemented groups and unsupplemented groups in boys or girls born small, or in SGA infants. In adolescence, there was no difference between supplemented groups and unsupplemented groups in blood pressure, triglycerides, LDL concentrations and HDL concentrations, fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance, and fasting insulin concentrations (all P > 0.05). Limitations include considerable heterogeneity, low to very low quality of the evidence, and limited data beyond early childhood. In this review and analysis of trials, we found no evidence that early macronutrient supplementation for infants born small altered later cognitive outcomes, although there was some evidence that supplementation may decrease motor impairment in toddlers. Contrary to the findings from studies, evidence from trials suggests that early macronutrient supplementation for infants born small improves some metabolic outcomes in childhood. CRD42019127858.
lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::2: Objectives Recently, two point-of-care (PoC) feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) antibody test kits (Witness and Anigen Rapid) were reported as being able to differentiate FIV-vaccinated cats from FIV-infected cats at a single time point, irrespective of the gap between testing and last vaccination (0-7 years). The aim of the study was to investigate systematically anti-FIV antibody production over time in response to the recommended primary FIV vaccination series. Methods First, residual plasma from the original study was tested using a laboratory-based ELISA to determine whether negative results with PoC testing were due to reduced antibodies as opposed to absent antibodies to gp40. Second, a prospective study was performed using immunologically naive client-owned kittens and cats given a primary FIV vaccination series using a commercially available inactivated whole cell/inactivated whole virus vaccine (Fel-O-Vax FIV, three subcutaneous injections at 4 week intervals) and tested systematically (up to 11 times) over 6 months, using four commercially available PoC FIV antibody kits (SNAP FIV/FeLV Combo [detects antibodies to p15/p24], Witness FeLV/FIV [gp40], Anigen Rapid FIV/FeLV [p24/gp40] and VetScan FeLV/FIV Rapid [p24]). Results The laboratory-based ELISA showed cats from the original study vaccinated within the previous 0-15 months had detectable antibodies to gp40, despite testing negative with two kits that use gp40 as a capture antigen (Witness and Anigen Rapid kits). The prospective study showed that antibody testing with SNAP Combo and VetScan Rapid was positive in all cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination, and remained positive for the study duration (12/12 and 10/12 cats positive, respectively). Antibody testing with Witness and Anigen Rapid was also positive in a high proportion of cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination (8/12 and 7/12, respectively), but antibody levels declined below the detection level in most cats (10/12) by 1 month after the third (final) primary FIV vaccination. Consequently, Witness and Anigen Rapid antibody test kits can be used reliably to determine FIV infection status at the time of annual booster FIV vaccination to help detect 'vaccine breakthroughs' and in cats that have not received a primary FIV vaccination course within the preceding 6 months. The antibody response duration following annual booster FIV vaccination and the resulting effect on antibody testing using PoC kits needs to be determined by further study research investigation. The mechanism(s) for the variation in FIV antibody test kit performance remains unclear and requires additional study investigation research to determine the underlying causes of these testing differences.
lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::3: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare monogenic disorder characterized by benign tumors in multiple organs as well as a high prevalence of epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism. TSC is caused by inactivating mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Heterozygocity induces hyperactivation of mTOR which can be inhibited by mTOR inhibitors, such as rapamycin, which have proven efficacy in the treatment of TSC-associated symptoms. The aim of the present study was (1) to identify molecular changes associated with social and cognitive deficits in the brain tissue of Tsc1 +/- mice and (2) to investigate the molecular effects of rapamycin treatment, which has been shown to ameliorate genotype-related behavioural deficits. Molecular changes in the frontal cortex and hippocampus of Tsc1 +/- and control mice, with or without rapamycin treatment, were investigated. A quantitative mass spectrometry-based shotgun proteomic approach (LC-MS E ) was employed as an unbiased method to detect changes in protein levels. Changes identified in the initial profiling stage were validated using selected reaction monitoring (SRM). Protein Set Enrichment Analysis was employed to identify dysregulated pathways. LC-MS E analysis of Tsc1 +/- mice and controls ( n = 30) identified 51 proteins changed in frontal cortex and 108 in the hippocampus. Bioinformatic analysis combined with targeted proteomic validation revealed several dysregulated molecular pathways. Using targeted assays, proteomic changes in the hippocampus validated the pathways "myelination", "dendrite," and "oxidative stress", an upregulation of ribosomal proteins and the mTOR kinase. LC-MS E analysis was also employed on Tsc1 +/- and wildtype mice ( n = 34) treated with rapamycin or vehicle. Rapamycin treatment exerted a stronger proteomic effect in Tsc1 +/- mice with significant changes (mainly decreased expression) in 231 and 106 proteins, respectively. The cellular pathways "oxidative stress" and "apoptosis" were found to be affected in Tsc1 +/- mice and the cellular compartments "myelin sheet" and "neurofilaments" were affected by rapamycin treatment. Thirty-three proteins which were changed in Tsc1 +/- mice were normalized following rapamycin treatment, amongst them oxidative stress related proteins, myelin-specific and ribosomal proteins. Molecular changes in the Tsc1 +/- mouse brain were more prominent in the hippocampus compared to the frontal cortex. Pathways linked to myelination and oxidative stress response were prominently affected and, at least in part, normalized following rapamycin treatment. The results could aid in the identification of novel drug targets for the treatment of cognitive, social and psychiatric symptoms in autism spectrum disorders. Similar pathways have also been implicated in other psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders and could imply similar disease processes. Thus, the potential efficacy of mTOR inhibitors warrants further investigation not only for autism spectrum disorders but also for other neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders and diseases. The molecular changes and pathways affected by rapamycin treatment in Tsc1 +/- mice suggest that mTOR inhibitors could potentially treat molecular changes in multiple disorders.
lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::4: Silica nanoparticles (nanoSiO 2 ) are nanoparticles that can deliver biologically active compounds to cardiac tissues such as cardiac heart tissues in a controllable manner. However, cardiac toxicity induced by nanoSiO 2 has been recently related to abnormal calcium handling and energetic failure in cardiac cardiomyocytes. Moreover, the mechanisms underlying this energetic failure remain unclear. In order to elucidate these mechanisms, this article explores the ex vivo cardiac heart function and cardiac mitochondria after exposure to nanoSiO 2 . The cumulative administration of nanoSiO 2 reduced the mechanical performance of the cardiac heart with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) of 93 μg/mL, affecting the cardiac relaxation. In isolated cardiac mitochondria nanoSiO 2 was found to be internalized, inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation and significantly reducing the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m ). The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) was also induced with an increasing dose of nanoSiO 2 and partially recovered with, a potent blocker of the mPTP, Cyclosporine A (CsA). The activity of aconitase and thiol oxidation, in the adenine nucleotide translocase, were found to be reduced due to nanoSiO 2 exposure, suggesting that nanoSiO 2 induces the mPTP via thiol modification and ROS generation. In cardiac cells exposed to nanoSiO 2 , enhanced viability and reduction of H 2 O 2 were observed after application of a mitochondrial antioxidant, MitoTEMPO. Concomitantly, CsA treatment in adult cardiac cells reduced the nanoSiO 2 -triggered cardiac cell death and recovered ATP production (from 32.4 to 65.4%). Additionally, we performed evaluation of the mitochondrial effect of nanoSiO 2 in human cardiac cardiomyocytes. We observed a 40% inhibition of maximal oxygen consumption in cardiac mitochondria at 500 μg/mL. Under this condition we identified a remarkable diminution in the spare respiratory capacity. This capacity indicates that a reduction in the amount of extra ATP that can be produced by cardiac mitochondria during a sudden increase in cardiac energy demand. In human cardiac cardiomyocytes, increased LDH release and necrosis were found at increased doses of nanoSiO 2 , reaching 85 and 48%, respectively. Such effects were partially prevented by the application of CsA. Therefore, exposure to nanoSiO 2 affects cardiac heart function via mitochondrial dysfunction through the opening of the mPTP. The effects can be partially avoided reducing ROS or retarding the opening of the mPTP. These strategies which resulted in cardioprotection could be considered as therapies to decrease the cardiac effects of nanoSiO 2 exposure.
lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::5: Return to play (RTP) of National Football League (NFL) athletes after isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears has been reported. However, no reports have reported on RTP of NFL athletes after multiligament knee injuries. NFL athletes with multiligament knee injuries have lower RTP rates and longer RTP recoveries than athletes with isolated ACL tears. Second, athletes with ACL and medial collateral ligament (MCL) injuries will have higher RTP rates and shorter RTP time than athletes with an ACL tear and posterolateral corner injuries. Retrospective study. Level 4. Publicly available NFL injury reports were reviewed for all multiligament knee injuries incurred between 2000 and 2016 with RTP reports. Athletes were excluded if RTP was limited for reasons unrelated to the injury. Extracted reports included type of injury, RTP, RTP time (days), number and percentage of plays played, and play performance. Mean RTP time for all 50 athletes was 388.71 ± 198.52 days. The mean RTP time for athletes with ACL/MCL injuries was 305.1 ± 58.9 days, compared with 459.2 ± 245.1 days ( P = 0.004) and 609.3 ± 183.1 days ( P < 0.0001) for athletes with combined ACL and PCL/LCL injuries and frank knee injuries, respectively. lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::6: Pulmonary pressure in response to exercise is a marker of the pressure severity of mitral stenosis (MS). However, the factors related to elevated pulmonary pressure with exercise are not well defined. The aim of this study was to assess the factors associated with the pulmonary pressure response to exercise in patients with pure rheumatic MS. An additional aim was to determine the impact of exercise-induced pulmonary pressure on outcome. One hundred thirty patients with MS (94% women; mean age, 45 ± 11 years) underwent exercise testing. A range of parameters were obtained at rest and at peak exercise. Exercise was performed in the supine position. The primary end point was mitral valve intervention, either percutaneous or surgical. Increases in mean mitral gradient, right ventricular function, left atrial volume, and net atrioventricular compliance were independently associated with SPAP at peak exercise, after adjusting for changes in rate. By analysis adjusted for age and sex, SPAP achieved at peak exercise was an important predictor of adverse outcome (adjusted ratio, 1.025; 95% CI, 1.010-1.040; P = .001). New York Heart Association functional class (adjusted ratio, 2.459; 95% CI, 1.509-4.006; P < .001) and the interaction between valve area and net atrioventricular compliance (P = .001) were also significant predictors of adverse events. The pulmonary pressure response to exercise reflects multiple factors and provides important prognostic information for patients with mitral stenosis beyond resting pressure measurements alone.
lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::7: The impact of chronic liver disease on outcomes in patients with COVID-19 is uncertain. Hence, we aimed to explore this association. We explored the outcomes of all adult inpatients with COVID-19 in France, in 2020. We computed adjusted odds ratios to measure the associations between chronic liver disease, alcohol use disorders, mechanical ventilation and day-30 in-hospital mortality. The sample comprised 259,110 patients (median [IQR] age 70 (54-83) years; 52% men), including 15,476 (6.0%) and 10,006 (3.9%) patients with chronic liver disease and alcohol use disorders, respectively. We explored the outcomes, including mechanical ventilation and day-30 mortality, of all adult patients with COVID-19 in France in 2020 (N = 259,110). Patients with mild liver disease; compensated cirrhosis; liver transplantation; or immunodeficiency were not at increased mortality from COVID-19. Patients with alcohol use disorders, decompensated cirrhosis, or primary liver cancer were at increased mortality from COVID-19 but were less likely to receive mechanical ventilation. Our outcomes suggest that therapeutic effort limitation may have contributed to the increased mortality in French patients with liver disease or alcohol use disorders.
lexical_diversity_down_s.academic_abstracts::8: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has caused a significant number of mortalities worldwide. COVID-19 causes a serious threat to human life. The clinical manifestations of COVID-19 are diverse manifestations and severe manifestations and 20% of infected patients are reported to be in a critical condition. A loss in lung function and pulmonary fibrosis are the main manifestations of patients with the severe form of the disease. The lung function is affected, even after recovery, thereby greatly affecting the psychology and well-being of patients, and significantly affecting their quality of life.
