words_common_s.xsum::7: Zack Hider, from Portsmouth, was born with a heart problem he had from birth. A "mistake" was made during the heart operation at Southampton General Hospital on 11 November last year, the inquest in Winchester was told. Zack's parents said they did not blame any individual but hoped lessons were learned to prevent similar mistakes. Recording a story-like verdict, coroner Graham Short said pressure from the too-large dose of the heart-stopping liquid had been the main cause of death. Moments after the mixture of blood and chemicals was put in, Zack's heart turned "stiff" and looked "bruised", surgeon Michael Kaarme told the inquest. "I didn't know what was happening," he said, adding, "I didn't have any experience like this." The man operating the machinery that controlled the liquid, perfusionist Richard Hartshorne, did not appear in court. In a statement, he said it had not been made clear a procedure requiring the heart to be stopped was being carried out, until part way through the operation. An inquiry found Zack had been given a dose of the liquid for a much larger child, like the previous patient in the theatre. Mr Short said: "The amount was not changed before delivery for reasons that I've not been able to fully work out." He said even when the operation was stopped, Zack's heart could not be started and he died in hospital nine days later. "By that time, the damage had been done," he said. In a statement, Zack's parents, Gary and Sarah Hider, said they "did not blame any individual but only hope lessons are learned to make sure similar mistakes are not made in future." Neil Pearce, associate medical director for patient safety at University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, said: "We accept full responsibility for the incident and have said sorry without holding back for it. "The error made was very rare and led to a serious reaction in Zack's heart muscle which took away his chance of surviving the difficult surgery he was due to undergo." He said an "immediate investigation" had led to the bringing in of a number of "important new safety measures" which he added had later been shared with all children's heart centres in the UK "to try to remove the risk of a similar incident occurring again".
words_common_s.xsum::8: Pauline Carmichael, 61, was found dead on the shores of Lough Neagh in February 2015. The mother of seven had died from drowning. Alan Norman Foster, of Hillside in Antrim, said he was guilty of her murder. Foster carried Ms Carmichael over his shoulder while she was still in her nightclothes, and threw her off a bridge with a 40ft drop. Speaking outside court, Ms Carmichael's daughter told people that her mother had a fear of water and would have been "very frightened" in the moments leading up to her death. Noreen Brown said: "We feel justice has not been done today. It should be a life for a life. "Her biggest fear was of water - anyone who knew her knew that. She would have been very frightened on that bridge, knowing the river was below," she said. Ms Brown and her sister, Jeanette Hall, said Ms Carmichael was a loving mother and grandmother, but was also a "lost soul" because of her need for alcohol. Ms Hall spoke well of both the police and the Public Prosecution Service, but said she felt the punishment given to Foster was not enough. "The things we have had to listen to about what she went through has hurt us as a family. We have never hidden the fact she had a drinking problem, but even with this fact, she was a good and loving person." Belfast Crown Court heard Foster was angry because Ms Carmichael, from Ballyclare in County Antrim, called police to remove him from the flat, where he was "having a party with two females". She was heard by a neighbour screaming: "At least let me get my other shoe." Foster told people Ms Carmichael had gone to Ballyclare with her dog. He was first arrested because they thought he had taken her before being arrested for murder once her body was found. A body check after death showed Ms Carmichael drowned and had also broken a bone in her throat as well as broken many ribs. The court had earlier heard Foster was dealing with "the ticking time bomb of post traumatic stress disorder" after serving with the Royal Irish Rangers in Bosnia, Iraq and Northern Ireland. It was heard he had seen "horrible scenes of killing" while on active duty. But a lawyer working against him said: "He knew exactly what he was doing, he went through with it and then tried to cover up what he had done." Foster said he was guilty of murder last month, after the group of people for his trial had been sworn in, but before the trial began. A judge said the way the murder happened was "especially cruel" and called it a "evil act". He said Foster had murdered a woman who was "hurt, small and drunk". He added: "She ended up in a moving river where she drowned and was washed away." The judge said he had thought about Foster's feeling sorry and his guilty answer. Foster had already been given a life sentence, but Wednesday's hearing decided that he would spend at least nine years in prison before being thought about for early release, if ever.
words_common_s.xsum::9: Nadia Eweida took her case to the ECHR after BA made her stop wearing her white gold cross where people could see it. The court said BA had not struck a fair balance between Ms Eweida's religious beliefs and the company's wish to "project a certain company image". It ruled the rights of three others had not been broken by their employers. But they said Ms Eweida's rights had been broken under Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The four Christians had brought cases against the UK government for not protecting their rights but ministers, who fought against the claims, argued that the rights of the employees were only protected in private. By Robert Pigott Religious matters writer, BBC News Although Nadia Eweida's victory shows that Christians can see wearing a cross at work as part of behaving in line with their religion, the court's decision was based on special conditions - including the fact that a quiet cross would not have badly affected British Airways' public image. It's perhaps more important that Shirley Chaplin's case was dismissed, along with those of Gary McFarlane and Lillian Ladele. Today's judgement sets the legal seal on years in which traditional Christians have tried, and failed, to defend their values against non-religious ones in British courts. The message coming from Strasbourg is that although people are allowed to hold religious views, that right is badly limited in the workplace when it comes into fight with the rights of other people. The judgement also hands large freedom to employers to set reasonable policies and then demand that employees follow them whatever their religious beliefs. Ms Eweida, 60, a Coptic Christian from Twickenham in south-west London, told the BBC she was "jumping with joy" after the ruling, adding it had "not been an easy ride". British Airways said its uniform policy was changed in 2007 to allow Miss Eweida and others to "wear symbols of faith" and that she and other employees had been working under these arrangements for the last six years. It said Ms Eweida did not attend work for a period of time in 2006 while an internal appeal was held into her refusal to remove her cross but she remained a British Airways employee. The British government was ordered to pay Ms Eweida 2,000 euros (£1,600) in damages and 30,000 euros (£25,000) costs. A court decision was held up by the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court in the UK before she took her case to the ECHR. Prime Minister David Cameron said he was "delighted" that the "idea of wearing religious symbols at work has been held up", adding that people "shouldn't suffer unfair treatment due to religious beliefs". The other cases involved nurse Shirley Chaplin, 57, whose employer also stopped her wearing necklaces with a cross, Gary McFarlane, 51, a marriage helper fired after saying he might object to giving sex therapy advice to gay couples, and registrar Lillian Ladele who was punished after she refused to hold same-sex civil partnership ceremonies. The four had made individual requests to the ECHR after losing separate job courts but their cases were heard together. They argued their employers' actions went against articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protected their rights to "freedom of thought, conscience and religion" and stopped religious unfair treatment. Ms Ladele was punished by Islington Council, in north London, after saying she did not want to hold same-sex civil partnership ceremonies. Her lawyers said the service could have been done by other employees who were prepared to carry them out. ECHR judges said the council's action was right as it was required to consider the rights of same-sex couples. Mike Judge, of the Christian Institute, which backed Ms Ladele's case, said: "What this case shows is that Christians with traditional beliefs about marriage are at risk of being left out in the cold." Mr McFarlane, a Bristol relationship helper, worked for the Avon branch of national charity Relate but was fired for very bad behaviour in 2008 after saying on a training course he might have an objection to talking about sexual problems with gay couples. The court said clients of the service where he was employed could not be given out in line with their sexual direction. Source: BBC Religion and Ethics Why is the cross important to Christians? Mr McFarlane told the BBC that the decision in his case was "a sad judgment" for all faiths, not just Christians. Ms Chaplin, from Exeter, was moved to a desk job by Royal Devon and Exeter NHS Trust Hospital for failing to remove a confirmation cross on a small chain, which she had worn to work for 30 years. The court said the decision was needed to protect the health and safety of nurses and patients. She said she thought British Christians would be "destroyed" by the ruling. The three plan to ask for their cases to go to appeal to the Grand Chamber of the ECHR. Job lawyers at firm Slater and Gordon said the decision did not change the situation that treating someone badly purely because of their religion was against UK law. They said it also showed that company image did not beat a person's right to reasonable showing of their religious belief. Communities Secretary Eric Pickles and the Equalities Minister Maria Miller both welcomed the ruling. Keith Porteous-Wood, of the National Secular Society, said: "Religious people who feel parts of their job go against their conscience can always find work that better matches their needs. That is true religious freedom." Shami Chakrabarti, director of human rights group Liberty, said the judgment was "an excellent result for equal treatment, religious freedom and common sense". The Archbishop of York, Dr John Sentamu, said the Equality Act "pushes employers to welcome variety - including people of faith".
words_common_s.xsum::10: General Sir Richard Shirreff told The Times that politicians were "scared of any form of action" ahead of next year's general election. This comes as RAF Tornado jets are to be sent for possible use in a northern Iraq aid operation, as thousands of people run away from Islamist fighters. The government said on Monday the jets would leave within the next 48 hours. General Shirreff, who was the UK's most senior officer at Nato HQ until last March, said the UK government had "politicians who want to show off" but "do not have any stick". "What we have got is this commitment-scared government that is frightened of being seen to be putting boots on the ground at a time when they are trying to pull out from everything," he said. The general also said: "The longer we sit on our hands and delay, the more dangerous the situation is going to become. "These things don't go away. We have got a situation. There is no way round it. You have just got to go through it and sort it out." Prime Minister David Cameron has fought back pressure to recall Parliament to talk about a UK military role in the Iraq crisis. Islamic State (IS) fighters have made big gains in northern Iraq in recent months, forcing tens of thousands of people from religious minorities to leave their homes. The UK's Tornado jets are set to take off from RAF Marham in Norfolk, and could carry out watching to help delivery of aid supplies. On Sunday an attempt to deliver aid was called off when the RAF crew decided that the supplies could have hurt people below. "If you are going to do anything, if you are serious about stopping a human disaster, you have got to do it properly," said General Shirreff, who said he believed soldiers should be on the ground helping to deliver the aid to the right places. The UK government has said it will work with Iraqi, Kurdish and international people in the area "to reduce safety concerns". It also said it would look at how it could play a role in getting equipment to Kurdish forces so they were better able to fight back against IS fighters. US forces have carried out four rounds of air strikes aimed at IS militants near Irbil, the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan. The US has also begun giving weapons to the Kurdish Peshmergas, who are fighting the militants, senior US officials told the Associated Press.
words_common_s.xsum::11: A US appeals court on Tuesday granted a new hearing for Kris Maharaj, 78, who has been in jail for more than 30 years for a 1986 double murder in Miami. The ruling means that Maharaj's lawyers will be able to present new evidence which they say proves the two men were killed by members of a drug gang. His lawyer claims a Colombian killer killed Derrick and Duane Moo Young. Maharaj's lawyer, Clive Stafford Smith from human-rights group Reprieve, praised the decision, saying "it is a great day for Kris, and I hope now we will finally get him the justice he has long been denied". But a spokesman for the Miami-Dade State Attorney's office, Ed Griffith, told BBC News: "We stand by the outcome of the very long and fair hearing that Maharaj received in the state court, where the judge found these witnesses and claims to not be believable or have any value." The defence team plans to present new evidence from six gang members to argue that the two men, who were business partners of Maharaj, were killed after members of Pablo Escobar's Medellin drugs gang caught them stealing cleaned drug money. The new ruling from the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta says "new evidence" would show that Maharaj could not have been found guilty of the Moo Young murders "beyond a reasonable doubt". The judgment adds that the statements by the witnesses, which include Escobar's preferred hit man John Jairo "Popeye" Velasque, "separately support one another". They will also present evidence that one hotel guest on the night of the murders, Jaime Vallejo Mejia, was a member of the drug gang. The former businessman, who has been in poor health, had been on death row for 15 years but had his sentence changed to life in prison in 2002.
words_common_s.xsum::12: It comes after a two-year-old girl was left for dead after being run over by a van - and then ignored by 18 people walking by. She is right now in hospital fighting for her life. The law might never be put into place - but even talking about such a rule shows the level of anger created in China by this case. The effects from this incident, which happened in the city of Foshan in southern Guangdong Province, continue. Provincial groups from the ruling Communist Party, government departments and groups are talking about a new law. This could make it against the law for people to ignore those in need of help. "Many laws, including stopping drunk driving, in China have been passed after well-known individual cases," said lawyer Zhu Yongping, according to a report in the English-language China Daily. Other media outlets report that the introduction of a law will be talked about at a meeting of lawyers next month. First online polls, though, suggest most people are against it. "Talk about being civilised first. Is anyone paying attention to that?" read one posting. Groups in Guangdong are also looking at other ways to get people to act with caring when faced with an emergency. The provincial government's political and legal affairs committee is using its small-blog site to gather opinions about how to "guide brave acts for just causes" and support "socialist morals". This debate has been started by an accident last week involving the toddler Wang Yue. She was knocked down by a van while walking through a market, where her parents run a shop. The driver sped off without checking on the girl's condition. Over the following minutes, 18 people went past the bleeding toddler - and another van ran over her legs - but no one stopped to help. It was all recorded by a security camera, with the upsetting footage shown on television. There have been millions of internet comments about how to get good Samaritans to help - and many more showing anger that so many people refused to help.
words_common_s.xsum::13: Lord Naseby's question followed complaints from viewers about "mumbled" speech in TV shows, including the recent BBC drama SS-GB. Minister Lord Ashton of Hyde told him "it would not be right" for the government to step in. The discussion at Lords questions brought in Downton Abbey writer Lord Fellowes and House of Cards creator Lord Dobbs. "TV viewers should be able to hear and understand their favourite shows," said Culture, Media and Sport Minister Lord Ashton. "It's a long-standing rule, however, that government does not get involved in broadcasters' day-to-day activities so it would not be right for government to ask people about this matter." Lord Naseby said he was disappointed with the minister's answer, telling the House of Lords: "All these problems started in 2014 with that drama called Jamaica Inn, when there were well over 1,000 written complaints to the BBC about the difficulty of hearing that particular show. "Is it right for the ordinary viewer to go to written words on screen to understand what the talking is? "If he can't put pressure on the chairman of the BBC, will he understand that someone will have to make a complaint to Ofcom?" Lord Ashton replied that, since 2014, the BBC had made "66,000 hours of new material and I think there have been six programmes which have had hearing problems". Lord Fellowes, another Conservative peer and the writer of dramas including ITV's Downton Abbey, said the "unfortunate fashion" for mumbled talking was not new. "We had a lot of trouble with it in the 1950s and 60s," he said, adding: "The government has no proper role other than to hope it will soon pass." After the minister suggested that "one person's mumbling is another person's feeling", Labour peer Lord Blunkett, who is blind, said: "Feeling's fine if you can lip read." For people like him, he told peers, mumbling was "not just a bother but an impossibility" and he called on the government to "lean on" media regulator Ofcom. House of Cards author Lord Dobbs came in to say the problem could lie with modern flat-screen televisions. They are "all screen and the speakers face backwards", he said, though he admitted: "We are all getting a little older and, perhaps, losing our hearing." Earlier this year the BBC promised to "look at" sound levels for its new drama SS-GB after viewers complained about mumbling. A version of Daphne du Maurier's novel Jamaica Inn brought in almost 2,200 complaints by the end of its run in 2014.
words_common_s.xsum::14: Action was brought against Bideford Town Council by the National Secular Society (NSS) after atheist councillor Clive Bone complained. Mr Justice Ouseley ruled the prayers were not lawful under section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972. However, he said prayers could be said as long as councillors were not formally called to attend. The judgement was being seen as a test case which could affect local councils across England and Wales. Mr Justice Ouseley ruled the prayers as done by Bideford Town Council had been unlawful because there was no legal power allowing them to continue. The NSS, which said prayers had no place in "a non-religious place concerned with local business", argued the "unsuitable" practice broke articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protect a person's right to freedom of belief and not to face unfair treatment. However, the case was not won on human rights grounds but on a point of legal understanding of local government law. By Robert PigottBBC News religious matters reporter By and large, judges have been unsympathetic to the Christian case when people have argued that they don't want to do things like advising homosexual couples. The tide has been flowing pretty firmly against Christianity in public life and it's caused huge concerns for the churches. They say it's being driven out of public life. There is a lot of concern that this is not just about pure religion but this is about some of the values that support the British way of life. Of course, from the other side, people like the National Secular Society say the Church and Christianity should not have undue privileges in having their values and their way of doing things supported. So there's an argument on both sides but certainly it's been very noticeable in the last few years that the tide's been turning against Christian practices which we've just taken for granted for centuries. Mr Justice Ouseley said: "A local authority has no power under section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972, or otherwise, to hold prayers as part of a formal local authority meeting, or to call councillors to such a meeting at which prayers are on the list of things to do." He told the court: "There is no clear power to say prayers or to have any period of quiet thinking as part of the business of the council." Talking about Bideford, he said: "The council has on two occasions by a majority voted to keep public prayers at its full meetings. "But that does not give it power to do what it has no power to do." The judge accepted the case raised issues of general public importance and gave the council permission to appeal. Speaking after Friday's outcome, Eric Pickles, Secretary of State for Communities and Local Government, said the ruling was "surprising and disappointing". He said: "Public authorities - be it Parliament or a parish council - should have the right to say prayers before meetings if they wish." Anthony Inch, a Bideford town councillor and Torridge district councillor, said he hoped there would be an appeal leading to the ruling being turned over. "I'm disgusted, surprised and saddened by the decision," he said. Simon Calvert, of the Christian Institute, said: "We are pleased that the court has said the saying of prayers at meetings does not break human rights laws. "But it is strange that they should be declared unlawful because of the 1972 Local Government Act." He added: "The judge's finding that the Local Government Act doesn't give local authorities power to include prayers as part of their formal meetings - we think that's very unusual. "I mean we're talking about a practice that goes back to the time of Queen Elizabeth. "And the reasoning of the judge's ruling may be that it could also be unlawful for a council to start its meeting with the beginning of the national anthem. It may even throw local authorities' Diamond Jubilee celebrations up in the air." Keith Porteous Wood, head director of the National Secular Society said: "This judgement is an important victory for everyone who wants a non-religious society, one that neither helps nor hurts people because of their religion or lack of it." He added: "Acts of worship in council meetings are key to the separation of religion from politics, so we're very pleased with the judgement, and the clear non-religious message it sends - particularly the statement made about the 1972 Act." The Bishop of Exeter, the Right Reverend Michael Langrish, said he would encourage councils in his area to continue holding prayers before the start of their legal business. He added: "I think it's a great pity that a tiny minority are seeking to ban the majority, many of whom find prayers very, very helpful, from continuing with a process in which no-one actually has to take part." The legal challenge was started in 2010 after the NSS was contacted by Mr Bone, who was a Bideford town councillor at the time. Mr Bone, who ended up leaving the council because of its "refusal to adjust" its prayers policy, said on Friday: "Quite frankly delighted. I'm not surprised, I expected to win. "The law is the law and local authorities have to obey the law." He added: "Local government is for everybody, it should be equally welcoming to everybody, whatever they believe. "This has got nothing to do with hatred towards religion. "Religious freedom is a complete right and so is freedom from religion a complete right, in my view."
words_common_s.xsum::15: Mike Powell's now-deleted message said Labour and Tory supporters were involved in "why so many deaths lie at the feet" of their parties. words_common_s.xsum::16: Prosecutors think Manuel Trillo helped Joaquin "Shorty" Guzman break out of the Altiplano jail in July. Now Mr Trillo has been sent to that very same prison. A search is under way to catch Guzman, who leads the Sinaloa drug group, since he got away through a 1.5km-long (one mile-long) underground passage on 11 July. According to investigators, Mr Trillo is the money handler of the Sinaloa group and paid for Guzman's escape. He is also blamed for using illegal money to buy properties from 2012 to 2015 under false names. More than 30 people have been arrested in connection with Guzman's escape, including the prison boss and several guards. Guzman's arrest in February 2014 was seen as a big success for Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto. The group leader had been on the run for 13 years since getting away from another top security jail in 2001, reportedly hidden inside a laundry cart. But his amazing break-out from the Altiplano prison caused huge embarrassment. Video recordings showed how guards failed to notice his escape until more than 20 minutes had passed. Questions have also been raised how the prison authorities could have failed to notice the building of the underground passage leading directly into Guzman's cell. On camera recordings leaked to the media, the sound of drilling can be heard echoing through his cell. Investigators say Guzman's partners must have been planning the jailbreak since shortly after his arrest. Not only would the building of the underground passage have taken time, but Guzman's partners also bought a piece of land outside the jail and built a house to hide the underground passage's exit. Attempts to catch Guzman again have so far failed although authorities said he was hurt when he barely got away from a police operation last month. He is believed to be hiding in his home state of Sinaloa, in north-west Mexico.
words_common_s.xsum::17: The cinema, Maratha Mandir, will now continue to show the film just days after it stopped showing it, saying it was no longer making money. Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, a romantic drama, was first shown in October 1995. The cinema said it received hundreds of calls from broken hearted fans within hours of deciding to end the run. Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge means "The Brave-Hearted Will Take The Bride" and is commonly known as DDLJ. It follows two Indians living in Britain and the problems they face as they fall in love. Featuring Indian stars Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol, the movie is one of the most popular in Bollywood history. "After we put up a board outside the theatre last Thursday saying we were taking down the film, we received more than 230 calls in the first two hours from unhappy fans," Maratha Mandir owner Manoj Desai told the BBC. "We received calls not just from Mumbai but also from Delhi and Ahmedabad. We even got a call from a radio station in Dubai - they said whenever people from there visit Mumbai, they make it a point to watch this film. "We never expected this kind of response," he added. The decision to stop the film was taken by Yash Raj Films (YRF), the Bollywood studio that made DDLJ, and Mr Desai says the decision to continue with the screening has also been taken by YRF. Both Mr Desai and the YRF have refused to tell the details of what they say is a "mutually agreed deal" to keep the film going, for the near future at least. In recent years, the film had not been making any money - the theatre screened the film at 0915 local time and the cost of the ticket was low at 10, 15 or 20 rupees (20-30 US cents). "For most people 9:15am was too early so we have changed the show time to 11:30am and ticket prices have also been raised by 5 rupees at all levels," YRF official Vinay Choksi said, adding, "let's see if it improves the collection". The two people living abroad featured in the story fall in love on a trip to mainland Europe, despite the promised marriage of the female lead to a man in India. But in the end they manage to convince their families to allow the union to go ahead. With its unbroken 1,009-week run, DDLJ beat all other Bollywood records for long-running films. It is so well known that US President Barack Obama quoted one of its lines during a speech in India last month.
words_common_s.xsum::18: Mohammed Zahid Mahmood, from Walthamstow, eight members of his family and two other children checked in on Tuesday for the Norwegian Airlines flight to Los Angeles. They had received travel permission under the Visa Waiver programme. The family say they were told an official in the US had said no. At the boarding gate Mr Mahmood said they were told they could not travel but no reason was given. He said in order to use the VWP, the family's request to travel had been approved by the Department for Homeland Security a month before the flight. "We checked in, there were no problems," Mr Mahmood told the BBC. "Just before the final check we were picked out. "Border control came and said 'Can we have your passports?'. He asked us to point out the difference between my brother's children and my children. "Then he came back and said, 'I'm sorry you can't board this flight. We received a call from Washington DC that we can't allow this family to board the flight'." Mr Mahmood said he had taught his children "to live in this country peacefully" and had been invited to speak at local schools about Islamophobia. He said he had once been refused entry to Israel, and was held at Tel Aviv airport for two days before returning to the UK. "No-one is taking the blame. We are just going round in circles. It's about £8,000-£9,000 we've spent on tickets." A spokesperson for Norwegian Airlines said: "We can confirm that a group of passengers were refused the right to board a flight from London Gatwick to Los Angeles yesterday at the request of US Homeland security. Norwegian fully follows all requests from the border controls of each country we serve." The US Embassy could not be reached for comment and Gatwick Airport said they had no information about the incident. The airline company said they had no choice but to follow the orders given by American security officials at the time. Correction 23 December 2015: This story has been changed to make clear the amount of time Mr Mahmood says he was held in Israel.
words_common_s.xsum::19: Phillip Smith, 40, was taken by police officers onto a plane that left Rio de Janeiro for Auckland through the Chilean capital, Santiago. Smith used a passport in his birth name, Phillip Traynor, to fly to Chile and then on to Brazil on 6 November. He got away while on a three-day release from a prison south of Auckland. Smith was sentenced to life in prison in 1996 after he murdered the father of a 13-year-old boy he had sexually hurt between 1992 and 1995. The family had moved house but he had followed the boy to their new home in Wellington in December 1995. He repeatedly stabbed the father, killing him. The boy managed to get away and raise the alarm. Smith was caught a week after he arrived in Brazil, when somebody knew who he was at a youth hostel. His New Zealand lawyer said that he was surprised that Smith had been sent back so quickly, because he had been fighting against his being held in Brazil. "They must have heard the question yesterday and dismissed it, otherwise there will be questions about whether his being sent back was legal," said Tony Ellis. Brazilian police had earlier said that when Smith entered the country he probably lied about his criminal past, which is a reason to send someone back. He now faces a further sentence of up to five years for getting away from custody. Smith's getting away led to calls for a complete change of New Zealand's short-term prison release program and the watching of high-risk offenders. In an email Smith sent to Radio New Zealand he said he had planned the getting away by running a criminal check on his birth name and finding out that it had not been marked with a warning. "My only worry was that somebody that knew me might happen to be at the airport at the same time to know who I was,'' he wrote, according to Radio NZ. He also said he had been able to pay for the getting away with money from different businesses he had run from prison. Smith said he chose Brazil because he thought it would be harder to send him back if he was caught, as the two countries do not have a formal agreement to send criminals back. Sending someone back is, however, a more simple legal process.
words_common_s.xsum::20: Another student reported the claimed close hug and kiss between 50-year-old Tad Cummins and Elizabeth Thomas, but he was allowed to continue working. There have been more than 450 reported sightings of the girl since she and the teacher disappeared on 13 March. Mr Cummins is believed to be traveling with two handguns. He is wanted on charges of sexual contact with a minor and very serious kidnapping. The family is angry that Mr Cummins was not stopped from working after a middle school student reported the claimed kiss in January. Mr Cummins was allowed to continue teaching crime investigation at the high school in the town of Culleoka, 56 miles (90km) south of Nashville. He was stopped from working in February for ignoring the head teacher's order to keep his distance from Ms Thomas. The Maury County School District officially fired Mr Cummins last week after the first missing-person warning was sent out. The missing girl's father has asked for his daughter's safe return in an interview with Nashville news station WZTV. Anthony Thomas said: "Izzy, please come home, get away from him. Come home." Both Mr Cummins and Ms Thomas said no to Culleoka Unit School officials that there had been a kiss. The girl's family were never told of the claimed kiss, said Thomas family lawyer Jason Whatley. But the teacher admitted that the girl is "a really good friend and she does leave her other classes to come see him when she needs someone to calm her down", according to school records dated 30 January. Workers for the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) "believe Cummins could have Thomas hidden from view of the general public or far away from Tennessee". But they add that due to the lack of confirmed sightings, "the individuals could be anywhere". One week after the disappearance, TBI spokesman Josh Devine took to local television to deliver a message to the teenager. "Our message to her tonight: you are a victim," Mr Devine said. "You're 15 years old. He's 50. We are going to do everything we can to bring you home." Two nationwide warnings, known as Amber Alerts, have been sent out since she was first reported missing. People living in far away or country areas have been asked to check their property for any sign of damage or suspicious vehicles.
words_common_s.xsum::21: Gunshots were heard and smoke was seen rising from the scene after special forces entered and took control of the building. Mehmet Selim Kiraz was apparently taken as a prisoner because he had led an investigation into the death of a boy during protests against the government in 2013. A forbidden Marxist revolutionary group is said to be behind the taking of the prisoner. A statement posted online had said the prosecutor would be killed if the group's demands were not met. Istanbul's police chief Selami Altunok said that police had talked with the gunmen for six hours, but eventually entered and took control of the courthouse "because of gunshots heard from inside the prosecutor's office". The two gunmen died during the operation, while Mr Kiraz was badly wounded and later died of his injuries, officials said. The gunmen had released shocking images of a gun being held to the head of Mehmet Selim Kiraz as the prisoner crisis happened. The Turkish government stopped live TV coverage of the incident, giving security concerns as the reason. Sukriye Erden, a lawyer talking with the people holding the prisoner, told the BBC that they had demanded that the police announce the names of four members of the security services whom they said were connected to the death of the boy, Berkin Elvan. Elvan, who was then 14, was hit in the head by a police tear gas container in June 2013 as he went to buy bread during large demonstrations that began in Istanbul and spread across Turkey. He died in an Istanbul hospital last year, after spending nine months in a coma. Recep Tayyip Erdogan, now Turkey's president, made feelings stronger shortly after the teenager's death when he said the boy had been carrying a slingshot and had been "taken up into terrorist organisations". Suspected members of the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party-Front (DHKP-C) took the prosecutor as a prisoner on the sixth floor of the Caglayan court house. The DHKP-C is considered a terrorist group by Turkey, the European Union and US. It said it carried out a suicide bombing in February 2013 at the US embassy in Ankara, where a security guard was killed. In January, a man connected to the banned Marxist group was arrested near the prime minister's offices in Istanbul, reportedly after throwing two grenades that failed to go off and blow up.
words_common_s.xsum::22: Linda Norgrove, 36, from Lewis in the Western Isles of Scotland, was working for US aid group DAI. She was taken with three local staff on 26 September. Their two-car group was attacked in the eastern area of Kunar. Ms Norgrove was killed by her kidnappers on Friday during a rescue mission by US forces. Her workmates were let go safely last week. The British woman is believed to have been taken by her kidnappers from village to village as British, Afghan and other spy agencies worked in the far away and hilly area of Kunar area to find her. Both the prime minister and Foreign Secretary William Hague were kept fully told about what was happening and British approval was given for a rescue mission to be carried out on Friday night, with US forces taking part and British officials giving advice. In a statement, Mr Hague said the aid worker was "killed at the hands of her kidnappers in the course of a rescue attempt". He said: "Working with our friends we received news about where Linda was being held and we decided that, given the danger she was facing, her best chance of safe release was to act on that news. "Blame for this sad outcome rests completely with the hostage takers. "From the moment they took her, her life was under great threat. Given who held her, and the danger she was in, we judged that Linda's best chance lay in trying to rescue her." Prime Minister David Cameron said: "My thoughts are with Linda's family, who will be destroyed by this sad news. She was doing valuable work for the Afghan people. "Decisions on actions to free hostages are always difficult. But where a British life is in such danger, and where we and our friends can act, I believe it is right to try. I pay respect to the courage and skill of all those involved in this effort, and join the foreign secretary in speaking against hostage taking." International Security Help Force Commander General David Petraeus said Afghan and combined security forces did everything in their power to rescue Ms Norgrove. He said: "Linda was a brave person with a strong desire to improve the lives of Afghan people, and sadly she lost her life in their service. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family during this difficult time." And Alex Salmond, Scotland's first minister, said he felt his "deepest sadness" following her "very sad and upsetting" death. "Ms Norgrove was a committed aid worker who was doing everything she could to help people in Afghanistan - hopefully that memory of service in a helping cause can be of some comfort to her loved ones in their time of sadness," he said. Ms Norgrove had been based in Jalalabad where she watched over US-funded rebuilding programmes in the eastern region of Afghanistan. 'Wonderful woman' DAI president James Boomgard said the loss of a "beloved friend and respected workmate" was "destroying news" and sent his sadness to her family. In a statement, he said: "We are saddened beyond words by the death of a wonderful woman whose only purpose in Afghanistan was to do good, to help the Afghan people reach a measure of wealth and steadiness in their everyday lives as they set about rebuilding their country. "Linda loved Afghanistan and cared deeply for its people, and she was deeply committed to her development mission. She was a source of hope to many of us here at DAI and she will be deeply missed." A workmate who was working with her in Jalalabad told the BBC Ms Norgrove was a "very kind and hard-working lady". They said: "You know she didn't need to go for the finishing ceremony of that project, but the only reason she wanted to go there was to show her love and commitment to the people of Kunar area. "Everyone in our office is crying including our Afghan and foreign workmates. Starting from the boss of the office even to drivers and guards are shocked and crying. No one thinks that she was a workmate, but it looks like she was part of everyone's family and we have lost one of our dearest." Ms Norgrove, who had travelled widely, was an experienced aid worker who had been based in a number of countries. She worked for the United Nations in Afghanistan and Laos and, before that, led a nature protection and poverty reduction project in Peru. The BBC's Bilal Sarwary in Kabul said the Dewagal valley, in eastern Kunar area, where she was held, is known for its difficult ground. It is hilly and thickly covered with trees. The valley is very far away. There has never been any government control; it is almost ruled by fighters, tribal elders and powerful families. Different armed groups work in the area, Afghans and foreigners can be targeted by gangs looking for ransom money, but they are sometimes sold on to fighter groups. DAI carries out aid work, often hired by the United States Agency for International Development. In July, a British private security guard was among four people killed in an attack on DAI offices in Kunduz, northern Afghanistan. Shaun Sexton, 29, from Northumberland, a former member of the Parachute Regiment, was working for the firm's security hired company, Edinburgh International. A month later, British doctor Karen Woo and nine other aid workers and language helpers were killed by gunmen, in the north-eastern area of Badakhshan, in what police said was a robbery. Dr Woo worked for Christian charity the International Assistance Mission, giving eye care in far away villages.
words_common_s.xsum::23: Reading University's stress-reducing offer is the latest example of the competition to attract students. The university sees it as a more "honest" approach to applications. A University of Reading spokesman said it reflected a "very aggressive, competitive undergraduate market". With the removal of limits on student numbers and a population dip in 18-year-olds, there is intense competition between universities, which last year accepted more than half a million students. This has seen a growth in "unconditional offers", where universities try to tempt applicants with an offer of a place regardless of the exam grades eventually achieved. Universities have run advertising campaigns and marketing events and provided rewards such as free tablet computers, as well as offering scholarships and money for students. Mary Curnock Cook, head of the Ucas admissions service, said last week that more than half of students accepted on to degree courses last year had missed their required results by two or more grades. She also warned some teachers were "over-predicting" applicants' grades to improve their chances of university offers. University vice-chancellor and former Universities Minister Bill Rammell has said it would be fairer for the admissions process to take place after students have their A-level results. There have also been concerns about the trustworthiness of predicted grades when GCSE and A-level qualifications are being changed. A University of Reading spokesman said: "We've had record intakes and applications in the last two years, but we can't afford to stand still. "More planned, targeted offer-making is the reality of a very aggressive, competitive undergraduate market. "Universities are not wrapped in cotton wool any more by student number caps - we need to be much more active and forward-thinking. "Every application is judged equally and individually on merit. "We are testing new approaches to drive up the number of firm acceptances, convert students who may otherwise have put us as insurance and to make sure we attract high-quality students who will succeed in their studies and contribute positively to our community."
words_common_s.xsum::24: The firing of Mike Rice from Rutgers University in New Jersey happened right away, a college spokesman said. New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and NBA star LeBron James were among those who spoke out against the coach's behavior. Mr Rice said sorry on Wednesday, saying there was no reason for his actions caught on video. He was hired in 2010 to be head basketball coach at Rutgers, which finished last season near the bottom of their league, the well-known Big East Conference. "I've let so many people down: my players, my bosses, Rutgers University, the fans," Mr Rice told ABC News in an interview outside his home on Wednesday. "My family are sitting in their house just gathered together because of the fact that their father was a shame to them." Showing clips recorded between 2010-12, the video shown on sports network ESPN shows Mr Rice shouting rude words, throwing balls at team members, as well as kicking and grabbing them. Rutgers sports director Tim Pernetti reportedly watched the recording late last year. The university then stopped Mr Rice from working for three games, made him pay $75,000 (£50,000) as punishment and ordered him to go to anger management classes. On Wednesday, Rutgers President Robert Barchi said in a statement on the university website: "Coach Rice's hurtful language and actions are deeply upsetting and badly break the university's main values." Mr Barchi added that the video showed a "long-lasting and widespread pattern of troubling behavior", which led to his firing. The choice to fire Mr Rice comes during growing pressure at both state and national level for the university to take action. Gov Christie said in a statement that he was "deeply troubled" by the recording. "This was a sad event for the university, but I completely support the choice to remove Coach Rice," he said. New Jersey Assembly Speaker Sheila Oliver said the coach's behavior was "not fitting for our state". She called for a study into why Rutgers decided not to fire Mr Rice when it first became aware of the video. One of the most famous basketball players in the US, the Miami Heat forward LeBron James, tweeted: "If my son played for Rutgers or a coach like that he would have some real explaining to do and I'm still gone whoop on him afterwards! C'mon.'' Sports director Mr Pernetti said sorry for not taking stronger action when the recording first came to his attention. "I am responsible for the choice to try a recovery of Coach Rice," he said in a written statement. Saying that Rutgers had thought about firing him at the time, Mr Pernetti added: "I thought it was in the best interest of everyone to help him improve, but I was wrong."

words_common_s.xsum::26: The bill would pardon men only if they had sex without "force or threat" and if they married the victim. Critics say it makes rape and child marriage seem acceptable, and lets off men who know about their crime. Violence against women in Turkey has increased in the past ten years - 40% of women report sexual or physical abuse. Numbers also show the murder rate of women increased by 1,400% between 2003 and 2010. The bill was first approved on Thursday evening after being brought to parliament by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP). On Tuesday, lawmakers will debate the bill a second time before casting their final vote. It is a highly argued bill that has divided Turkey along its traditional non-religious versus religious fault line. The aim, says the government, is not to excuse rape but to help those who may not have understood their sexual relations were against the law - or to prevent girls who have sex under the age of 18 from feeling pushed out by their community. There is opposition to the bill on the streets of Istanbul. Many say it will encourage men to rape. But the government will get support among its religious voter base in poorer areas where girls are married off young and the sexual abuse rate is higher. Supporters say Mr Erdogan has freed religious women by removing a ban on headscarves in public places. The vote on Tuesday could start mass protests. If it passes it will likely cancel the guilty findings of some 3,000 men accused of attacking an under-18-year-old. But critics say as well as overlooking underage rape it would make child marriage seem acceptable. "Sexual abuse is a crime and there is no agreement in it. This is what the AKP fails to understand," said Ozgur Ozel, lawmaker for the opposition Republican People's Party, according to AFP news agency. "Seeking the agreement of a child is something that world law does not provide for." But Justice Minister Bekir Bozdag said it could help couples who have engaged in agreed sex and want to marry. "When a child is then born from this unofficial union, the doctor warns the prosecutor and the man is sent to prison, putting the child and mother into money difficulties," he said.
words_common_s.xsum::27: Andrew Apperley, 38, from Eastbourne, was reported missing after failing to return to his hotel four days after going to the Full Moon party. Official identification has not yet taken place but Mr Apperley's family, from Gloucester, have been told. "The reasons for the death are unknown at this time," said a Gloucestershire Police speaker. Mr Apperley was staying at a hotel in Bophut and went to the full moon party on 12 February. He has not been heard from since. He told his mother he would be returning the following morning, but the hotel reported him missing four days later. A speaker for Gloucestershire Police said: "Following questions with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) we can say that a body has been found in the search for Andrew Apperley. "Our thoughts are with Andrew's friends and family." Mr Apperley had flown into Ko Samui from Bangkok to go to the party in Ko Phangan, his brother told the BBC.
