Before going out Andrew had a talk with his mother Linda on the messaging app WhatsApp and said he would be getting the boat back to the hotel the following morning. Workers at the Hotel ibis Samui Bophut said earlier he had still not been seen and his documents were still in their keeping. His bank told his family his cards had not been used since going to the party. Mrs Apperley sent a message to her son's mobile phone, but did not get a delivery report to say he had received it. Speaking before the body was found, a woman speaking for the FCO said: "We are giving support to the family of a British person who has been reported missing in Thailand. "We are in touch with local authorities."
words_common_s.xsum::28: 1917 - Britain takes over Palestine from the Ottoman Empire. Gives support to "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine through the Balfour Declaration, along with a strong statement that "nothing shall be done which may harm the everyday and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities". 1918 - First important Palestinian Arab groups working for their nation appear - the mainly cultural Muntada al-Adabi and the Damascus-based Nadi al-Arabi. 1920 - San Remo meeting of countries that won the war gives Palestine to Britain as a territory under its control, to prepare it for ruling itself. Jerusalem riots against Balfour Declaration show clear Palestinian Arab identity. 1921 - Britain chooses Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, a member of a leading Palestinian Arab family, as Grand Mufti of Jerusalem and leader of the Muslim community. He brings together the Arabs and Muslims against any further giving in to the Jews. 1922 - Palestinian Arab group says no to British idea for a group that makes laws, saying including terms of the Balfour Declaration in draft basic law not acceptable. 1929 - Arab rioters kill about 200 Jews in Jerusalem's Old City and Hebron. British soldiers kill 116 Arabs in putting down riots in Jerusalem. 1930 - British White Paper and Royal group of experts recommend limiting Jewish people coming into the country. 1930-35 - The Black Hand religious Muslim group led by Sheikh Izz al-Din al-Qassam starts campaign of violence against Jewish community and British rule. 1935 - Palestinian Arab leadership accepts British High Commissioner's idea for group that makes laws, but the British House of Commons says no to it the following year. 1936-39 - Arab revolt begins with a general strike in Jaffa. Britain declares military law and breaks up Grand Mufti Al-Husseini's Arab Higher Committee. More than 5,000 Arabs killed and 15,000 injured in putting down revolt, Al-Husseini runs away to French-run Syria to avoid being arrested. 1947 - United Nations recommends dividing Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states after Britain signals end to its control, with international control over Jerusalem and its surrounding areas. Arab High Committee says no to dividing the land. Birth of Israel 1948 - Israel declares freedom from outside rule as British control ends. More than four million Palestinians are thought to be living with refugee status in Arab countries, many pushed to the edges and trapped in camps Slideshow: Inside Shatila Arab armies fail to defeat new Jewish state of Israel after Britain leaves. Jordan takes over West Bank and East Jerusalem, Egypt takes over Gaza, and Israel holds the rest of what Britain controlled including West Jerusalem. At least 750,000 Palestinian Arabs either run away or are forced to leave. Arguments over the nature of their leaving continue to this day. United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) set up to look after the educational and health needs of Palestinian refugees and their children and grandchildren throughout the Middle East. 1949-1950s - Fedayeen Palestinian fighters based in Egypt and Gaza carry out raids into Israel with Egyptian support and encouragement. This increases after pan-Arab officers take power in Cairo in 1952. 1956-1957 - Israel works together secretly with Britain and France to invade Egypt during the Suez Crisis, partly to end Fedayeen attacks. UN buffer force in Sinai and Gaza greatly reduces raids. 1959 - Yasser Arafat forms Fatah fighting group in Egypt to carry out raids into Israel. 1964 - Arab League sets up Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and Palestine Liberation Army under Ahmad Shukeiri. 1967 June - Six-Day War leaves Israel taking over East Jerusalem, all of West Bank, Gaza, Golan Heights and Sinai. Jewish settlements are set up in all of these areas in coming years, with government approval and permission. 1969 - Yasser Arafat takes over PLO leadership after first appearance as military leader in fights with Israeli forces in Jordan in 1968, and makes clear the group's freedom from Egyptian control. 1970 - Increasing tension over the strength of the PLO in Jordan leads to the Black September fights with Jordanian forces, driving the PLO into being forced to leave to southern Lebanon. 1970s-1980s - PLO and other armed Palestinian groups turn to airplane takeovers and attacks on Israeli soldiers, government workers and everyday people within Israel and in other countries to bring attention to their cause. Leila Khaled took part in a wave of airplane takeovers which brought attention to the Palestinian cause Profile of a person who takes over airplanes On this Day: 1970: Fighters destroy jets 1972 - Palestinian "Black September" gunmen take the Israeli team as prisoners at the Munich Olympics. Two of the athletes are murdered at the place and nine more killed during a failed rescue attempt by the German authorities. Israel starts a series of revenge killings. 1973 - Israel raids PLO bases in Beirut and southern Lebanon before and during the October Yom Kippur/Ramadan War. 1974 April-May - Two hardline groups, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine General Command and Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, carry out raids into northern Israel and kill 43 everyday people, including many children, in a block of flats in Kiryat Shmona and a school in Maalot. 1974 June - After 1973 Yom Kippur/Ramadan war, PLO accepts Ten-Point Programme allowing giving in to some demands with Israel on the way to setting up complete Palestinian control over historic Palestine, including the land of Israel. Some hardline groups split away to form the Rejectionist Front and increase attacks on Israeli soldiers and everyday people. PLO recognised 1974 October - Arab League recognises PLO as the "sole legal representative of the Palestinian people'' and it admits it to full membership of the League. Yasser Arafat was for many years the argued-about symbol of the Palestinians' struggle with Israel BBC Obituary: Yasser Arafat The Economist: Arafat 1974 November - Yasser Arafat becomes first non-state leader to speak to the United Nations General Assembly, delivers "olive branch... and freedom fighter's gun" speech. 1975 - Rejectionist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and German far-left armed group take over Air France plane travelling from Israel to France, send it to Entebbe in Uganda. Israel special soldiers rescue most of passengers and crew, kill people who took over plane. 1977 May - The right-wing Likud party wins surprise election victory in Israel and encourages settlements policy on West Bank and Gaza. 1978 March - PLO attack kills 38 everyday people on Israel's coastal road. Israel carries out first major push into southern Lebanon, driving PLO and other Palestinian groups out of the area. 1978 September - Israel promises to expand Palestinian self-government in the West Bank and Gaza as part of the Camp David Accords setting up relations with Egypt. 1982 June - Israel invades Lebanon again to force out PLO leadership from Beirut after killing attempt by Palestinian group on Israeli representative to London. PLO leaders leave Lebanon Israel's taking over of Lebanon in 1982 saw the moving of the PLO, and the killing of hundreds of Palestinians in refugee camps by Israel's Phalangist friends Video: Sabra and Shatila BBC: Witness 1982 September - Killing of Palestinians in the Beirut Sabra and Shatila camps by Israel's Christian Phalangist friends. PLO leadership moves to Tunisia, where it remains until it moves to Gaza in 1994. 1985 October - Israeli air force strikes PLO headquarters in Tunis after PLO group kills three Israeli tourists on a yacht. Palestine Liberation Front PLO group takes over Achille Lauro cruise ship, demanding release of 50 Palestinians from Israeli prisons. People who took over ship kill elderly American wheelchair user Leon Klinghoffer. 1987 December - First Palestinian Intifada uprising begins in Palestinian Territories. Muslim Brotherhood in Gaza forms the Hamas movement, which quickly turns to violence against Israel. 1988 Jordan gives up claim to West Bank, giving it to PLO. Palestinian National Council meeting in Algiers announces State of Palestine. 1990 - PLO backs Iraq over its taking over of Kuwait, which cuts ties with the PLO and later forces out about 400,000 Palestinians. 1991 October - US-Soviet supported meeting in Madrid brings Israeli and Palestinian representatives together for the first time since 1949. 1992 - Israeli Labour government of Yitzhak Rabin promises to stop settlement growth programme and begins secret talks with PLO. 1993 September - Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat sign Oslo Declaration to plan Palestinian self-government and officially end the First Intifada, which had been running out of steam since the Madrid Conference. Violence by different Palestinian groups that reject the Oslo Declaration continues. 1994 February - Baruch Goldstein of the hardline Jewish Kach movement kills 29 Palestinians at prayer at the Cave of the Patriarchs holy place in Hebron on the West Bank. Progress towards self-rule 1992 May-July - Israel withdraws from most of Gaza and the West Bank city of Jericho, allowing Yasser Arafat to move his PLO government from Tunis and set up the Palestinian National Authority. 1992 December - Yasser Arafat, along with Yitzhak Rabin and Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres, are together awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. 1995 - Temporary Agreement sets out path for transfer of further power and land to Palestinian National Authority. Forms basis of 1997 Hebron Protocol, Wye River Memorandum of 1998 and internationally-supported "Road Map for Peace" of 2003. 2000-2001 - Talks between Israeli Labour Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat break down over the timing and amount of a proposed further Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank. Palestinian protests grow into new Intifada. 2001 December - Israel sends soldiers to surround Ramallah after series of deadly Palestinian attacks inside Israel. Yasser Arafat is unable to leave his government building. Barrier goes up 2002 March - Israeli army starts Operation Defensive Shield on the West Bank and begins building barrier there to stop armed Palestinians entering Israel. The path of the barrier causes arguments as it often moves away from the pre-1967 ceasefire line into the West Bank. 2002 March - Arab League meeting in Beirut offers to recognise Israel in return for its full withdrawal from all lands taken over since 1967, agreement to a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital and "fair solution" to refugee question - the "Arab League Peace Plan". 2003 March - Yasser Arafat creates job of prime minister and chooses Fatah old member Mahmoud Abbas to lead contacts with US and Israel, both of which refuse to deal with Arafat. 2003 May - Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon says the taking over of Palestinian lands cannot continue forever. 2003 June - Arab League meeting in Egypt shows support for "road map" proposed by US, European Union, Russia and UN and accepted by Palestinian National Authority and Israel, suggesting an independent Palestinian state and a freeze on West Bank Jewish settlements. 2003 September - Mahmoud Abbas quits as prime minister, pointing to US and Israeli stubbornness as well as internal Palestinian opposition to his government. Followed by Fatah old member Ahmed Qurei. 2004 March - Israeli forces kill Sheikh Yassin, the founder and leader of Hamas, and his follower Abd al-Aziz al-Rantissi, the following month. 2004 July - International Court of Justice gives advisory opinion that the Israeli separation barrier breaks international law and must be removed. 2004 November - Yasser Arafat dies in hospital in France, where he went for urgent medical treatment in October. 2005 January - Mahmoud Abbas elected Mr Arafat's follower as head of the Palestinian National Authority. 2005 September - Israel withdraws all Jewish settlements and military people from Gaza, while keeping control over airspace, ports and border crossings. Hamas wins elections 2006 March - Hamas religious Muslim group's Ismail Haniyeh forms government after winning lawmaking elections in January. Struggle for being first with Fatah begins. United States and European Union stop aid, and Israel ends tax transfers, because of Hamas's refusal to recognise Israel, give up violence and accept previous peace agreements. The religious Muslim movement won lawmaking council elections in 2006 and has since controlled Gaza. It has proved itself a tough opponent in its fight with Israel, as well as with other Palestinian groups Who are Hamas? 2006 June - Hamas fighters from Gaza take Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit near border crossing and hold him prisoner for five years, demanding release of Palestinian prisoners. Major fights between Israel and Hamas forces in Gaza follow. Israel puts limits on Gaza. 2006 September - Fights break out between Fatah and Hamas supporters in Gaza. Different Arab states and Palestinian groups try to help them reach agreement in coming months in order to prevent civil war. 2007 March - Fatah and Hamas form national unity government to end months of on-and-off fights in Gaza. 2007 June - Unity government fails. Hamas forces out Fatah from Gaza and strengthens its control of the land. Israel tightens blockade after increase in rocket attacks from Gaza; Egypt closes border with Gaza. Mahmoud Abbas chooses Salam Fayyad as prime minister, but Hamas refuses to recognise him. Two rival governments in West Bank and Gaza appear. US and European Union start again aid to the Fayyad government. 2007 November - US-hosted Annapolis Conference for the first time sets up the "two-state solution" as the basis for future talks between Israel and the Palestinian Authority. 2008 March - Efforts at bringing back together between Fatah and Hamas begin in Yemen, but next round in Cairo in November stops when Hamas objects to Fatah arrest of its West Bank members. The Israeli raid on a group of vessels carrying pro-Palestinian people trying to break the Gaza blockade caused international anger Q&A: Raid on the Mavi Marmara 2008 November - Israel starts push into Gaza, seen by Hamas as a ceasefire breaking. Hamas responds by starting rockets. 2008 December - Israel starts Operation Cast Lead month-long invasion of Gaza to stop Hamas and other fighter groups firing rockets into Israel. 2010 February - Fatah and Hamas start again talks on national bringing back together. Direct talks start again between Israel and the Palestinian Authority, only to fail over the question of settlements. 2010 May - Nine Turkish pro-Palestinian people killed in Israeli capture of ships attempting to break sea blockade of Gaza. 2011 April-May - Fatah and Hamas agree at talks in Cairo to reform a unity government and hold fresh elections, but no practical putting into action follows. Bid for UN membership 2011 - Palestinian National Authority starts campaign for UN membership of "State of Palestine", as means of bringing attention to stopped talks with Israel. Bid fails, but UNESCO cultural agency accepts Palestine as member in October. 2012 May - After early talks in Qatar, Fatah and Hamas sign Cairo Agreement promising to maintain non-violent resistance to Israeli taking over in pursuit of an independent state within the 1967 ceasefire lines. Palestinians are hopeful that putting money in tech start-ups will help lift them out of a struggling economy Meeting the West Bank's tech start-ups 2012 October - Local elections on West Bank weaken Fatah's position, as it wins only two-fifths of the seats fought over on a turnout of 55%. Lists led by Fatah rebels win four of the 11 major towns and cities, and independents and leftists take control of a fifth. Hamas refuses to take part in the poll and allows no elections in Gaza. 2012 November - UN raises Palestinian representation to that of "non-member observer state", allowing it to take part in General Assembly debates and improving chances of joining UN agencies. 2012 December - Fatah allows Hamas celebration rally on West Bank over UN status raising, a gesture given back by Hamas in Gaza the following month. 2013 April - Prime Minister Fayyad quits after long-standing argument with Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas. He is followed by academic Rami Hamdallah in May. 2013 Newly chosen US Secretary of State starts a series of Israeli-Palestinian talks aimed at reaching a framework peace deal by April 2014. Palestinian government workers say continuing Israeli approval of Jewish housing in taken over East Jerusalem weakens progress. Israel accuses the Palestinians of encouraging hatred. 2013 July - Fall of Morsi government in Egypt destroys Palestinian hopes for lifting of Egyptian blockade of border with Gaza, and stops Egyptian helping to reach agreement in the Fatah-Hamas bringing back together process. 2013 December - Israel, Jordan and Palestinian Authority sign water-sharing agreement to stop and eventually reverse the drying-out of the Dead Sea by laying pipeline to carry salt water from Red Sea salt-removing plant while providing drinking water to region. 2014 March - Egypt bans Hamas activities and takes its property because of links to Egypt's illegal Muslim Brotherhood. 2014 April - Fatah and Hamas agree to form unity government, which takes office in June. Fatah complains that separate Hamas cabinet continues to rule Gaza. 2014 June - Israel responds to the kidnapping and murder of three Jewish teenagers in the West Bank by arresting numerous Hamas members. Fighters respond to the arrests and the killing of a Palestinian teenager by Jewish hardliners by firing rockets from Gaza. 2014 July-August - Israel responds to attacks from armed groups in Gaza with a military campaign by air and land to knock out missile starting places and attack tunnels. Fights end in uneasy Egyptian-helped ceasefire in August. 2014 December - Minister Without Portfolio Ziad Abu Ein dies at fight with Israeli soldiers at West Bank protest. 2015 May - The Vatican announces that it is to officially recognise Palestinian statehood.
words_common_s.xsum::29: Philip Cullen, 57, was given a six-month delayed sentence for catching two butterflies at protected areas in Somerset and in Gloucestershire in 2015. He was found guilty in March of six charges, relating to killing, catching and keeping the threatened species. His is believed to be the first case in the UK involving crimes related to the species. Bristol Magistrates' Court heard that Cullen was seen chasing a Large Blue with a child's net at Daneway Banks in Gloucestershire in June 2015. He was later spotted with a small net at Collard Hill in Somerset. It was reported to police who searched his home and found up to 30 boxes of butterflies, including Large Blues. Prosecutor Ian Jackson told the court the charges had been brought "on the grounds of putting a species in danger". Michael Hartnell, defending, said in his defence the 57-year-old had accepted the "seriousness" of what he had done and was "extremely sorry". Cullen, of The Grove, Warmley, Bristol, was given a six-month prison sentence delayed for two years and ordered to carry out 250 hours of unpaid work. He was also given a five-year criminal behaviour order banning him from three nature reserves popular with the Large Blue and was ordered to pay £300 case costs and an £80 victim payment. The Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust (GWT), said it was the "first UK guilty finding for collecting a butterfly" and a "major step forward in the battle against wildlife crime". Source: Butterfly Conservation The Large Blue (Maculinea arion) species became extinct in Britain 1979. It was brought back at sites, including Collard Hill and Daneway Banks, in the 1980s and in 2004 it was found at nine locations in the country. It has a wingspan of more than two inches and can be identified by a row of black spots on its upper front wing. A person who collects and studies butterflies is called a lepidopterist after the branch of animal science that deals with butterflies and moths.
words_common_s.xsum::30: David Souleman of the UK Forest Products Association said there was a clear lack of "openness and honesty" in the deal. The deal had been said to be wrong by checkers. NRW said the contracts were given out in "unusual" conditions. In 2014 a company was given a series of contracts worth £39m to buy both spruce and larch timber - the second one from forests where a fungus disease causing wide damage, Phytophthora ramorum, was present. The contracts were part of action NRW - which sells timber from publicly opened woodlands - took to deal with the disease, in the middle of a fast increase in its spread the earlier year. But a report by checker general Huw Vaughan Thomas in March showed doubt over whether the decision met state aid rules and said the decision-making process was not honest. Mr Thomas showed that the deal was made without other companies being allowed to offer their bids - but NRW argued against his findings. The agreements were going to be stopped after the company failed to meet a key promise to build a new handling line for cutting timber. Mr Souleman, who is top director of the UK Forest Products Association which stands for the home timber business, said: "It's a very serious, troubling and worrying situation for businesses across the forestry and forest public area in Wales, and indeed further away. "Our main concern here is that in the past businesses who have dealt with Natural Resources Wales have always been told that dealings with NRW would be fair, open and honest. "In this case, from what we can see there appears to have been a large lack of fairness, openness and honesty, and that is really what is giving rise to such serious concern across the area at the moment." "There probably are businesses out there who feel they were refused chances," he said. Fears that the market for larch was on the edge of falling apart at the time of the deal have been given as one of the reasons why NRW went ahead with the deal - but whether this was the case has been asked about by Mr Souleman. Facts given by chief leader Emyr Roberts at a meeting of the assembly's public accounts group in March said that, at the time of the deal: "We had a real emergency on our hands." "There was a danger of the timber market falling apart at that time," he said. But Mr Souleman said the statement was "wildly wrong" and "misleading". "Events have shown, in the time between through 2014 through today, that the diseased larch that was cut down has been equally well handled and sold in the market place," he said. He said a full look into the matter by the public accounts group was "probably needed given the seriousness of the situation". Mr Souleman will give facts to the assembly's public accounts group, which is also calling NRW in again to look at the issue again, on Monday. Emyr Roberts, chief leader of Natural Resources Wales, said in a statement: "The long-term contracts were given out at a point in time when we were dealing with an unusual set of conditions. "Our main goal at the time was to get a market for the diseased larch and we did so following our agreed processes. "We are sure that the facts we gave to the earlier public accounts group was right and good." Neither NRW or the Wales Audit Office have shown the name of the firm that was given the contracts.
words_common_s.xsum::31: Denbighshire council wanted to create a new school that teaches in two languages by closing Ysgol Pentrecelyn and Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd in Ruthin and opening a new place. Pentrecelyn parents had fought hard against the plan, saying the school's Welsh character would be lost. Councillors have been told to keep the school when they vote later. In August, the High Court cancelled the closure decision following a complaint brought by former Pentrecelyn student Aron Wyn Jones, who said the council had failed to think about the language and community effect of a single place school. All students in Ysgol Pentrecelyn are taught in Welsh, whilst in the Church in Wales Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd students can be taught in either Welsh or English, with 80% choosing Welsh-medium teaching at present. At the time of the ruling, Denbighshire council said it was disappointed with the outcome of the decision and would think about the guidance given by the court. In a report to Tuesday's cabinet meeting, head of education and children's services Karen Evans said as the court review did not criticise the goals, it would be "perfectly logical" for the authority to consider whether to restart the talks on the original proposals whilst recognising criticism of the process. However she continued: "The authority also needs to consider the wider effect based on the current situation." She said the council must give proper attention to the effect of any future proposal on community togetherness, in particular that which had an effect on the learners themselves. "It is clear from discussions with both school communities that there is no desire to look at the same proposal in the current circumstances," Ms Evans added. "The authority agrees that conducting a talk on the same proposal, even with a perfect process, risks further community divisions and legal challenges. "It is equally clear that the current state for Ysgol Llanfair cannot continue and that the area is in need of a lasting category 2 school that teaches in two languages." Councillors have been told to allow Ysgol Pentrecelyn, which currently has 56 students, to remain open and for a new Church in Wales school to be built in Llanfair on a safer place closer to many of the students' homes.
words_common_s.xsum::32: Iain Pocock, who lives near Tomich in the Highlands, caught a foot on a raised stone and fell during a visit to Inverness on 9 February 2012. Mr Pocock, who appeared in a BBC documentary in 2013, sought £500,000 in payment for an injury to his leg. A judge said Mr Pocock had failed to show that the stone had been at a height that required it to be fixed. Mr Pocock said the trip caused injury to a knee and this affected his ability to carry out tasks at his croft. He raised an action at the Court of Session in Edinburgh against Highland Council. The local authority, which denied responsibility, said that during 2012 and the following year Mr Pocock and his family were the subject of the documentary Power to the Pococks: A year in the life of a crofting family. In its defences to the action, the council said: "The pursuer's wife in particular, during the documentary, discusses the fact that they rely on own generator for power and that they cannot be linked to the National Grid other than at large expense to their family. "There is reference to them being quoted the sum of up to £230,000 for them to be connected and the pursuer's wife says they do not have that money unless they 'win the lottery'." During the court action parts of the documentary were played to Mr Pocock. Judge Lord Clark said: "Excerpts of the documentary were played which showed the pursuer doing such things as using an axe and a chainsaw to cut firewood, carrying out animal care tasks, carrying out maintenance of a wind turbine by climbing up a metal scaffold and in doing so being able to place weight on his left leg, driving a tractor, kneeling while milking, carrying a stockpot and sliding on a sheet of ice, spinning round a pole in a barn and working on a diesel generator." The judge said: "The pursuer explained that he was not filmed during periods when the knee was bad and that when he was carrying out some of the activities that had been filmed he was focused and aware of what he was doing, and was holding his leg steady to avoid unexpected injury." Documentary director Stephen Bennett explained to the court that he would not switch on the camera and begin filming when Mr Pocock said he was in pain. Lord Clark said in his newly issued judgement issued Mr Pocock, his wife and other relatives struck him as being honest witnesses and he had no hesitation in accepting them as believable and trustworthy. The judge said: "It may be the case that the pursuer's evidence to some degree made too much of the effects of the accident and that the BBC documentary supported the view that his injuries were not quite so severe as he had stated, but I regard any difference as being largely unimportant. "In relation to the documentary, I accept the evidence from the pursuer and Mr Bennett to the effect that there were points in time when filming could not take place because of the pursuer's knee injury." The judge said that in light of Mr Pocock's testimony of symptoms of the knee locking during 2012 and supporting evidence he concluded he had suffered a medial meniscal tear in the accident. In the action it was argued that there was a duty to repair a paving defect with a height difference greater than 20mm within seven days or at most within 21 days. The location of the accident in Baron Taylor Street was known to be prone to problems and was regularly checked. Lord Clark said he had concluded that Mr Pocock had failed to show the key factual basis of his case - that the defect at of the date of its identification involved a height difference greater than 20mm. The judge added that Mr Pocock had not shown that a roads authority of ordinary ability applying reasonable care would have taken the steps identified in his claim to correct the defect.
words_common_s.xsum::33: Their study, in Science Translation Medicine, showed caffeine was more than just a wake-you-up drug and actually slowed down the body's internal clock. A double espresso three hours before bedtime delayed the production of the sleep hormone melatonin by about 40 minutes, making it harder to fall asleep. Experts said our own actions had a huge influence on sleep and the body clock. One of the researchers, Dr John O'Neill, from the Medical Research Council's Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, told the BBC News website: "If you're tired and having a coffee at night to stay awake, then that is a bad idea, you'll find it harder to go to sleep and get enough sleep." In his half of the study, cells grown in a dish were put in contact with caffeine to work out how it changed their ability to keep time. It showed the drug was able to change the chemical clocks ticking away in every cell of the human body. Meanwhile, five people at the University of Colorado Boulder, in the US, were locked in a sleep room for 50 days. And as light coming in is the main way we normally control our body clock, they spent most of their time locked up in very dim light. In a series of tests over the month and a half, the scientists showed that an evening amount of caffeine slowed the body clock by 40 minutes. It had roughly half the effect of three hours of bright light at bedtime. Dr O'Neill said it would be "complete guessing" to set a stopping time for drinking caffeine in the evening but he personally never drank coffee after 17:00. He said the findings may help treat some sleep problems and people who naturally woke up too early - known as larks - to help keep them in step with the rest of the world. "It could be useful with jet lag if you are flying east to west where taking caffeine at the right time of day might speed up the time it takes to get over jet lag," he added. Prof Derk-Jan Dijk, from the University of Surrey, told the BBC: "People differ in how easily they are affected by caffeine, and if coffee drinkers have problems with falling asleep, they may try to avoid drinking coffee in the afternoon and evening." He added that people "too often" thought they were a "slave" to their body clocks and set up to wake up early or late. "These and other facts clearly show that we can to some degree change these rhythms and that part of the reason why we sleep so late relates to things such as caffeine intake and the coming in of man-made light in the evening," he said.
words_common_s.xsum::34: After 10 weeks of talks, a way forward has been agreed on armed groups and welfare reform. However, they failed to break the deadlock over past issues arising from Northern Ireland's Troubles. Prime Minister David Cameron said the agreement was "an important turning point for Northern Ireland". "The agreement makes sure Northern Ireland's budget can continue, sets out how we'll deal with armed groups, and could provide a basis for a shared future for the people of Northern Ireland," he said. The deal includes a new set of rules politicians will be asked to follow in relation to armed groups and a reworked money package to help those affected by welfare reforms and tax credit cuts. While the Democratic Unionist Party and Sinn Féin have backed the deal, the executive's Justice Minister David Ford, who leads the Alliance Party, said his party refused to support it today. Other parties said they needed more time to study the document. The US government has welcomed the deal. Victims' groups have said they are disappointed the deal does not include any movement on the past issues of the Troubles. Stormont crisis: How the story unfolded Reaction to the Stormont deal Read BBC News NI political editor Mark Devenport's analysis New rules are in place expecting politicians to work towards the breaking up of armed group structures. Politicians must not take instructions from anywhere other than those who have given them their right to govern through voting. The new rules will apply not only to ministers in Northern Ireland's ruling executive but to all MLAs, it is understood. An international body will be set up to watch armed group activity, with people chosen by the British and Irish governments and the Northern Ireland Executive. It will have a £3.2m budget. Unlike the old armed group watching body, the Independent Monitoring Commission, the new body will not have the power to recommend the removal of any parties from the assembly. A new cross-border task force will bring together agencies like HM Revenue and Customs, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) and the National Crime Agency - the UK's equivalent of the FBI - with their equivalents in the Republic of Ireland. The task force is expected to have a budget of about £50m. The PSNI will also get an extra £160m over the next five years. Read BBC News NI economics editor John Campbell's analysis Last year's Stormont House Agreement fell on the issue of welfare reform, when Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) refused to let the changes pass through the Northern Ireland Assembly. Social Development Minister Mervyn Storey is due to bring a law-making consent motion to the assembly on Wednesday that will allow the government to push the changes through. Westminster is expected to start the process either this week or next. The last Stormont deal included a help package on welfare reform that amounted to £564m over a six-year period. The new deal includes a four-year programme, with a value of £585m. The cash will be split, with £345m for measures designed to reduce the harm of the welfare changes. The remaining £240m will be spent on measures to help families who will lose out on tax credits. An independent benefit expert has been asked to make sure that £30m a year is devoted to assist people affected by the spare room payment rule, better known as the bedroom tax. Stormont sources are hopeful that they will recover around £40m of so-called fines linked to welfare that would have gone to the Treasury. They also expect to benefit by as much as £150m from a promise to cut down on benefit fraud and error, under a scheme in which any savings would be split with the Treasury. Northern Ireland's major parties have campaigned for corporation tax to be handed over to them, believing that cutting the tax would help tackle problems in the economy. The new agreement puts back the target date for cutting corporation tax by a year. The new date will be April 2018 and the rate will be 12.5%, the same as in the Republic of Ireland. Executive sources claim there is no fresh borrowing in the package, but when added together it contains more than £500m in extra new money. Earlier loans, such as £700m for a public sector voluntary exit scheme remain in place. A promise for £500m towards shared education will now be moved so some of the money may be spent on shared housing. It is also understood there is £60m to carry out work connected with Belfast's peace walls. It is believed the Irish government is ready to provide £75m towards making better the A5, part of a road link between Dublin and the north-west of Northern Ireland. It is thought Stormont will match this funding.
words_common_s.xsum::35: The so-called "International Checking Group" says it has put a small part of Eta's weapons under lock and key. The Spanish government has dismissed the taking away of weapons move, and the checkers' role, calling the Eta action "like theatre". Eta declared a final end to fighting in 2011. words_common_s.xsum::43: The so-called Egtved Girl was discovered in 1921 in a burial mound in the Jutland Peninsula, along with the burned bones of a young child. words_common_s.xsum::48: The University of Strathclyde's Fraser of Allander Institute is putting money into new research and students studying for higher degrees. A new director who has been chosen will also join the institute in April, while a group of advisers with well-known economists will be set up. It also plans to grow its economic research services for the third area, government, business and industry. The university said the move was "especially well-timed", with the Scottish Parliament soon to take on greater tax and spending powers. It added that the bigger institute would be able to provide decision-makers, the media and the public "with even greater top-quality independent economic study than before". The institute's new director who has been chosen will be Prof Graeme Roy, a former senior economic adviser in the Scottish government. The group of advisors will be led by Prof Andrew Goudie and include the chief economists of both the Scottish and UK governments. More details will be announced at an event at the Scottish Parliament to mark the institute's fortieth birthday. Before the event, University of Strathclyde head Prof Sir Jim McDonald described the money being put in as a "step change" for the institute. He said: "At a time when the Scottish Parliament is gaining important new powers and duties and the future of the UK's economic and money system is going through a major re-think, the need for independent economic and tax study has never been greater. "With more than four periods of ten years of economic guessing experience behind it, the Fraser of Allander Institute is in a special position to provide the independent research and study needed to shape public talk and decision making. "This new money will allow the institute to lead new research into public spending and money matters that will be of use not just in Scotland and the UK, but also around the world." The institute regularly puts out an economic report, which includes guesses and detailed study of the Scottish economy. It also carries out surveys of the economy on a regular basis.
words_common_s.xsum::49: Dr Fatoumata Nafo-Traoré, who leads the Roll Back Malaria (RBM) Partnership, said after visiting west Africa: "It makes sense that all the health workers' attention is on Ebola." Children's wards which used to be full of malaria patients were becoming "ghost areas," she added. In 2012, malaria killed 7,000 people in the three countries worst hit by Ebola. Most of these will have been young children - although malaria can be cured. The disease caused almost 4,000 deaths in Sierra Leone in 2012 - as well as around 2,000 deaths in Liberia and about 1,000 in Guinea. Now the three countries are fighting with the Ebola virus and Dr Nafo-Traoré said she feared that recent gains in preventing malaria could be threatened by the crisis. She said: "These countries have been really hit by malaria in the past. But five years ago, it was even worse - the deaths were double. "We all agree that no child should die from malaria, because we have the tools to prevent and treat it. "But now, it makes sense that all the health workers' attention is on Ebola. "We used to see hospital beds with three children in them at a time, because there was not enough space. "Now those children's wards are becoming ghost areas, because of the lack of workers there. "So we don't know who has malaria, and who is dying from it. "Even if the situation is at the same level as last year, that was still very bad in those countries. We're really worried that Ebola will cause a setback to the work on malaria. "And there's a lack of trust and confidence in health workers. There's still a feeling it's them who are bringing the virus to people." RBM is a partnership of more than 500 groups. It was formed 16 years ago to bring together world efforts against malaria. It says Guinea and Sierra Leone met key targets last year for handing out bed nets - an important weapon for protecting children from insects which spread malaria. The situation in Liberia was less positive. Officials there are trying to work out how they can increase their handing out efforts while trying to contain Ebola too. One problem is that the early signs of Ebola and malaria can be similar. Dr Nafo-Traoré travelled by road from Conakry in Guinea to Sierra Leone earlier this month. She told me: "The Ebola treatment centres have a way of treating cases of fever with anti-malaria drugs too, because the patient might be suffering from both diseases. "But at the moment when people have fevers, they are often afraid to go to healthcare places because they want to avoid being held in the Ebola treatment centres. "We are working with the countries to make sure people are tested for malaria and get the drugs. "It's important to have a working-together approach. A key aim is to decrease cases of malaria-related fever, so the Ebola centres don't get filled up with too many people. "I'm worried because of the weak health systems. And travel is so easy between all 15 of the West African countries. "In the past Ebola happened in far-away bush areas. But today it's happening in capital cities. "People are getting well-prepared now. As I travelled by road there, I saw checkpoints where people were having their temperature taken and were washing their hands. "Luckily the world has received a wake-up call - but the response was slow at the beginning."
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::0: For several decades, government testing plans for genetic damage have been made the same across the board where the tests being used looked at changes and physical and number-related chromosome damage. This has served the genetic harmfulness community well when most of the substances being tested were suitable for such checks. The outcome from this testing is usually a two-choice (yes/no) review of test results, and in many instances, the information is only used to decide whether a substance has cancer-causing ability or not. Over the same time period, processes and ways of action (MOAs) that explain a wider range of gene-related damage involved in many harmful health outcomes have been recognized. In addition, a major change in thinking in applied genetic harmfulness study is moving the field toward a more number-based dose-response study and point-of-departure (PoD) finding with a focus on risks to people who are exposed. This is directing attention on gene-related damage that is likely to cause changes connected with a variety of harmful health outcomes. This major change in thinking is moving the testing attention for genetic damage from a danger identification only review to a more complete risk measurement approach that provides more helpful information for decision makers regarding the possible risk of genetic damage to people who are exposed. To make possible this broader setting for looking at genetic damage, a next generation testing plan needs to take into account a broader, more bendable approach to testing, and in the end modeling, of gene-related damage as it relates to human contact with substances. This is in line with the larger risk measurement setting being used in government decision making. As presented here, this bendable approach for looking at gene-related damage focuses on testing for related gene-related effects that can be, as best as possible, connected with a harmful health effect. The most wanted connection for risk to humans would be changes in locations connected with human diseases, whether in body or reproductive cells. The outline of a bendable approach and connected thoughts are presented in a series of nine steps, some of which can occur at the same time, which was developed through a working together effort by leading genetic harmfulness scientists from universities, government, and industry through the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI) Health and Environmental Sciences Institute (HESI) Genetic Toxicology Technical Committee (GTTC). The final goal is to provide number-based data to model the possible risk levels of substances, which cause gene-related damage adding to human harmful health outcomes. Any good risk measurement begins with asking the right risk management questions in a planning and scoping effort. This step sets up the problem to be dealt with (for example, broadly, does gene-related damage need to be dealt with, and if so, how to move forward). The next two steps bring together what is known about the problem by building a knowledge base about the substance of concern and developing a sensible biological argument for why testing for gene-related damage is needed or not. By focusing on the risk management problem and possible gene-related damage of concern, the next step of test selection takes place. The work-up of the problem during the earlier steps provides the understanding to which tests would most likely produce the most meaningful data. This discussion does not detail the wide range of gene-related damage tests available, but points to types of testing systems that can be very useful. Once the tests are performed and looked at, the related data sets are selected for modeling possible risk. From this point on, the data are reviewed and modeled as they are for any other harmfulness study endpoint. Any observed gene-related damage or effects (or genetic event or events) can be modeled through a dose-response study and finding of an estimated PoD. When a number-based risk study is needed for decision making, a side-by-side contact measurement effort is performed (contact measurement is not detailed here as this is not the focus of this discussion; guidelines for this measurement exist elsewhere). Then the PoD for gene-related damage is used with the contact information to develop risk guesses (for example, using reference dose (RfD), margin of exposure (MOE) approaches) in a risk description and presented to risk managers for helping decision making. This approach is usable now for bringing in gene-related damage results into the decision-making process for measuring possible harmful outcomes in chemically exposed humans and is in line with the ILSI HESI Risk Assessment in the 21st Century (RISK21) roadmap. This applies to any substance to which humans are exposed, including drugs, farming products, food additives, and other chemicals. It is time for government bodies to bring in the broader knowledge and understandings provided by gene-related damage results into the measurements of risk to more fully understand the possibility of harmful outcomes in chemically exposed humans, thus improving the measurement of risk due to gene-related damage. The past use of gene-related damage data as a yes or no gateway for possible cancer risk has been too narrowly focused in risk measurement. The recent advances in checking for and understanding gene-related damage, including in the future changes in gene expression without DNA changes, obviously add a greater wealth of information for deciding possible risk to humans. Government bodies need to embrace this major change in thinking from danger identification to number-based study and to bring in the wider range of gene-related damage in their measurements of risk to humans. The number-based studies and ways of working discussed here can be easily applied to gene-related damage testing results now. Indeed, with the passage of the recent update to the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) in the US, the new generation testing plan for gene-related damage described here provides a government agency (here the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), but suitable for others) a golden opportunity to look again at the way it deals with risk-based gene-related damage testing (including danger identification and contact with substances). Environ. Mol. Mutagen. 58:264-283, 2017. © 2016 The Authors. Environmental and Molecular Mutagenesis Published by Wiley Periodicals, Inc.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::1: Food supplements may improve development of babies born small (early or small for pregnancy age [SGA]) but may increase the risk of later body chemical disease. We did a careful review and combined study to judge the effects of large food part supplements for babies born small on later development and body chemistry. We searched OvidMedline, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Cochrane Database of Careful Reviews from beginning to April 1, 2019, and controlled-trials.com, clinicaltrials.gov, and anzctr.org.au. Random or almost random trials were included if the plan was to increase large food part intake to improve growth or development of babies born small and measured after-hospital outcomes. Main outcomes were thinking damage and body chemical risk, looked at in young children (less than 3 years), childhood (3 to 8 years), and teenage years (9 to 18 years). Two reviewers separately took out data. Quality was judged using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and data were brought together using random-effect models. Twenty-one random and one almost random trial of different method quality involving 3,680 babies were included. In young children born small, extra food did not change thinking damage (relative risk [RR] 1.00; 95% confidence range [CI] 0.67 to 1.49; P = 0.99), and there were no differences in thinking scores (mean difference [MD] 0.57; 95% CI -0.71 to 1.84; P = 0.38) or movement scores (MD 1.16; 95% CI -0.32 to 2.65; P = 0.12) between extra food and no extra food groups. However, fewer children with extra food had movement damage (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; P = 0.01). In smaller group studies, extra food improved thinking scores in boys (MD 5.60; 95% CI 1.07 to 10.14; P = 0.02), but not girls born small (MD -2.04; 95% CI -7.04 to 2.95; P = 0.42), and did not change thinking or movement scores in the smaller group of children born SGA. In childhood, there was no difference in thinking damage (RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.26 to 2.57; P = 0.72) or thinking scores (MD 1.02; 95% CI -1.91 to 3.95; P = 0.50) between extra food and no extra food groups. There were also no differences in blood pressure, fat in blood, and low-quality fat carrier (LDL) amounts (all P greater than 0.05). However, children with extra food had lower no-food blood sugar (mmol/L: MD -0.20; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.06; P = 0.005) and higher high-quality fat carrier (HDL) amounts (mmol/L: MD 0.11; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19; P = 0.02). In smaller group studies, there was no sign of differences in blood pressure between extra food and no extra food groups in boys or girls born small, or in SGA children. In teenage years, there was no difference between extra food and no extra food groups in blood pressure, fats in blood, LDL and HDL amounts, no-food blood sugar, sugar resistance, and no-food body sugar control chemical amounts (all P greater than 0.05). Limits include large unexplained differences, low to very low quality of the facts, and small data beyond early childhood. In this careful review and combined study of random trials, we found no sign that early large food part extra food for babies born small changed later thinking function, although there was some sign that extra food may decrease movement damage in young children. Opposite to the findings from watching studies, facts from random trials suggest that early large food part extra food for babies born small improves some body chemical outcomes in childhood. words_common_s.academic_abstracts::2: Goals Recently, two bedside (PoC) cat disease (FIV) antibody test kits (Witness and Anigen Rapid) were reported as being able to tell apart FIV-vaccinated from FIV-infected cats at a single time point, regardless of the gap between testing and last vaccination (0-7 years). The aim of the current study was to look at carefully anti-FIV antibody production over time in response to the recommended primary FIV vaccination series. Methods First, leftover plasma from the original study was tested using a laboratory-based ELISA to find out whether negative results with PoC testing were due to reduced as opposed to absent antibodies to gp40. Second, a forward-looking study was performed using never-exposed client-owned kittens and cats given a primary FIV vaccination series using a store-bought killed whole cell/killed whole virus vaccine (Fel-O-Vax FIV, three under-the-skin injections at 4 week breaks) and tested carefully (up to 11 times) over 6 months, using four store-bought PoC FIV antibody kits (SNAP FIV/FeLV Combo [finds antibodies to p15/p24], Witness FeLV/FIV [gp40], Anigen Rapid FIV/FeLV [p24/gp40] and VetScan FeLV/FIV Rapid [p24]). Results The laboratory-based ELISA showed cats from the original study vaccinated within the previous 0-15 months had findable levels of antibodies to gp40, despite testing negative with two kits that use gp40 as a capture substance (Witness and Anigen Rapid kits). The forward-looking study showed that antibody testing with SNAP Combo and VetScan Rapid was positive in all cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination, and remained positive for the length of the study (12/12 and 10/12 cats positive, in that order). Antibody testing with Witness and Anigen Rapid was also positive in a high share of cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination (8/12 and 7/12, in that order), but antibody levels dropped below the level of finding in most cats (10/12) by 1 month after the third (final) primary FIV vaccination. All cats tested negative using Witness and Anigen Rapid 6 months after the third primary FIV vaccination. Endings and meaning This study has shown that a primary course of FIV vaccination does not get in the way of FIV antibody testing in cats using Witness and Anigen Rapid, provided primary vaccination has not happened within the previous 6 months. As a result, Witness and Anigen Rapid antibody test kits can be used safely to find out FIV infection status at the time of yearly booster FIV vaccination to help find 'vaccine breakthroughs' and in cats that have not received a primary course of FIV vaccination within the going before 6 months. The length of antibody response following yearly booster FIV vaccination and the resulting effect on antibody testing using PoC kits needs to be found out by further research. The reason(s) for the difference in FIV antibody test kit performance remains unclear.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::3: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare single-gene disorder marked by non-cancerous tumors in many organs as well as a high rate of epilepsy, thinking disability and autism. TSC is caused by damaging changes in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Having one changed gene causes overactivity of mTOR which can be blocked by mTOR blockers, such as rapamycin, which have proven effectiveness in the treatment of TSC-related symptoms. The aim of the present study was (1) to identify molecular changes linked with social and thinking problems in the brain tissue of Tsc1 +/- mice and (2) to look at the molecular effects of rapamycin treatment, which has been shown to improve gene-related behaviour problems. Molecular changes in the frontal cortex and hippocampus of Tsc1 +/- and control mice, with or without rapamycin treatment, were looked at. A number-based mass measurement shotgun protein approach (LC-MS E ) was used as an unbiased method to detect changes in protein levels. Changes identified in the initial profiling stage were confirmed using selected reaction watching (SRM). Protein Set Enrichment Analysis was used to identify badly working pathways. LC-MS E analysis of Tsc1 +/- mice and controls ( n = 30) identified 51 proteins changed in frontal cortex and 108 in the hippocampus. Computer analysis combined with targeted protein confirmation revealed several badly working molecular pathways. Using targeted tests, protein changes in the hippocampus confirmed the pathways "myelination", "dendrite," and "damaging stress", an increase of ribosomal proteins and the mTOR kinase. LC-MS E analysis was also used on Tsc1 +/- and wildtype mice ( n = 34) treated with rapamycin or vehicle. Rapamycin treatment had a stronger protein effect in Tsc1 +/- mice with important changes (mainly decreased presence) in 231 and 106 proteins, each one. The cell pathways "damaging stress" and "cell death" were found to be affected in Tsc1 +/- mice and the cell parts "myelin sheet" and "neurofilaments" were affected by rapamycin treatment. Thirty-three proteins which were changed in Tsc1 +/- mice were brought back to normal following rapamycin treatment, amongst them damaging stress related proteins, myelin-specific and ribosomal proteins. Molecular changes in the Tsc1 +/- mouse brain were more noticeable in the hippocampus compared to the frontal cortex. Pathways linked to myelination and damaging stress response were strongly affected and, at least in part, brought back to normal following rapamycin treatment. The results could help in the finding of new drug targets for the treatment of thinking, social and mental symptoms in autism spectrum disorders. Similar pathways have also been involved in other mental and brain-damaging disorders and could suggest similar disease processes. Thus, the possible effectiveness of mTOR blockers deserves further study not only for autism spectrum disorders but also for other mental and brain-damaging diseases.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::4: Silica nanoparticles (nanoSiO 2 ) are promising systems that can deliver biologically active compounds to tissues such as the heart in a controllable manner. However, heart poisoning caused by nanoSiO 2 has been recently related to unusual calcium handling and energy failure in heart muscle cells. Moreover, the exact ways behind this energy breakdown remain unclear. In order to explain these ways, this article explores the outside the body heart function and mitochondria after exposure to nanoSiO 2 . The building up administration of nanoSiO 2 reduced the mechanical performance measure of the rat heart with a half-greatest blocking concentration (IC 50 ) of 93 μg/mL, affecting the relaxation rate. In separated mitochondria nanoSiO 2 was found to be taken inside, blocking oxygen-based energy production and greatly reducing the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m ). The mitochondrial opening change pore (mPTP) was also caused with an increasing dose of nanoSiO 2 and partly recovered with, a powerful blocker of the mPTP, Cyclosporine A (CsA). The activity of aconitase and thiol change, in the adenine nucleotide translocase, were found to be reduced because of nanoSiO 2 exposure, suggesting that nanoSiO 2 causes the mPTP through thiol change and ROS production. In heart cells exposed to nanoSiO 2 , improved ability to survive and reduction of H 2 O 2 were seen after use of a specific mitochondrial substance that fights damage, MitoTEMPO. At the same time, CsA treatment in adult rat heart cells reduced the nanoSiO 2 -caused cell death and recovered ATP production (from 32.4 to 65.4%). Also, we performed checking of the mitochondrial effect of nanoSiO 2 in human heart muscle cells. We saw a 40% blocking of greatest oxygen use rate in mitochondria at 500 μg/mL. Under this condition we found a remarkable lowering in the spare breathing capacity. This information shows that a reduction in the amount of extra ATP that can be made by mitochondria during a sudden increase in energy demand. In human heart muscle cells, increased LDH release and tissue death were found at increased doses of nanoSiO 2 , reaching 85 and 48%, in that order. Such harmful effects were partly stopped by the use of CsA. Therefore, exposure to nanoSiO 2 affects heart function through mitochondrial problems through the opening of the mPTP. The mentioned effects can be partly avoided reducing ROS or slowing down the opening of the mPTP. These new approaches which resulted in heart protection could be thought about as possible treatments to lower the side effects of nanoSiO 2 exposure.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::5: Return to play (RTP) of National Football League (NFL) athletes after single anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears has been reported. However, no studies have reported on RTP of NFL athletes after multiple ligament knee injuries. NFL athletes with multiple ligament knee injuries have lower RTP rates and longer recoveries than athletes with single ACL tears. Second, athletes with ACL and medial collateral ligament (MCL) injuries will have higher RTP rates and shorter time to RTP than athletes with an ACL tear and back outer corner involvement. Looking back group study. Level 4. Publicly available NFL injury data were reviewed for all multiple ligament knee injuries that happened between 2000 and 2016 with RTP information. Athletes were left out if RTP was limited for reasons not connected to the injury. Collected data included type of injury, RTP, time to RTP (days), number and percentage of games played, and performance. A total of 50 NFL athletes with multiple ligament knee injuries met the requirements for being included and left out. The overall RTP rate was 64.0%. Athletes with ACL/MCL tears had an RTP rate of 70.8%, whereas athletes with ACL and posterior collateral ligament/lateral collateral ligament (PCL/LCL) tears had an RTP rate of 55.6% ( P = 0.26). Average time to RTP for all 50 athletes was 388.71 ± 198.52 days. The average time to RTP for athletes with ACL/MCL injuries was 305.1 ± 58.9 days, compared with 459.2 ± 245.1 days ( P = 0.004) and 609.3 ± 183.1 days ( P < 0.0001) for those with combined ACL and PCL/LCL injuries and complete knee dislocations, in that order. Athletes with ACL/MCL injuries were more likely to return to earlier performance level (43.5%) than those with ACL and PCL/LCL injuries (18.5%) ( P < 0.001). The RTP rate for athletes with multiple ligament knee injuries is much less than the RTP rate for athletes with single ACL tears. In addition, athletes with ACL and MCL tears have a higher RTP rate, a much shorter time to RTP, and a greater chance of returning to earlier performance than athletes with ACL and PCL/LCL tears. Multiple ligament knee injuries greatly affect the ability of a football player to return to sport. ACL and MCL tears are connected with better RTP outlook compared with ACL and PCL/LCL tears.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::6: High blood pressure in the lungs in response to exercise is a sign of the blood flow seriousness of mitral narrowing (MS). However, the things related to raised lung pressure with exercise are not well understood. The aim of this study was to measure the features connected with the lung pressure response to exercise in patients with pure rheumatic MS. An additional aim was to find out the effect of exercise-caused high blood pressure in the lungs on medical outcome. One hundred thirty patients with MS (94% women; mean age, 45 ± 11 years) went through exercise heart imaging. A range of heart imaging measurements were collected at rest and at top exercise. Symptom-limited stepped ramp bicycle exercise was done in the lying-back position. The main end point was mitral valve treatment, either through-the-skin or surgical. In the overall group, pumping lung artery pressure (SPAP) went up from 38.3 ± 13.4 mm Hg at rest to 65.8 ± 20.7 mm Hg during exercise. Increases in average mitral difference, right heart pumping chamber function, left upper heart chamber size, and net between-chamber flexibility were separately connected with SPAP at top exercise, after correcting for changes in heart rate. During the follow-up time (middle value, 17 months; range, 1-45 months), 46 harmful medical events were seen. By multiple-factor analysis method corrected for age and sex, SPAP reached at top exercise was an important predictor of harmful outcome (corrected danger ratio, 1.025; 95% CI, 1.010-1.040; P = .001). New York Heart Group working class (corrected danger ratio, 2.459; 95% CI, 1.509-4.006; P < .001) and the working together between valve opening and net between-chamber flexibility (P = .001) were also meaningful predictors of harmful events. Time-related areas under the receiver working feature curve for the model with SPAP during exercise were better than for the model with SPAP at rest, with a meaningful improvement from 3 years onward. In patients with MS, the lung artery pressure response to exercise is decided by a combination of things, including across-mitral mean difference at exercise, net between-chamber flexibility, left upper heart chamber size, and right heart pumping chamber function. Lung artery pressure at top exercise is a predictor of medical outcomes and adds step-by-step prediction value beyond that given by standard resting measurements, including valve opening.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::7: The effect of long-term liver disease on results in patients with COVID-19 is not clear. So, we wanted to look at this connection. We looked at the results of all adult hospital patients with COVID-19 in France, in 2020. We calculated adjusted odds ratios to measure the connections between long-term liver disease, alcohol use problems, breathing machine use and day-30 in-hospital death. The group included 259,110 patients (middle [IQR] age 70 (54-83) years; 52% men), including 15,476 (6.0%) and 10,006 (3.9%) patients with long-term liver disease and alcohol use problems, in that order. Death happened in 38,203 (15%) patients, including 7,475 (28%) after breathing machine use, and 2,941 (19%) with long-term liver disease. The adjusted odds ratios for breathing machine use and day-30 death were 1.54 (95% CI 1.44-1.64, p <0.001) and 1.79 (1.71-1.87, p <0.001) for long-term liver disease; 0.55 (0.47-0.64, p <0.001) and 0.54 (0.48-0.61, p <0.001) for mild liver disease; 0.64 (0.53-0.76; p <0.001) and 0.71 (0.63-0.80, p <0.001) for stable cirrhosis; 0.65 (0.52-0.81, p <0.001) and 2.21 (1.94-2.51, p <0.001) for unstable cirrhosis; 0.34 (0.24-0.50; p <0.001) and 1.38 (1.17-1.62, p <0.001) for main liver cancer; and 0.82 (0.76-0.89; p <0.001) and 1.11 (1.05-1.17; p <0.001) for alcohol use problems. Long-term viral liver swelling; non-viral, non-alcohol long-term liver swelling; organ, including liver, moving from one body to another, and acquired immune weakness condition were not connected with COVID-19-related death. Long-term liver disease raised the risk of COVID-19-related death in France in 2020. Treatment effort limits may have played a role in COVID-19-related death in French people with a liver-related problem or an alcohol use problem. We studied the results, including breathing machine use and day-30 death, of all adults with COVID-19 who were sent home from short-term and after-care in France in 2020 (N = 259,110). Patients with mild liver disease; stable cirrhosis; organ, including liver, moving from one body to another; or acquired immune weakness condition were not at raised risk of COVID-19-related death. Patients with alcohol use problems, unstable cirrhosis, or main liver cancer were at raised risk of COVID-19-related death but were less likely to receive breathing machine use. Our results point to the idea that treatment effort limits may have played a role in the extra deaths in French people with a liver-related problem or an alcohol use problem.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::8: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute breathing illness coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to a large number of deaths worldwide. COVID-19 creates a serious danger to human life. The health signs of COVID-19 are different and serious and 20% of sick patients are reported to be in a very bad condition. A loss in lung function and lung scarring are the main problems of patients with the serious form of the disease. The lung function is harmed, even after getting better, which greatly affects the mental state and health of patients, and greatly reduces their quality of life. People in the study must meet the following conditions at the same time: over 18 years of age, should have gotten better from serious or very bad COVID-19 cases, should show lung scarring after getting better, and should show Qi-Yin shortage problem as shown in the system of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). The people who can join will be placed randomly into treatment or control groups. The treatment group will receive modern medicine (pirfenidone) plus TCM whereas the control group will be given modern medicine plus TCM fake treatment. The lung function measure will be watched over time and written down. By looking at the treatment result between the two groups, the study wants to find out whether TCM can improve the strength of modern medicine in patients with lung scarring happening as a lasting problem after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Lung scarring is one of deadly lasting problems for some serious or very bad COVID-19 cases, some studies show that pirfenidone leads to a delay in the drop of forced breathing out ability, which reduces the death rate partly. Also, although TCM has been shown to be helpful in treating lung scarring, its role in treating lung scarring related to COVID-19 has not been looked at. So, a many-center, side-by-side-group, randomly controlled, action-based, forward-looking medical trial has been planned and will be done to find out if a new complete treatment for lung scarring related to COVID-19 is possible and if it can improve the quality of life of patients. This many-center, side-by-side-group, randomly controlled, action-based, forward-looking trial was recorded at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000033284) on 26th May 2020 (forward-looking recorded).
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::9: Temperature and water availability are two of the most important things affecting all parts of a frog's key body processes such as body temperature ( T b ), water loss through the skin (EWL) and standard rate of energy use (SMR). Since frogs show clear differences between males and females, evidence suggests that these processes are further affected by other things such as the dryness of the air (VPD), sex and body weight ( M b ). However, only a small number of studies have tested whether these results hold true across a wide range of surrounding temperatures ( T a ) that matter in nature, while taking where animals live into account. Thus, the aim of this study was to look at the role of T a on T b , whole-animal EWL and whole-animal SMR in three wild caught African frog species with different ways of living in their surroundings: the mainly water-dwelling African clawed frog ( Xenopus laevis ), stream-breeding common river frog ( Amietia delalandii ), and the mostly land-dwelling raucous toad ( Sclerophrys capensis ). Tests were done at a range of test temperatures (5-35 °C, at 5 °C steps). We found that VPD better predicted rates of EWL than T a in two of the three species looked at. What is more, we found that T b , whole-animal EWL and whole-animal SMR increased with increasing T a , while T b increased with increasing M b in A. delalandii and S. capensis but not in X. laevis . Whole-animal SMR increased with increasing M b in S. capensis only. We did not find any clear effect of VPD, M b or sex on whole-animal EWL within species. Lastly, M b did not affect T b , whole-animal SMR and EWL in the mainly water-dwelling X. laevis . These results suggest that M b may not have the same effect on key body-related things, and that the effect of M b may also depend on the species way of living in its surroundings. Thus, whether M b is an important thing should be understood in the setting of both body processes and species living place preferences and habits.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::10: Chronotaraxis is a problem with how people sense the order of time. This change in how time feels has been described as being typically linked with damage to the thalamus, more exactly in the dorsomedial part. We report the medical cases of two patients with sudden blocked blood flow strokes located in that area, with a medical appearance based on this sign and the noticing of which was needed in the treatment method. In the first and second cases, it is described how the sense of how time feels was needed for the finding of the blocked blood flow condition in both patients. Knowledge and spreading of this link may be very important in the care of patients with thalamus problems. This is because of the chance of affecting and changing the first treatment method, since the noticing of a particular sign, such as chronotaraxis, can stop the spreading of thalamus damage, in addition to the long-term problems that it causes, particularly those of a thinking nature. Cronotaraxis como síntoma guía de un infarto talámico medial. Introducción. La cronotaraxis es una afectación de la percepción de la secuencia temporal. Esta alteración de la temporalidad se ha descrito asociada de forma característica a la afectación talámica, concretamente al núcleo dorsomediano. Casos clínicos. Presentamos los casos clínicos de dos pacientes con ictus isquémicos agudos de localización en dicho territorio, con una clínica basada en este síntoma y cuyo reconocimiento resultó esencial en el abordaje terapéutico. Tanto en el primero como en el segundo caso se describe cómo la percepción de la temporalidad fue esencial para el diagnóstico de la patología isquémica de ambos pacientes. Discusión. El conocimiento y la divulgación de esta asociación pueden resultar fundamentales en el manejo de los pacientes con alteraciones talámicas. Esto se debe a la posibilidad que surge de influir y modificar el abordaje inicial, puesto que el reconocimiento de un síntoma específico, como es la cronotaraxis, puede evitar la extensión del daño talámico, y prevenir de esta manera las secuelas, sobre todo cognitivas, que ocasiona a largo plazo.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::11: Some catching diseases, such as flu, tuberculosis, and SARS-CoV-2, may be passed on when virus-carrying bits pushed out from a sick person are breathed in by someone else, which is known as the airborne passing-on route. These virus-carrying bits are more packed together in the breathing-out stream of a sick person than elsewhere in a well-mixed room, but this close-by increase in virus contact has not been well measured. Passing on of airborne viruses depends on things that are naturally changing and, in many cases, poorly limited, and measuring this uncertainty needs large groups of model runs that cover the changing nature in starting information. However, models that are well-suited to copy the close-by change of breathing bits are also expensive in terms of computer power, which limits the looking into of information uncertainty. In order to perform many runs that cover the wide changing nature in things controlling airborne passing-on, we built the Quadrature-based model of Respiratory Aerosol and Droplets, which we call QuaRAD. QuaRAD is an effective working structure for copying the change of virus-carrying bits after they are pushed out from a sick person, their landing to the nose hole of a person who can catch it, and the following risk of first infection. We copied ten thousand different situations to measure the risk of first infection by a particular virus, SARS-CoV-2. The predicted risk of infection was highly changing among situations and, in each situation, was strongly increased near the sick person. In more than fifty percent of situations, the physical keeping apart needed to avoid close-by increases in airborne passing-on was beyond the recommended safe distance of two meters, which is six feet, if the sick person is not wearing a mask, though this distance marking the close-by reach was also highly changing among situations; the changing nature in the close-by reach is explained mainly by changing nature in breathing-out speed. Our findings suggest that keeping at least two meters of distance from a sick person greatly reduces contact with airborne viruses; guards against airborne passing-on, such as N95 breathing masks, should be available when keeping apart is not possible.
words_common_s.academic_abstracts::12: Open fractures are dirty wounds that contain two types of germs called gram-positive and gram-negative organisms; therefore, broad-range antibiotic treatment should be included in the treatment plan. Antibiotics should be started as soon after injury as possible, preferably within 3 hours of injury, after which time the rate of infection has been reported to increase. Time to surgical cleaning within 12 hours of injury has not been reported to affect the rate of infection, given that a patient is being treated with antibiotics. An antibiotic bead pouch and vacuum-helped wound closure may help reduce the risk for secondary and hospital-acquired dirt and later infection. Open fractures are always connected with a soft-tissue injury; therefore, they can be thought of as a soft-tissue injury that involves a fracture. The management of the bone and the soft tissues in a patient with an open fracture is the major factor in fracture healing and functional restoration of the injured arm or leg. The creation of a soft-tissue treatment plan must occur during the initial wound check and the initial fixing of an open fracture and should not be thought of as a secondary or following process. A soft-tissue surgeon should be called the night of the injury. Selection of fracture fixing depends on the broken bone, the location of the fracture, which could be inside the joint, near the joint, or in the shaft of the bone, the amount of soft-tissue injury and dirt, and the body condition of the patient.
