"Hey, check out that chickadees over in the birdbath." Kylo shouted and puffed out his chest, nearly falling off his perch.

"Don't be a cave-dweller, bro," Atticus complained, pecking at his seeds, "You're a wren. That isn't even the same family."

"I don't care. I'm gonna go talk to them." Kylo took off, turning through the air like a leaf trapped in a wind. Atticus sighed and took off after him. He'd have to keep close watch on Kylo or else they'd get kicked out again.

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash. Drops flew in every direction, soaking the birds in the birdbath. They squawked with anger as Kylo came up from beneath the surface, shaking the wetness from his head. He walked up to a group of soaked finches and gave his wings a shake. "Hey, birds. Nice tits."

"We're not tits." A purple finch stepped forward from the group, and she started a long angry speech on how overused that pickup line was. Atticus landed on the rim of the bath and began to walk around, saying sorry to everyone for Kylo's behavior and begging them not to call the bouncer over.

"Okay, sorry," Kylo interrupted, "let me make it up to you: how about you and I head over there—" He pointed to the bird feeder. "—and I share my seeds with you?" If birds had lips, Kylo would be smiling in a cocky way right now.

The finches began to flap their wings angrily, splashing Kylo with water. "You're such a rude jerk. Get out of here!" Many of the watchers chirped in agreement, and some of the bigger birds began to puff their chests in a threatening way. Atticus shoved Kylo to the side and raised his wings. "On behalf of my friend here, I apologize. He's clearly had too much nectar; we'll just be going now..."

"Oh, you think we're going to fall for that?" The purple finch spat a nut shell at his feet. "He's just trying to play wingbird for you, isn't he? Let him take the fall for you, and swoop in to look better by comparison." The other birds sang out in agreement.

"I think these two need to be taught a lesson." A blue jay flew over to Atticus, standing a full inch above him. He spread his wings in a threatening way, blocking Atticus from taking off. "Why don't you peck on someone your own size?" The watchers broke into cheers, shouting for a fight.

"Well, you're kind of bigger than me." Atticus took a step back into the bath. He felt feathers brush against him as the crowd pressed around him, pushed him back towards the jay. "That wouldn't be my own size now, would it?"

Kylo walked unsteadily in front of him and began to hop around. "Don't worry, Atticus; we got this."

"Hey, this is a one-on-one fight." The jay looked around. "If you get back-up, then—"

"Who on earth placed all this here?" A door opened, and the birds began to scatter, screaming, "Human!" Atticus grabbed Kylo and pushed him into the air, and the two lost themselves among the cloud of running birds. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw the human scratching his head in front of the birdbath.

"Make sure to thank that human for saving you from yet another mess," Atticus said.

Kylo laughed in a mocking way. "We could've totally taken that guy." As the two flew over the Toyota in the driveway, he let loose a dropping that landed right in the center of the windshield.
words_common_s.writingprompts::37:
He used to hit me so much.

I'd never even had a drink, and he beat broken ribs, hurt kidneys and loose teeth into me. To make sure I never became what he was.

Once when he was not drunk he told me he drank because of how he grew up. He said it like he wanted me to understand him, to forgive him. Like he couldn't see that my arm was broken from him protecting me from drink the week before. Like he couldn't see himself standing over me crying blood and snot and tears, making fun of me. Like he couldn't remember what was so bad about how he grew up, couldn't remember why he needed it to let him sleep at night, to stop waking up screaming in the night, to stop wetting himself when he had a bad dream.

He made me sick, my dad. My breath catches sometimes, and one of my wrists never healed right, leaving me half unable to use that hand. I have eleven fake teeth. At twenty three, all this.

I didn't go to his funeral, I celebrated it though. I didn't take a drink though, I could never do that. I cry myself to sleep most nights, I can't help myself screaming if someone comes up to me suddenly. Lately I've noticed a lot of blood coming up when I cough. I won't let him beat me though, I won't give him this little victory.

When my son was born it was the happiest day of my life. For the first time in my life, someone wanted and needed me. His mother left soon after that, saying she didn't want to be trapped in a way of living she didn't choose, after carrying a child for nine months, she leaves it in three weeks. Never in those nine months did she not choose that way of living.

Honestly, after she left it all got too much for me. I left my son with my mother for the night, and went and had a drink. It was perfect. It was the best I've felt in my whole life. For a few hours, I wasn't scared or hating myself or on edge. Just calm and ok, I could deal with everything a little better. I think I'll probably have a few more now, just to keep the good feeling going. Being sober now scares me even more, now that I know that there's such an easy other choice, which is so much better.

When I picked my son up in the morning mom looked at me funny, but I ignored her. I was in a bit of a rush, I'd heard good things about whisky, and was wanting to try it.

But don't worry, I won't let my son grow up like I did, I'll make sure he knows alcohol is evil. I won't put him through that pain, to that fear. I'll make sure he hates me for as long as possible as much as possible. He'll connect alcohol with me, and I'm bad, so he'll break the cycle. I'm not strong enough, but he will be. I know he'll be strong enough. I'll make him tough enough outside, and cold and hard enough inside. He'll be able to beat it. Like I can't.
words_common_s.writingprompts::38:
Craig was walking home from the shops when he met God. He wasn't expecting to run into God, normal people rarely do. In fact he didn't really ever think about God. He didn't believe in a God, but he also didn't disbelieve enough to ever think about Gods not existing. Religion and God weren't really topics he cared about.

A topic he cared deeply about was that of Caramels. If you don't know Caramels are a rather delicious chocolatey biscuit type thing made of several layers of wafer covered in chocolate, and Craig was crazy about them. He may not have been religious, but his feelings on Caramels came close. The reason behind his trip to the shops was to buy more Caramels, and his mind was full of looking forward to them as he headed back home.

He was about two minutes away from his home, and Caramel happiness when God first spoke to him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His Caramel thinking interrupted, Craig turned round to see who had spoken to him. Behind him stood a tall person in a loose fitting suit. Craig wasn't really sure of the person's sex, they were pretty neither male nor female, looking not different to Diamond Dogs time David Bowie. They looked familiar to Craig, but he couldn't quite put his finger on where he might have seen them before. He understood he'd been staring, and looked for something to say.

"Hi," he began slowly and carefully. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," replied the Bowie lookalike. "I'm God."

"Well good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye." Said Craig before starting back towards his house. He had Caramels in his bag, and didn't want to be wasting time on a crazy person.

"Wait, don't go yet. Please." Called out the person. "What would it take for you to believe me?"

Craig let out a breath and turned back, deciding that playing along with the person would probably get him to his Caramels faster.

"I don't know," said Craig, tired and annoyed. "A miracle or something. Some special thing which couldn't just be done by any old person. Something more than just saying that you're god."

"Hmm. How about....*this*!" God pointed at a bush which burst into flames. The fire shaped itself into a dragon which roared at the two of them. Then, with a snap of God's fingers, the fire was put out leaving the bush burned but still whole. God turned back to Craig with arms spread wide as if to say'Tada!'

Craig, looking mildly impressed, turned back to God.

"Yeah, that was pretty good. Looked very impressive. I have to admit I have no idea how you did it. A fake three dimensional image maybe? It worked for Tupac, so I can see it working for a dragon."

God stared at him for a few seconds before responding.

"I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle. I showed you one. What more do you want from me?"

"Don't get me wrong, it's very good. But the whole God thing probably isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you're a wizard."

"But I'm not a damn wizard!" Shouted God. "I'm God. Why would I say I'm a wizard?"

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in front of him in the worldwide sign of'I don't want any trouble, let's all just calm down'.

"Hey calm down buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh, but it's just helpful advice to make things better. This is for a T.V. show or YouTube thing right? You're not going to get anyone with the whole'God' thing."

God, clearly angry and upset by this point, held Craig's look for a few more seconds before letting out an angry breath and walking off quickly in anger.

Craig watched them leave, then shook his head and returned to his journey. He thought about checking out the bush to see if he could get any hints as to how the trick had been done, but decided against it. Whoever had been recording the meeting was probably still watching, waiting for Craig to do exactly that. So he pushed it out of his mind, and set off home. After all, there were Caramels waiting for him.
words_common_s.writingprompts::39:
"Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy?" 
 
 "Get it yourself, Ser Whyte. I'm not your bloody helper no more." 
 
 "Right. Well then, my lord. Would you do me the honor of getting me my wine so I can die drunk and happy?" 
 
 "As you wish, sir-knight." 
 
 "I hate you, Patsy." 
 
 The bed-stuck shell of a former knight let out a harsh cough. His rusty suit of white armor made noisy metal sounds as he jerked up hard. Dirty, gray hair shot up in an instant. Still choking and coughing, he drank down the little glass bottle of wine in his hand. The burp was loud as the lightning's thunder, striking down on a rainy night. 
 
 Next to him, there sat a young man. A little silver crown, broken and beaten from torn away jewels, sat upon his short locks of brown. Deep green eyes, far too young to know what it means to rule, look down upon the Knight Whyte. His knight. 
 
 "Tell me." The knight's arm, weak and tired, placed his bottle on the bedside. "How is Isabella doing? I haven't been able to get a letter from you for months." 
 
 "We've shut down the mail service, remember? The delivery service handles delivery for boxes, but messages go through that fancy message-by-wire system." 
 
 "Hah. What an age your kingdom has come to. Weapons that shoot steel and fire. Writers who control entire towns. Pretty soon, even my kind will be out of work." 
 
 The king laughed, though it sounded forced and awkward through his lips. He had no need for knights anymore. Neither did any nearby kingdom. They were now just old things. Old things that talked and drank and fought. No, war in this time was decided by how much gold you could carry, how many people you could take, and how many flags you can put on some hill. 
 
 "What's with that look, king? Has that queen kicked you out of your castle again? You're more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here. Just remember to clean the dead bodies out from their beds." 
 
 "That's a terrible joke, Whyte." 
 
 "So, we're dropping the titles? I don't think we need another repeat of Georgie bringing about another uprising. The head-cutting machines, they were only a little uncomfortable." 
 
 "A little?" 
 
 "A little." 
 
 The rain outside appeared to stop, the lightning-storm ended in its steps. The king got up to the window edge to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time. 
 
 "Hmm. You see that, Whyte?" 
 
 The knight in rusting armor had gotten up out of his bed, placing his brownish-orange metal gloves on the young king's shoulder. A rush of wind came blowing through, slapping its cold blanket of winter wind against the faces of the two men. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who answered in kind. With wet eyes, the young man turned to the knight. 
 
 "How strange. I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this." 
 
 "And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too." 
 
 "I'm glad to have called you my knight." 
 
 "And you my king." 
 
 The knight turned back to his bed. His legs suddenly shook with a wild force, sending him down to the hard wood floor. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised glove, still reddish-brown and faded. With a great effort, the knight made it to his bed, taking his gloves off and throwing them right out the window opening. 
 
 "I guess it's about time I've gotten rid of those. Too old for me." 
 
 "I've seen older. Take a look at the man who wore them." 
 
 "You always were a bold little patsy." Skin falls over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink. "I grow tired. Would you tell me a story?" 
 
 "What am I, your mother?" 
 
 "Just tell me that story." 
 
 "That story. Yes, after all, we only know that one story." 
 
 "Don't play cute with me, Patsy." 
 
 "Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after?" 
 
 The king breathed out, taking a knee on the side of the bed. The knight smiled, eyelids finally falling over his eyes. Hands held together over his chest as the beating of the heart grew slow. The winter cold must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold. Through hot tears, the king began speaking the words of the story they both knew so well. 
 
 "Once upon a time, in a village far, far away..."

One metre high and as wide across, the blackened and dusty car roared down the desert road. Ahead ran the group with their tank of helium, the motorized unicycle blazing as they tried in vain to stay ahead of Kinko. The fifteen clowns inside readied their weapons as they closed fast upon their rivals on the unicycle ahead.

"Boffo, Luffy, Bobo," grated Kinko, "fucking clowns fucked with us for the last fucking time. When we catch up to those assholes, I want you to fucking *whitewash* their asses. Fuck them up *so bad* that they can honk their noses from the *inside*." They nodded, and gripped their slapsticks all the tighter.

With a roar, the car pulled ahead of the clowns in front and slid to a halt. The doors opened in unison and the fifteen of them tumbled out and rolled to their feet. Two of them grabbed the weaponized ladder from the roof, knocking over another three as they stood readying their automatic pielaunchers - and the same three again as the original two turned to see what they hit. Two others ran into each other and fell to the ground, stretched out and still. To one side, Bobo and Kinko lifted their pails of custard, and started towards the unicycle.

"Bastards!" screamed a whitefaced warrior as she fell from the shoulders of the topmost clown. Rolling as she landed, she sprayed a stream of water from the flower on her lapel, knocking Kinko to the ground with a highly amusing 'parp!'. Grabbing a rubber chicken from the driver, she waded into the fray, knocking Kinko's clowns over like bowling pins. "That helium is *ours!*"

"The hell it is!" roared Luffy, pulling the pin on his rubber nose before tossing it at the jokers falling from the unicycle seat. "That helium is *ours*, for *our* balloons! Balloon zoos are *ours*, you hear? ***Ours!***" Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo upended the bucket of custard into them before pushing her to the ground. As she bounced up and started running in circles, he grabbed the container from the unicycle and tossed it in the car. "*Our* group!" he cheered, as the rest of the clowns piled into the car. One cranked the front handle to life, and with a cheery melody, they drove off down the road, to their big top in the wasteland.

As they disappeared in the horizon, the whitefaced warrior sadly blew her horn, and watched the dust cloud fade in the distance. She stood there alone in the empty desert, her group beaten and scattered around her.
words_common_s.writingprompts::41:
The air is cool here. Fog rises off the gardens and the air is heavy with the smell of flowers. A shout comes from the tower. Stranger coming from the south.


There is nothing to the south. Just sand and dust and maybe, if the wild people are to be believed, the bones of monsters.


He is a torn up man. Along the walk he lost his shoes. The bottom of his feet are bloody. Torn cloth hangs off the bones of his shoulders and hips. He only alive through the kindness of the gods.


Before he can be shown to the leader he must be cleaned. Fed and dressed as well. Rewarded - not yet. It is not known if he ran away.


The water almost kills him. He screams like a baby, fighting in the pool and crying for his mother, his father, his leader... He begs for death.


It is not given to him. Soon he is quiet. The slaves wash him until he is clean. His cuts are not bad. As he is being dressed a guard says quietly that he is not yet a man. The armor must be stolen.


When food is brought to him, he does not eat. Bread sits well with him though. He is not allowed to stuff himself.


The leader asks about the others. A hundred thousand strong, it had been whispered, a group of the strongest and most faithful. The men who feared nothing.


They are all dead. The boy looked small and weak. Fear had stolen his courage and his will, but not his honor.


They had walked for thousands of miles. When they entered a valley the sun and stars were lost to them. There were huge things - half men with bent bodies and sharp teeth, cats twice the size of a horse made of fire and smoke, animals with snakes for noses and long teeth like a pig that roared like a thousand horns.


Deeper they must have walked. The thick forest must have been the god of death's garden. Everything brought death.


They did not have a hundred thousand men, only five thousand. By the time they found it - the thing of bad dreams, the giant's unborn child - they numbered in the hundreds.


It came at night, pulled by the fires.


It was here the boy stopped. He shook. His teeth ground so hard they might have broken in his mouth. But he had honor, and spoke of what he had seen.


It must have been pulled by the fires. Maybe it remembered the burning place it had come from, or in the flames it saw strength.


The appearance was sudden. It fell near the fire, stirring it up and sending bright pieces into the air. It had small claws and was covered like a fish. It was not large. The boy pointed to his waist. He was missing half his hand. About the size of war dog. It had wings like a bat.


It drank the fire. The gods gave it power and it rose up and killed a hundred the first night.


The group ran through the death garden. Some were killed by the plants, the animals. One man woke screaming in the darkness. Bugs had eaten away at his flesh. They moved through his mouth and nose and the holes of his eyes.


After that no one slept.


Was that how the boy lost his hand? No. That was on the fifth day.


The men had begun to go crazy. Every tree was the same. Every rock and pool and spot of dirt.


They came to a cliff. They must climb it, someone said. So they did.


The boy was quick. Some men were quicker and stood along the top of the world and helped the others up. When the boy pulled himself over he saw the piles of bodies and called below. There is death above, wearing the face of their brothers. One of the men tried to kill him. Instead he lost half of his hand to a rock. It was broken and twisted. The boy pulled himself up and ran away.


He left the men and headed north. The group was broken apart. The boy walked north. He could see the sky again. His hand felt tight and hot. His fingers turned white, then red. On the fifth day he bit them off.


The seventh he lost one shoe. He threw the other away, and in a fit of craziness took off his clothes. The forest became thinner. He was burnt by the sun. There was no water, no food. Once he saw a golden eagle and followed it. But there was no eagle. On the ninth day he found a man hung from a tree.


The boy took the clothes from the body and dressed himself in the dead man's things.


As he walked north his hand leaked blood and his feet hurt and shook. One night he built a fire. It started a great fear in him. He was brave enough to put his hand inside and stop the rot from spreading. Afterwards he crawled away and cried until the sun rose again.


As he walked he left the grasslands. He wanted to see water. He wanted to die.


On the tenth day he saw the animal again. Or it may have been a different one. It had the body of dog, standing up. It had long claws and made sounds like a bird. It was the size of a man's leg, from the ground to his knee. There was a group of them. They called to each other. The boy followed them.


The dog animals took down an animal - the one with a snake for a nose. It had leather for skin and cried out as it died. After the dog animals left the boy ate what he could.


The boy stopped there. What else? There was nothing else. He had come to the sand and walked. His voice was quiet. Tired. His body told the cost his voice could not.


Could he die now? No. Not yet. More would want to hear of this. The story needed to be shared with others who would listen and understand what had happened to the great group of men.

The subway stopped suddenly. Laurentius woke up with a quick breath. He tried to understand his surroundings: It was cold, that was certain. He looked at his clothes: His hands were covered with gloves that seemed to be made of cow skin. His boots were black, lined with fur and warm. Underneath a thick black coat was a soft white shirt, with fasteners holding it together in the front. A red strip of cloth reached around his neck and made its way to just past his stomach. "*What is this, *" he thought. "*Is that how I died? Do we wear signs of our death? *" His eyes met those of a round darker-skinned woman, who was reading a strange folded-paper thing on her lap. He looked around her neck: a cross. He looked at her with understanding. "*I suppose so. *" 
 
 
 Tubes of light lit up the metal room he was in. A smooth sound made itself heard, and the doors closed shut. To Laurentius' surprise, the metal room began to move again. He stood, and made his way to a man he thought was in charge. The man, covered in what seemed to be traditional dress for the time, with the exception of a large silver wig, and glasses that read "2015" across the front. 
 
 
 "*Salve*," Laurentius began. 
 
 
 The man returned a confused look, then returned to looking out the window. He smelled of wine. 
 
 
 "*Aut ubi sum? Quis hic locus? *" 
 
 
 The metal room shook once again, slightly, throwing off Laurentius' balance. A voice rang out over the loudspeaker, but Laurentius couldn't make out what it had said. The metal room made another stop, but Laurentius wasn't ready. He fell onto the floor below as a wave of people left. He got up and followed the crowd, which moved through tunnels. He tried to take everything in: Musicians lined the closed-in street. Few sellers, from what he understood. He continued until he reached a flight of stairs. He went up, and was amazed by what he saw. 
 
 
 Bright lights flashed around him, in all directions. What was the steady noise of voices, broken up sometimes by an outburst, had now turned into a flood of voices and action. To his left and right, the streets were lined with people all moving towards a central place, where a large tall tower reached into the sky. On top of this tower was a round ball. He looked into the sky. 
 
 
 No stars? 
 
 
 No stars. He thought about this. Suddenly, an understanding came to him, and with it, a wave of happiness and relief. There were no stars, for he was above them all: Might these be the plains of Asphodel? They were more beautiful than he'd ever imagined. They were more wonderful than he'd ever thought possible. The beauty filled him with wonder and joy. 
 
 
 Suddenly, a man in a similar outfit – a black coat, black pants, white shirt – ran up to him. Black metal covered his eyes, and cold breath came out of his mouth when he spoke. 
 
 
 "Dick!" he said, grabbing Laurentius by the arm. So overcome with everything, Laurentius had no thought of arguing. He followed this man. 
 
 
 "Dick, where have you been? We've been looking all over – the crowd's waiting, and they ain't happy. Kathy's been doing what she can, but..." 
 
 
 Laurentius stopped. Clearly, he must learn the language of the afterlife. He noticed some of the crowd had begun to turn their attention towards him. He returned the same greeting he was offered. 
 
 
 "Dick," he said, moving his head at the people walking by as he was carried off by the man he had met. 
 "Dick," he said once more, this time at a young girl. Her ears were covered right away by her mother, who left an angry stare in her wake. 
 
 
 A few minutes of moving through the busy streets passed, and Laurentius passed by other similarly-dressed men who patted him down. After greeting both of them properly, he was pushed up steep metal stairs, and onto a raised floor which looked out over the huge crowd below. The raised floor held a woman, red-haired, who was holding a microphone. "Dick!" she said, "Where have you been? We're on in 2." 
 
 
 "Dick," Laurentius smiled. 
 
 
 "Well, you know what I like." 
 
 
 Someone handed Laurentius a plastic cord with a small piece on the end. He looked at the woman, who had it placed in her ear, and did the same. Perhaps this was part of the welcoming ceremony. 
 
 
 He heard the woman speak with the man behind a larger metal thing, one with a folded glass mirror in the middle. 
 
 
 "Live in 30." 
 
 
 "Alright. You ready?" she said, looking directly at Laurentius. He moved his head up and down. She handed him another metal stick with fur at the end, much like the one she was holding. She stared into the thing. Her lips formed a smile, and Laurentius couldn't help but smile himself. 
 
 
 A small red light went on in the corner of the metal-glass thing. There was a brief pause. The woman pushed Laurentius with her elbow in a way that showed she expected something. 
 
 
 Laurentius smiled and breathed in deeply. "Dick," he said, and looked with expectation once again at the woman to his right.

It was hard to find a pizza company that would still bring food to my home. You know, since the person bringing the food usually came back confused, a little paler, a little thinner, with an untouched thin crust pizza still in its box.

A vampire had to eat after all.

I had thought myself so smart all those thousands years ago. Rome! Home of every religion but the one that mattered, away from those damn crosses made of cheap wood that had begun to rest against every doorway in Jerusalem. I would make my home in Italy, I thought. Never would Christianity follow me to what had been the greatest nation the world had ever seen!

How wrong I had been.

Almost overnight the religious teachers had shown up, and within a hundred years there was a cross on every door and a church on every block. I was trapped, certain death just waiting outside if I so much as stuck my head out of my beautiful wood door.

Outside, I could sense three children laughing as they pushed each other outside on my doorstep. Finally, one of them jumped up to ring the doorbell, and laughing, they ran away. Ringing the doorbell of the person who never comes out, and running away to tell the story! How very exciting.

"I hate humans," I said to myself.

Looking through the seemingly eight hundredth phone book they had left pushed in my mail slot the last year, I tried to find a restaurant that maybe had not heard the tale of the feared Pale Master of The Takeout.

One could hope.

The wizard held the small garden slug in the palm of his hand.

He was Marvolio IV. He had called up demons the size of castles, he had created new rivers, he had figured out a spell that stopped you from getting nose itches when your hands were busy. He wouldn't accidentally call up a slug when he was looking for god?

He carefully placed the slug down. Even if it clearly wasn't God maybe it was God's favorite slug or something.

He spent hours looking through his notes, measuring the holy calling circles, checking the element mixtures for any dirt or bad bits. A mistake was somewhere in here. The slug ate at the corner of his work book.

After the moon began falling to the ground and the sun started peeking over the edge of the world God decided to speak.

'LETTUCE'

'Wh-what' Marvolio whispered. The voice had appeared directly in his head and though his mostly healthy mind could barely take it. He knew. He knew that voice was the voice from which all came and all were kept alive. He knew that voice was older than time. he knew that voice came from the three inch slug on his work bench.

'BRING ME LETTUCE. IT IS NOT SMART TO REFUSE ME'

Marvolio walked in a fog into his kitchens and found a basket of lettuce. He looked at it. it was a bit dried out and some blue fuzzy stuff had begun moving around the edges. wizards didn't go in for vegetables much.

Though the slug was on the other side of the house it's voice came again unwelcome into Marvolio's brain.

'YES THAT'LL DO NICELY'

'Surely not, I mean for God? It's not- I mean? I can run down to the market and get some of that black Italian cabbage tha-'

'NO I LIKE IT LIKE THAT. NICE AND SOFT.'

Marvolio talked quietly to himself in a confused way as he brought the rotting vegetable back to the one true lord of life.

God enjoyed the lettuce fully while Marvolio sat and talked to himself some more in a confused way.

'WELL'

'Well what? - I mean Um, Yes- L-lord'

'YOU WANTED TO KNOW SOMETHING? YOU PUT A LOT OF EFFORT INTO BRINGING ME HERE SO YOU SHOULD PROBABLY ASK'

'Oh um. Well. Why did you create everything? I mean there's so much suffering and-'

'LETTUCE'

'I don't think I have any more'

'NO I CREATED THIS WORLD TO PRODUCE THE CORRECT KIND OF LETTUCE. THIS IS THE MOST LETTUCY OF ALL POSSIBLE WORLDS'

'That actually explains a lot'

If God could shrug he would have, instead he stared at Marvolio without expression with his holy eye stalks.

'Should I try to send you back'

'NO JUST POP ME OUT IN THE BACK GARDEN THAT'S A GOOD LAD'

Marvolio never spoke of his experience, nor did wizardry again, but he did take up gardening and became famous across the whole nation for his impressive variety of award winning lettuce and cabbages.

I knew I wouldn't be able to see right away. I knew it would take a lot of work, and I was even warned that I might feel too much at once. I had unclear memories of what sight was like. I had been hurt in a car accident that had left me blind in both eyes at the age of three. I do think it helped, though; being able to take in light and color for three years before going blind may have made it a bit easier for my brain to remember rather than to learn everything new.

James helped me a lot. Sometimes I would close my eyes to get around like I had before. He would suddenly get in front of me and block my way, playing with me. It wasn't mean; if I complained, he'd raise his arms out and stop my movement until he closed them around me, hugging me tight.

"I won't let go until you open your eyes," he'd say. No one had ever loved me this much. I could hear it in his voice and feel it every time he hugged me.

I worked at it often. Sometimes I'd get headaches from trying to look at everything. Spots of dark spread across the table as I tried to eat breakfast. James told me it was the shadows from the tree outside. That tree had never bothered me before. Now it was breaking up my breakfast, trying to make it even harder to simply eat a bowl of cereal. I still felt around to make sure I could trust what I was seeing. I can't tell you how strange it was to see my own hands before me, two badly shaped unclear shapes feeling around with everything I tried to touch. I used to love my hands.

After a while, the dark spots became shadows, and James's face became clear to me. I think that was the happiest moment in my life. I woke up one morning and he turned over, and I could see his eyes. They shone bright, as if they themselves held light inside them. He was beautiful. I never knew how beautiful he really was.

The spots no longer mixed up his face and I was able to see him clearly. My problems began when I noticed that my own face wasn't clearing. The ugly spots on my own face weren't tricks of the light. I had a bunch of skin problem scars around my jawline. My skin felt smooth to me, but I didn't know the dark marks were there. I had a few lines on my face, which I had known about, but the sickly green circles under my eyes looked bad with my dark eye color. My eyes didn't shine like James's eyes. My eyes looked dead and sad.

I didn't want to ask James about it. I never knew I was so ugly. Even if I was ugly, I thought James must be just as ugly. Why would a good-looking man choose an ugly, blind girlfriend? I could finally see how women looked at him. Nobody ever looked at me that way. A trip to the food store used to be a fun time for both of us. Now, it was another chance to see every other woman who he could easily have if he wanted stealing quick looks at him, or smiling if he looked in their direction.

I have no idea what to think. Sometimes I think he smiles back at them. I caught him looking at two women walking by us at a place where we ate. My stomach was in knots. I didn't say anything. I just looked down at my pasta and tried not to lose my hunger.

"Is something wrong?" James asked.

"No, why?" I said, forcing my scarred face into a look of fun.

"Just asking," he said. "I love you," he said, with a smile.

I wish I could believe it.
words_common_s.writingprompts::48:
*** 
 The Author 
 *** 
 
 I can't shake the feeling. You know, that feeling creeping along your back waiting to take up a place in the bottom of your head like some kind of bug living inside you. It's an unclear feeling you're being watched. I can't shake it off. I am sure I know what it is, but I'm not ready to say I know. The... *author* let's call him. He is watching, waiting, building. Even as I think this, he is writing it down in his messy handwriting, touching the pen against his teeth in thought. I can feel it; I can see it in my mind. He's trying to figure out how to kill me. 
 
 I suppose it is my own fault. See I kept asking, I needed to understand. I had to find out if there was some guiding hand to life. If people had a goal, a reason, I needed to understand what goal we worked toward. There's a moment, one of special understanding, which caught me and held tight. Like my worry about an observer; only, this feeling was deeper, more basic. I *knew*, I mean really *understood*; all of it is a story. Life is a story. Which naturally led me to the end thought -- there needs to be a builder, an *author*. 
 
 The car barely missed me. I had a hint of a pushing against my chest getting close to the edge of fear. I didn't cross when the green man showed on the crossing signal, instead I took a step back. My *danger-sense* tingled. The taxi-cab driver never saw me, I hadn't seen him either. His drunken out of control car slammed into the same traffic signal post I had been, until recently, standing by. Can I tell you how messed up that is, I have this understanding, followed by a sudden feeling of fear. If I hadn't listened to my gutless push, I might have been crushed between the cabbie's car and the hard place which was the traffic signal pole. I turned my look upward, burning eyes and tightening jaw aside, and yelled at whoever worked at putting together this story. 
 
 "What the actual hell was that?" I said. 
 
 Okay, so I realize my choice of words probably did not fall into the meaning of careful, but damn we're talking about some kind of god-figure deciding on my time to die. 
 
 *Are you sure? * My thinking brain asked. 
 
 I thought about my place, both in the real and beyond-real sense. 
 
 *Yeah, I'm damn sure, * I replied to myself inside my head. *How else do you explain the sudden understanding and right after that my almost quick death. There's an* author *and he doesn't want to be known. * 
 
 I'm not sure how I knew the *author* didn't want to be known, or the fact he was a man, but I figured it was something in my general make-up giving me the knowledge. Oh don't get all high and mighty and talk at me now, I'm not talking religion or belief in spirits, I want to live for crying out loud. I stood, still staring up at the sky, trying to show my total disgust and anger when the signal pole made a noise, strangely so. I moved my head so my eyes were level with the pole. 
 
 The metal looked bent, and I saw that the car had burst into flames. 
 
 *When had that happened? * I thought. *Never mind, run stupid. * 
 
 My inside talk is not always the most kind; I'm a direct sort. So, I ran. What I was running from, if Mr. All-knowing *author* was already in my head, he could follow me anywhere. Hell, I could have an badly-timed looking back to the past, and he could hit me with a huge truck. If this *author* decided I was going to die, why didn't he do it already? 
 
 *Damn me, * I thought. *It's about the excitement; the story. * 
 
 "Sick bastard," I said. I knew he'd hear me, or he'd write that in his childish handwriting, knowing I meant it for him. 
 
 *What if I stop? * 
 
 I looked up again, and said, "What are you going to do with a person in your story who won't work with you, huh?" 
 
 Of course, he didn't answer back. It wasn't like I expected a voice from the sky, but I figured he might hit me down with lightning or something, I mean he possibly it's within his power, right? He might decide my knowledge of the plan made me a danger to keep around. 
 
 *What the hell is the plan anyway? * 
 
 I don't know, I guess the plan is for me to die. Perhaps, he's not into the ordinary. Maybe, just maybe, he wants my death to be something important, something of a show. I bet that's it. I got the sense again; a punch to my stomach making my insides turn like they were spilling to the outside, and the noise in my stomach told me to take a step back. I did. Something pushed through the skin in my back. It was a smooth, easy movement that opened the skin. I felt the warm blood mixing with my sweat as it soaked the back of my checked shirt made of soft cloth. 
 
 A quiet voice spoke in my ear. "Hello main character," she said. "I'm your enemy, the *author* says hello." 
 
 That was all she said. She didn't have a smell, like you would expect. She was a ghost from the shadows. I don't know who she was, or why her, but she'd made it clear... I was right. Take that you bastard. I didn't have the strength to say it, but I know he heard me. 
 *** 
 subscribe to /r/djmauthor for more stories

**A wise man, in a rare try at humor, once said "Heaven was eating pâté de foie gras to the sound of trumpets."** 

 Page of a journal of a Chef - Recently Dead. 
 
 
 
 As a chef, I completely agree with the foie gras but I have never had much of an ear for trumpets. Foie gras for those who don't know ( and do not worry, many don't ) is a dish as old as the art of cooking. Foie Gras, French for *fat liver* is the main dish of any self respecting chef. Take a duck, better a goose, but more often a duck. Put it in a cage, give it no room, movement will ruin the feel. Take it by the neck and pump corn boiled in fat down its throat. Do this seven times a day, pump it full. Kill the bird, remove the liver and a good chef would pay a good price for it. With mustard, with honey, with chopped onions and balsamic vinegar. Never has anything been so tasty and good. 
 See, it is not the taste that pushes people away, it is the way we make it. "Does the end make the means okay?" is a question often asked. No, if you have no talent, if you lack a sense of taste. Yes, Yes! Believe me anyone would scream "YES!" if they tried my Foie gras. But then again, mine is different, mine is better and mine stands above all others. 
 
 See, they say that beauty is skin deep. It is, and taste is far less deep than that. I am a chef. A good chef, not a good man but I say again: A GOOD chef. If I had been born a painter and my only way to get red was the blood of the innocent, do not doubt that I would paint in red. Of course I wasn't born a painter, I was born a chef. A GOOD chef. Foie gras, as most chefs make it, is against the law in many countries: the UK, Germany, and Italy to name a few. I do not need to say that I do not get my ways of cooking from law books. Foie gras as I make it, is against the law in every country. The pope once said Foie Gras was cruel, that was of course before he tried mine. Mine is different, mine is better and mine stands alone. 
 
 A cardinal said to me that if god again came to earth, he would make sure I cooked. Another said that "I once spoke against your dish Chef. I am sorry Chef. I owe you a thousand apologies Chef. I have now tried your dish Chef, and I now know that the joy from the soft cooked flesh on my tongue is greater than all the pain of all the geese and ducks that God has ever tried to make." They were in awe of me. Anyone who I talk into putting aside their morals, will at moment of contact with my Foie gras, be in awe of me. Mine is different, mine is better and mine is the best. 
 
 People would kill for a spoonful, Good people, religious people, moral people who care about right and wrong… They would kill for a spoonful of my Foie Grois. Believe me, I would sell out if I charged a million per pound. But I don't. I don't do it for power or money, I do it for the art. I am a chef, A GOOD chef, not a good man but I say again: A GOOD chef. My way of cooking is worth kingdoms, my dish has made kings weak at the knees. So weak that they kneel before me, the Chef. 
 
 My thing I leave behind will be my way of cooking. If you are reading this, good for you, you have been given it. Here it is: 
 
 Take a baby, take it by force, buy it, steal it, it makes no difference. Any baby without parents or home will do. Boy or girl, it makes no difference. Black, White, Arab, Asian, it makes no difference at all to the taste. Though they must be newborn! They must be pure and clean, they must be tender and juicy. 
 
 Put it in a cage, give it no room, movement will ruin the feel. Take it by the neck and pump corn boiled in fat down its throat. Do this seven times a day, pump it full. Two months should be enough. Add a pinch of salt and an ounce of butter per pint of corn. Two pints of fat, per pint of corn. Pig fat is best, the more of the special acid the better. When killed, take the liver and cook it in the way you are most able. I would soak in honey and mustard seed. Cooked sesame seeds, chopped red onions and a thimble full of rum.

Kai quietly walked back up the stairs from the kitchen. Getting caught by Mom and Dad would be bad. Getting caught with the leftover broccoli that Mom planned to serve for dinner tomorrow night would be worse. Lucky for Kai, he wouldn't have to eat any of it.

Closing his bedroom door behind him, the six-year old went straight to his closet. Bravely opening the closet, he smiled at the lump of eyes, hair and tentacles he found there.

"Here ya go, Blergh," Kai whispered. Blergh took the open Tupperware container with one tentacle and emptied the entire thing into a mouth the size of a basketball hoop before swallowing it whole. Kai could never see if Blergh had teeth or not, but the monster never chewed.

Kai began laying a trail of crackers out to the middle of the floor. Tempted by the salty circles, the monster slowly left the closet. Kai got a box out of his toy chest and dumped its contents on the floor.

"We're playing army men tonight," Kai said. Blergh merely grunted in agreement. Kai loved playing with Blergh because he could move lots of pieces at once and he was really good at pretending to be surprised when things "blew up."

***

Julia used to be annoyed when she woke up in the morning to find her son not only sleeping on the floor but also in the middle of a bunch of plastic men just waiting to be stepped on. By now it had happened so many times that being annoyed wasn't worth the effort.

"Wake up, sweetie," she said, softly shaking his shoulder. "How's Blergh?"

As they walked toward the breakfast table, Julia settled in for another story how Kai and his made-up friend had beaten some great evil. Kids are so cute at that age.

***

Ten years later, Kai no longer had to quietly walk around. All boys his age eat a lot in the middle of the night, right? Kai sat in front of his X-Box and passed one bag of Doritos and one bottle of Mountain Dew to his left.

"Here ya go, Blergh." Blergh grunted in thanks before swallowing everything whole. (Dude still hadn't learned to chew.) Blergh grunted again and (with his many tentacles) at the same time pointed to the tv, the three controllers in his tentacles and the fourth one at Kai's feet. They were all ready to play Call of Duty. It was going to be another great night.
words_common_s.writingprompts::52:
As the ship reached the signal point, the pilot nervously turned on his direction-finding scanner - he had used the last of his jump fuel making it this area.

The pilot felt a strange chill as he looked out his window. He figured it was jump nerves, but he sent power to his security flying robot anyways. The detection equipment didn't find anything; he should have known it was a waste of time. He had more important things to think about like finding fuel.

The direction-finding scanner beeped and drew his attention to a large body floating some distance from his ship, a thick cloud of gas partly blocking it. The ship was turned off, which is why the first system scan had not found it. He brought the push engines online and moved towards the empty ship while at the same time calling the ship.

No response. That was interesting, but empty ships were not unheard of. More unusual was the perfect condition of the ship, which did not have so much as a dent. He had found empty bodies before, but they were covered with burn marks from a light weapon blast or short range moving device, some sign of battle was always clear.

He briefly thought about putting on his outside space suit. Instead he headed to the flying robot room and took remote control of the security flying robot - it was meant for boarding defense, but in a tight spot it could be used as a scouting unit.

Moments later the flying robot slid through the air door, a smooth machine armed to the teeth with a collection of light weapons and close fighting weapons that had saved the pilot's life more than once. He had building plans for this body, and the flying robot made a straight line for the engine room. Any remaining fuel would be found there.

The problem with remotely controlling the flying robot was that it demanded the full attention of the pilot. The air door had not closed - if the pilot was paying attention, he would have noticed his door system had broken down.

His dying screams rang out as he was torn to pieces.

The pilot should have known that giant alien spiders are no joke.

Elwood and Shara were leaning against a concrete post in the yard of a high school, watching Elwood's newest person to work on, a quiet young man named Dale.

"So how did you get given this one, Elwood?" Shara said while looking at her claws.

"I'm pretty sure this is an easy job from the bosses downstairs." Elwood said, arms crossed against his chest. A group of girls walked over to the post and leaned against it, taking up the same space as the two demons. A strong blast of wind blew the papers and folders out of the hands of the girls, who screamed in surprise and ran after them.

Shara, angry said, "I'll never get used to that. I don't care if we *can* take up the same space." turning to the girls, she held her arm out to them, claws held behind her thumb and flicked them outwards with a snap, sending the books and papers again flying out of the screaming girls hands. "Little pests..."

Dale was chewing on his bean and cheese burrito looking at the scene across the yard with the look of a calm cow chewing on grass.

"What's with that kid?" Shara asked.

"I don't know. Maybe he's stupid?" Elwood chewed on his thumb for a bit, planning. "Let's jump time to sixth period."

Shara gave Elwood a sideways look and raised an eyebrow, "Sure...."

With a sound like tearing cloth they were moved and rested on the edge under the window in the back of Dale's sixth period class.

"So what's your plan, big boy?"

Elwood pressed a long-clawed finger to his lips and said, "Sssshhhh." As he did that Dale's head hit the desk, he was out cold. Throwing his arms out wide and then bringing them in together in a grand gathering movement, every student in the class turned to face Dale without a word.

"That's cute." said Shara.

Elwood smiled and said, "It's time to wake up, Dale." As he said that, every single student in the class in a very flat tone said the same thing at the same time with Elwood. Dale, face half-wet with drool sat up and rubbed his eyes, looking around at the class looking back at him.

"Dale, it's time to wake up." All the students and Elwood said again. No one blinked. Dale looked from side to side, "I'm awake." Elwood threw his arms apart and the class went back to normal, no one but Dale aware of what happened.

 -

A small lamp burned steadily on the shiny desk. The human wore a pair of thin glasses on the edge of his nose. Piles of paper filled a far corner of the work surface. He read through pages at a time, writing notes on another sheet. Empty ink bottles on the floor showed the man was rather busy.

From the entrance, Ronn readied his flail, letting the heavy chains hang down, their sounds filling the room. But the man refused to look up at the people entering. Instead, he held up a finger and continued reading. Ronn and the rest of his group looked at each other and lifted their shoulders. For a moment, they stood still. With a disappointed click of the tongue, the man put down the paper, pushed his glasses closer to his eyes, called for his guests to come forward. They did.

"Sorry, my friends," he said. His voice cracked slightly as though it had gone unused for some time. "Come. Come."

The adventurers stepped forward slowly. Wilm's head turned around as he looked for dangerous stones in the floor or another tripwire. The stones turned to green when the hanging edge of the rug stood before them. The group stopped.

"Come," the man said quietly, any impatience hard to notice.

Firrel's boot tested its weight against the rug. There was solid ground beneath. The rest followed the same action.

"Wait!" the man screamed. The group wasted no time taking a defensive position, their weapons and shields drawn. "I meant the carpet."

The adventurers looked towards their feet. The green threads took on a purple color as the blood from their persons dripped freely. Querth's face turned red.

"Sorry," the wizard whispered.

The man rolled his eyes. "It's already ruined. Nothing we can do now. Let's just get this over with."

The adventurers were finally within a step of the desk when the open palm of the man asked them to stop. The crowds of evil creatures had led them to that chamber. The supposed throne room of terrible evil was little more than a study with a librarian.

"Well, then. I suppose congratulations are in order!" The man clapped his hands together. "Great job. I'm Pollock and I'll be handling your processing from here."

"Processing?" Edmund repeated.

"Yes," replied Pollock. "You're almost done in this awful castle and on your way back home to enjoy the rewards. All that's left is to handle the last odds and ends."

The adventurers nodded in happiness, but kept their weapons handy. The armies they had to cut through in order to reach that chamber began to feel finished.

"Excellent! Let's get started. In total you've killed... one hundred and fifty three goblins, twenty nine orcs, eighteen kobolds... and two dragons. Impressive."

Edmund smiled and rolled the handle of his axe to catch the light to the unhappy sounds of Ronn and Dismal. They had enjoyed the mess that had followed as it stopped their fellow warrior from bragging.

"In addition, you broke down forty one doors, set off two fire traps, six spike snares, three boulders, and one acid spill. Plus, it says you freed the prisons of ten prisoners."

"All in a day's work," Wilm said suddenly.

"Quite," responded Pollock, not the least impressed. "And adding up your little adventure, that comes to a total of eight million, eight hundred thirty seven thousand, two hundred and fifty one gold pieces."

Even Querth's mind could not understand such a number. They were used to generous rewards, but several hundred was the most any had ever seen.

"We couldn't possibly carry that much coin," Dismal said. "Or spend it."

"That's quite expected," Pollock laughed. "You can just pay in installments."

"Pay?" shouted Firrel. "What do you mean pay?"

"Your fines. Your damages. You can't just go around killing things, damaging property, and setting off traps that require professional adjustment."

"But we were on a quest," begged Ronn. "We were trying to save the village."

"I see," sneered Pollock. "Does that mean the village is going to pay the fines, rebuilt the castle, reset the protections, mop the floors, rehire the guards, retrain dragons, and inform the families of those lost?" The group stood in wide-eyed silence. "I didn't think so."

"B-but, it was a quest," Ronn repeated.

"Do you have a license, a Writ of Pacification for this 'quest' of yours?" Ronn shook his head. "No need to answer, I already know you don't. If you had bothered to apply for one, *this* castle would have been better protected and *I* wouldn't have been needed. Just a little '[WP]' at the start would have been enough to save us all the mess of your unauthorized rampage."

"Who was supposed to file our WP?" Querth asked the group. They thought about the question for a moment before turning to face /u/dismaldreamer. "You've ruined us!"

"I'm sorry," cried Dismal. "I didn't know! I didn't know this would happen!"

The circle closed around him as the group looked to destroy their greatest enemy: the enemy within.

-- -- -- -- --
