1921 - Britain appoints Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, who is a member of a leading Palestinian Arab family with considerable influence, as Grand Mufti of Jerusalem and leader of the Muslim community. He rallies the Arabs and Muslims against any further concessions to the Jews, becoming a focal point of resistance.

1922 - Palestinian Arab delegation rejects the British proposal for a Legislative Council, saying that the inclusion of terms of the Balfour Declaration in the draft constitution is not acceptable to them under any circumstances.

1929 - Arab rioters, acting in waves of violence that sweep through the region, kill about 200 Jews in Jerusalem's Old City and Hebron. British troops, responding to the unrest with force, kill 116 Arabs in the suppression of riots that erupt in Jerusalem.

1930 - British White Paper and Royal Commission, examining the causes of the previous year's violence, recommend limiting Jewish immigration to reduce tensions in the region.

1930-35 - The Black Hand Islamist group, which is led by Sheikh Izz al-Din al-Qassam who becomes a legendary figure, launches a sustained campaign of violence against both the Jewish community and British rule.

1935 - Palestinian Arab leadership accepts the British High Commissioner's proposal for a Legislative Assembly, but the British House of Commons, responding to pressure from various quarters, rejects it the following year.

1936-39 - Arab revolt begins with a general strike in Jaffa that spreads throughout Palestine. Britain declares martial law and dissolves Grand Mufti Al-Husseini's Arab Higher Committee, which had been coordinating resistance. More than 5,000 Arabs are killed and 15,000 injured in the suppression of the revolt, which is conducted with considerable force, while Al-Husseini flees to French-run Syria to avoid arrest by British authorities.

1947 - United Nations recommends partition of Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states after Britain signals its intention to end the Mandate, with international control over Jerusalem and its environs being maintained. Arab High Committee, representing Palestinian interests, rejects the partition plan outright.

Birth of Israel

1948 - Israel declares independence as the British mandate ends after three decades of administration. More than four million Palestinians are thought to be living with refugee status in Arab countries, with many marginalised and trapped in camps that offer few opportunities. Arab armies, coming from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq, fail to defeat the new Jewish state of Israel after Britain withdraws its forces. Jordan occupies the West Bank and East Jerusalem, Egypt occupies Gaza, and Israel holds the rest of Mandate Palestine including West Jerusalem. At least 750,000 Palestinian Arabs either flee or are expelled from their homes in what becomes known to Palestinians as the Nakba. Disputes over the nature of their departure, whether voluntary or forced, endure to this day. United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) is set up to cater to the educational and health needs of Palestinian refugees and their descendants throughout the Middle East.

1949-1950s - Fedayeen Palestinian guerrillas, who are based in Egypt and Gaza, carry out raids into Israel with Egyptian encouragement and support. This activity increases significantly after pan-Arab officers seize power in Cairo in 1952, bringing a more militant approach.

1956-1957 - Israel colludes with Britain and France to invade Egypt during the Suez Crisis, partly to end Fedayeen incursions that have been causing casualties. UN buffer force, which is deployed in Sinai and Gaza, drastically reduces raids in the following period.

1959 - Yasser Arafat, who will become the most recognizable Palestinian leader, forms Fatah fighting group in Egypt to carry out raids into Israel.

1964 - Arab League sets up the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and Palestine Liberation Army under Ahmad Shukeiri, creating an umbrella organization for Palestinian nationalism.

1967 June - Six-Day War, which lasts less than a week but transforms the regional map, leaves Israel occupying East Jerusalem, all of the West Bank, Gaza, the Golan Heights and Sinai. Jewish settlements are set up in all of these areas in the coming years, with government approval that becomes increasingly systematic.

1969 - Yasser Arafat takes over PLO leadership after making his debut as a military leader in clashes with Israeli forces in Jordan in 1968, and asserts the group's independence from Egyptian control, which had previously constrained its actions.

1970 - Increasing tension over the strength of the PLO in Jordan, where armed Palestinian groups have established a state within a state, leads to the Black September clashes with Jordanian forces, driving the PLO into exile in southern Lebanon.

1970s-1980s - PLO and other armed Palestinian groups turn to airline hijackings and attacks on Israeli soldiers, officials and civilians within Israel and abroad to highlight their cause, which they feel is being ignored by the international community.

1972 - Palestinian "Black September" gunmen, operating under a name commemorating the Jordanian clashes, take the Israeli team hostage at the Munich Olympics. Two of the athletes are murdered at the site and nine more are killed during a failed rescue attempt by the German authorities, who are criticized for their handling of the crisis. Israel launches a series of reprisal assassinations targeting those it holds responsible.

1973 - Israel raids PLO bases in Beirut and southern Lebanon before and during the October Yom Kippur/Ramadan War, which catches Israeli forces by surprise.

1974 April-May - Two hardline factions, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine General Command and Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, carry out raids into northern Israel and kill 43 civilians, including many children, in a block of flats in Kiryat Shmona and a school in Maalot, shocking Israeli society.

1974 June - After the 1973 Yom Kippur/Ramadan war, which has altered the political landscape, the PLO adopts the Ten-Point Programme allowing compromise with Israel on the way to establishing complete Palestinian control over historic Palestine, including the territory of Israel. Some hardline factions, rejecting any compromise whatsoever, split away to form the Rejectionist Front and step up attacks on Israeli soldiers and civilians.

PLO recognised

1974 October - Arab League recognises the PLO as the "sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people" and admits it to full membership of the League, giving it diplomatic legitimacy.

1974 November - Yasser Arafat becomes the first non-state leader to address the United Nations General Assembly, where he delivers his famous "olive branch... and freedom fighter's gun" speech that captures international attention.

1975 - Rejectionist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and German far-left armed group, working together in an unusual alliance, hijack an Air France plane en route from Israel to France, diverting it to Entebbe in Uganda. Israeli commandos, in a daring raid that becomes legendary, rescue most of the passengers and crew, killing the hijackers in the process.

1977 May - The right-wing Likud party, which opposes territorial compromise, wins a surprise election victory in Israel and encourages an expanded settlements policy on the West Bank and Gaza.

1978 March - PLO attack, launched from Lebanon, kills 38 civilians on Israel's coastal road. Israel carries out its first major incursion into southern Lebanon, driving the PLO and other Palestinian groups out of the area near the border.

1978 September - Israel pledges to expand Palestinian self-government in the West Bank and Gaza as part of the Camp David Accords, which are establishing diplomatic relations with Egypt.

1982 June - Israel invades Lebanon again to expel the PLO leadership from Beirut after an assassination attempt by a Palestinian faction on the Israeli ambassador to London, which provides the pretext.

1982 September - Massacre of Palestinians in the Beirut Sabra and Shatila camps by Israel's Christian Phalangist allies, who enter while Israeli forces control the area, shocks international opinion. PLO leadership, having been forced out, moves to Tunisia, where it remains until it moves to Gaza in 1994.

1985 October - Israeli air force strikes PLO headquarters in Tunis after a PLO group kills three Israeli tourists on a yacht. Palestine Liberation Front PLO faction, operating independently, hijacks the Achille Lauro cruise ship, demanding the release of 50 Palestinians from Israeli prisons. Hijackers kill elderly American wheelchair user Leon Klinghoffer, throwing his body overboard.

1987 December - First Palestinian Intifada uprising, which is largely spontaneous, begins in the Palestinian Territories. Muslim Brotherhood in Gaza forms the Hamas movement, which rapidly turns to violence against Israel as its primary strategy.

1988 - Jordan abandons its claim to the West Bank, ceding it to the PLO in a significant diplomatic shift. Palestinian National Council meeting in Algiers proclaims the State of Palestine, declaring independence symbolically.

1990 - PLO backs Iraq over its annexation of Kuwait, which severs ties with the PLO and subsequently expels about 400,000 Palestinians who had been working there.

1991 October - US-Soviet sponsored conference in Madrid, which represents a breakthrough, brings Israeli and Palestinian representatives together for the first time since 1949.

1992 - Israeli Labour government of Yitzhak Rabin pledges to halt the settlement expansion programme and begins secret talks with the PLO, which had previously been considered a terrorist organization.

1993 September - Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat, former enemies meeting on the White House lawn, sign the Oslo Declaration to plot Palestinian self-government and formally end the First Intifada, which had been running out of steam since the Madrid Conference. Violence by various Palestinian groups that reject the Oslo Declaration, viewing it as a betrayal, continues.

1994 February - Baruch Goldstein of the extremist Jewish Kach movement kills 29 Palestinians at prayer at the Cave of the Patriarchs shrine in Hebron on the West Bank, shocking both communities.

Progress towards self-rule

1994 May-July - Israel withdraws from most of Gaza and the West Bank city of Jericho, allowing Yasser Arafat to move his PLO administration from Tunis and set up the Palestinian National Authority, which begins governing.

1994 December - Yasser Arafat, along with Yitzhak Rabin and Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres, are jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their efforts toward reconciliation.

1995 - Interim Agreement, which is painstakingly negotiated, sets out the path for transfer of further power and territory to the Palestinian National Authority. It forms the basis of the 1997 Hebron Protocol, the Wye River Memorandum of 1998 and the internationally-sponsored "Road Map for Peace" of 2003.

2000-2001 - Talks between Israeli Labour Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat break down over the timing and extent of a proposed further Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank. Palestinian protests, beginning after Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount, escalate into a new Intifada.

2001 December - Israel sends troops to encircle Ramallah after a series of deadly Palestinian attacks inside Israel that kill dozens. Yasser Arafat is unable to leave his government compound, which becomes his prison.

Barrier goes up

2002 March - Israeli army launches Operation Defensive Shield on the West Bank and begins building a barrier there to stop armed Palestinians from entering Israel. The route of the barrier is controversial as it frequently deviates from the pre-1967 ceasefire line into the West Bank, effectively annexing land.

2002 March - Arab League meeting in Beirut offers to recognise Israel in return for its full withdrawal from all territories occupied since 1967, agreement to a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital and a "fair solution" to the refugee question - the "Arab League Peace Plan" that offers comprehensive peace.

2003 March - Yasser Arafat establishes the post of prime minister and appoints Fatah veteran Mahmoud Abbas to lead contacts with the US and Israel, both of which refuse to deal with Arafat directly.

2003 May - Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon, in a significant statement, says the occupation of Palestinian territories cannot continue indefinitely.

2003 June - Arab League meeting in Egypt expresses support for the "road map" proposed by the US, European Union, Russia and UN and accepted by the Palestinian National Authority and Israel, which is positing an independent Palestinian state and a freeze on West Bank Jewish settlements.

2003 September - Mahmoud Abbas resigns as prime minister, citing US and Israeli intransigence as well as internal Palestinian opposition to his government. He is succeeded by Fatah veteran Ahmed Qurei, who faces similar challenges.

2004 March - Israeli forces kill Sheikh Yassin, who is the founder and leader of Hamas, and his successor Abd al-Aziz al-Rantissi, the following month in targeted strikes.

2004 July - International Court of Justice issues an advisory opinion stating that the Israeli separation barrier violates international law and must be removed.

2004 November - Yasser Arafat dies in a hospital in France, where he went for urgent medical treatment in October under mysterious circumstances that fuel conspiracy theories.

2005 January - Mahmoud Abbas is elected as Mr Arafat's successor as head of the Palestinian National Authority in elections that are deemed free and fair.

2005 September - Israel withdraws all Jewish settlements and military personnel from Gaza in a unilateral move, while retaining control over airspace, ports and border crossings.

Hamas wins elections

2006 March - Hamas Islamist group's Ismail Haniyeh forms a government after winning parliamentary elections in January that surprise international observers. A struggle for primacy with Fatah begins immediately. The United States and European Union suspend aid, and Israel ends tax transfers, because of Hamas's refusal to recognise Israel, renounce violence and accept previous peace accords.

2006 June - Hamas militants from Gaza seize Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit near a border crossing and hold him hostage for five years, demanding the release of Palestinian prisoners. Major clashes between Israel and Hamas forces in Gaza follow the kidnapping. Israel imposes restrictions on Gaza that tighten over time.

2006 September - Clashes break out between Fatah and Hamas supporters in Gaza as the power struggle intensifies. Various Arab states and Palestinian groups seek to mediate between them in the coming months in order to avert civil war.

2007 March - Fatah and Hamas, under pressure from Saudi Arabia, form a national unity government to end months of intermittent clashes in Gaza that have killed dozens.

2007 June - Unity government founders after only three months. Hamas ousts Fatah from Gaza and reinforces its control of the territory in what amounts to a coup. Israel tightens its blockade after an increase in rocket attacks from Gaza; Egypt closes its border with Gaza. Mahmoud Abbas appoints Salam Fayyad as prime minister, but Hamas refuses to recognise him or his authority. Two rival governments in the West Bank and Gaza emerge, dividing Palestinian governance. The US and European Union resume aid to the Fayyad government while boycotting Hamas.

2007 November - US-hosted Annapolis Conference for the first time establishes the "two-state solution" as the basis for future talks between Israel and the Palestinian Authority.

2008 March - Efforts at reconciliation between Fatah and Hamas begin in Yemen, but the next round in Cairo in November stalls when Hamas objects to Fatah's arrest of its West Bank activists.

2008 November - Israel launches an incursion into Gaza, which is seen by Hamas as a ceasefire violation. Hamas responds by launching rockets into Israeli territory.

2008 December - Israel launches Operation Cast Lead, which is a month-long invasion of Gaza designed to stop Hamas and other militant groups from firing rockets into Israel.

2010 February - Fatah and Hamas resume talks on national reconciliation, which have stalled repeatedly. Direct talks resume between Israel and the Palestinian Authority, only to falter over the question of settlements once again.

2010 May - Nine Turkish pro-Palestinian activists are killed in the Israeli capture of ships attempting to break the maritime blockade of Gaza, causing international outrage.

2011 April-May - Fatah and Hamas agree at talks in Cairo to form a unity government and hold fresh elections, but no practical implementation follows despite repeated pledges.

Bid for UN membership

2011 - Palestinian National Authority launches a campaign for UN membership of the "State of Palestine", as a means of highlighting the stalled talks with Israel. The bid fails due to US opposition, but UNESCO cultural agency accepts Palestine as a member in October.

2012 May - After preliminary talks in Qatar, Fatah and Hamas sign the Cairo Agreement pledging to maintain non-violent resistance to Israeli occupation in pursuit of an independent state within the 1967 ceasefire lines.

2012 October - Local elections on the West Bank undermine Fatah's position, as it wins only two-fifths of the seats contested on a turnout of 55%. Lists led by Fatah rebels win four of the 11 major towns and cities, and independents and leftists take control of a fifth. Hamas boycotts the poll and allows no elections in Gaza, maintaining its authoritarian control.

2012 November - UN upgrades Palestinian representation to that of "non-member observer state", allowing it to take part in General Assembly debates and improving its chances of joining UN agencies.

2012 December - Fatah allows a Hamas celebration rally on the West Bank over the UN status upgrade, which is a gesture reciprocated by Hamas in Gaza the following month.

2013 April - Prime Minister Fayyad resigns after a long-standing dispute with Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas over governance issues. He is succeeded by academic Rami Hamdallah in May, who lacks political experience.

2013 - Newly appointed US Secretary of State John Kerry launches a series of Israeli-Palestinian talks aimed at reaching a framework peace deal by April 2014. Palestinian officials say continuing Israeli approval of Jewish housing in occupied East Jerusalem undermines progress toward an agreement. Israel accuses the Palestinians of incitement against Jews.

2013 July - Fall of the Morsi government in Egypt dashes Palestinian hopes for the lifting of the Egyptian blockade of the border with Gaza, and suspends Egyptian mediation in the Fatah-Hamas reconciliation process.

2013 December - Israel, Jordan and the Palestinian Authority sign a water-sharing pact to halt and eventually reverse the drying-out of the Dead Sea by laying a pipeline to carry brine from a Red Sea desalination plant while providing drinking water to the region.

2014 March - Egypt bans Hamas activities and seizes its assets because of the organization's links to Egypt's illegal Muslim Brotherhood, which has been outlawed.

2014 April - Fatah and Hamas agree to form a unity government, which takes office in June amid international hopes. Fatah complains that a separate Hamas cabinet continues to rule Gaza independently.

2014 June - Israel responds to the kidnapping and murder of three Jewish teenagers in the West Bank by arresting numerous Hamas members throughout the territory. Militants respond to the arrests and the killing of a Palestinian teenager by Jewish extremists by firing rockets from Gaza into Israel.

2014 July-August - Israel responds to attacks from armed groups in Gaza with a military campaign by air and land designed to knock out missile launching sites and attack tunnels that extend into Israeli territory. Clashes end in an uneasy Egyptian-brokered ceasefire in August after thousands of casualties.

2014 December - Minister Without Portfolio Ziad Abu Ein dies at a clash with Israeli troops at a West Bank protest against settlements.

2015 May - The Vatican announces that it is to formally recognise Palestinian statehood, becoming one of the few European states to do so.
syntax_complex_s.xsum::30: David Sulman of the UK Forest Products Association criticised what appeared to be a lack of "openness and transparency" in the deal, which had been criticised by auditors, while NRW said the contracts were awarded in "extraordinary" circumstances. In 2014 a company was awarded a series of contracts worth £39m to purchase both spruce and larch timber - the latter from forests where a fungus disease causing extensive damage, Phytophthora ramorum, was present. The contracts, which were part of action NRW - an organisation that sells timber from publicly opened woodlands - took to deal with the disease, came amid a rapid increase in its spread during the previous year. But a report by auditor general Huw Vaughan Thomas in March expressed doubt over whether the decision met state aid rules, saying that the decision-making process was not transparent. Mr Thomas revealed that the deal was made without other companies being allowed to bid - although NRW disputed his findings. The agreements were set to be pulled after the company failed to meet a key promise to build a new processing line for cutting timber. Mr Sulman, who is executive director of the UK Forest Products Association which represents the domestic timber industry, said: "It's a very serious, disturbing and worrying situation for businesses across the forestry and forest public sector in Wales, and indeed further afield. "Our principal concern here is that historically businesses who have dealt with Natural Resources Wales… have always been assured that dealings with NRW would be fair, open and transparent. "In this case, from what we can see there appears to have been a considerable lack of fairness, openness and transparency, and that is really what is giving rise to such serious concern across the sector at the moment." "There probably are businesses out there who feel they were denied opportunities," he said. Fears that the market for larch was on the brink of collapse at the time of the deal have been given as one of the reasons why NRW went ahead with the deal - but whether this was the case has been questioned by Mr Sulman. Evidence given by chief executive Emyr Roberts at a meeting of the assembly's public accounts committee in March said that, at the time of the deal: "We had a real crisis on our hands." "There was a danger of the timber market collapsing at that time," he said. But Mr Sulman said the statement was "wildly inaccurate" and "misleading", adding that events have proved, in the intervening period through 2014 through today, that the diseased larch that was harvested has been equally well processed and sold in the market place. He said a full investigation by the public accounts committee was "probably warranted given the seriousness of the situation". Mr Sulman will give evidence to the assembly's public accounts committee, which is also calling NRW in again to re-examine the issue, on Monday. Emyr Roberts, chief executive of Natural Resources Wales, said in a statement: "The long-term contracts were awarded at a point in time when we were dealing with an extraordinary set of circumstances. "Our prime objective at the time was to secure a market for the diseased larch and we succeeded in doing so following our agreed processes. "We are confident that the evidence we gave to the previous public accounts committee was accurate and valid." Neither NRW or the Wales Audit Office have revealed the name of the firm that was awarded the contracts.
syntax_complex_s.xsum::31: Denbighshire council had wanted to create a new bilingual school by shutting both Ysgol Pentrecelyn and Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd in Ruthin and opening a new site, a plan against which Pentrecelyn parents had campaigned vigorously, saying that the school's Welsh character would be lost. Councillors, having been advised to keep the school, will vote later on this matter. In August, following a claim brought by former Pentrecelyn pupil Aron Wyn Jones, who argued that the council had failed to take into account the language and community impact of a single site school, the High Court quashed the closure decision. While all pupils in Ysgol Pentrecelyn are educated in Welsh, pupils in the Church in Wales Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd can be educated in either Welsh or English, with 80% choosing Welsh-medium education at present. At the time of the ruling, Denbighshire council, expressing disappointment with the outcome of the decision, said it would reflect on the guidance given by the court. In a report to Tuesday's cabinet meeting, head of education and children's services Karen Evans said that, as the judicial review did not criticise the objectives, it would be "perfectly logical" for the authority to consider whether to restart the consultation on the original proposals whilst acknowledging criticism of the process that had been followed. However, continuing her assessment, she stated that the authority also needs to consider the wider impact based on the current situation that now exists. She said the council must give due regard to the impact of any future proposal on community cohesion, in particular that which had an impact on the learners themselves, who remain central to all considerations. Ms Evans added that it is clear from discussions with both school communities that there is no appetite to revisit the same proposal in the current circumstances that have developed. She noted that the authority agrees that conducting a consultation on the same proposal, even with a perfect process being followed, risks further community divisions and legal challenges that could prove costly. She also stated that it is equally clear that the status quo for Ysgol Llanfair cannot continue and that the area is in need of a sustainable category 2 bilingual school serving local families. Councillors have been recommended to allow Ysgol Pentrecelyn, which currently has 56 pupils attending, to remain open and for a new Church in Wales school to be built in Llanfair on a safer site closer to many of the pupils' homes.

Iain Pocock, who lives near Tomich in the Highlands, caught a foot on a raised slab and fell during a visit to Inverness on 9 February 2012, an incident that would lead to protracted legal proceedings. Mr Pocock, who appeared in a BBC documentary in 2013, sought £500,000 in compensation for an injury to his leg, claiming significant impairment to his daily activities. A judge said Mr Pocock had failed to establish that the slab had been at a height that required it to be fixed, thereby undermining the fundamental basis of his claim.

Mr Pocock said the trip caused injury to a knee and this impacted on his ability to carry out tasks at his croft, prompting him to raise an action at the Court of Session in Edinburgh against Highland Council. The local authority, which denied liability, said that during 2012 and the following year Mr Pocock and his family were the subject of the documentary Power to the Pococks: A year in the life of a crofting family, footage that would become central to the case.

In its defences to the action, the council said: "The pursuer's wife in particular, during the documentary, discusses the fact that they rely on own generator for power and that they cannot be linked to the National Grid other than at significant expense to their family, there being reference to them being quoted the sum of up to £230,000 for them to be connected and the pursuer's wife saying they do not have that money unless they 'win the lottery'."

During the court action parts of the documentary were played to Mr Pocock, revealing activities that appeared inconsistent with his claimed limitations. Judge Lord Clark said: "Excerpts of the documentary were played which showed the pursuer doing such things as using an axe and a chainsaw to cut firewood, carrying out animal husbandry tasks, carrying out maintenance of a wind turbine by climbing up a metal scaffold and in doing so being able to place weight on his left leg, driving a tractor, kneeling while milking, carrying a stockpot and sliding on a sheet of ice, spinning round a pole in a barn and working on a diesel generator."

The judge said: "The pursuer explained that he was not filmed during periods when the knee was bad and that when he was carrying out some of the activities that had been filmed he was focused and aware of what he was doing, and was bracing his leg to avoid unexpected injury," an explanation supported by testimony from the documentary's director. Documentary director Stephen Bennett explained to the court that he would not switch on the camera and begin filming when Mr Pocock said he was in pain, corroborating the pursuer's account of selective filming.

Lord Clark said in his newly issued judgement Mr Pocock, his wife and other relatives struck him as being honest witnesses and he had no hesitation in accepting them as credible and reliable, despite apparent contradictions. The judge said: "It may be the case that the pursuer's evidence to some degree over-emphasised the effects of the accident and that the BBC documentary supported the view that his injuries were not quite so severe as he had stated, but I regard any difference as being largely immaterial, and in relation to the documentary, I accept the evidence from the pursuer and Mr Bennett to the effect that there were points in time when filming could not take place because of the pursuer's knee injury."

The judge said that in light of Mr Pocock's testimony of symptoms of the knee locking during 2012 and supporting evidence he concluded he had suffered a medial meniscal tear in the accident, establishing that injury had occurred.

In the action it was contended that there was a duty to repair a paving defect with a height difference greater than 20mm within seven days or at most within 21 days, given that the location of the accident in Baron Taylor Street was known to be prone to problems and was regularly inspected. Lord Clark said he had concluded that Mr Pocock had failed to establish the key factual basis of his case - that the defect at of the date of its identification involved a height difference greater than 20mm - adding that Mr Pocock had not established that a roads authority of ordinary competence applying reasonable care would have taken the steps identified in his claim to correct the defect.

Their study, published in Science Translation Medicine, showed that caffeine was more than just a stimulant, actually slowing down the body's internal clock in ways that had significant implications for sleep patterns. A double espresso consumed three hours before bedtime delayed the production of the sleep hormone melatonin by about 40 minutes, making it considerably harder to nod off when the time came to rest. Experts said that our own actions, including our consumption of stimulants and exposure to various environmental factors, had a huge influence on both sleep quality and the body clock's functioning.

One of the researchers, Dr John O'Neill, from the Medical Research Council's Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, told the BBC News website that if you're tired and having a coffee at night to stay awake, then that is a bad idea, explaining that you'll find it harder to go to sleep and get enough sleep afterward. In his half of the study, which involved laboratory work at the cellular level, cells grown in a dish were exposed to caffeine to work out how it changed their ability to keep time accurately. It showed that the drug was able to alter the chemical clocks ticking away in every cell of the human body, demonstrating a fundamental biological mechanism.

Meanwhile, five people at the University of Colorado Boulder, in the US, were locked in a sleep laboratory for 50 days, participating in carefully controlled experiments. And as light exposure is the main way we normally control our body clock, they spent most of their incarceration in very dim light, eliminating this confounding variable. In a series of experiments conducted over the month and a half, the scientists showed that an evening dose of caffeine slowed the body clock by 40 minutes, having roughly half the impact of three hours of bright light at bedtime.

Dr O'Neill said it would be "complete speculation" to set a cut-off time for drinking caffeine in the evening but acknowledged that he personally never drank coffee after 17:00. He said the findings may help treat some sleep disorders and people who naturally woke up too early—known as larks—to help keep them in sync with the rest of the world, which operates on different schedules. He added that it could be useful with jet lag if you are flying east to west, where taking caffeine at the right time of day might speed up the time it takes to overcome jet lag and adjust to new time zones.

Prof Derk-Jan Dijk, from the University of Surrey, told the BBC that individuals differ in their sensitivity to caffeine, noting that if coffee drinkers experience problems with falling asleep, they may try to avoid drinking coffee in the afternoon and evening. He added that people "too often" thought they were a "slave" to their body clocks, programmed to wake up early or late without any control. These and other data clearly indicate that we can to some extent modify these rhythms and that part of the reason why we sleep so late relates to factors such as caffeine intake and the exposure to artificial light in the evening, both of which are within our control.

After 10 weeks of talks, a way forward, which addresses paramilitarism and welfare reform, has been agreed upon by the parties involved. However, despite these intensive negotiations spanning more than two months, they failed to break the deadlock over legacy issues arising from Northern Ireland's Troubles, which have remained contentious throughout the process. Prime Minister David Cameron, speaking about the outcome, said the agreement was "an important turning point for Northern Ireland," emphasizing its significance for the region's future. "The agreement secures sustainability for Northern Ireland's budget, sets out how we'll deal with paramilitary groups, and could provide a basis for a shared future for the people of Northern Ireland," he said, outlining the key elements that had been resolved. The deal, having been negotiated over an extended period, includes a new set of principles that politicians will be asked to follow in relation to paramilitarism and a reworked financial package designed to help those impacted by welfare reforms and tax credit cuts that have affected vulnerable populations. While the Democratic Unionist Party and Sinn Féin, representing the two largest political blocs, have backed the deal that emerged from the negotiations, the executive's Justice Minister David Ford, who leads the Alliance Party, said his party refused to support it today, citing concerns about its provisions. Other parties, needing additional time to examine the complex document thoroughly, said they needed more time to study its implications before committing their support. The US government, monitoring developments closely given its historical involvement in the peace process, has welcomed the deal as a positive step forward. Victims' groups, representing those who suffered during the decades of conflict, have said they are disappointed the deal does not include any movement on the legacy issues of the Troubles, which remain deeply important to many families seeking justice and acknowledgment.

New principles are in place expecting politicians to work towards the disbandment of paramilitary structures that have persisted despite the peace process. Politicians, under these binding principles, must not take instructions from anywhere other than those who have given them their democratic mandate through legitimate electoral processes. The new principles, representing a significant commitment to democratic norms, will apply not only to ministers in Northern Ireland's ruling executive but to all MLAs, it is understood from sources familiar with the agreement.

An international body, established to provide independent oversight, will be set up to monitor paramilitary activity, with appointees nominated by the British and Irish governments and the Northern Ireland Executive working collaboratively. It will have a £3.2m budget allocated for its operations. Unlike the old paramilitary monitoring body, the Independent Monitoring Commission which had stronger enforcement powers, the new body will not have the power to recommend the exclusion of any parties from the assembly, a significant difference in its mandate.

A new cross-border task force, bringing together law enforcement capabilities from both jurisdictions, will bring together agencies like HM Revenue and Customs, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) and the National Crime Agency—the UK's equivalent of the FBI—with their equivalents in the Republic of Ireland, creating an integrated approach to tackling organized crime. The task force, equipped with substantial resources, is expected to have a budget of about £50m dedicated to its mission. The PSNI, recognizing the need for enhanced capacity, will also get an extra £160m over the next five years for operational improvements.

Last year's Stormont House Agreement, which had seemed promising initially, fell on the issue of welfare reform, when Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), representing nationalist constituencies, refused to let the changes pass through the Northern Ireland Assembly, creating a political crisis. Social Development Minister Mervyn Storey, tasked with moving the process forward, is due to bring a legislative consent motion to the assembly on Wednesday that will allow the government to push the changes through despite local opposition. Westminster, having the constitutional authority to intervene, is expected to start the process either this week or next, moving quickly to implement the agreed measures.

The last Stormont deal, negotiated under different circumstances, included a mitigation package on welfare reform that amounted to £564m over a six-year period to cushion the impact. The new deal, offering enhanced protections, includes a four-year programme, with a value of £585m allocated for various support measures. The cash, divided according to specific needs, will be split, with £345m for measures designed to mitigate the welfare changes affecting vulnerable groups. For a party with 232 MPs, it is an insight into two other things: firstly, it is not just the Conservative Party that is subjecting itself to long, internal discussions about the European Union, and secondly, the legacy of a crushing defeat at the general election has left a party nervous, unsure of itself and far from sure footed.
syntax_complex_s.xsum::46: Chloe Rutherford, 17, and Liam Curry, 19, both from South Shields, were among 22 victims killed in the Manchester Arena explosion that occurred on 22 May. In a joint tribute, their relatives said that the couple, who both "adored each other," had wanted to be "together forever". The couple's families and friends, wearing pink and blue for the occasion, attended the funeral service at St Hilda's Church. Funeral of Grande 'superfan' bomb victim Funeral due of 'true gent' bomb victim Family members and friends, beginning to arrive at St Hilda's Church in South Shields more than an hour before the service began, gathered in anticipation. syntax_complex_s.xsum::47: David Poole, appearing before Cardiff Crown Court, told the court that he had trapped Adnan Khalid, 27, who was charged with grooming a 14-year-old. Mr Poole, 38, was accused of giving misleading evidence in the trial of Mr Khalid, of Porth, Rhondda Cynon Taff. Judge Thomas Crowther QC, entering a formal not guilty verdict, criticised the paedophile hunting group for the trial collapsing. Mr Poole, who founded the group H Division from his base in Hereford, set up a fake profile on dating website Plenty of Fish, claiming to be a 14-year-old called Chloe. Having arranged to meet Mr Khalid in Cardiff after messaging him on Whatsapp, he filmed the sting. Mr Khalid, denying the offence, told police that he believed he was speaking to a woman aged over 18. Mr Poole, arriving four hours late to the trial, then said he had passed photo evidence to the police before admitting this was not true. Judge Crowther said his answer was "at best inaccurate and at worst a lie". Discharging the jury, he said: "This case underlines why criminal investigations should be conducted carefully, meticulously and by those who are trained and qualified to do so. When you are talking about a conviction, especially a sexual offence conviction, a high degree of reliability is needed in the evidence. The prosecution have taken the view that you could not find that degree of reliability in Mr Poole's evidence." During the trial, Mr Poole said this was one of the group's "first stings" and was "a learning curve". Speaking after the court case, a NSPCC Wales spokesman said that online abuse and grooming was "one of the biggest child protection challenges we face". "While we have every sympathy for people concerned about suspected abusers, we believe that identifying offenders and investigating crimes is best left to the police," he said. "When members of the public take the law into their own hands it can run the risk of driving offenders underground, jeopardise on-going police work and the legal process or result in innocent people being harassed, all of which may put more children at risk of harm in various ways."
syntax_complex_s.xsum::48: The University of Strathclyde's Fraser of Allander Institute, investing in new research and postgraduate fellows, will also welcome a new director designate who will join the institute in April, while simultaneously creating a board of advisers featuring leading economists. It also plans to expand its economic research services for the third sector, government, business and industry, marking a significant development for the organisation. The university said the move was "particularly timely", given that the Scottish Parliament will soon assume greater tax and spending powers, adding that the expanded institute would be able to provide decision-makers, the media and the public "with even greater leading-edge independent economic analysis than before". The institute's new director designate will be Prof Graeme Roy, who previously served as a senior economic adviser in the Scottish government, bringing considerable experience to the role. The board of advisors, which will be chaired by Prof Andrew Goudie, will include the chief economists of both the Scottish and UK governments, ensuring high-level expertise and guidance. Further details will be announced at an event taking place at the Scottish Parliament to mark the institute's 40th anniversary, celebrating four decades of contribution. Ahead of the event, University of Strathclyde principal Prof Sir Jim McDonald, describing the investment as a "step change" for the institute, said: "At a time when the Scottish Parliament is gaining significant new powers and responsibilities and the future of the UK's economic and financial system is undergoing a major re-think, the need for independent economic and fiscal analysis has never been greater. With more than four decades of economic forecasting experience behind it, the Fraser of Allander Institute is uniquely placed to provide the independent research and analysis needed to inform public debate and decision making. This new investment will enable the institute to spearhead new research into public spending and finance that will be of relevance not just in Scotland and the UK, but also internationally." The institute regularly publishes an economic commentary, which includes forecasts and detailed analysis of the Scottish economy, while also carrying out surveys of the economy on a regular basis, providing ongoing insights.
syntax_complex_s.xsum::49: Dr Fatoumata Nafo-Traoré, who heads the Roll Back Malaria (RBM) Partnership, said after visiting west Africa that, understandably, all the health workers' attention was focused on Ebola. She added that children's wards, which used to be full of malaria patients, were becoming "ghost areas." In 2012, malaria killed 7,000 people in the three countries worst hit by Ebola, most of these victims having been young children despite the fact that malaria is curable. The disease caused almost 4,000 deaths in Sierra Leone in 2012, as well as around 2,000 deaths in Liberia and approximately 1,000 in Guinea. Now that the three countries are wrestling with the Ebola virus, Dr Nafo-Traoré said she feared that recent gains in preventing malaria could be threatened by the crisis unfolding before them. She explained that these countries, having previously been really hit by malaria, had experienced even worse conditions five years ago when the deaths were double what they are now. Agreeing that no child should die from malaria because the necessary tools to prevent and treat it exist, she noted that now, understandably, all the health workers' attention was focused on Ebola. She recalled seeing hospital beds with three children in them at a time because there was not enough space available, whereas now those paediatric wards were becoming ghost areas because of the lack of manpower there. This meant that nobody knew who had malaria and who was dying from it. Even if the situation remained at the same level as last year, which was still very bad in those countries, she expressed real concern that Ebola would cause a setback to the efforts on malaria. She also mentioned that there was a lack of trust and confidence in health workers, with people still feeling that it was the health workers themselves who were bringing the virus to communities. RBM, being a partnership of more than 500 organisations that was formed 16 years ago to co-ordinate global efforts against malaria, reports that Guinea and Sierra Leone met key targets last year for distributing bed nets, which represent a crucial weapon for protecting children from mosquitoes that spread malaria. The situation in Liberia was less positive, with officials there trying to work out how they could boost their distribution efforts while simultaneously trying to contain Ebola. One problem complicating matters is that the early symptoms of Ebola and malaria can be similar. Dr Nafo-Traoré, having travelled by road from Conakry in Guinea to Sierra Leone earlier this month, told me that the Ebola treatment centres have a protocol for treating cases of fever with anti-malarial drugs too, because the patient might be suffering from both diseases simultaneously. She explained that at the moment when people have fevers, they are often afraid to go to healthcare facilities because they want to avoid being held in the Ebola treatment centres. Working with the countries to ensure people are tested for malaria and get the drugs, she stressed that having a co-ordinated approach was important, with a key aim being to decrease cases of malaria-related fever so the Ebola centres don't get overwhelmed. She expressed worry because of the weak health systems, noting that communication is so easy between all 15 of the West African countries. Pointing out that in the past Ebola occurred in remote bush areas whereas today it's happening in capital cities, she observed that people are getting well-organised now. As she travelled by road there, she saw checkpoints where people were having their temperature taken and were washing their hands. Fortunately, she concluded, the world has received a wake-up call, although the response was slow at the beginning.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::0: For several decades, regulatory testing schemes for genetic damage have been standardized, with the tests being utilized examining mutations along with both structural and numerical chromosomal damage, an approach that has served the genetic toxicity community well during the period when most of the substances being tested were amenable to such assays. The outcome from this testing, which is usually a dichotomous (yes/no) evaluation of test results, in many instances provides information that is only used to determine whether a substance has carcinogenic potential or not. Over the same time period, mechanisms and modes of action (MOAs) that elucidate a wider range of genomic damage involved in many adverse health outcomes have been recognized, while a paradigm shift in applied genetic toxicology is moving the field toward a more quantitative dose-response analysis and point-of-departure (PoD) determination with a focus on risks to exposed humans. This shift, which is directing emphasis on genomic damage that is likely to induce changes associated with a variety of adverse health outcomes, is moving the testing emphasis for genetic damage from a hazard identification only evaluation to a more comprehensive risk assessment approach that provides more insightful information for decision makers regarding the potential risk of genetic damage to exposed humans. To enable this broader context for examining genetic damage, a next generation testing strategy needs to take into account a broader, more flexible approach to testing, and ultimately modeling, of genomic damage as it relates to human exposure, which is consistent with the larger risk assessment context being used in regulatory decision making. As presented here, this flexible approach for examining genomic damage, focusing on testing for relevant genomic effects that can be, as best as possible, associated with an adverse health effect, identifies the most desired linkage for risk to humans as being changes in loci associated with human diseases, whether occurring in somatic or germ cells. The outline of a flexible approach and associated considerations are presented in a series of nine steps, some of which can occur in parallel, having been developed through a collaborative effort by leading genetic toxicologists from academia, government, and industry through the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI) Health and Environmental Sciences Institute (HESI) Genetic Toxicology Technical Committee (GTTC), with the ultimate goal being to provide quantitative data to model the potential risk levels of substances, which induce genomic damage contributing to human adverse health outcomes. Any good risk assessment begins with asking the appropriate risk management questions in a planning and scoping effort, a step that sets up the problem to be addressed (e.g., broadly, whether genomic damage needs to be addressed, and if so, how to proceed). The next two steps, assembling what is known about the problem by building a knowledge base about the substance of concern and developing a rational biological argument for why testing for genomic damage is needed or not, focus on the risk management problem and potential genomic damage of concern before the next step of assay(s) selection takes place. The work-up of the problem during the earlier steps, providing the insight to which assays would most likely produce the most meaningful data, does not detail the wide range of genomic damage tests available in this discussion, but points to types of testing systems that can be very useful. Once the assays are performed and analyzed, the relevant data sets, being selected for modeling potential risk, are evaluated and modeled from this point on as they are for any other toxicology endpoint. Any observed genomic damage/effects (or genetic event(s)) can be modeled via a dose-response analysis and determination of an estimated PoD, and when a quantitative risk analysis is needed for decision making, a parallel exposure assessment effort is performed (exposure assessment is not detailed here as this is not the focus of this discussion; guidelines for this assessment exist elsewhere). Then the PoD for genomic damage is used with the exposure information to develop risk estimations (e.g., using reference dose (RfD), margin of exposure (MOE) approaches) in a risk characterization and presented to risk managers for informing decision making. This approach, being applicable now for incorporating genomic damage results into the decision-making process for assessing potential adverse outcomes in chemically exposed humans, is consistent with the ILSI HESI Risk Assessment in the 21st Century (RISK21) roadmap and applies to any substance to which humans are exposed, including pharmaceuticals, agricultural products, food additives, and other chemicals. It is time for regulatory bodies to incorporate the broader knowledge and insights provided by genomic damage results into the assessments of risk to more fully understand the potential of adverse outcomes in chemically exposed humans, thus improving the assessment of risk due to genomic damage, given that the historical use of genomic damage data as a yes/no gateway for possible cancer risk has been too narrowly focused in risk assessment. The recent advances in assaying for and understanding genomic damage, including eventually epigenetic alterations, obviously add a greater wealth of information for determining potential risk to humans, meaning that regulatory bodies need to embrace this paradigm shift from hazard identification to quantitative analysis and to incorporate the wider range of genomic damage in their assessments of risk to humans. The quantitative analyses and methodologies discussed here, being readily applicable to genomic damage testing results now, are particularly relevant given that, with the passage of the recent update to the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) in the US, the new generation testing strategy for genomic damage described here provides a regulatory agency (here the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), but suitable for others) a golden opportunity to reexamine the way it addresses risk-based genomic damage testing (including hazard identification and exposure). Environ. Mol. Mutagen. 58:264-283, 2017. © 2016 The Authors. Environmental and Molecular Mutagenesis Published by Wiley Periodicals, Inc.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::1: Nutritional supplements, while potentially improving the development of infants born small (either preterm or small for gestational age [SGA]), may simultaneously increase the risk of later metabolic disease. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis with the aim of assessing the effects that macronutrient supplements given to infants born small have on later development and metabolism. Having searched OvidMedline, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews from inception to April 1, 2019, as well as controlled-trials.com, clinicaltrials.gov, and anzctr.org.au, we included randomised or quasirandomised trials if the intention was to increase macronutrient intake to improve growth or development of infants born small and assessed post-discharge outcomes. Co-primary outcomes, which were cognitive impairment and metabolic risk, were evaluated in toddlers (<3 years), childhood (3 to 8 years), and adolescence (9 to 18 years). Two reviewers, working independently, extracted data, while quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and data were pooled using random-effect models. Twenty-one randomised and one quasirandomised trial of variable methodological quality, involving 3,680 infants, were included. In toddlers born small, supplementation did not alter cognitive impairment (relative risk [RR] 1.00; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.49; P = 0.99), and there were no differences in cognitive scores (mean difference [MD] 0.57; 95% CI -0.71 to 1.84; P = 0.38) or motor scores (MD 1.16; 95% CI -0.32 to 2.65; P = 0.12) between supplemented and unsupplemented groups. However, fewer supplemented children had motor impairment (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; P = 0.01). In subgroup analyses, supplementation improved cognitive scores in boys (MD 5.60; 95% CI 1.07 to 10.14; P = 0.02), but not girls born small (MD -2.04; 95% CI -7.04 to 2.95; P = 0.42), and did not alter cognitive or motor scores in the subgroup of children born SGA. In childhood, there was no difference in cognitive impairment (RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.26 to 2.57; P = 0.72) or cognitive scores (MD 1.02; 95% CI -1.91 to 3.95; P = 0.50) between supplemented and unsupplemented groups. There were also no differences in blood pressure, triglyceride, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) concentrations (all P > 0.05), although supplemented children had lower fasting glucose (mmol/L: MD -0.20; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.06; P = 0.005) and higher high-density lipoprotein (HDL) concentrations (mmol/L: MD 0.11; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19; P = 0.02). In subgroup analyses, there was no evidence of differences in blood pressure between supplemented and unsupplemented groups in boys or girls born small, or in SGA children. In adolescence, there was no difference between supplemented and unsupplemented groups in blood pressure, triglycerides, LDL and HDL concentrations, fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance, and fasting insulin concentrations (all P > 0.05). Limitations include considerable unexplained heterogeneity, low to very low quality of the evidence, and limited data beyond early childhood. In this systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, we found no evidence that early macronutrient supplementation for infants born small altered later cognitive function, although there was some evidence suggesting that supplementation may decrease motor impairment in toddlers. Contrary to the findings from observational studies, evidence from randomised trials suggests that early macronutrient supplementation for infants born small improves some metabolic outcomes in childhood. syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::2: Objectives Recently, two point-of-care (PoC) feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) antibody test kits (Witness and Anigen Rapid) were reported as being able to differentiate FIV-vaccinated from FIV-infected cats at a single time point, irrespective of the gap between testing and last vaccination, which ranged from 0-7 years. The aim of the current study was to investigate systematically anti-FIV antibody production over time in response to the recommended primary FIV vaccination series. Methods First, residual plasma from the original study was tested using a laboratory-based ELISA to determine whether negative results obtained with PoC testing were due to reduced as opposed to absent antibodies to gp40. Second, a prospective study was performed using immunologically naive client-owned kittens and cats that were given a primary FIV vaccination series using a commercially available inactivated whole cell/inactivated whole virus vaccine (Fel-O-Vax FIV, consisting of three subcutaneous injections administered at 4 week intervals) and tested systematically (up to 11 times) over 6 months, using four commercially available PoC FIV antibody kits (SNAP FIV/FeLV Combo [which detects antibodies to p15/p24], Witness FeLV/FIV [gp40], Anigen Rapid FIV/FeLV [p24/gp40] and VetScan FeLV/FIV Rapid [p24]). Results The laboratory-based ELISA showed that cats from the original study vaccinated within the previous 0-15 months had detectable levels of antibodies to gp40, despite testing negative with two kits that use gp40 as a capture antigen (Witness and Anigen Rapid kits). The prospective study showed that antibody testing with SNAP Combo and VetScan Rapid was positive in all cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination, and it remained positive for the duration of the study (12/12 and 10/12 cats positive, respectively). Antibody testing with Witness and Anigen Rapid was also positive in a high proportion of cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination (8/12 and 7/12, respectively), but antibody levels declined below the level of detection in most cats (10/12) by 1 month after the third (final) primary FIV vaccination, with all cats testing negative using Witness and Anigen Rapid 6 months after the third primary FIV vaccination. Conclusions and relevance This study has shown that a primary course of FIV vaccination does not interfere with FIV antibody testing in cats using Witness and Anigen Rapid, provided that primary vaccination has not occurred within the previous 6 months. Consequently, Witness and Anigen Rapid antibody test kits can be used reliably to determine FIV infection status at the time of annual booster FIV vaccination to help detect 'vaccine breakthroughs' and in cats that have not received a primary course of FIV vaccination within the preceding 6 months. The duration of antibody response following annual booster FIV vaccination and the resulting effect on antibody testing using PoC kits needs to be determined by further research, while the mechanism(s) for the variation in FIV antibody test kit performance remains unclear.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::3: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), which is a rare monogenic disorder, is characterized by benign tumors in multiple organs as well as a high prevalence of epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism, being caused by inactivating mutations occurring in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Heterozygocity, inducing hyperactivation of mTOR, can be inhibited by mTOR inhibitors, such as rapamycin, which have proven efficacy in the treatment of TSC-associated symptoms. The aim of the present study was (1) to identify molecular changes associated with social and cognitive deficits in the brain tissue of Tsc1 +/- mice and (2) to investigate the molecular effects of rapamycin treatment, which has been shown to ameliorate genotype-related behavioural deficits. Molecular alterations in the frontal cortex and hippocampus of Tsc1 +/- and control mice, with or without rapamycin treatment, were investigated using a quantitative mass spectrometry-based shotgun proteomic approach (LC-MS E ), which was employed as an unbiased method to detect changes in protein levels. Changes identified in the initial profiling stage were validated using selected reaction monitoring (SRM), while Protein Set Enrichment Analysis was employed to identify dysregulated pathways. LC-MS E analysis of Tsc1 +/- mice and controls ( n = 30) identified 51 proteins changed in frontal cortex and 108 in the hippocampus, with bioinformatic analysis combined with targeted proteomic validation revealing several dysregulated molecular pathways. Using targeted assays, proteomic alterations observed in the hippocampus validated the pathways "myelination", "dendrite," and "oxidative stress", including an upregulation of ribosomal proteins and the mTOR kinase. LC-MS E analysis was also employed on Tsc1 +/- and wildtype mice ( n = 34) treated with rapamycin or vehicle, with rapamycin treatment exerting a stronger proteomic effect in Tsc1 +/- mice, producing significant changes, mainly consisting of decreased expression, in 231 and 106 proteins, respectively. The cellular pathways "oxidative stress" and "apoptosis" were found to be affected in Tsc1 +/- mice, while the cellular compartments "myelin sheet" and "neurofilaments" were affected by rapamycin treatment. Thirty-three proteins which were altered in Tsc1 +/- mice were normalized following rapamycin treatment, amongst them oxidative stress related proteins, myelin-specific and ribosomal proteins. Molecular changes in the Tsc1 +/- mouse brain were more prominent in the hippocampus compared to the frontal cortex, with pathways linked to myelination and oxidative stress response being prominently affected and, at least in part, normalized following rapamycin treatment. The results could aid in the identification of novel drug targets for the treatment of cognitive, social and psychiatric symptoms in autism spectrum disorders, given that similar pathways have also been implicated in other psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders and could imply similar disease processes. Thus, the potential efficacy of mTOR inhibitors warrants further investigation not only for autism spectrum disorders but also for other neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::4: Silica nanoparticles (nanoSiO 2 ), being promising systems that can deliver biologically active compounds to tissues such as the heart in a controllable manner, have nonetheless been recently related to cardiac toxicity induced through abnormal calcium handling and energetic failure occurring in cardiomyocytes. Moreover, the precise mechanisms that underlie this energetic debacle remain unclear, necessitating further investigation. In order to elucidate these mechanisms comprehensively, this article explores the ex vivo heart function and mitochondria following exposure to nanoSiO 2 . The cumulative administration of nanoSiO 2 , affecting the relaxation rate, reduced the mechanical performance index of the rat heart with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) of 93 μg/mL. In isolated mitochondria, nanoSiO 2 was found to be internalized, thereby inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation and significantly reducing the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m ). The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), which was also induced with an increasing dose of nanoSiO 2 , was partially recovered with Cyclosporine A (CsA), a potent blocker of the mPTP. The activity of aconitase and thiol oxidation occurring in the adenine nucleotide translocase were found to be reduced due to nanoSiO 2 exposure, suggesting that nanoSiO 2 induces the mPTP via thiol modification and ROS generation. In cardiac cells exposed to nanoSiO 2 , enhanced viability and reduction of H 2 O 2 were observed after application of MitoTEMPO, a specific mitochondrial antioxidant. Concomitantly, CsA treatment in adult rat cardiac cells reduced the nanoSiO 2 -triggered cell death while recovering ATP production from 32.4 to 65.4%. Additionally, we performed evaluation of the mitochondrial effect of nanoSiO 2 in human cardiomyocytes, observing a 40% inhibition of maximal oxygen consumption rate in mitochondria at 500 μg/mL. Under this condition we identified a remarkable diminution in the spare respiratory capacity, which indicates that a reduction in the amount of extra ATP that can be produced by mitochondria occurs during a sudden increase in energy demand. In human cardiomyocytes, increased LDH release and necrosis, reaching 85 and 48% respectively, were found at increased doses of nanoSiO 2 . Such deleterious effects were partially prevented by the application of CsA. Therefore, exposure to nanoSiO 2 affects cardiac function via mitochondrial dysfunction occurring through the opening of the mPTP. The aforementioned effects can be partially avoided by reducing ROS or retarding the opening of the mPTP. These novel strategies, which resulted in cardioprotection, could be considered as potential therapies to decrease the side effects resulting from nanoSiO 2 exposure.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::5: Return to play (RTP) of National Football League (NFL) athletes after isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears has been reported; however, no studies have reported on RTP of NFL athletes after multiligament knee injuries, which represents a significant gap in the literature. NFL athletes sustaining multiligament knee injuries have lower RTP rates and longer recoveries than athletes suffering isolated ACL tears. Second, athletes presenting with ACL and medial collateral ligament (MCL) injuries will have higher RTP rates and shorter time to RTP than athletes sustaining an ACL tear with posterolateral corner involvement. Retrospective cohort study. Level 4. Publicly available NFL injury data, covering all multiligament knee injuries incurred between 2000 and 2016 with RTP information documented, were reviewed systematically. Athletes were excluded if RTP was limited for reasons unrelated to the injury itself. Extracted data, which were analyzed comprehensively, included type of injury, RTP, time to RTP (days), number and percentage of games played, and performance metrics. A total of 50 NFL athletes with multiligament knee injuries met inclusion and exclusion criteria that had been established. The overall RTP rate, calculated across all injury patterns, was 64.0%. Athletes with ACL/MCL tears had an RTP rate of 70.8%, whereas athletes with ACL and posterior collateral ligament/lateral collateral ligament (PCL/LCL) tears had an RTP rate of 55.6% (P = 0.26), demonstrating a trend toward significance. Mean time to RTP for all 50 athletes included in the analysis was 388.71 ± 198.52 days. The mean time to RTP for athletes with ACL/MCL injuries was 305.1 ± 58.9 days, compared with 459.2 ± 245.1 days (P = 0.004) and 609.3 ± 183.1 days (P < 0.0001) for those with combined ACL and PCL/LCL injuries and frank knee dislocations, respectively, showing statistically significant differences. Athletes with ACL/MCL injuries were more likely to return to prior performance level (43.5%) than those with ACL and PCL/LCL injuries (18.5%) (P < 0.001), representing a clinically meaningful difference. The RTP rate for athletes with multiligament knee injuries is significantly less than the RTP rate for athletes with isolated ACL tears. In addition, athletes with ACL and MCL tears have a higher RTP rate, a significantly shorter time to RTP, and a greater likelihood of returning to prior performance than athletes with ACL and PCL/LCL tears. Multiligament knee injuries significantly affect the ability of a football player to return to sport. ACL and MCL tears are associated with better RTP prognosis compared with ACL and PCL/LCL tears.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::6: Pulmonary hypertension occurring in response to exercise, which serves as a marker of the hemodynamic severity of mitral stenosis (MS), has been recognized, though the factors related to elevated pulmonary pressure developing with exercise remain not well defined. The aim of this study, which we undertook to address this gap, was to assess the parameters associated with the pulmonary pressure response to exercise in patients presenting with pure rheumatic MS, while an additional aim was to determine the impact that exercise-induced pulmonary hypertension exerts on clinical outcome. One hundred thirty patients with MS (94% women; mean age, 45 ± 11 years), who were recruited for this investigation, underwent exercise echocardiography, during which a range of echocardiographic parameters were obtained at rest and at peak exercise. Symptom-limited graded ramp bicycle exercise, which was performed in the supine position, constituted the testing protocol. The primary end point was mitral valve intervention, either percutaneous or surgical. In the overall population studied, systolic pulmonary artery pressure (SPAP) increased from 38.3 ± 13.4 mm Hg measured at rest to 65.8 ± 20.7 mm Hg recorded during exercise. Increases in mean mitral gradient, right ventricular function, left atrial volume, and net atrioventricular compliance, when analyzed together, were independently associated with SPAP at peak exercise, after adjusting for changes occurring in heart rate. During the follow-up period, which had a median duration of 17 months with a range extending from 1 to 45 months, 46 adverse clinical events were observed among participants. By multivariate Cox proportional-hazards analysis, which was adjusted for age and sex, SPAP achieved at peak exercise emerged as an important predictor of adverse outcome (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.025; 95% CI, 1.010-1.040; P = .001). New York Heart Association functional class (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.459; 95% CI, 1.509-4.006; P < .001) and the interaction between valve area and net atrioventricular compliance (P = .001), when examined, were also significant predictors of adverse events. Time-dependent areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for the model incorporating SPAP during exercise were better than for the model using SPAP at rest, demonstrating a significant improvement from 3 years onward. In patients with MS, the pulmonary artery pressure response to exercise is determined by a combination of factors, including transmitral mean gradient at exercise, net atrioventricular compliance, left atrial volume, and right ventricular function, while pulmonary artery pressure at peak exercise serves as a predictor of clinical outcomes, adding incremental prognostic value beyond that provided by standard resting measurements, including valve area.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::7: The impact of chronic liver disease on outcomes in patients with COVID-19, which remains uncertain, prompted us to explore this association. We explored the outcomes of all adult inpatients with COVID-19 in France during 2020, computing adjusted odds ratios to measure the associations between chronic liver disease, alcohol use disorders, mechanical ventilation and day-30 in-hospital mortality. The sample, which comprised 259,110 patients with a median [IQR] age of 70 (54-83) years and included 52% men, contained 15,476 (6.0%) and 10,006 (3.9%) patients with chronic liver disease and alcohol use disorders, respectively. Death occurred in 38,203 (15%) patients, including 7,475 (28%) after receiving mechanical ventilation, and 2,941 (19%) with chronic liver disease. The adjusted odds ratios for mechanical ventilation and day-30 mortality, measuring these critical outcomes, were 1.54 (95% CI 1.44-1.64, p <0.001) and 1.79 (1.71-1.87, p <0.001) for chronic liver disease; 0.55 (0.47-0.64, p <0.001) and 0.54 (0.48-0.61, p <0.001) for mild liver disease; 0.64 (0.53-0.76; p <0.001) and 0.71 (0.63-0.80, p <0.001) for compensated cirrhosis; 0.65 (0.52-0.81, p <0.001) and 2.21 (1.94-2.51, p <0.001) for decompensated cirrhosis; 0.34 (0.24-0.50; p <0.001) and 1.38 (1.17-1.62, p <0.001) for primary liver cancer; and 0.82 (0.76-0.89; p <0.001) and 1.11 (1.05-1.17; p <0.001) for alcohol use disorders. Chronic viral hepatitis; non-viral, non-alcoholic chronic hepatitis; organ transplantation, including liver; and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome were not associated with COVID-19-related death. Chronic liver disease increased the risk of COVID-19-related death in France during 2020, with therapeutic effort limitation potentially contributing to COVID-19-related death in French residents who had a liver-related complication or an alcohol use disorder. Having studied the outcomes, including mechanical ventilation and day-30 mortality, of all adults with COVID-19 who were discharged from acute and post-acute care in France during 2020 (N = 259,110), we found that patients with mild liver disease; compensated cirrhosis; organ transplantation, including liver; or acquired immunodepression syndrome were not at increased risk of COVID-19-related mortality, whereas patients with alcohol use disorders, decompensated cirrhosis, or primary liver cancer were at increased risk of COVID-19-related mortality but were less likely to receive mechanical ventilation, suggesting that therapeutic effort limitation may have contributed to the excess mortality observed in French residents with a liver-related complication or an alcohol use disorder.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::8: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), which is caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), has led to a significant number of mortalities worldwide, posing a serious threat to human life. The clinical manifestations of COVID-19, being diverse and severe, result in 20% of infected patients being reported to be in a critical condition. A loss in lung function and pulmonary fibrosis, which are the main manifestations of patients with the severe form of the disease, affect the lung function even after recovery, thereby greatly affecting the psychology and well-being of patients and significantly reducing their quality of life. Participants must meet the following simultaneous inclusion criteria: being over 18 years of age, having recovered from severe or critical COVID-19 cases, exhibiting pulmonary fibrosis after recovery, and exhibiting Qi-Yin deficiency syndrome as indicated in the system of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). The eligible candidates, after being randomized into treatment or control groups, will receive either modern medicine (pirfenidone) plus TCM in the treatment group or modern medicine plus TCM placebo in the control group, while the lung function index will be continuously surveyed and recorded. By comparing the treatment effect between the two groups, the study intends to explore whether TCM can improve the effectiveness of modern medicine in patients with pulmonary fibrosis arising as a sequelae after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Pulmonary fibrosis, being one of fatal sequelae for some severe or critical COVID-19 cases, has been shown in some studies to respond to pirfenidone, which leads to a delay in the decline of forced expiratory vital capacity, thereby reducing the mortality partly. Additionally, although TCM has been proven to be efficacious in treating pulmonary fibrosis, its role in treating pulmonary fibrosis related to COVID-19 has not been explored. Hence, a multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled, interventional, prospective clinical trial, having been designed to determine if a new comprehensive treatment for pulmonary fibrosis related to COVID-19 is feasible and if it can improve the quality of life of patients, will be conducted. This multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled, interventional, prospective trial was registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000033284) on 26th May 2020, being prospectively registered.
syntax_complex_s.academic_abstracts::9: Temperature and water availability, being two of the most important variables, affect all aspects of an anuran's key physiological processes such as body temperature ( T b ), evaporative water loss (EWL) and standard metabolic rate (SMR). Since anurans display pronounced sexual dimorphism, evidence suggests that these processes, already complex in nature, are further influenced by other factors such as vapour pressure deficit (VPD), sex and body mass ( M b ). However, a limited number of studies have tested the generality of these results across a wide range of ecologically relevant ambient temperatures ( T a ), while simultaneously taking habitat use into account. Thus, the aim of this study was to investigate the role that T a plays on T b , whole-animal EWL and whole-animal SMR in three wild caught African anuran species possessing different ecological specialisations: the principally aquatic African clawed frog ( Xenopus laevis ), the stream-breeding common river frog ( Amietia delalandii ), and the largely terrestrial raucous toad ( Sclerophrys capensis ). Experiments, designed to test these relationships, were conducted at a range of test temperatures spanning from 5 to 35 °C, progressing at 5 °C increments.
