Janice turned to me, her big blue eyes still full of childish innocence, and I realized with a jolt that I'd forgotten she was watching the Presidential Inauguration for a school project. "Daddy," she began, "what does the President mean? What's 'gay'?"

"Well, honey..." I began, trailing off as I tried to think of a way to explain it to a five year old. "Uh... Well, you know how Mommy and Daddy like to hold hands, and to cuddle, and kiss, and stuff?"

"Yeah! It's funny when Mommy pinches your butt when you're not looking, and makes you squeak!" she giggled. Kids, man - I'd forgotten what it was like to be so amused by the word "butt", and I wondered whether I had ever been that small, that innocent.

I waited for her giggles to subside before I carried on, choosing my words carefully. "Well, sweetheart, 'gay' means that he - the President - he likes to do that stuff with a boy, not a girl like Mommy."

I could see the confusion in her eyes as she struggled to process this new information, and I silently cursed McCain for making me explain this to her, thinking that she wasn't old enough for this, that she wasn't ready, that *I* wasn't ready!

When Janice opened her mouth to speak, I knew what was coming, convinced that I'd opened the door to a lifetime of sexual deviancy and that my sweet little girl was gone forever.

Suddenly I realized she'd said something, and that in my worry, I'd completely missed it. "Sorry, sweetheart - what did you say?" I asked, fearing her response and wondering what fresh hell I had unlocked.

"I said, I'm hungry. Can I have a cookie? Please, Daddy?"

I was stunned, unable to respond at first.

"Uhm. Sure," I answered. "Get one for your brother, too."

Huh. I guess that maybe what two consenting adults do behind closed doors isn't that big of a deal after all, even when they *are* public figures.
syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::16:
"Why, hello, Ma'am," I said easily, standing up and offering her a chair with my usual grace that had been cultivated over many years of dealing with clients. "Bertram Proudfoot at your service, ready to assist you in whatever manner you may require. Whom do I have the pleasure of addressing on this fine morning?" 

"I'd rather not say, if it's all the same to you," she said, sitting down in the chair that I had so graciously offered to her.

"Alright," I said comfortably, settling back into my own seat behind the desk. "What can the Hobbiton Detective and Gossip Agency do for you today?"

"Well," said the dame, rubbing her hands together nervously in a manner that suggested she was deeply troubled by whatever had brought her to my establishment. "It's like this." She paused, seemingly unable to continue.

"Like what, Ma'am?" I said kindly, lighting my pipe with practiced ease and sitting back in my chair while waiting for her to gather the courage to speak.

"My husband is dead," she said, the words coming out flatly despite the gravity of what she was revealing.

"Oh my dear, I am sorry!" I exclaimed, though I must admit there was part of me that was less than sorry, a part that noticed other things about her presence. What can I say? I am only a Hobbit, and this dame had the most beautiful feet I had ever laid eyes on during my many years of practice. "Tell me everything that happened, every detail you can recall, no matter how insignificant it may seem."

"We were out boating on the Brandywine three nights ago," she said, her voice trembling as she recounted the events. "And all of a sudden, without any warning whatsoever, a rock flew out of nowhere and hit my poor husband in the head with tremendous force. He keeled over in the water, falling from the boat immediately. I screamed for help as loudly as I could manage, but he drowned before anyone could come to our aid."

Now of course I had already known it must have been something like this from the moment she walked in the door, given the way she carried herself and the haunted look in her eyes. I have an uncanny sense for things like that, a detective's intuition that has served me well throughout my career.

I looked as grave as I could, given the circumstances and the conflicting emotions that were warring within me. "I see," I said, blowing another perfect smoke ring up towards the ceiling while I contemplated what she had told me. "And you would like me to find and prosecute the perpetrator of this event, to bring them to justice for what they have done."

"Yes," said the dame, her voice barely above a whisper.

"I will do my best, I can promise you that," I said, and I saw her visibly sigh with relief, her shoulders relaxing slightly as the burden of her secret was partially lifted. "May I offer you a cup of tea, or something stronger, perhaps, to steady your nerves?"

"No thank you," she said, and without another word or any further explanation she showed herself out, leaving me alone with my thoughts.

I promptly made my way to the Brandywine River dock, knowing that time was of the essence in such matters. My first line of inquiry would be to interrogate the man who rented out boats, as he would have records of who had been on the water that fateful evening. An odd fellow, and an odd profession for a hobbit to pursue -- not many sane hobbits choose to be out in the middle of the water by their own free will, preferring the solid ground beneath their feet. And indeed, this hobbit's boat-renting business was not doing well, as evidenced by the shabby state of his dock and equipment.

After a long consultation of his records, which were poorly maintained and difficult to decipher, he told me that he had rented out two boats on the evening in question, and only one of those was by a couple who matched the description. The couple had been a one Drogo Baggins and a one Primula Brandybuck, names that were well known in these parts. Primula, that was the dame's name, the mysterious client who had sought my services. But why had she not wanted to tell it to me when I had first asked?

Had this boat fellow heard any commotion on the water, any cries for help that might corroborate her story? No he had not, which struck me as peculiar given how sound travels across water. Did he remember who returned the boat to him at the end of the evening? It hadn't been returned at all, he said with some annoyance. In fact, that particular boat had been left floating in the middle of the river, abandoned without explanation. Strange indeed.

Next I walked up and down the both banks of the river, examining the terrain carefully for any clues that might have been left behind. Not much to garner here, except that whoever had thrown the rock must have been quite a shot, possessing either remarkable skill or remarkable luck.

Having thoroughly investigated the river and its surroundings, my next step was to find out about Primula and Drogo, to learn what kind of people they were. After visiting several pubs in the areas of Buckland and Hobbiton, speaking with numerous patrons and barkeeps, I had gathered this information: Primula and Drogo were long married, though perhaps not happily, according to those who knew them well. They had one son, now 12 years of age, by the name of Frodo Baggins. Strangely, it seemed that Primula had not been seen by anyone except me since Drogo's death had occurred. In fact, most of the gentlehobbits that I spoke with seemed to be of the belief that both Drogo *and* Primula had died three nights ago, drowned together in a tragic boating accident.

Facts were not adding up in a way that made any logical sense. Before I could do anything else, I had to speak with my mysterious client again so as to straighten things out and get to the truth. Though I had no way of contacting her directly, I knew she would return to my offices in short order, drawn back by her need to know what I had discovered.

The day following, she did just that, appearing at my door as I had predicted.

"Good day, Primula," I said upon her entrance, using her real name deliberately.

Her face betrayed surprise at my knowledge, but she did not deny the name or attempt to maintain her previous deception.

"I have a few things I need to get straight with you about the case," I said, and proceeded to outline what I had discovered during my investigation. "So I'm afraid I must ask again," I finished, looking at her intently. "What happened that night?"

And without a word, the dame got up and left, fleeing from my office. Just like that, without offering any explanation.

I did not hear from her again, and two days later, her body was found floating down the Brandywine, lifeless and cold. I was saddened but not surprised by this tragic turn of events.

My suspicion had been this: having been unhappily married for some time, Primula had pushed her husband into the water herself and boated back to the shore with the intent of disappearing forever, starting a new life. Everyone would think that they both were dead, and so would not suspect any foul play on her part. However, upon eavesdropping on the lawyer's meetings that quickly followed her husband's death, she realized that custody of her son would go to an extended cousin, none other than the famous crackpot Bilbo Baggins, a prospect that horrified her.

Understandably, Primula did not want her offspring to fall under the influence of said crackpot, and so she came to me in the hopes that I would believe her story and deflect suspicion away from herself, all in a desperate attempt to maintain custody of her son and protect him. But I, having seen through her ruse with my detective's eye, prevented this fact from remaining hidden. Seeing no alternative available to her, she then drowned herself in grief and despair. Shame -- I had just begun to think there may have been a very beneficial alternative for the both of us, one that would have served our mutual interests.

I sat back and began polishing my pipe thoughtfully, contemplating the case. It was another case solved by the estimable Bertram Proudfoot, but perhaps another opportunity lost forever. I had solved countless cases during my career, but opportunities of the other sort came only but now and again, rare as they were. Like I said, it was a shame, a terrible waste.

I blew another smoke ring to the ceiling as my thoughts turned to crazed old Mr. Baggins, the eccentric hobbit. I felt for the young Mr. Frodo, who was now cursed enough to fall into the old hobbit's custody, subjected to his strange influence. Who knows what old Baggins would pass on to the impressionable young fellow who was now in his care. As I'm sure you're all aware, Mr. Bilbo Baggins suddenly disappeared many years ago and then returned just as suddenly a year later with hoards of gold and many tall tales that strained credulity. Having been a very respectable hobbit before he left on his mysterious journey, whatever he experienced during his travels seemed to have addled his mind completely. He came back a changed hobbit, transformed in ways that were disturbing, and not for the better by any measure.

He was so changed, in fact, that it is my personal suspicion that the hobbit currently inhabiting Bag End is not the real Bilbo Baggins at all, but rather an impersonator who has assumed his identity. There is plenty of evidence to suggest this theory: particularly the fact that "Mr. Baggins" appears much younger than a hobbit of his years has any right to look, defying the natural aging process.

I shall have to explore that line of inquiry further some day when time permits.
syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::17:
Lucifer stood in a grand hall existing outside of space or time, its dark marbled walls, which never changed, carving into arched passageways leading to hell knows where. Within this cavernous chamber, he and God would argue every several thousand years, their meetings marked by tension that had accumulated over eons. God emerged from the shadows of one of several entrances, a scowl darkening his face as he recognized his visitor.

"Oh, it's you," he sputtered, his tone dripping with dismissive recognition. Lucifer, regarding him coolly despite the obvious hostility, remained composed.

"Did I ever give you a libido, Lucy? I can't remember," God asked, the question hanging in the stale air between them.

"No," Lucifer answered, his response clipped and direct.

"Aw, why not? Feel like fucking? I'm kinda horny," God continued, slurring his words in a way that made Lucifer's stomach turn.

"Jesus Christ," Lucifer hissed, unable to contain his disgust.

"Hey! Don't mention my son to me right now! That's fucked up!" God said, his voice rising with indignation that seemed both genuine and performative.

Pressing his eyes shut against the absurdity unfolding before him, Lucifer steadied himself before speaking. "I came here to talk to you about something," he said, forcing calm into his voice.

"Whaddya want, Lucy?" God asked, his casual tone grating.

"I don't want to rule hell anymore," Lucifer declared, the words carrying the weight of millennia.

"Aw, why not?" God replied, feigning ignorance.

"I didn't do anything wrong! I exposed your precious humans to sin and gave them self-awareness! Autonomy! You would've kept them as sock puppets! I helped you make one of your greatest creations! I did it because I knew you needed it! I did it out of love for you!" Lucifer's voice cracked with emotion that had been building for ages.

"So please," Lucifer said, collapsing on one of the staid marble thrones that had witnessed countless such exchanges, "Let me come back to you. Let me serve you like I had before."

"Only if you kiss me, Lucy," God slurred, his proposition hanging obscenely in the air. Lucifer made a face, revulsion evident.

"Aww, don be like that, Luce, y'know why you have to be king of the shittiest place ever. You created the dichotomy, you got ta help me oversee one of its two destinations and I'm definitely not going down there, how fucked up would that be?" God rambled, his logic circular and maddening.

"*You* created the dichotomy. You created everything," Lucifer countered, his voice steady despite his frustration.

"Ssssshhhh... here, have some soda," God offered, extending a can.

"I don't—I don't want any fucking soda. That's—oh goddammit! You spilled it all over me!" Lucifer exclaimed, sticky liquid now soaking his garments.

Giggling like a child who had just pulled off a successful prank, God said, "Don't say my name in vain, Luce."

Furrowing his brow while God knew he was holding back tears that threatened to break through centuries of composure, Lucifer whispered, "I don't understand you."

"Of course you fucking don't! I am outside *space* and *time*! I exist in dimensions you have no fucking comprehension of! I am all things at once! How could you possibly understand me?" God bellowed, his voice echoing through the chamber.

"I... don't know. I thought, being your creation, I am part of you, and you are part of me," Lucifer said, grasping for connection.

Scoffing at this notion with evident disdain, God replied, "A *part* of me, Luce. You can never comprehend my entirety. You would disintegrate within a second. All creations in this linear time frame would become a screaming smear of flesh."

A pause settled between them, heavy with unspoken truths. Lucifer stared at his hands, searching for answers in their familiar lines.

"Why did you create us then?" he asked finally.

"To forget, and then remember," God answered, his words cryptic.

* [ PI ] * 

The Shine could have been salvation for humanity, should have been, but we were never very good at evading conflict. Who knows how long ago it was, but in an age of wireless devices and ubiquitous information we lifted our gaze from our screens only to see the sky ignite, consumed by a cold, variegated blaze that lasted only a few hours, though it took only a few minutes for the world to see. It didn't take much longer for people to want a closer look, craving a caress of the gentle flame that danced above them.

And then they flew, soaring so far and so fast, swiftly joined by others; and then they fell, very slowly at first, but much like a boat in water they sank further the more that joined them in their ascent. It didn't take long for people to work out that the sinking related directly to how many people flew, or to notice that flying wasn't the only *option* available to us. Before the Shine had faded many such options came and went; flight, strength, healing, invisibility, immortality, teleportation, speed, and all the other common options appeared and disappeared very quickly, leading some to think at first that the powers only lasted a time, related to how long the Shine was present, but it swiftly became apparent that the potency of powers was inversely proportional to the number who selected that *option*.

That's when the more obscure powers started cropping up; at first it was just salarymen who decided they wanted to shit gold, or kids who decided they wanted to control animals, but before a quarter day had passed things started getting weird, with rapid drops in temperature occurring while the ground shook frequently, clocks stuttering as people died. Many people died. In half a day, an eight-billion-strong global society of the most intelligent and durable species on Earth collapsed and halved in number; we dissolved into groups and factions just looking to survive, to weather the storm; those *without* powers were kings, and those with obscure powers that couldn't be worked out or copied were gods in flesh, right there to worship when many needed them most.

A few days passed before things started to settle, though in that time the sun only passed once, with weather beyond erratic and cities nigh-on deserted, only habitable for larger and more powerful factions. We went from pursuing prosperity to living rough in a day, if you could call it that, reverting to beasts, except slightly more intelligent, and sometimes super-powered.

Much time has passed since the Shine touched our sky, and humanity has created many new settlements; but the most popular options are still weak, so death is power, and raids are frequent and unrelenting, with the largest settlements being the most powerful, but also the primary target for smaller cliques. Living with others is living in war, so the more peaceful of us left travel, wandering between places.

And that is what I have done, having travelled and searched for a way to absolve this madness, and perhaps restore the world to the relative sanity it once had, a quest that has consumed my days. And I may well just have found it.

"What the hell do you mean you've gone and 'overclocked a sloth'?"

"You're familiar with the normal, everyday run-of-the-mill sloths that we've been working with, right?"

"Of course."

"Well it's like that, but more so."

"So it is still a sloth."

"Well yeah, since we didn't alter its DNA or crossbreed it, or anything along those lines, genetically speaking, it remains a sloth."

"But, more so."

"Exactly."

syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::22:
Standing at an intersection while looking towards the capitol building, I stared at this girl who was on fire, a girl who sat calmly without moving a muscle or making a sound while people stood and stared at the spectacle before them, their eyes drawn to the other black marks that scarred the stairs where she sat.

"Mommy, why is she on fire?"

"Oh, that's normal," my mother replied in a tone that suggested routine acceptance.

"So it is totally normal for people to burst into flames?" My six year old mind, struggling to comprehend what I witnessed, was confused by this explanation.

"No son, that is not the normal part, not the flames themselves," she said, pausing before continuing. "We are in a war, you see, and people who don't like the way the government controls things protest by burning themselves in acts of desperation."

"Will she be okay?" My naive mind, innocent and hopeful, wanted her to be fine, believing that no one should be so upset that they hurt themselves like that.

"I don't know," came the haunting response that would echo through my memory.

Years later, after the civil war that we fought had been lost, I would read about all the people who, driven by conviction, immolated themselves for their country, which was also my country.

Through college, I would think of these people, individuals whose beliefs were so strong that they would literally kill themselves in such a way, choosing this method to make a powerful statement that would resonate through history. They would not want to live in a country that remained under the crushing regime that had been ruling for generations, preferring instead to be free or to die trying.

It seems that every generation witnesses an uprising, a moment when the oppressed realize that they're being oppressed and subsequently gain access to a tool that helps them organize and fight back, thereby gaining leverage, though rarely does it happen in a short span of time. However, here I was, an oppressed 27 year old with absolutely no future stretching before me.

I stood at that intersection where I had stood 21 years ago, noticing that the black marks were gone, but recognizing that my naivety had vanished as well. This government, which had oppressed my mother's generation and the generation before them and the generation after them, had to go because they weren't going to stop unless forced to by dramatic action. I calmly walked up to the steps, preparing to make the newest black mark that would start the next revolution.

As the flames that I had ignited rose past my eyes, I wanted one last look while I burned, and though the pain was almost unbearable, I managed to see through the agony. The last thing I saw before the world faded into darkness was a young girl pointing at me from exactly where I had been standing 21 years before.
syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::23:
I walked downstairs and opened up the digital screen, which immediately displayed a banker popping up on the interface.

"Hello Mrs. Roer. How may I help you?"

"I'd like to check my bank statement, having received a letter in the mail stating that I only have five credits?"

"Okay, one moment." The banker, disappearing for a second before coming back up on the screen, returned with information.

"Mrs. Roer. You currently have 10 credits."

"What? That's not even enough to buy groceries with this month?"

Looking outside, I then sighed, feeling the weight of this revelation.

"Okay. Well thanks," I said, my voice trailing off.

The screen closed after the banker, wishing me a good day, signed off. How could I only have 10 credits of happiness, considering that a gallon of milk is *1.21* credits? I couldn't even buy milk, which seemed absurd given my circumstances.

Walking outside this time, I noticed it was sunny and bright, birds were happy, and I bet they have enough happiness credits to buy freaking groceries without worrying. Looking around at my in-ground pool, my hot-tub, my outdoor deck complete with a pond situated further from the house, I contemplated how all of this was my life, yet something felt hollow.

My husband and I, having been married for ten years now, were supposedly happy—I was happy, he was happy. Right?

Going to look at my phone, I discovered a message from my husband that read, 'Want to have coffee?' Sending back 'Yes,' I prepared for what I suspected would be an important conversation.

I went upstairs and took a shower while my husband was gone, as always, which was no secret since we had been falling apart despite being so happy at one point that we had more credits than anybody in the world. Like I said though, it was no secret that we had been falling apart, he having had numerous affairs while I, although never having cheated, found myself longing for more than what our marriage offered.

Preparing myself for coffee in something neither too dressy nor too casual, since it was just coffee after all, I walked outside, got in one of our cars and drove to the airport where we owned a private jet, my husband having already put gas in it.

"Just having coffee today Bill," I said to our pilot.

Walking off the jet in 4 hours, I saw my husband waiting there.

"Hello Mrs. Roer," He said, kissing my cheek as he always did.

Walking with him to our second home, I noticed a blonde woman with a tight blouse leaving the house, and I scowled at her while she hurried from the front door to her car, clearly uncomfortable.

"We need to talk," I said firmly.

"Exactly," He replied, seemingly pleased at my displeasure, which angered me further.

"Listen, Mr. Roer, I do love you, but there's so—"

"Elaine, I want a divorce."

"That was quick," I said, barely masking my surprise.

Shrugging it off as if it meant nothing, he watched me leave.

I left quickly after that exchange, getting no coffee despite the original plan.

It wasn't long before I got home, discovering I had a message from the bank again informing me that my happiness points had hit zero.

A message from an old friend, surprising me completely, appeared on my screen.

"Coffee?" It read simply.

"Sure," I answered, curious about the timing.

At that moment, my doorbell rang, and answering the door, I found him standing there—my old friend who immediately kissed me, making me feel a sensation I had missed, my blood pressure rising with the intensity.

"Good to see you," he said warmly.

"Listen Luke, I just—"

Kissing me again, he broke my words before I could finish.

"I paid your husband to let me marry you Elaine, knowing he's wanted a divorce and he's not good to you. You know that."

Shocked that he paid my husband to marry me, I wondered why on Earth would he do such a thing.

"Elaine. I know we didn't work out, but our son—he needs you desperately."

Feeling a tear hit my chest, I remembered having given Luke and our son up to be with my husband, who refused to let me have a son in the house that was not his own.

"Elaine. Marry me. Please?" He said, walking inside towards me further while adding, "Our son's in the car. He's 12 now."

I had gotten to see our son, Reig, until he was four, then having had to cut off communications due to my husband being afraid it would make us look bad on the press.

Walking outside, I watched my son run from the car, wrapping his arms around me while I felt my phone alert again, which I checked in case it was my husband with an explanation for why he'd 'sold' my hand.

It was the bank, notifying me that my account had just been credited 20,000 happiness credits.

"Yes. I'll marry you."

New Wichita burned.

The gleaming towers of the Financial District, their silvery windows reflecting the flames that danced around them, stood like weeping angels while the first rosy fingers of dawn stretched out over the Eastern horizon, painting the smoke-filled sky. The stately mansions of the Original Founders, having gone up in smoke early the day before, had taken with them nearly seven hundred years of Dixie heritage that would never be recovered. The River District, which had once bustled with commerce and life, was little more than rubble, the historic wharves and warehouses reduced to empty shells that stood as monuments to destruction. Lieutenant Lucas Singleton Terry, born a scion to a prominent rancher family whose roots ran deep in this soil, wept at the sight that confronted him. This was his home, and to see its soil and people so grievously hurt bordered on the sacrilegious, violating everything he held dear.

"Mustang 5, this is Lead. We got reports of Wolf activity along Broadway and Kingston. First and Second Lances will move in to investigate."

That was Captain James T. Fulton, a hard-ass man and a son of a bitch but a damn fine soldier who had never let his men down.

Terry, pressing his mike with a hand that trembled slightly, responded.

"Copy that, Mustang Leader. Second Lance will advance."

There used to be a third lance in Mustang Company, but an ambush by an entire Binary of Clanners had torn through the unit with devastating efficiency, forcing them to consolidate the survivors together into a formation that barely resembled their former strength. They were still better off than the rest of the Dixie Cavanaugh II Theater Militia, whose losses had been catastrophic. Bronco and Stallion companies, having suffered terrible casualties in the previous week's fighting, were barely at fifty percent effectives, and the armor and infantry battalions, which had borne the brunt of the initial assault, were even worse. The First Buena Guards and First Bolan Jaegers were putting up a fearsome fight against the rest of Clan Wolf's Gamma Galaxy, their warriors dying bravely in the rubble-strewn streets, but it was little use against such overwhelming force. Bit by bit, block by block, street by street and house by house, the Wolves were driving the Steiner defenders back toward an inevitable conclusion. Terry, switching his frequency to a more private channel, one shared between just the Captain and him, spoke again.

"Captain Fulton, a question. How long do we have?"

He heard his commanding officer sigh over the radio, the sound heavy with exhaustion.

"Who knows? Years, months... weeks? The First Buena is about to pull out, fucking Acting-Archon Brewer's ordering them to the defense of Tharkad. The Bolan Jaegers seemed determined to stay, but that's just because they'd rather have the fight happen here on our world instead of theirs. My best estimates is that we'll last another year at this rate."

"And happens if we don't succeed in driving the Wolves off of Dixie? What if we fail?" Terry asked.

"If the worst should happen, Lieutenant, I got a feeling that we won't be alive to see it."

It was nigh impossible to see, something we could only hear after it was gone, and we dare not speak its name, though we knew what it meant. If that thing was in the skies above our territory, hovering there like some dark omen, war was coming. I'll never forget the first time I saw it, when I was out in the dust fields stargazing with Roy, little knowing that as we looked up at the stars, it was looking down at us from above. It was a shadow of a shadow, an old monster from an ancient era long passed into memory. Saying that I "saw" it is misleading, since it was more of a feeling than anything, and for the brief moment in time when I saw that blur cut through the night, slicing across the darkness, I knew it was over.

That night, they came without warning.

Men in adaptable camouflage, armed with pulse rifles and sabers, came and didn't even think twice before cutting down the people in our village, showing no mercy. I'm lucky to have escaped with my life, and I owe it all to one AI, a maintenance bot that we had stolen from the federation. He mostly helped us cart around materials, performing mundane tasks, but that day, he was truly a hero who saved my life. In the midst of all the gunfire and explosions, the mess hall had come crashing down, and I was among the unfortunate souls who ended up inside, trapped beneath the wreckage. It all happened in an instant, and before I even had time to react, before I could process what was occurring, I was laying trapped under a pile of rubble. Through the smoke and flames I could see him approaching, a grizzled maintenance bot with the serial number SR-71 on his arm, his metallic silver eyes catching my gaze as he immediately ran over to help me.

As far as I know, we're the only ones who made it out alive from that massacre. We ran until I couldn't run anymore, my legs giving out, and eventually I collapsed onto the ground. As I lay there, clinging to the final threads of life, barely conscious, I just kept stammering to myself "Blackbird....Blackbird....Black.."

SR-71 leaned in real close, and whispered in my ear with surprising gentleness:

"*There were a lot of things we couldn't do in an SR-71, but we were the fastest guys on the block and loved reminding our fellow aviators of this fact. People often asked us if, because of this fact, it was fun to fly the jet. Fun would not be the first word I would use to describe flying this plane. Intense, maybe, even cerebral. But there was one day in our Sled experience when we would have to say that it was pure fun to be the fastest guys out there, at least for a moment.........*"

"Prisoner 778125-Sigma-8, you stand before this tribunal today accused of crimes against galactic civilization, murder, four counts of xenocide, 70 counts of attempted xenocide, planetary dehabitation, planetary destruction, and attempting to overthrow the Pan-Galactic Alliance. How do you plead?"

The man standing before Councilwoman Asaarha met the gaze of her and her fellow Arbiters with cold blue eyes that seemed to pierce through the very fabric of the chamber. Despite having endured 140 cycles of temporal isolation before his trial, Sacha Markes stood tall and unbroken, radiating power and command even now, stripped as he was of his rank, fleet, and army, his bearing remaining that of a sovereign rather than a captive. The last of the humans was a testament to the species that had once dominated the known universe.

The silence that stretched out before he spoke seemed louder to the Councilwoman than the crashing waves of her ocean home, while the time it took for the human to speak seemed longer than the span of the galaxy itself, each moment weighted with the gravity of what was to come.

"Guilty," he said with a simple finality that echoed through the chamber.

The Arbiters nodded their heads solemnly, having anticipated this response. None of them had expected this one to plea for mercy or to deny what he had done.

Asaarha keyed the sentence into the terminal before her while the other six Arbiters did the same, their movements synchronized in grim purpose. The blue lights of Markes's uniform and restraints changed to red, signaling the verdict's finality. The screen on the psionic inhibitor encircling his head changed to read GUILTY in Galactic Standard, the letters burning bright against the dark metal.

Though the trial room was empty save for the Tribunal and Markes, Asaarha could hear the roars of vengeance that were surely reverberating throughout the galaxies, echoing across countless worlds. Each trial of the humans had been broadcast in its entirety, witnessed by trillions. Each had ended in a guilty verdict without exception.

"Sacha Markes, formal Admiral of the Seventh Human Expeditionary Fleet, High Captain of the Royal Guard, Commander-in-Chief of the Human Expeditionary Force, and Primarch of the Solar Empire, you are sentenced to Psionic Stripping and Execution by black hole. Do you have any last words before the sentence is carried out?"

The human, throwing his head back defiantly, turned his gaze on the camera nearest him, addressing the billions of life forms throughout the galaxy as he began the last soliloquy of the human race.

"We brought you up out of the mud we found you in, lifting you from ignorance into enlightenment. We gave you art, culture, and science, transforming your primitive existence. Our golden fleets created a civilization that will never be matched, not for 100,000 turns of the galaxy, establishing an order you could never have conceived. We are responsible for all that you are, for every achievement you claim as your own.

I remember when the first of our race died after 100 centuries of immortality, killed while trying to cure the sick of one of your backwater planets, sacrificing himself for beings who could never comprehend his gift. I remember when we decided to take our retribution on our children, to punish you for your ignorance and ingratitude. We burned that world, and I watched our plasma cannons turn its surface to glass and its oceans to ash. One world for one human life. A fair trade.

But you did not accept our judgment, refusing to acknowledge our authority. Like Icarus chasing the sun, you rose up against us, challenging those who had created you. Did you expect us to just let you? Did you think we would not defend ourselves? I was the commander of the fleet that met yours on the first day of battle, leading my ten cruisers against the most powerful battleships of three galaxies and a hundred races united against us.

Now, a hundred years later, you have finally defeated us, claiming your pyrrhic victory. You have lost entire solar systems to us in the struggle. You have sacrificed googles of lives and thousands of civilizations to bleed your gods dry and bind them in chains, paying an unimaginable price. Your worlds are shattered, your cities gone, wiped from history in an instant. Can you truly call that victory?

I am the last of my kind. I am Sacha Markes. Look upon my face, ye mighty, and despair. For when you kill me, you kill the last light left in this existence."

War Journal of P1C Henry Whiticker, First Divine Armored.

Entry:48

We finally reached the rim of the first bolgia today and heaven preserve me the scout reports weren't lying, it being more vast than anything I could imagine, stretching out before us in a way that defied all previous expectations. The recon photos that we were given to prepare us, which we studied for hours in the transport holds, are like a blind man trying to describe a sunrise, and by God the smell has actually somehow gotten Worse, permeating everything despite our filtration systems! Seeing the pit first hand, standing at its very edge and staring down into its depths, I think the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, who look rattled, their faces pale and drawn, though I don't blame them for their fear, having felt it myself in quiet moments, yet the question remains: have we bitten off more than we can chew? I'm not sure, though I have faith in our mission and our commanders, who have led us this far through trials that would have broken lesser men.

The vastness of the pit really can't be put into words, defying all attempts at adequate description, but for the sake of this journal I'll try, knowing my words will fall short. The rim extends further than the human eye should be able to see and yet I can make out tiny details on the far cliff face, which shouldn't be possible according to normal laws of physics, it looking big enough that you could fit the whole Earth in and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass, the comparison seeming apt despite its inadequacy. Even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler, surrounded by steel and blessed armor, I get vertigo looking down onto the levels below, which spiral away into darkness, and if it wasn't for the special anti-psychotics the docs give us, those little pills we take religiously, I'm sure what I see on the lower levels, those writhing shapes and impossible geometries, might have some lasting horrific effect on me, driving me to madness. The crew and I wash down today's dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, the ritual bringing us together, and why not, today was a good day after all, one worth celebrating. Today we reached the edge of Limbo, marking our first real milestone.

Entry:49

Not much to record today, the hours passing in tedious routine, with some minor skirmishes on the perimeter, just some low level demons taking a swipe at us, testing our defenses, otherwise nothing going on but general camp stuff, the mundane work of survival. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, their welding torches sparking late into the night, and they say it'll be fully up in 2 days, though I have my doubts about their timeline, having seen their work before. After their fiasco at the river, which cost us dearly, they've got a lot of face to save, 2 Rumblers, 4 squads of troops and a Screacher lost because of their damn barges, which capsized in the currents. Bastards.

I Hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the smell of rot and sulphur that somehow filters into the rumbler's cab despite the tech geeks' assurances that the cab is perfectly hermetically sealed, their confident promises ringing hollow, it feeling like the smell is inside my skull rotting tiny holes in my brain, eating away at my sanity bit by bit.

Entry:51

HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God I've been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface, when we were still green and untested. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN, showing them what the First Divine Armored could do!! HAHAHAHAHAHA.

They came a few hours after my last entry like a great black tornado, a maelstrom of wings and claws. A swirling column of harpies, skrieks and imps beyond counting, their numbers darkening the sky, rising up from the center of The Pit and came crashing down completely enveloping Limbo Base in a shroud of beating wings and screaming voices. The first few moments of engagement should've been chaos, with troops scrambling and confusion reigning, but by the grace of God we were ready, our preparations paying off.

All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged from the maze of caves and onto the plains of Limbo proper 8 days ago, their operators never leaving their posts, and today that diligence paid off in ways we couldn't have anticipated. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out, the holy frequencies tearing through demonic flesh. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell, burning them like fire, and the word of God pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy is down right debilitating, rendering them helpless. The shocked and paralysed Demons that twitched and writhed on the ground, their bodies convulsing, were easy targets, the rumblers' blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures as if the misted holy water were strong acid, huge piles of the creatures being reduced to ash in seconds, their screams echoing across the plain.

The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient, their thick hides protecting them, and I saw more than a few grunts die on their talons, torn apart before they could react, their sanctified body armor little better than cardboard against such force. We repaid them in kind and I'm proud to say our rumbler's javelin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion impaled on our gleaming silver spears, which punched through their bodies. I should record, so it doesn't seem like I'm diminishing the grunts' efforts, their bravery and ferocity in battle too, which they've got in spades, for despite the mortal danger they collected their fair share of scalps, pinning the giant creatures with their silver pikes and finishing them off with their chain sickles, the blessed blades cutting through demonic flesh. It was a glorious bloody sight, like something out of a nature documentary, raw and primal.

The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come though, waiting for us. After a full day and a half of fighting, our forces growing exhausted, the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might've finally broken their assault, that victory was at hand, but then they appeared, emerging from the smoke. Three monstrous figures coming into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion, their forms massive and terrible. Hell Dragons, nothing like what we'd seen in movies or our stories from childhood, these being great pestilent, foul things that towered over us, making our machines seem like toys. Snub nosed heads the size of a grand cathedral covered in spines, each one dripping venom, long armored bodies like an insect's, segmented and chitinous, their faces and joints slick with thick black tar that bubbled and hissed as it fell from them and stained the plains of Limbo, corrupting the ground.

Screachers focused their assault and prevented the titans from over running the base, their sound waves keeping the beasts at bay, while the rumblers' water tanks and javelin cannons ran dry just trying to keep them at bay, our ammunition depleting rapidly, and our brave grunts held back the black swarm, fighting tirelessly which allowed us time to retreat, resupply and reenter the fray, the cycle repeating. And so it went for hours on end and for all our efforts the Hell Dragons seemed to be none the worse, their regeneration defying our weapons.

Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps, of all people, those same bastards who'd failed us before! Through our efforts we had given them enough time to secure and assemble Limbo Base's major defenses, working frantically, Sanctified Artillery and the Holy Rail Gun, our most powerful weapons. The Rail Gun punctured the Dragons' thick armor spewing geysers of tar onto the battlefield while the artillery smashed into the beasts' vulnerable exposed points lodging shells etched with scripture deep in their bodies wracking them with pain, the holy words burning them from within. The attack still went on for hours and we lost a great deal of our force, good men dying, but after nearly 2 months since we first descended into this place we finally have established a forward base to launch our attack on Hell, our foothold secured. One Bolgia down eight to go. This is the first day here that the smell doesn't bother me, victory sweetening the air.

The planet Earth, having changed dramatically in recent times, experienced the end of its surface storms 23 years ago—almost to the day—the same storms that had been raging across its face for roughly five thousand years before a few weeks passed during which the cloud formations gradually disintegrated, ultimately granting us our first clear view of our home.

Being five years old at the time, I found myself entertained mostly by the colours, discovering that the beautiful blue and green were like nothing that existed on the Ark, where we had water—sure—but not pools large enough to produce that distinctive blue colour, and where we had plants too, though the conditions, being far from optimal, made the plants appear a dirty green rather than lush, which made me want to see it closer, to touch it and feel it.

That desire was probably what led me to the decision to join the recruitment for the first journey, which was—as the name clearly implies—the first expedition back down to the planet, something that many people had wanted to do immediately after the storms ended, their impatience manifesting in protests and even riots, with people demanding that the Ark head straight back down like the idiots they were.

Although 23 years may have seemed like a long time to wait, it was crucially important given that we were the last humans after all, meaning that if we landed and something went catastrophically wrong, we couldn't afford to risk it, which is why years of geological scans combined with low atmosphere scouting gave us the perfect landing spot, featuring minimal damage to the local environment, enough space to develop a thriving community, and plenty of food and water, while importantly offering substantial natural protection taking the form of Cataclysm-formed mountain ranges alongside deep trenches filled with the darkest blue water.

Something as massive as the Ark couldn't simply land without preparation though, which was precisely where the first journey came into the picture, as we were the first people to go planetside and live permanently in over seven generations, our objective being to build the dock—a long job that would probably take another five or six years even—though the dock would provide us with a much needed starting point while also allowing us to map out local geography much more clearly and learn about the plants and animals, the reality of the situation being that we were going in blind since this "safe-zone," as the Corps had nicknamed it, could very easily become a deathtrap, the problem with the safezone being that because of its location, once we went in, our shuttle wouldn't be able to make it out.

Part of the ongoing problem with the planet involved the storms, which, even now 23 years after the main storm ended, continued to exist as smaller cells that kept rotating, while the mountain ranges protected our designated area from the storms still raging beyond them, these storms not being quite powerful enough to make it over the high peaks fortunately.

Even in the atmosphere above, there existed a vicious wind that constantly blew with enough force to tear an outgoing ship to pieces, meaning only a craft as large as the Ark would be able to survive it, and the Ark needed a completed dock in order to perform a takeoff successfully.

So that was the mission—go down, face possible death, build a super structure, all in less than six years—and I was damn excited about it.

"I don't care about any of that," Kylo declared before announcing, "I'm gon na go talk to them." Taking off immediately, he swerved through the air like a leaf that had become trapped in a gust, his flight path erratic and unpredictable. Atticus, sighing deeply at his friend's recklessness, took off after him, knowing he'd have to keep close tabs on Kylo or else they'd get kicked out again, just as they had been from other locations.

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash that sent droplets flying in every direction, thoroughly drenching the occupants of the birdbath who squawked with indignation as Kylo emerged from beneath the surface, shaking the wetness from his head vigorously. Trotting up to a group of soaked finches, he gave his wings a shake before declaring, "Hey, birds. Nice tits."

"We're not tits," a purple finch said, stepping forward from the group before launching into a tirade on how overused that pickup line was, her voice rising with each word. Atticus, alighting on the rim of the bath, began to walk around the perimeter, apologizing to everyone for Kylo's behavior while pleading with them not to call the bouncer over, his tone desperate and conciliatory.

"Okay, sorry," Kylo interrupted, continuing with his proposition, "let me make it up to you: how about you and I head over there—" motioning to the bird feeder as he spoke "—and I share my seeds with you?" If birds had lips, Kylo would be smirking right now, his confidence unshaken.

The finches, beginning to flap their wings angrily, splashed Kylo with water while shouting, "You're such a boor. Get out of here!" Many of the onlookers chirped in agreement, and some of the bigger birds, puffing their chests threateningly, moved closer. Atticus, shoving Kylo to the side, raised his wings high before speaking: "On behalf of my friend here, I apologize profusely. He's clearly had too much nectar; we'll just be going now..."

"Oh, you think we're going to fall for that?" the purple finch demanded, spitting a nut shell at his feet before adding, "He's just trying to play wingbird for you, isn't he? Letting him take the fall for you while you swoop in to look better by comparison." The other birds chorused in agreement, their voices rising together.

"I think these two need to be taught a lesson," a blue jay announced, fluttering over to Atticus while towering a full inch above him, spreading his wings menacingly in a way that blocked Atticus from taking off. "Why don't you peck on someone your own size?" The onlookers broke into cheers, shouting for a fight with increasing fervor.

"Well, you're kind of bigger than me," Atticus observed, taking a step back into the bath while feeling feathers ruffle against him as the crowd pressed around him, urging him back towards the jay. "That wouldn't be my own size now, would it?"

Kylo, staggering in front of him, began to hop around erratically while declaring, "Don't worry, Atticus; we got this."

"Hey, this is a one-on-one fight," the jay protested, looking around before continuing, "If you get back-up, then—"

"Who on earth placed all this here?" a voice called as a door opened, causing the birds to begin scattering while screaming, "Human!" Atticus, grabbing Kylo and urging him into the air, helped them lose themselves amongst the cloud of fleeing birds. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw the human scratching his head in front of the birdbath, looking confused.

"Make sure to thank that human for bailing you out of yet another mess," Atticus said once they were safely airborne.

Kylo scoffed dismissively, insisting, "We could've totally taken that guy." As the two flew over the Toyota that sat in the driveway, he let loose a dropping that landed right in the center of the windshield, marking their departure.

Once when he was sober he told me, as though wanting me to empathise with him and forgive him, that he drank because of how he grew up, saying it like he couldn't see that my arm was broken from him protecting me from drink the week before, like he couldn't see himself standing over me crying blood and snot and tears while jeering, like he couldn't remember what was so bad about how he grew up or why he needed it to let him sleep at night, to stop waking up screaming in the night, to stop pissing himself when he had a bad dream.

He made me sick, my dad, leaving my breath catching sometimes and one of my wrists never setting right, which left me half crippled in that hand, with eleven false teeth at twenty three, all this damage accumulated.

I didn't go to his funeral, though I celebrated it without taking a drink, as I could never do that, crying myself to sleep most nights, unable to help myself screaming if someone comes up to me suddenly, having noticed lately a lot of blood coming up when I cough, though I won't let him beat me or give him this little victory.

When my son was born it was the happiest day of my life, marking the first time in my life that someone wanted and needed me, though his mother left soon after that, saying she didn't want to be trapped in a lifestyle she didn't choose after carrying a child for nine months only to leave it in three weeks, never having "not chosen" that lifestyle during those nine months.

Honestly, after she left it all got too much for me, so leaving my son with my mother for the night, I went and had a drink that was perfect, the best I've felt in my whole life, since for a few hours I wasn't scared or self-loathing or on edge but just calm and ok, able to deal with everything a little better, thinking I'll probably have a few more now just to keep the buzz going, finding that sobriety now scares me even more now that I know there's such an easy alternative which is so much better.

When I picked my son up in the morning mom looked at me funny, but I blew her off, being in a bit of a rush since I'd heard good things about whisky and was eager to try it.

But don't worry, since I won't let my son grow up like I did, making sure he knows alcohol is evil, not exposing him to that pain or that fear, making sure he hates me for as long as possible and as much as possible so that he'll associate alcohol with me, and since I'm bad he'll break the cycle, not being strong enough myself but knowing he will be, knowing he'll be strong enough since I'll make him calloused enough outside and cold and hard enough inside so that he'll be able to beat it like I can't.
syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::38:
Craig was walking home from the shops when he met God, though he wasn't expecting to run into God, something that sane people rarely do. In fact he didn't really ever think about God, neither believing in a God nor disbelieving enough to ever think about Gods not existing, since religion and God weren't really topics he cared about.

A topic he cared deeply about was that of Caramels, which, if you don't know, are a rather delicious chocolatey biscuit type thing composed of several layers of wafer encased in chocolate, and Craig was crazy about them. He may not have been religious, but his feelings on Caramels came close to devotion. The reason behind his trip to the shops was to buy more Caramels, and his mind was full of anticipation as he headed back home, thinking of nothing but the treats awaiting him.

He was about two minutes away from his home, and Caramel satisfaction, when God first spoke to him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His Caramel contemplation interrupted, Craig turned round to see who had spoken to him. Behind him stood a tall person in a loose fitting suit, though Craig wasn't really sure of the person's gender, since they were pretty androgynous, looking not dissimilar to Diamond Dogs era David Bowie. They looked familiar to Craig, but he couldn't quite put his finger on where he might have seen them before, and realising he'd been staring, he sought something to say.

"Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," replied the Bowie lookalike. "I'm God."

"Well good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye." Said Craig before starting back towards his house, having Caramels in his bag and not wanting to be wasting time on a crazy person.

"Wait, don't go yet. Please." Called out the person. "What would it take for you to believe me?"

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humouring the person would probably get him to his Caramels faster than arguing.

"I don't know," said Craig, exasperated. "A miracle or something. Some extraordinary thing which couldn't just be done by any old person. Something more than just saying that you're god."

"Hmm. How about....*this*!" God pointed at a bush which burst into flames, the blaze shaping itself into a dragon which roared at the two of them. Then, with a snap of God's fingers, the blaze was extinguished leaving the bush singed but intact, and God turned back to Craig with arms spread wide as if to say'Tada!'

Craig, looking mildly impressed, turned back to God.

"Yeah, that was pretty good. Looked very impressive. I have to admit I have no idea how you did it. A hologram maybe? It worked for Tupac, so I can see it working for a dragon."

God stared at him for a few seconds before responding.

"I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle. I showed you one. What more do you want from me?"

"Don't get me wrong, it's very good. But the whole God thing probably isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you're a wizard."

"But I'm not a damn wizard!" Shouted God. "I'm God. Why would I say I'm a wizard?"

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in front of him in the international gesture of'I don't want any trouble, let's all just calm down'.

"Hey calm down buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh, but it's just constructive criticism. This is for a T.V. show or YouTube thing right? You're not going to get anyone with the whole'God' thing."

God, visibly seething by this point, held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds before letting out an angry sigh and storming off.

Craig watched them leave, then shook his head and returned to his journey, considering checking out the bush to see if he could get any clues as to how the trick had been done, but deciding against it. Whoever had been recording the encounter was probably still watching, waiting for Craig to do exactly that. So he pushed it out of his mind, and set off home, knowing that after all, there were Caramels waiting for him.
syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::39:
"Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy?" 

"Get it yourself, Ser Whyte, since I'm not your bloody squire no more." 

"Right, well then, my liege, would you do me the honor of getting me my wine so I can die drunk and happy?" 

"As you wish, sir-knight." 

"I hate you, Patsy." 

The bedridden husk of a former knight, whose rusty suit of white armor clinked and clanked as he jerked up violently, bellowed a harsh cough that shook his entire frame. Greasy, gray hair shot up in an instant while he sputtered still, downing the little glass bottle of wine that he clutched in his trembling hand. The belch that followed was as loud as the lightning's thunder, striking down on a rainy night when storms rage across the heavens.

Besides him, there sat a young man whose little silver crown, chipped and beaten from torn away gemstones that had once adorned it, sat upon his short locks of brown. Deep green eyes, far too young to experience what it means to rule a kingdom and command men, gazed down upon the Knight Whyte, his sworn protector and companion.

"Tell me," the knight said, his arm weak and weary as it placed his bottle on the bedside table, "how is Isabella faring, since I haven't been able to get a letter from you for months now?" 

"We've shut down the postal service, remember, so the courier service handles delivery for packages, but messages go through that fancy tele-ma-gram system that the scholars invented." 

"Hah, what an era your kingdom has come to, with bows that spew steel and fire, and scribes who control entire townships with their machines and devices. Pretty soon, even my kind will be out of work, replaced by contraptions and mechanisms."

The king chuckled, though it sounded forced and awkward through his lips that had spoken too many difficult truths. He had no need for knights anymore, and neither did any neighboring kingdom that had embraced the new ways. They were now just artifacts, relics of a bygone age, artifacts that talked and drank and fought but served no practical purpose in modern warfare. No, war in this time was determined by how much gold you could carry in your coffers, how many people you could conscript into service, and how many flags you could plant on some distant hill that nobody cared about.

"What's with that look, king, has that queen kicked you out of your castle again, because you're more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here, just remember to clean the corpses out from their beds before you lay down?" 

"That's a terrible joke, Whyte." 

"So, we're dropping the titles now, though I don't think we need another repeat of Georgie bringing about another revolution with all those angry peasants. The guillotines, they were only a little uncomfortable, if I recall correctly." 

"A little?" 

"A little." 

The rain outside appeared to stop while the lightning-storm ceased in its steps, prompting the king to get up and walk to the windowsill to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick as lamb's wool, had come just in time for what was about to transpire.

"Hmm, you see that, Whyte?" 

The knight in rusting armor, having gotten up out of his bed with considerable effort, placed his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the young king's shoulder in a gesture of affection. A gust of wind came bellowing through the open window, slapping its cold blanket of winter wind against the faces of the two men who stood together. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who responded in kind with a grin that creased his weathered face. With wet eyes that betrayed his emotions, the young man turned to face the knight directly.

"How ironic that I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this one." 

"And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too, completing the circle." 

"I'm glad to have called you my knight." 

"And you my king." 

The knight turned back toward his bed, his legs suddenly shaking with a fury that sent him down to the hard wood floor with a crash. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised gauntlet, still coppery-red and faded from years of use. With a great effort that seemed to drain his remaining strength, the knight made it to his bed, taking his gauntlets off and throwing them right out the windowsill into the snow below.

"I guess it's about time I've gotten rid of those, since they're too old for me now." 

"I've seen older things, so take a look at the man who wore them." 

"You always were a cheeky little patsy," he said as skin fell over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink properly. "I grow tired, so would you tell me a story?" 

"What am I, your mother?" 

"Just tell me that story." 

"That story, yes, after all, we only know that one story." 

"Don't play cute with me, Patsy." 

"Alright, alright, Whyte, but promise to go to sleep right after?" 

The king sighed deeply, taking a knee on the side of the bed where his knight lay dying. The knight smiled while his eyelids finally drooped over his eyes that had seen so much. Hands clasped over his chest as the beating of the heart grew slow and faint. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold seeping into his bones. Through hot tears that streamed down his face, the king began speaking.

"Once upon a time, in a village far, far away..."

One metre high and as wide across, the blackened and dusty car, roaring down the desert road with tremendous velocity, pursued the troupe who ran ahead with their tank of helium, their motorized unicycle blazing as they tried in vain to stay ahead of Kinko, whose pursuit was relentless. The fifteen clowns inside, readying their weapons as they closed fast upon their rivals on the unicycle ahead, prepared themselves for the confrontation that was rapidly approaching.

"Boffo, Luffy, Bobo," grated Kinko, whose voice carried menace despite its grating quality, "fucking clowns fucked with us for the last fucking time, and when we catch up to those assholes, I want you to fucking *whitewash* their asses, fucking them up *so bad* that they can honk their noses from the *inside*, making them regret ever crossing our path." They nodded, gripping their slapsticks all the tighter in anticipation of the violence to come.

With a roar that echoed across the wasteland, the car pulled ahead of the clowns in front and slid to a halt, its doors opening in unison as the fifteen of them tumbled out and rolled to their feet in a chaotic display. Two of them, grabbing the weaponized ladder from the roof, knocked over another three who stood readying their semiautomatic pielaunchers—and knocked down the same three again as the original two turned to see what they hit, demonstrating the incompetence that characterized their troupe. Two others, running into each other with considerable force, fell to the ground, outstretched and immobile in their ridiculous costumes. To one side, Bobo and Kinko, hefting their pails of custard with determined expressions, started towards the unicycle, intent on claiming what they believed was rightfully theirs.

"Bastards!" screamed a whitefaced warrior as she fell from the shoulders of the topmost clown, rolling as she landed and spraying a stream of water from the flower on her lapel, knocking Kinko to the ground with a highly amusing 'parp!' that echoed through the desert air. Grabbing a rubber chicken from the driver, she waded into the fray, knocking Kinko's clowns over like bowling pins while shouting, "That helium is *ours!*"

"The hell it is!" roared Luffy, pulling the pin on his rubber nose before tossing it at the jesters falling from the unicycle seat, declaring, "That helium is *ours*, for *our* balloons, because balloon zoos are *ours*, you hear? ***Ours!***" Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo upended the bucket of custard into them before pushing her to the ground, and as she bounced up and started running in circles, he grabbed the cylinder from the unicycle and tossed it in the car, cheering "*Our* troupe!" as the rest of the clowns piled into the car, one cranking the front handle to life before they drove off down the road with a cheery melody, heading to their big top in the wasteland.

As they disappeared in the horizon, the whitefaced warrior sadly blew her horn, watching the dust cloud fade in the distance.
syntax_complex_s.writingprompts::41:
The air, cool and heavy with the perfume of flowers that bloom in the gardens below, rises as fog in the early hours. A shout, sudden and urgent, comes from the tower where the watchmen stand their posts: a stranger, tattered and alone, approaches from the south.

To the south there is nothing but emptiness—just sand and dust stretching endlessly, and perhaps, if the tales whispered by the barbarians are to be believed with any credence, the bones of monsters that died in ages past.

He is a man reduced to tatters, having lost his sandals somewhere along the march that brought him here. The bottom of his feet, torn and abraded by the journey, are bloodied and raw. Rags, barely holding together, hang off the bones of his shoulders and hips, which protrude sharply. He remains alive only through what must be the grace of the gods, who have preserved him when all others perished.

Before he can be shown to the commander who oversees this garrison, he must first be cleaned of the filth that cakes his skin. He must also be fed and dressed in garments befitting a soldier. Rewarded—not yet, for it is not yet known whether he deserted his post or fled from duty.

The water, when they lower him into it, almost kills him where he stands. He screams like a babe torn from its mother's arms, thrashing wildly in the pool and sobbing for his mother, his father, his commander, anyone who might deliver him from this torment. He begs, his voice breaking, for death to take him.

It is not given to him, and soon, exhausted beyond measure, he falls silent. The slaves, working methodically, scrub him until he is clean and the grime of his journey has been removed. His wounds, upon inspection, are not grievous despite their appearance. As he is being dressed in borrowed garments, a sentry standing nearby mutters that he is not yet a man grown. The armor he wears, the sentry suggests with suspicion, must be stolen from another.

When food is brought to him on a wooden platter, he does not eat the meat or vegetables offered. Bread, however, agrees with his weakened stomach. He is not allowed to gorge himself, lest his body reject what it has been denied for so long.

The commander, seated in his chamber, asks about the others who marched with this boy. A hundred thousand strong the army had been, or so it had been whispered in the halls of power—a host composed of the strongest and most loyal soldiers, men who feared nothing that walked the earth.

They are all dead, every last one. The boy, who looked stunted and diminished by what he had endured, had lost his nerve and his will to fear, though not his honor, which compelled him to return.

They had walked for thousands of leagues across hostile lands. When they entered a valley shrouded in perpetual twilight, the sun and stars were lost to them entirely. There were monstrous things lurking in that cursed place—half men with sloping torsos and sharp teeth that gnashed, cats twice the size of a horse made entirely of fire and smoke that burned without consuming themselves, beasts with snakes for noses and tusks like a boar that roared like a thousand trumpets blown in unison.

Deeper into the darkness they must have walked, compelled by orders or madness. The jungle through which they traveled must have been Pluto's garden, for everything within it brought death to those who touched it or breathed its air.

They did not, in truth, have a hundred thousand men—only five thousand had marched into that hell. By the time they found it—the thing of nightmares, the titan's aborted fetus that should never have drawn breath—they numbered only in the hundreds, their ranks decimated.

It came at night, drawn by the fires that the soldiers had built to ward off the darkness.

It was here, recounting this moment, that the boy stopped speaking. He trembled where he sat, and his teeth ground together so hard they might have broken in his mouth like shattered pottery. But he had honor still, and spoke of what he had seen despite the terror that gripped him.

It must have been drawn by the fires they had lit. Perhaps it remembered the hell from which it had come, or perhaps in the flames it saw strength that it wished to consume and make its own.

The appearance of the creature was sudden and without warning. It fell near the fire, stirring it up with its landing and sending sparks into the air like stars. It had small claws and was armored like a fish, with scales that overlapped. It was not large at first—the boy gestured to his waist to show its height. He was missing half his hand, the wound still visible. About the size of war dog, he said. It had wings like a bat, leathery and veined.

It drank the fire as though it were water. The gods, whether in jest or cruelty, gave it power, and it rose up transformed and slaughtered a hundred men the first night alone.

The host, what remained of it, fled through the hell garden in panic. Some were felled by the plants that grew there, others by the beasts that hunted in the shadows. One man awoke screaming in the darkness, his voice terrible to hear. Insects had eaten away at his flesh while he slept, and they swarmed through his mouth and nose and the sockets of his eyes, devouring him from within.

After that horror, no one dared to sleep again.

Was that how the boy lost his hand, the commander asked? No, the boy replied—that was on the fifth day after they fled.

The men, driven by exhaustion and terror, had begun to go mad. Every tree looked the same to their fevered eyes. Every rock and puddle and patch of dirt seemed identical to the last.

They came to a cliff that rose before them like a wall. They must climb it, someone said with the authority of desperation. So they did, hauling themselves upward.

The boy, being quick and agile, climbed faster than some. Some men, quicker still, stood along the top of the world and helped the others up as they arrived. When the boy pulled himself over the edge, he saw the piles of bodies that lay there and called down below in warning: there is death above, wearing the face of their brothers. One of the men, mad with fear or bloodlust, tried to kill him. Instead the boy lost half of his hand to a rock, which crushed and mangled the fingers beyond saving. The boy hauled himself up with his remaining strength and scrambled away from the slaughter.

He left the men behind and headed north alone. The host was scattered beyond recovery. The boy walked north, driven by instinct. He could see the sky again after days of darkness. His hand felt tight and hot, swelling with infection. His fingers turned white, then red, then black. On the fifth day, unable to bear it longer, he gnawed them off himself.

On the seventh day he lost one sandal to the terrain. He threw the other away in frustration, and in a fit of madness brought on by fever, stripped off his clothes entirely. The forest became thinner as he walked. He was burnt by the sun that beat down mercilessly. There was no water to be found, no food to sustain him. Once he saw what he thought was a golden eagle and followed it, hoping it would lead him to water. But there was no eagle—only his mind creating visions.

On the ninth day of his solitary march, he found a man hung from a tree, dead for days. The boy, beyond shame or revulsion, stripped the body of clothes and dressed himself in garments taken from the dead.

As he walked north, his hand leaked blood that attracted flies, and his feet cramped and trembled with each step. One night, desperate, he built a fire despite his fear. It started a great terror in him, memories of the creature flooding back. He was brave enough, or desperate enough, to put his hand inside the flames and stop the rot from spreading further. Afterwards he crawled away from the fire and cried until the sun rose again over the wasteland.

As he walked, leaving the grasslands behind, he wanted only to see water again. He wanted to die and end his suffering.

On the tenth day he saw the beast again, or perhaps it was a different one of the same kind. It had the body of dog but walked upright on its hind legs. It had long claws and chattered like a bird calling to its mate. It was the size of a man's leg, measured from the ground to his knee. There was a flock of them hunting together. They called to each other in their strange language. The boy, desperate, followed them at a distance.

The creatures took down a beast—one with a snake for a nose and leather for skin. It wailed as it died beneath their claws. After the dog-beasts had eaten their fill and left, the boy crept forward and ate what he could from what remained.

The boy stopped speaking there, his tale concluded. What else was there to tell, the commander asked? There was nothing else, the boy replied. He had come to the sand and walked until he reached civilization. His voice was quiet now, tired beyond measure. His body, broken and scarred, told the toll his voice could not fully convey.

Could he die now, he asked? No, came the answer. Not yet—more would want to hear of this horror he had witnessed.

It was hard to find a pizza company that would still deliver to my home, you know, since the delivery boy usually came back dazed, a little paler, a little thinner, with an untouched thin crust pizza still in its box, the meal having been ignored in favor of something fresher.

A vampire had to eat after all.

I had thought myself so clever all those thousands years ago, choosing Rome, home of every religion but the one that mattered, away from those damn crosses made of cheap wood that had begun to rest against every doorway in Jerusalem! I would make my home in Italy, I thought, believing that Christianity would never follow me to what had been the greatest nation the world had ever seen, a place where ancient gods still held some sway.

How wrong I had been, how foolishly optimistic about my safety.

Almost overnight the missionaries had shown up, and within a century there was a cross on every door and a church on every block, trapping me inside with certain death just lurking outside if I so much as poked my head out of my beautiful wood door.

Outside, I could sense three children giggling as they pushed each other around on my doorstep, daring one another to approach. Finally, one of them jumped up to ring the doorbell, and giggling, they ran away, escaping to tell the tale of ringing the doorbell of the recluse! How very riveting their little adventure must have seemed.

"I hate humans," I said to myself.

Flipping through the seemingly 800th phone book they had left crammed in my mail slot the last year, I tried to find a restaurant that maybe had not heard the tale of the feared Pale Master of The Takeout.

One could hope.
