I picked up this little beauty. It replaced an ancient and cranky 5-disc CD Player. It also replaced a single disc DVD player. I now have breathing room in the old entertainment center. My antique turntable can take a creaky spin every now and again.

I can't connect a toaster without help. I called on my trusty better half. My better half unraveled the mystery of setting it up. This is what you need to know about this mighty machine. I will use non-technical language. I will use plain English.

1. The manual needs a lot of work. It's not user-friendly. It's not idiot-proof. The same goes for the boxy silver remote.

2. The setup is easy. You need to already know how to do that sort of thing. We have component video connections to the TV. We have digital coaxial connections to the receiver.

3. It gives excellent sound from both CDs and DVDs. You get the benefit of 5.1 surround. Movies like Master and Commander can literally move you. CDs have never sounded better.

4. It is convenient as a 5-disc CD changer. It is convenient as a 5-disc DVD player. You might play more than one CD. You'll need to put it in "CD Mode" first.

5. It can easily play different types of media. It plays audio CDs. It plays MP3s. It plays DVDs. It plays those other mysterious formats. You just put in the discs. You play away.

6. The video quality is very good on a regular TV. You can set up different pre-defined picture quality modes. You can customize to suit your own taste. You need to be a techie or a buff. You might have difficulty making up your mind. You should ignore this option.

7. The player is chock full of options. You have to explore for yourself. This can be a bit confusing. You need to get the hang of it. You say to read the manual? See Item 1 above.

8. There's on-screen information for MP3s. There's on-screen information for photo CDs. Different views are available for the contents. You can see groups. You can see folders. You can see entire playlists.

9. I can't comment on the progressive scan feature. I don't have an HD TV. I don't have an HD-ready TV. I am still waiting for that lottery win.

10. It is supposed to play DVD-Audio discs. You need 6.1 channel inputs on your receiver. You need these inputs to play them. Our receiver is lacking these inputs. I am also lacking any DVD-Audio discs.

Electronics buffs will probably say something. It needs a bit of "tweaking." The tweaking will get it to look just right. The tweaking will get it to sound just right. It looks great to me. It sounds great to me. All in all this is a very good player. It is perhaps excellent. You should factor in the price.

Amanda Richards, October 1, 2004

*Day 0, 00:20*

~

"… there was an explosion. It happened right when I looked up…"

"… this is the largest death toll in this country. It is the largest since…"

"… this is unprecedented…"

Sirens blare from the TV. I sit on the floor. I feel dazed.

*What had just happened?*

The words "BREAKING NEWS" splash across the screen. Every pair of eyes in the country must be glued to their TVs. No, every pair of eyes in the world must be watching. Plumes of smoke continue to rise. They rise from the side of the towers. Witnesses cry. They scream about the carnage. They had witnessed the carnage.

"Mommy," Emma stumbles into the living room. "It's time for school, Mommy."

"Oh honey," I say. I am on the brink of tears. "Come here." She walks to me. I hold her in my arms tightly. I run my hands through her hair. "We won't be going to school today, dear."

News continues to pour in from the TV.

In the corner of the screen: Monday, 11 September 2001.

________

*Shanghai, China*

*Day 0, 01:00*

~

"Dr. Wu, you have to look at this."

"Not now, Lin. There are enough people freaking out about this! We need to focus on our research." I take off my thin glasses. They have metal rims. I look at my assistant. She has helped me so much in the past seven years. We're so close now. We can't afford to be distracted. "We have a deadline. If we don't meet it, all our efforts would have gone to waste."

Lin shakes her head. "No, doctor. I'm not talking about the attack. I… I…"

"What is it, then? Speak up."

"You should see this for yourself." Lin takes out a massive sheet of paper. She lays it out on my table.

"This is the oceanic temperature table today. Why did you print it out? These fluctuations are perfectly normal. The fluctuations are—" Something at the end of the graph catches my eyes. I see a massive spike. "This… this…"

"Yes, doctor. You were right all along."

My heart skips a beat. I check the time of the spike. It matches perfectly.

"Lin,"

"Yes, doctor?"

*This is the end, isn't it?*

The thought struck Josh suddenly. It struck him almost by accident. It pierced through his frustration. It dissolved his frustration. The car had allowed him to break down. He was so far from home. The phone company had neglected to build towers. This barren desert road had no towers. The sun had audaciously beaten him. He was sweaty. He was tired. The sun had beaten him to the ground.

*This is the end.*

This thought remained prominent in his mind. It remained there. He realized something. He had already seen Heather for the last time. And... and Joey. Joey was still so proud about that geometry test. And Dale. Dale would inherit the business. The business would serve as an unexpected legacy.

*This is it.*

Dale had told him something. This trip was a fool's errand. Dale had made a joke. The joke was about what he would say at Josh's funeral. This memory failed to shake the thought from Josh's head.

*The end of...*

The thought lingered there. It was static. It lingered for a time. Josh wasn't able to comprehend the time. Everything else in his mind seemed to fade away. It faded from his periphery. It faded inward. It faded toward this single idea. It faded toward this solitary idea.

*This is the end of me.*

Nothing else was left. Josh found it fitting. This idea of finality should itself be his final thought.

But it wasn't.

It vanished. It vanished as abruptly as it came. And then --

Josh would have cried. He was no longer physically capable.

His regrets came flooding back. They came all at once. His anger came back. His sorrow came back. His despondency came back. He felt despondency at his own powerlessness. The tranquil peace of the "end" was over. It was replaced with the angst of a life incomplete. The life had failed to come to terms with itself.

And then Josh felt **fear**. He felt fear like he had never felt before. He felt the terror of fate incarnate. He felt the terror of the great unknown. He was utterly unprepared for it. The sheer horror overwhelmed his memory. The total horror overwhelmed his memory. It overwhelmed his pain. It overwhelmed all his other emotions.

That fear was the last thing Josh thought about.

Nervous? Whatever she was. Something wasn't quite right. She was doing that little nose twitch. That never happens when she's calm.

"Imani," he called out. Her head tipped down to where he was seated. This was acknowledgement. "It's going to be fine." She gave him a weak smile. It didn't quite reach her eyes. She reached out to squeeze his hand. Of course he said it to comfort her. He honestly felt like everything was going to be okay. They already crossed the worst bits. He survived the car accident. Then he survived the surgery. The surgery made sure the universe didn't decide to change its mind later. Then later came the amputations. Then came the implants. He rolled his eyes. He squeezed her hand back. "Honestly, this has been the easy part. We have plenty of time."

"The easy part? Since when do we ever get easy!" She reached out to swat his ears. Her eyes crinkled with mirth. "That's up there with 'What could possibly go wrong?' Don't jinx it." She scolded him. He leaned in. He wanted to tell her something. All that worrying could do nothing good. Then the door slammed open. The solid thump echoed through the large room.

"Oops," the tall man in the doorway looked sheepish. "I tripped into the door there. How are you two today?" He inquired in a friendly way. He strode into the room. The sunlight from the windows poured over his lanky form. "Ready to give it another go?" Daniel flexed his legs. They were neat. They were secured into his new running blades.

"Since the second I put these on Mason!" He replied earnestly. The easy going man gave him a thumbs up. Then he reached out his hands.

"That's what we like to hear! Alright lets get you up and moving then." Daniel took one last look at his wife. She was standing back. She had an apprehensive look. But she held up crossed fingers. He reached for the other man's hands. These were the fourth pair of running blades he had tried. The other ones had issues. This was despite their so called custom fits. Too long. Too short. These hurt. Those felt like they were going to fall off. But Daniel wobbled to his feet. He knew these were it. It took a moment to steady himself. They had a different sort of balance. They had a different give to them. This was different than his normal prosthetic. His fitness wasn't quite where he wanted it to be. His heart raced. He shifted his weight from one foot to the other. He heard the blades flex in response. Left. Right. Left. Right. Left right, left right, left right, bounce. They felt nothing like his old legs. But all the same they felt right. Slowly Mason let go. Then he backed away to the other side of the room. His eyes never left Daniel's. He hit the wall. He called out to them.

"Great! Now start at a walk. Work up to as fast as you feel comfortable doing." A sly tone crept into his voice. "And remember, the room is padded. We're all friends here. His arms wheeled around a bit. Then he braced his core to maintain balance. Then he took another. And another. Soon he had a slow bobbing jog going. He carefully moved between his wife and physical therapist. He did this until finally Mason signaled for him to stop. Mason sprinted down the room to the happy couple. He had a look of great excitement.

"It looks like we got it this time!" He stepped back. He gave him one final look over. "We just need to run a few more tests. We need to make sure that everything is adjusted correctly. But I think we found your golden pair here. So, how do you feel?"

His mind began to wander. He turned inward. He was trying to find the words. The words could even begin to describe what he was feeling. All he could think about were the things he thought he had lost forever. He hazily woke up from surgery that faithful day. He looked down. He saw the sheet cave in. His lower legs had once been there. The sound of the crowd screaming his name. He tore down the field. The heady feeling of sprinting down a track. The world narrowed almost into blackness. He pushed himself to the limit. The lightness of a casual game of tag with his wife. He caught thin air. She slipped by him. Laughter danced in her eyes. He bounced on his new legs once more. He felt weightless. Invincible. He felt a strength. He hadn't felt it in a long time. He hugged Imani. He spoke over her head. His face ached with a smile.

"Alive."

They were bearing down on the carriage with weapons drawn. I knew something right away. There were too many for me to handle. But I couldn't bear a certain thought. "Why, hello, Ma'am," I said easily. I stood up. I offered her a chair with my usual grace. "Bertram Proudfoot at your service. Whom do I have the pleasure of addressing?"

"I'd rather not say," she said. "That is, if it's all the same to you." She sat down.

"Alright," I said comfortably. "What can the Hobbiton Detective and Gossip Agency do for you?"

"Well," said the dame. She rubbed her hands together nervously. "It's like this." She paused.

"Like what, Ma'am?" I said kindly. I lit my pipe. I sat back in my chair.

"My husband is dead," she said.

"Oh my dear, I am sorry!" I exclaimed. I must admit there was part of me. That part was less than sorry. What can I say? I am only a Hobbit. This dame had the most beautiful feet. I had ever laid eyes on such feet. "Tell me everything. Tell me what happened."

"We were out boating on the Brandywine three nights ago," she said. "All of a sudden, a rock flew out of nowhere. It hit my poor husband in the head. He keeled over in the water. I screamed for help. He drowned."

I had already known it must have been something like this. I knew from the moment she walked in the door. I have an uncanny sense for things like that.

I looked as grave as I could. The circumstances made this difficult. "I see," I said. I blew another perfect smoke ring up towards the ceiling. "You would like me to find the perpetrator of this event. You would like me to prosecute him."

"Yes," said the dame.

"I will do my best," I said. "I can promise you that." I saw her visibly sigh with relief. "May I offer you a cup of tea? Something stronger, perhaps?"

"No thank you," she said. She showed herself out without another word.

I promptly made my way to the Brandywine River dock. My first line of inquiry would be simple. I would interrogate the man. This man rented out boats. He was an odd fellow. He had an odd profession. Not many sane hobbits choose to be out in the middle of the water. They do not do this by their own free will. This hobbit's boat-renting business was not doing well.

He consulted his records for a long time. He told me something. He had rented out two boats on the evening in question. Only one of those was by a couple. The couple had been a one Drogo Baggins and a one Primula Brandybuck. Primula was the dame's name. But she had not wanted to tell it to me. Why was that?

Had this boat fellow heard any commotion on the water? Had he heard any cries for help? No he had not. Did he remember something? Did he remember who returned the boat to him? It hadn't been returned, he said. That particular boat had been left floating in the middle of the river. Strange.

Next I walked up and down the both banks of the river. There was not much to garner here. I did learn one thing. Whoever had thrown the rock must have been quite a shot.

I had thoroughly investigated the river. My next step was to find out about Priscilla and Drogo. I visited several pubs. These pubs were in the areas of Buckland and Hobbiton. I had gathered this: Primula and Drogo were long married. Perhaps they were not happily married. They had one son. He was now 12. His name was Frodo Baggins. Strangely, it seemed that Primula had not been seen by anyone except me. This was since Drogo's death. Most of the gentlehobbits that I spoke with seemed to be of a certain belief. They believed that both Drogo and Primula had died three nights ago.

Facts were not adding up. I had to speak with my mysterious client again. I had to do this before I could do anything else. I needed to straighten things out. I had no way of contacting her. I knew she would return to my offices in short order.

The day following, she did just that.

"Good day, Primula," I said upon her entrance.

Her face betrayed surprise. She did not deny the name.

"I have a few things," I said. "I need to get them straight with you. They are about the case." I proceeded to outline what I had discovered. "So I'm afraid I must ask again," I finished. "What happened that night?"

The dame got up without a word. She left. Just like that.

I did not hear from her again. Two days later, her body was found. It was floating down the Brandywine. I was saddened. I was not surprised.

My suspicion had been this: Primula had been unhappily married for some time. She had pushed her husband into the water herself. She had boated back to the shore. Her intent was to disappear forever. Everyone would think that they both were dead. They would not suspect any foul play. She eavesdropped on the lawyer's meetings. These meetings quickly followed. She realized something. Custody of her son would go to an extended cousin. This cousin was none other than the famous crackpot Bilbo Baggins.

Primula did not want her offspring to fall under the influence of said crackpot. This was understandable. She came to me. She had hopes. She hoped that I would believe her story. I would deflect suspicion away from herself. This was all in a desperate attempt. She wanted to maintain custody of her son. But I had seen through her ruse. I prevented this fact. She saw no alternative. She then drowned herself in grief. Shame. I had just begun to think there may have been a very beneficial alternative. This alternative was for the both of us.

I sat back. I began polishing my pipe thoughtfully. It was another case. The estimable Bertram Proudfoot had solved it. Perhaps it was another opportunity lost. I had solved countless cases. Opportunities of the other sort came only but now and again. Like I said, it was a shame.

I blew another smoke ring to the ceiling. My thoughts turned to crazed old Mr. Baggins. I felt for the young Mr. Frodo. He was now cursed enough to fall into the old hobbit's custody. Who knows what old Baggins would pass on to the impressionable young fellow. I'm sure you're all aware of this. Mr. Bilbo Baggins suddenly disappeared many years ago. He returned just as suddenly a year later. He had hoards of gold. He had many tall tails. He had been a very respectable hobbit before he left. Whatever he experienced on his journey seemed to have addled his mind. He came back a changed hobbit. The change was not for the better.

He was so changed. It is my personal suspicion. The hobbit currently inhabiting Bag End is not the real Bilbo Baggins at all. He is rather an impersonator. There is plenty of evidence to suggest this. There is particularly one fact. "Mr. Baggins" appears much younger than a hobbit of his years has any right to look.

I shall have to explore that line of inquiry further some day.

I went through college. I would think of these people. The people had beliefs. Their beliefs were so strong. They would literally kill themselves. They did this in such a way. They wanted to make a powerful statement. They would not want to live in a country. The crushing regime ruled that country. It had been ruling for generations. They wanted to be free. Or they wanted to die. Those were their only choices.

It seems every generation has an uprising. The oppressed realize something. They realize that they're being oppressed. They get a tool. This tool helps them organize. It helps them fight back. They gain leverage. Rarely does it happen in a short span. However, here I was. I was an oppressed 27 year old. I had absolutely no future ahead of me.

I walked downstairs. I opened up the digital screen. A banker popped up on the screen.

"Hello Mrs. Roer. How may I help you?"

"I'd like to check my bank statement. I got a letter in the mail. The letter said I only have five credits."

"Okay, one moment." The banker disappeared for a second. Then the banker came back up.

"Mrs. Roer. You currently have 10 credits."

"What? That's not even enough to buy groceries with this month."

I looked outside. Then I sighed.

"Okay. Well thanks." I said.

The screen closed. The banker wished me a good day first. How could I only have 10 credits of happiness? A gallon of milk is 1.21 credits. I couldn't even buy milk. I couldn't buy basic necessities.

I walked outside this time. It was sunny. It was bright. Birds were happy. I bet they have enough happiness credits to buy freaking groceries. I looked around. My in-ground pool was there. My hot-tub was there. My outdoor deck was complete with a pond further from the house. All of this was my life. All of this surrounded me.

My husband and I had been married for ten years now. I was happy. He was happy. Right?

I went to look at my phone. I had a message from my husband.

'Want to have coffee?'

I sent back,'Yes.'

I went upstairs. I took a shower. My husband was gone. He was gone as always. It was no secret we had been falling apart. We were so happy at one point though. We had more credits than anybody in the word. Like I said though, it was no secret. We had been falling apart. He had numerous affairs. I never cheated. I frankly found myself longing for more.

I prepared myself for coffee. Nothing too dressy. Nothing too casual. It was just coffee. I walked outside. I got in one of our cars. I drove to the airport. We owned a private jet. My husband had already put gas in it.

"Just having coffee today Bill," I said.

I was walking off the jet in 4 hours. I saw my husband there.

"Hello Mrs. Roer," He said. He kissed my cheek. He always did this.

I walked with him to our second home. A blonde woman with a tight blouse was leaving the house. I scowled at her. She hurried from the front door to her car.

"We need to talk," I said.

"Listen, Mr. Roer, I do love you, but there's so --."

"Coffee?" It read.

At that moment my doorbell rang. I answered the door to him. My old friend stood there. He immediately kissed me. I had missed that feeling. I felt my blood pressure rise.

"Good to see you."

He kissed me again. He broke my words.

"I paid your husband to let me marry you Elaine. He's wanted a divorce. He's not good to you. You know that."

I was shocked. He payed my husband to marry me? Why on Earth would he do this?

"Elaine. I know we didn't work out, but our son. He needs you."

"Yes. I'll marry you."

HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God. I've been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents. WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA.

They came a few hours after my last entry. They came like a great black tornado. A swirling column rose up. It contained harpies. It contained skrieks. It contained imps beyond counting. The column rose up from the center of The Pit. It came crashing down. It completely enveloped Limbo Base. The first few moments of engagement should've been chaos. By the grace of God we were ready.

All the Screachers had been on high alert. We emerged from the maze of caves 8 days ago. We came onto the plains of Limbo proper. Today that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled. It crumbled before the wall of sound. Our blessed Screachers blasted out this sound. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell. The word of God gets pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers. A devout member of the clergy pilots it. This is down right debilitating. The Demons were shocked and paralyzed. They twitched and writhed on the ground. They were easy targets. The rumblers have blessed water cannons. These cannons burned away swaths of the foul creatures. The misted holy water acted as if it were strong acid. Huge piles of the creatures were reduced to ash in seconds.

The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient. I saw more than a few grunts die on their talons. The grunts wore sanctified body armor. It was little better than cardboard. We repaid them in kind. I'm proud to say our rumblers javalin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion. They were impaled on our gleaming silver spears. I should record the grunts efforts too. I don't want to seem like I'm diminishing them. They showed bravery. They showed ferocity in battle. They've got that in spades. They faced mortal danger. They collected their fair share of scalps. They pinned the giant creatures with their silver pikes. They finished them off with their chain sickles. It was a glorious bloody sight. It was like something out of a nature documentary.

The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come though. We fought for a full day and a half. The black swarm began to thin out. We thought we might've finally broken their assault. But then they appeared. Three monstrous figures came into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion. Hell Dragons. They were nothing like what we'd seen in movies. They were nothing like our stories from childhood. These were great pestilent foul things. They towered over us. They had snub nosed heads the size of a grand cathedral. The heads were covered in spines. They had long armored bodies like an insects. Their faces were slick with thick black tar. Their joints were slick with thick black tar. The tar bubbled and hissed. It fell from them. It stained the plains of Limbo.

Screachers focused their assault. They prevented the titans from over running the base. The rumblers water tanks ran dry. The javlin cannons ran dry. We were just trying to keep them at bay. Our brave grunts held back the black swarm. They fought tirelessly. This allowed us time to retreat. This allowed us time to resupply and reenter the fray. So it went for hours on end. The Hell Dragons seemed to be none the worse for all our efforts.

Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps. Of all people! We had given them enough time through our efforts. They could secure and assemble Limbo Bases major defenses. These included Sanctified Artillery. These included the Holy Rail Gun. The Rail Gun punctured the Dragons thick armor. It spewed geysers of tar onto the battlefield. The artillery smashed into the beasts vulnerable exposed points. It lodged shells etched with scripture deep in their bodies. This wracked them with pain. The attack still went on for hours. We lost a great deal of our force. Nearly 2 months have passed since we first descended into this place. We finally have established a forward base. We can launch our attack on Hell. One Bolgia down. Eight to go. This is the first day here. The smell doesn't bother me.

The planet Earth has changed a lot recently. The storms on the surface ended 23 years ago. This was almost to the day. The same storms had been raging for roughly five thousand years. A few weeks passed. The cloud formations disintegrated during this time. Then we got our first clear view of our home.

I was five years old at the time. The colours entertained me mostly. The beautiful blue and green were like nothing on the Ark. We had water. This was sure. But we didn't have pools large enough to give that blue colour. We had plants too. The conditions were far from optimal. This made the plants a dirty green rather than lush. I wanted to see it closer. I wanted to touch it. I wanted to feel it.

That was probably when I decided to join the recruitment for the first journey. The first journey was the first expedition back down to the planet. The name implies this. A lot of people wanted to go back down as soon as the storms ended. There were protests. There were riots even. People wanted the Ark to head straight back down. They were idiots.

23 years may have been a long time to wait. But it was important. We were the last humans after all. What if we landed and something went wrong? We couldn't risk it. Years of geological scans gave us the perfect landing spot. Low atmosphere scouting helped too. The site had minimal damage to local environment. It had enough space to develop a community. It had plenty of food. It had water. It importantly had a lot of natural protection. This protection took the form of Cataclysm-formed mountain ranges. It also included deep trenches. These trenches were filled with the darkest blue water.

Of course something as large as the Ark couldn't simply just land though. That was where the first journey came into the picture. We were the first guys to go planetside. We would live permanently there. This hadn't happened in over seven generations. Our objective was to build the dock. It'd be a long job. It would probably take another five or six years even. But the dock would provide us with a much needed start. It would help us map out local geography much more clearly. We would learn about plants. We would learn about animals. The reality of the situation is clear. We were going in blind. The Corps had nicknamed it the safe zone. This safe zone could very easily become a deathtrap. The problem with the safezone was its location. Once we went in, our shuttle wouldn't be able to make it out.

Part of the problem with the planet was the storms. The main storm ended 23 years ago now. Smaller cells continued to rotate even now. The mountain ranges protected the area from the storms still raging. These storms were not quite powerful enough to make it over the high peaks though.

Even in the atmosphere above there was a vicious wind. This wind constantly blew. It would tear an outgoing ship to pieces. Only a craft as large as the Ark would be able to survive it. The Ark needed a Dock in order to perform a take off.

So that was the mission. We would go down. We would face possible death. We would build a super structure. All in less than six years. And I was damn excited.

"Hey, check out that chickadees over in the birdbath." Kylo whooped. He puffed out his chest. He nearly toppled off his perch.

"Don't be a troglodyte, bro," Atticus groused. He pecked at his seeds. "You're a wren. That isn't even the same family."

"I don't care. I'm gonna go talk to them." Kylo took off. He swerved through the air like a leaf trapped in a gust. Atticus sighed. He took off after him. He'd have to keep close tabs on Kylo. Otherwise they'd get kicked out again.

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash. Droplets flew in every direction. They drenched the occupants of the birdbath. The birds squawked with indignation. Kylo emerged from beneath the surface. He shook the wetness from his head. He trotted up to a group of soaked finches. He gave his wings a shake. "Hey, birds. Nice tits."

"We're not tits." A purple finch stepped forward from the group. She launched into a tirade. The pickup line was overused. Atticus alighted on the rim of the bath. He began to walk around. He apologized to everyone for Kylo's behavior. He pleaded with them. They should not call the bouncer over.

"Okay, sorry," Kylo interrupted. "Let me make it up to you. How about you and I head over there?" He motioned to the bird feeder. "I can share my seeds with you." Birds don't have lips. But Kylo would be smirking right now.

The finches began to flap their wings angrily. They splashed Kylo with water. "You're such a boor. Get out of here!" Many of the onlookers chirped in agreement. Some of the bigger birds began to puff their chests threateningly. Atticus shoved Kylo to the side. He raised his wings. "I apologize on behalf of my friend here. He's clearly had too much nectar. We'll just be going now."

"Oh, you think we're going to fall for that?" The purple finch spat a nut shell at his feet. "He's just trying to play wingbird for you. Isn't he? He'll let himself take the fall for you. Then you swoop in. You look better by comparison." The other birds chorused in agreement.

"I think these two need to be taught a lesson." A blue jay fluttered over to Atticus. He towered a full inch above him. He spread his wings menacingly. This blocked Atticus from taking off. "Why don't you peck on someone your own size?" The onlookers broke into cheers. They shouted for a fight.

"Well, you're kind of bigger than me." Atticus took a step back into the bath. He felt feathers ruffle against him. The crowd pressed around him. They urged him back towards the jay. "That wouldn't be my own size now. Would it?"

Kylo staggered in front of him. He began to hop around. "Don't worry, Atticus. We got this."

"Hey, this is a one-on-one fight." The jay looked around. "If you get back-up, then—"

"Who on earth placed all this here?" A door opened. The birds began to scatter. They screamed, "Human!" Atticus grabbed Kylo. He urged him into the air. The two lost themselves amongst the cloud of fleeing birds. Out of the corner of his eye, Atticus saw something. The human scratched his head in front of the birdbath.

"Make sure to thank that human. He bailed you out of yet another mess," Atticus said.

Kylo scoffed. "We could've totally taken that guy." The two flew over the Toyota in the driveway. Kylo let loose a dropping. It landed right in the center of the windshield.

I had never even had a drink. He beat cracked ribs into me. He beat bruised kidneys into me. He beat loose teeth into me. He wanted to make sure I never became what he was.

Once he was sober. He told me he drank because of how he grew up. He said it. He wanted me to empathise with him. He wanted me to forgive him. My arm was broken. He had broken it the week before. He was protecting me from drink. He could not see that. He could not see himself standing over me. I was crying blood. I was crying snot. I was crying tears. He was jeering. He could not remember what was so bad about how he grew up. He could not remember why he needed it. It let him sleep at night. It stopped him waking up screaming in the night. It stopped him pissing himself. He had bad dreams.

He made me sick. He was my dad. My breath catches sometimes. One of my wrists never set right. That leaves me half crippled in that hand. I have eleven false teeth. I am twenty three. All this has happened to me.

I did not go to his funeral. I celebrated it though. I did not take a drink though. I could never do that. I cry myself to sleep most nights. I cannot help myself screaming. Someone comes up to me suddenly. I scream. Lately I have noticed a lot of blood. It comes up when I cough. I will not let him beat me though. I will not give him this little victory.

Craig was walking home from the shops. He met God. He wasn't expecting to run into God. Sane people rarely do. He didn't really ever think about God. He didn't believe in a God. He also didn't disbelieve enough to ever think about Gods not existing. Religion and God weren't really topics he cared about.

He cared deeply about one topic. That topic was Caramels. You might not know about Caramels. Caramels are a rather delicious chocolatey biscuit type thing. They are composed of several layers of wafer. The wafer is encased in chocolate. Craig was crazy about them. He may not have been religious. His feelings on Caramels came close to religion. The reason behind his trip to the shops was simple. He wanted to buy more Caramels. His mind was full of anticipation. He headed back home.

He was about two minutes away from his home. He was two minutes from Caramel satisfaction. God first spoke to him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His Caramel contemplation was interrupted. Craig turned round. He wanted to see who had spoken to him. Behind him stood a tall person. The person wore a loose fitting suit. Craig wasn't really sure of the person's gender. They were pretty androgynous. They looked not dissimilar to Diamond Dogs era David Bowie. They looked familiar to Craig. He couldn't quite put his finger on where he might have seen them before. He realised he'd been staring. He sought something to say.

"Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," replied the Bowie lookalike. "I'm God."

"Well good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye." Craig said this. He started back towards his house. He had Caramels in his bag. He didn't want to be wasting time on a crazy person.

"Wait, don't go yet. Please." The person called out. "What would it take for you to believe me?"

Craig sighed. He turned back. He decided something. Humouring the person would probably get him to his Caramels faster.

"I don't know," said Craig. He was exasperated. "A miracle or something. Some extraordinary thing. It couldn't just be done by any old person. Something more than just saying that you're god."

"Hmm. How about this!" God pointed at a bush. The bush burst into flames. The blaze shaped itself into a dragon. The dragon roared at the two of them. God snapped his fingers. The blaze was extinguished. It left the bush singed but intact. God turned back to Craig. His arms spread wide. His gesture seemed to say 'Tada!'

Craig looked mildly impressed. He turned back to God.

"Yeah, that was pretty good. It looked very impressive. I have to admit I have no idea how you did it. A hologram maybe? It worked for Tupac. I can see it working for a dragon."

God stared at him for a few seconds. Then God responded.

"I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle. I showed you one. What more do you want from me?"

"Don't get me wrong. It's very good. But the whole God thing probably isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you're a wizard."

"But I'm not a damn wizard!" God shouted. "I'm God. Why would I say I'm a wizard?"

Craig backed off a few meters. He held his hands up in front of him. This was the international gesture of 'I don't want any trouble, let's all just calm down'.

"Hey calm down buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh. It's just constructive criticism. This is for a T.V. show or YouTube thing right? You're not going to get anyone with the whole 'God' thing."

God was visibly seething by this point. God held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds. Then God let out an angry sigh. God stormed off.

Craig watched them leave. He shook his head. He returned to his journey. He considered checking out the bush. He wanted to see if he could get any clues. The clues would explain how the trick had been done. He decided against it. Whoever had been recording the encounter was probably still watching. They were waiting for Craig to do exactly that. So he pushed it out of his mind. He set off home. After all, there were Caramels waiting for him.

"Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy?"

"Right. Well then, my liege. Would you do me the honor of getting me my wine? I want to die drunk and happy." 

"As you wish, sir-knight."

He was sputtering still. He downed the little glass bottle of wine in his hand. The belch was loud. It was loud as the lightning's thunder. Thunder strikes down on a rainy night. 

A young man sat besides him. A little silver crown sat upon his short locks of brown. The crown was chipped and beaten. Gemstones had been torn away from it. Deep green eyes gazed down upon the Knight Whyte. These eyes were far too young. They were too young to experience what it means to rule. But this was his knight.

The king chuckled. It sounded forced and awkward through his lips. He had no need for knights anymore. No neighboring kingdom did either. They were now just artifacts. You needed flags you could put on some hill. 

"What's with that look, king? Has that queen kicked you out of your castle again? You're more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here. Just remember to clean the corpses out from their beds."

The rain outside appeared to stop. The lightning-storm ceased in its steps. The king got up. He walked to the windowsill. He saw that snow had started to fall. A snowfall had come. It was white and thick. It had come just in time. 

"Hmm. You see that, Whyte?" 

The knight in rusting armor had gotten up out of his bed. He placed his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the young king's shoulder. A gust of wind came bellowing through. It slapped its cold blanket of winter wind against the faces of the two men. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight. The knight responded in kind. The young man turned to the knight. His eyes were wet.

"And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too."

"Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after?" 

The king sighed. He took a knee on the side of the bed. The knight smiled. His eyelids finally drooped over his eyes. His hands clasped over his chest. The beating of the heart grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him. The king had felt the cold too. The king began through hot tears.

The Author
***

I can't shake the feeling. You know that sensation. It creeps along your spine. It waits to take up residence in the base of your skull. It acts like some kind of parasite. It's an indeterminable feeling. Someone is watching me. I can't shake it off. I am sure I know what it is. I'm not ready to admit I know. The *author* let's call him. He is watching. He is waiting. He is building. Even as I think this, he is scratching it down in his chicken-scratch scrawl. He touches the pen against his teeth in thought. I can feel it. I can see it in my mind's eye. He's trying to figure out how to kill me.

I suppose it is my own fault. See I kept asking. I needed to understand. I had to find out something. Was there some directing hand to life? I needed to know. Did mankind have a purpose? Did we have a reason? I needed to appreciate what purpose we worked toward. There's a moment. It is one of particular realization. It caught me. It held fast. It was like my apprehension regarding an observer. Only this feeling was deeper. It was more primal. I *knew*. I mean I really *understood* something. All of it is a narrative. Life is a story. This inevitably led me to the conclusion. There needs to be an architect. There needs to be an *author*.

The car narrowly missed me. I had an inkling of something. A pressure was pushing against my chest. It was verging on the edge of panic. I didn't cross. The green man displayed on the crossing signal. Instead I took a step back. My *spidey-sense* tingled. The taxi-cab driver never saw me. I hadn't seen him either. His drunken sprawling vehicle slammed into the same traffic signal post. I had been standing by that post until recently. Can I tell you how fucked up that is? I have this realization. Then a sudden sensation of fear follows. I hadn't heeded my gutless compulsion. I might have been splattered between the cabbie's car and the hard place. The hard place was the traffic signal pole. I turned my gaze upward. My eyes were burning. My jaw was clenching. I decried whoever worked at compiling this narrative.

"What the actual fuck was that?" I said.

Okay, so I realize something. My choice of words probably did not fall into the definition of circumspect. But hell we're talking about some kind of god-figure. He was deciding on my time to die.

*Are you sure?* My logical brain asked.

I pondered my position. I considered both the physical and meta-physical sense.

*Yeah, I'm fucking sure,* I replied to myself internally. *How else do you explain the sudden epiphany? How do you explain my almost immediate death afterward? There's an* author. *He doesn't want to be known.*

I'm not sure how I knew something. The *author* didn't want to be known. Also the fact he was a man. But I figured it was something in my general make-up. It was granting me the knowledge. Oh don't get all high and mighty. Don't preach at me now. I'm not talking religion or spirituality. I want to live damnit. I stood there. I was still staring up at the sky. I was trying to impart my utter disgust and frustration. Then the signal pole creaked. It sounded unnaturally so. I adjusted my head. My eyes were level with the pole.

The metal appeared warped. I realized something. The car had burst into flames.

*When had that happened?* I thought. *Nevermind, run stupid.*

My internal dialog is not always the most kind. I'm a blunt sort. So I ran. What was I running from? Mr. Omniscient *author* was already in my head. He could follow me anywhere. Hell, I could have an inopportune flashback. He could hit me with a mack truck. This *author* decided I was going to die. Why didn't he do it already?

*Fuck me,* I thought. *It's about the drama. It's about the story.*

"Sick fuck," I said. I knew he'd hear me. He'd write that in his juvenile scrawl. He would know I intended it for him.

*What if I stop?*

I looked up again. I said something. "What are you going to do with a character? The character won't cooperate. Huh?"

Naturally he didn't respond. It wasn't like I expected a voice from the sky. But I figured he might strike me down with lightning or something. I mean potentially it's within his ability. Right? He might decide something. My knowledge of the plan labeled me as a liability.

*What the hell is the plan anyway?*

I don't know. I guess the plan is for me to die. Perhaps he's not into the mundane. Maybe, just maybe, he wants my death to be something significant. He wants it to be something of a show. I bet that's it. I got the sense again. It was a gut punch to my stomach. It made my insides roil. They were leaking to the outside. The rumbling in my stomach suggested something. I should take a step back. I did. Something pierced the skin in my back. It was a fluid motion. It was a smooth motion. It parted the skin. I felt the warm blood. It was mixing with my sweat. It soaked the back of my flannel shirt.

A quiet voice whispered in my ear. "Hello protagonist," she said. "I'm your antagonist. The *author* says hello."

That was all she said. She didn't have a scent. You would expect that. She was a ghost from the shadows. I don't know who she was. I don't know why her. But she'd made it clear. I was right. Take that fucker. I didn't have the strength to say it. But I know he heard me.

"We're playing army men tonight," Kai said. Blergh merely grunted in agreement. Kai loved playing with Blergh. Blergh could move lots of pieces at once. He was really good at pretending to be surprised. Things would "blow up." He acted surprised then.

The ship reached the beacon. The pilot nervously activated his directional scanning. He had used the last of his jump fuel making it this sector.

The pilot felt an inexplicable chill. He glanced out his viewing port. He figured it was jump jitters. He routed power to his security drone anyways. Sensors didn't find anything. He should have known it was a waste of time. He had more important things to focus on. He needed to find fuel.

The directional scanner pinged. It drew his attention to a large hull. The hull was floating some distance from his vessel. A thick cloud of gas partially obscured it. The ship was powered-down. This is why the initial system scan had not detected it. He brought the impulse engines online. He moved towards the derelict vessel. He simultaneously hailed the ship.

No response came. That was curious. Abandoned vessels were not unheard of. More unusual was the pristine condition of the ship. The ship did not have so much as a dent. He had found abandoned hulls before. They were pocketed with scorch marks from a laser blast or short range teleporter. Some sign of battle was always evident.

He briefly considered donning his EVA suit. Instead he headed to the drone bay. He took remote control of the security drone. It was meant for boarding defense. In a pinch it could be used as an exploration unit.

Moments later the drone slid through the airlock. It was a sleek machine. It was armed to the teeth with an assortment of lasers and close combat weapons. These weapons had saved the pilot's life more than once. He had schematics for this hull. The drone made a beeline for engineering. Any remaining fuel would be found there.

The problem with remotely controlling the drone was simple. It demanded the full attention of the pilot. The airlock had not sealed. The pilot was not paying attention. He would have noticed his door system had malfunctioned.

His dying screams echoed. He was torn to pieces.

The pilot should have known something important. Giant alien spiders are no joke.

Elwood and Shara were leaning against a concrete pillar. The pillar was in the courtyard of a high school. They were watching Elwood's newest charge. His name was Dale. He was an unassuming young man.

"So how did you get assigned to this one, Elwood?" Shara said this. She was examining her claws at the same time.

"I'm pretty sure this is a softball pitch. The management downstairs sent it." Elwood said this. His arms were crossed against his chest. A group of girls walked over to the pillar. They leaned against it. They occupied the same space as the two demons. A strong gust of wind blew. It blew the papers out of the hands of the girls. It blew the binders out of their hands too. The girls shrieked in surprise. They ran after their papers and binders.

Shara was annoyed. She said, "I'll never get used to that. I don't care if we *can* occupy the same space." She turned to the girls. She held her arm out to them. Her claws were held behind her thumb. She flicked them outwards with a snap. This sent the books flying out of the girls' hands. The papers flew out too. The girls shrieked again. Shara said, "Little wretches..."

Dale was chewing on his bean and cheese burrito. He was looking at the scene across the courtyard. His expression was like a placid cow. The cow was chewing on grass.

"What's with that kid?" Shara asked this question.

"I don't know. Maybe he's stupid?" Elwood chewed on his thumb for a bit. He was strategizing. "Let's jump time to 6th period."

Shara gave Elwood a sideways glance. She raised an eyebrow. "Sure...."

A sound came. It was like tearing canvas. They were transported. They rested on the ledge under the window. The window was in the back of Dale's 6th period class.

"So what's your plan, big boy?"

Elwood pressed a long-clawed finger to his lips. He said, "Sssshhhh." He did that. Dale's head hit the desk at the same moment. Dale was out cold. Elwood flung his arms out wide. Then he brought them in together. It was a grand grouping gesture. Every student in the class turned to face Dale. They did this without a word.

"That's cute." Shara said this.

Elwood smiled. He said, "It's time to wake up, Dale." He said that. Every single student in the class said the same thing. They said it in a very flat tone. They said it in unison with Elwood. Dale's face was half-slick with drool. He sat up. He rubbed his eyes. He looked around at the class. The class was looking back at him.

"Dale, it's time to wake up." All the students said this. Elwood said it again too. No one blinked. Dale glanced from side to side. "I'm awake." Elwood flung his arms apart. The class resumed as normal. No one but Dale was aware of what happened.

"That's your plan?" Shara asked this. She was clearly unimpressed.

Dale noticed something. He was a little behind in taking notes. He began writing in a hurry.

"You're kidding me, right? That's a daytime creep! It's not even 3 am. That's some creepy shit. I don't care what you say."

"Uh huh." Shara said this. "Look at him. He's got no clue. That was out of the ordinary. C'mon, lets go." She flexed a claw over her shoulder. She walked away. She was begging for Elwood to follow.

They were leaving through the wall. Elwood spun around. He made a bitch-slapping motion. Dale grunted. His head jerked forward. Loose tangles of hair were at the back of his head. They flew up. His pencil shot out of his hand. It bounced off the back of the muscular kid. That kid was in front of him. The girl next to Dale looked at him. She looked at him with plain disgust. She said, "You're such a weirdo..." She shifted in her small desk. She wanted to be as far away as possible from him.

Shara laughed.

The two demons waited outside the classroom. They waited for the end of period. They waited for Dale. "You know this would be so much easier in the nighttime..." Shara said this. She was bored.

"Yeah but that's not my style." Elwood said this. "You get more *genuine* results during the day. Anyone can be spooked at night. The day comes. They're so quick to forget it. No. What really freaks them out is a daytime haunting."

Shara didn't say anything. She only yawned.

The bell sounded. It sounded for the end of the period. Dale was the last one out of the classroom. He was walking slowly. He was looking down at his phone. Elwood flapped his wings. He dove into the phone. An alert popped up on Dale's screen. Dale clicked on 'Read.' This cued Elwood. He jumped in to full-view on the screen. He yelled "DAAAAAAAAAAAALE" through the phone's speaker.

Dale hit the power button. He put his phone back in his pocket. "Just great." He thought this. "One of my friends has been messing with my alerts again." He continued walking to his next class.

Elwood stretched out of the phone. He was like elastic. There was a 'pop.' He took his place next to Shara. She was leaning against the wall. "I don't get this kid." He said this. He was watching Dale walk away.

"Still insistent on the daytime?" Shara asked him this question.

Elwood let out a heavy sigh. "Okay, let's try it your way." They both vanished. There was a pop and sizzle.

The two demons burst into the space above Dale's bed. They stared down at him. They were gently flapping their wings. "So what do you do now?" Elwood asked Shara this. She only gave a half smile. She extended her index claw out in front of her. She slowly curled it back into her palm. The bed sheet was covering Dale. It was pulled off him. This happened in sync with the flexing of Shara's finger. Dale only scratched his stomach. He rolled over.

"Wow... I'm.. I'm just at a loss for words, Shara. That's some scary stuff. Right there."

She narrowed her eyes at him. She shot a hand out. She wanted to grab something in the air. Dale screamed in pain. Shara then yanked her arm back. Dale flew off the foot of the bed. He crashed against the wall. This knocked several books off the shelf. They fell one after the other. They fell onto the top of his head.

Elwood's jaw dropped. He looked from Shara to Dale. He looked back again. "You have no subtlety at all, woman!"

"Just watch..."

Dale stood up. He picked up the books. He put them back on the shelf. The door to his room opened. His mom asked him a question. She asked him if he was alright. "Yeah, just had a really bad leg cramp. I fell when I got up."

"Oh for fuck's sake!" Shara said this. She threw her arms up.

"Yeah, the hell with this kid..." Elwood said this. They both popped out of the air.

Dr. Kevin Bruin.. Log Entry E72 -- The Moment
-
To whoever is investigating my dissaperance... In case I don't return.

No one knows when their turn will come. We quickly found ways to predict its movement. We found ways to avoid it. There is no stopping it. The worst attempts came under Marshall Law. The isolation periods were terrible. They were short. They were terrible. One of the iso-men once asked me something. He asked if it was worse that everyone lived. We had to interact with the people we selfishly isolated. He asked his question. "Would it have been best if the moment caused death instead?" His eyes locked into mine. Mine were filled with panic and guilt. His were peaceful. Why wouldn't they be peaceful? The moment had passed him. It hadn't passed me.

There are several rules we have identified. These rules correspond to the moment. The first rule is this. It only affects men. It affects each and every man. It affects them regardless of age. The second rule is this. Its intent is not to kill. Deaths have occurred. They usually happen to the very young or old. They can be prevented through medical intervention. Third rule is this. It affects men in singular basis. This means only one man can experience the moment at a time. There have been no reported cases of simultaneous experiences. Four is this. Its movement is proximity based. You are close to someone experiencing the moment. You are more likely to be next. Five is this. It can't be contained by any physical barrier. The isolation of an infected area failed. The moment had gone through the male population in the isolation area. Then it advanced outwards. Sixth is this. It is possible to out run it. It moves at speeds comparable to an average human. Finally there is this. The experience itself is said to be incredibly painful.

As to where I went.

I was asked what I thought the moment could be. This was when I first started. I claimed something explainable! I made observations. I formed hypothesis. I did experiments. I did testing month after month. A virus? A bacterium? A parasite? Mass hysteria? None of it fit. There was no explanation. People talked about aliens. People talked about god's punishment. I laughed. I exclaimed science will find the answer. Eventually thou it seemed no answer was coming. I doubted for a while. I started to believe the extremists. Few people know this about me. However there is one more rule. I choose to accept it. Others don't accept it. Its sentient. Extinction is it's end game. I am a man of science. I can't be scared anymore. I must test my hypothesis. You will now understand why i'm missing. Men my age are less likely to survive. We can find the answer. Science will prevail. I've performed an orchidectomy on myself. By the time you read this I should be within the moment's current spread. I wonder what people will think. They will see a naked old man walking into the fire. Is he mad? A religious nut? No pun intended. I will succeed. I believe I will. You will probably hear stories before I can make it back. Hence the log. Stories of a crazy old man. His faith made him immune to the moment. Well that will be so. Know that it was faith that triumphed. Faith in science.

If I don't return. Dan. Love always.

A small lamp burned steadily on the polished desk. The human wore a pair of thin spectacles on the edge of his nose. Stacks of parchment occupied a far corner of the work surface. He read through pages at a time. He scribbled notes on another sheet. Empty ink bottles sat on the floor. They suggested the man was rather busy.

From the entrance, Ronn readied his flail. He let the heavy chains dangle. Their echoes filled the room. But the man refused to look up at the intruders. Instead, he held up a finger. He continued reading. Ronn and the rest of his group exchanged glances. They shrugged shoulders. For a moment, they stood still. The man made a disappointed smack with his tongue. He replaced the parchment. He pushed his glasses closer to his eyes. He called for his guests to approach. They did.

"Apologies, my friends," he said. His voice cracked slightly. It sounded unpracticed. It had gone unused for some time. "Come. Come."

The adventurers stepped forward slowly. Wilm's head darted around. He scouted for suspicious stones in the floor. He looked for another tripwire. The cobbles turned to green. The tasseled edge of the rug stood before them. The group stopped.

"Come," the man muttered. Any impatience defied detection.

Firrel's boot tested its weight against the rug. There was solid ground beneath. The rest followed suit.

"Wait!" the man screamed. The group wasted no time. They assumed a defensive stance. They drew their weapons and shields. "I meant the carpet."

The adventurers looked towards their feet. The jade fibers assumed a purplish hue. The blood from their persons dripped freely. It stained the rug. Querth's face flushed.

"Sorry," the wizard whispered.

The man rolled his eyes. "It's already ruined. Nothing we can do now. Let's just get this over with."

The adventurers were finally within a pace of the desk. The open palm of the man begged their halt. The hordes of evil creatures had led them to that chamber. The supposed throne room of unspeakable villainy was little more than a study. It had a librarian.

"Well, then. I suppose congratulations are in order!" The man clapped his hands together. "Smashing job. I'm Pollock. I'll be handling your processing from here."

"Processing?" Edmund echoed.

"Yes," replied Pollock. "You're almost done in this dreadful castle. You're on your way back home. You can enjoy the spoils. All that's left is to handle the last odds and ends."

The adventurers nodded in content. They kept their weapons handy. The legions they had to cut through began to feel concluded. They had fought hard to reach that chamber.

"Excellent! Let's get started. In total you've slaughtered one hundred and fifty three goblins. You killed twenty nine orcs. You slew eighteen kobolds. You defeated two dragons. Impressive."

Edmund smirked. He rolled the handle of his axe to catch the light. Ronn and Dismal groaned. They had enjoyed the chaos. It had followed. It stopped their fellow warrior from gloating.

"In addition, you broke down forty one doors. You set off two fire traps. You triggered six spike snares. You activated three boulders. You caused one acid spill. Plus, it says you freed the dungeons of ten prisoners."

"Quite," responded Pollock. He was not the least impressed. "I'm adding up your little adventure. That comes to a total of eight million, eight hundred thirty seven thousand, two hundred and fifty one gold pieces."

Even Querth's mind could not comprehend such a figure. They were used to generous spoils. Several hundred was the most any had ever seen.

"We couldn't possibly carry that much coin," Dismal remarked. "Or spend it."

"That's quite expected," Pollock laughed. "You can just pay in installments."

"Pay?" shouted Firrel. "What do you mean pay?"

"But we were on a quest," pleaded Ronn. "We were trying to save the village."
